News.title: Navy has ‘lost its ability’ to fight beneath Arctic ice cap & is leaving seas to Russian subs, damning report warns
News.content:
Next

THE Navy has lost its ability to fight beneath the ice cap and is leaving the seas to Russian submarines, a damning report by MPs has warned.

Royal Navy crews need specialist training and subs with “hardened sails” to smash through the ice around the North Pole, like in the spy thriller Ice Station Zebra.



The skills were a Royal Navy staple until the late 1990s when it fell out of normal training cycle.

The last Navy exercise to smash through the ice was April 2018 and the last submarine fit to do it retired in 2024.



The lack of an under-ice capability was one of the “glaring gaps” in Britain’s High North defences identified by cross-party MPs.

Their report ‘Defence In The High North’ warned: “The UK has allowed its submarine under-ice capability to lapse just as the High North has become strategically more important.”



The report warned: “The lack of an under-ice capability allows Russia to leave its SSBNs [nuclear armed submarines] safe under the ice while its attack submarines surge forward to disrupt UK critical infrastructure, Nato sea lanes and allied [nuclear armed submarines] automatically putting the UK and Nato on the defensive.”

The Navy’s newer Astute class subs are still being “certified” for ice operations, MPs found.

It comes after The Sun revealed the Navy risks running out of captains due to record low numbers of offciers passing their “driving tests”.

And three more ships on the cutting board, bringing Labour’s scrap heap tally to 12.



As the ice caps melt the High North is increasingly contested. Russia wants access to military bases, undiscovered oil and gas fields and control of the merchant sea lanes linking Europe to Asia.

Labour’s Tan Dhesi MP, chair of the Defence Select Committee, said: “Russian submarine and sabotage forces in the High North pose direct risks to the North Atlantic and the UK, including the nuclear deterrent.

“Despite this, the Ministry of Defence has accepted a serious anti-submarine warfare gap.”

The report warned of chronic shortages of warships and submarines and cautioned against pretending that everything can be done by drones.

It said: “The MoD’s Hybrid Navy concept must not become a substitute for crewed capability before uncrewed systems have been proven in the specific conditions of the High North.”



It also warned against an over reliance on America after Donald Trump threatened Greenland and Canada, both essential High North Allies.

The report said: “Europe cannot count on the US returning to the European Arctic as the security partner and ally that the UK and Europe previously counted on.

The MoD said it was “clear-eyed about the threat Russia poses” and investing £1.8bn in Atlantic Bastion and subsea defences.

A spokesperson said: “We are leading allied activity across the High North, strengthening Nato’s northern flank and increasing our ability to respond rapidly to emerging threats.”

News.title: Huge number of cops feeling stressed and exhausted over workloads as ‘public health emergency’ in policing declared
News.content:
FEELING BLUE Huge number of cops feeling stressed and exhausted over workloads as ‘public health emergency’ in policing declared

Credit: Victor Golmer







Next

FOUR out of every five cops are feeling stressed over workloads, a survey reveals today.

And more than three-quarters of them say they are too exhausted to perform their duties properly.

The rank-and-file Police Federation of England and Wales has declared a public health emergency in policing.

Acting deputy national chairman Paul Williams will today tell its annual conference in London: “Policing is a service making its people sick.





“We are asking officers to respond to life-or-death emergencies and run towards danger, while routinely denying them the rest, resources and support they need to do their jobs safely.”

“The service has become so accustomed to operating under pressure that it no longer recognises the warning lights on its own dashboard.

“We cannot allow another generation of officers to believe that breakdown is simply part of the job.”

A pay and morale survey found 78 per cent of officers had experienced stress, low mood or anxiety in the past year.



Almost all of them said work had caused or worsened their depression.

And 76 per cent said they were exhausted.

There will also be a call for an independent investigation into the health, wellbeing and welfare of officers during their first five years of service.

That is where the deepest unhappiness is said to lie.

News.title: The difficult balancing act Burnham faces over immigration – and the trap he must avoid which brought down Starmer
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham arrived in Downing Street with something his predecessor had long since lost – the goodwill of Labour MPs.

But the real test is whether he can turn that popularity into getting difficult decisions over the line.



The PM inherited some of the biggest headaches of Sir Keir Starmer‘s premiership, not least immigration.

Shabana Mahmood‘s plans to make migrants wait longer before settling permanently in Britain sparked a backlash from around 100 Labour MPs under Starmer.



The Government is still weighing up the responses to a consultation that closed in February, with no final decision on the controversial 15-year wait.

And the longer ministers take, the more questions Mr Burnham faces about how much of the crackdown will survive.

The divisions have now reached his own Cabinet, with Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh yesterday refusing sixteen times to back the proposals.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has also voiced concerns, while the PM is reportedly considering exempting care workers to ease opposition.

It leaves Mr Burnham with a difficult balancing act.

Water down the reforms and he risks accusations of going soft on immigration, handing ammunition to Nigel Farage.



But press ahead and he could squander the goodwill he enjoys among Labour MPs.

There is also a warning from his predecessor’s downfall.

Sir Keir’s authority suffered a major blow when he caved to Labour rebels over welfare cuts, exposing a PM who appeared unable to stand up to his own backbenchers.

The retreat only emboldened MPs to demand further concessions.

Mr Burnham’s challenge is to avoid the same trap while proving he can deliver the tougher immigration system his Government has promised.



For a PM who came to power promising to unite Labour, the danger is that keeping his party happy comes at the expense of getting anything done.

News.title: Ukraine’s First Lady begs world leaders to act after Russian drone kills baby in her pram
News.content:
Next

UKRAINE’S First Lady has begged world leaders not to turn a blind eye after a baby in a pushchair was killed in a Russian drone strike.

A haunting image of lifeless one-year-old Angelina Mariukhna in her buggy was posted by Volodymyr Zelensky’s wife Olena.



The tot, her primary school teacher mum Inna, 28, and four others, including an 11-year-old girl, were killed on Monday when the drone exploded at a park in Kharkiv, Ukraine.

More than a dozen other people were hurt.



The First Lady said: “Parents seize every opportunity to let their children breathe fresh air after spending so much time in shelters.

“Russian killers took advantage of that moment, too.”



The image of little Angelina’s body slumped to one side shocked the world.

It went viral online after US President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House: “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven’t been doing much.”



The US has recently been accused of withholding intelligence during Russian strikes and limiting Ukraine’s access to its Starshield satellite network, while buying Russian diesel and dropping sanctions.

Mr Trump, who days ago said Ukraine should replace Mr Zelensky as President, sparked global outrage with yesterday’s comments.

And his special envoy Steve Witkoff fawned over Russian dictator Vladimir Putin yesterday as they held talks in St Petersburg, saying Mr Trump was “deeply grateful” for their diesel deal.

Mr Witkoff even called Putin, whose forces invaded Ukraine in February 2022, a “humanitarian” for releasing US prisoner Stephen Hubbard, 74, who Russia had claimed was fighting for Ukraine.

He told the Russian President: “Because of you, he’s going home to his family.



“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir.”

News.title: Runner, 24, dies after suffering sudden cardiac arrest during Cardiff Half Marathon – as devastated family pay tribute
News.content:
'LASTING LEGACY' Runner, 24, dies after suffering sudden cardiac arrest during Cardiff Half Marathon – as devastated family pay tribute







Next

THE HEARTBROKEN family of a runner who died after suffering a sudden cardiac arrest during a half marathon has paid a touching tribute to the 24-year-old.

Ross Williams-Griffith – described as “active, fit and full of life” – tragically collapsed while running alongside his girlfriend Katie in the Cardiff Half Marathon on Sunday, October 4.



He suffered a cardiac arrest while roughly 12 miles into the 13.1 mile race and died despite receiving urgent medical care.

His family said Ross “brought laughter, loyalty and warmth wherever he went” as they paid tribute to the much-loved sportsman.



The moving tribute says he approached everything with “enthusiasm and determination”, whether playing football, golf, snowboarding, bodyboarding or training for his next running challenge.

Ross, who was also a keen goalkeeper, had spent months preparing for the race that he died in alongside his partner Katie.



The pair were affectionately known as “Team Griff-Bow” and were running in support of Tenovus Cancer Care – a cause close to their hearts.

Ross had also recently started running with a local club alongside his brother Rhys and his fiancé Jayde.



His family described him as “kind, generous and hard-working”, adding that he was a friendly face who “never had a bad word to say about anyone”.

They said he had a “unique ability to make people feel welcome wherever he went”.

Ross had built a promising career with GE Aerospace and was admired by his colleagues.

In a statement released through Run 4 Wales, his family said: “Ross was a young, fit and healthy man who loved running and being part of the community that surrounded it.

“He was kind, caring and full of life, and brought laughter, loyalty and warmth wherever he went.



“The support we have received since losing Ross has been overwhelming and we are deeply grateful for the kindness shown to our family.”

They added that they hoped sharing his story would raise awareness of sudden cardiac arrest.

The family said: “While we are yet to learn the exact cause of Ross’ death, we hope that sharing his story may raise awareness of sudden cardiac arrest.

“If raising awareness in Ross’ memory helps even one family avoid the heartbreak we are experiencing, then that will be part of his lasting legacy.”

Matt Newman, chief executive of Run 4 Wales, said: “Everyone at Run 4 Wales continues to hold Ross’ family and friends in our thoughts.



“The loss of a runner at one of our events is felt deeply by all involved, and our focus remains on supporting Ross’ loved ones in any way we can.”

He also thanked the event and hospital medical teams who responded, praising their “extraordinary speed and professionalism”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Anyone wishing to donate in Ross’ memory to help fund cardiac screening can do here.

His family are also raising money for 2wish here.

News.title: Ex-Labour deputy leader Roy Hattersley left wife huge six-figure sum after death aged 93 plus two major gifts to charity
News.content:
Next

LABOUR grandee Roy Hattersley left £25,000 to a dog charity and another £25,000 to feed the hungry in his £590,000 will, The Sun can reveal.

The party’s former deputy leader, who died aged 93 in June, made a string of charitable donations as he gave the bulk of his fortune to his wife Maggie.



Probate documents seen by The Sun show his estate was worth £594,696, falling to £586,018 after debts and expenses were paid.

Lord Hattersley – considered one of the party’s greatest “nearly men” – signed his will in June 2024 while living in Great Longstone, Derbyshire.



Records show he left £25,000 to the Dogs Trust and a further £25,000 to charities which provide food to those in need.

Roy’s wife, Maggie Hattersley, 78, inherited the rest of his estate along with the rights to his popular books, manuscripts and letters.

Had she died before him, the money would have been split between nine charities including the RSPCA, Blue Cross, Oxfam, the Salvation Army and Macmillan.

Hattersley was MP for Birmingham Sparkbrook for more than 32 years and served as Neil Kinnock’s deputy from 1983 until 1992.

Then-PM Sir Keir Starmer led tributes after his death, saying: “Roy Hattersley was a giant of the Labour movement.

“Through decades of service, including as deputy leader and a minister, he never lost his belief in a more equal Britain.



“My thoughts are with his wife Maggie and his family.”

Lord Kinnock said: “Roy was a socialist of deep conviction, a dedicated democrat who believed that liberty should be unqualified by anything but responsibility and never by background or fortune.

“He was never solemn nor deferential and his common sense, humour and endless stories made him excellent company.”



Born in Sheffield in 1932, the political heavyweight fought his way into Parliament before being made Secretary of State for Prices and Consumer Protection under Jim Callaghan.

He stayed loyal to Labour when the Gang of Four quit to form the Social Democratic Party, now the Liberal Democrats, in 1981.

After losing the 1983 leadership race to Kinnock, he joined him on the so-called “dream ticket” to modernise the party after it was thumped by Margaret Thatcher.

He quit as deputy on the same day Kinnock resigned following Labour’s 1992 election defeat to John Major.

Hattersley was made a life peer as Baron Hattersley of Sparkbrook after leaving the Commons in 1997.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Later becoming an author, Hattersley wrote more than 20 books and worked as a columnist and broadcaster.

He was famously lampooned on Spitting Image and was also replaced by a tub of lard on BBC panel show Have I Got News For You after pulling out at the last minute.

News.title: Brit, 24, died from ‘catastrophic peanut allergic reaction after eating churros and hot chocolate in Argentina café’
News.content:
TRAGIC END Brit, 24, died from ‘catastrophic peanut allergic reaction after eating churros and hot chocolate in Argentina café’







Next

A BRIT died from a “catastrophic” allergic reaction after consuming hot chocolate and churros in a cafe, an inquest has heard.

Harry James Kitto was repeatedly reassured his order from the popular tourist spot in Buenos Aires did not contain nuts, a court heard.



But the 24-year-old – who had a severe peanut allergy – was rushed to hospital after biting into the food on October 30, 2025.

Harry had been travelling around South America with his girlfriend Naomi Pye when tragedy struck.



The pair had visited Mexico, Guatemala and Peru before arriving in Argentina.

They checked into their Buenos Aires accommodation before heading to a popular tourist spot, Café Tortoni, the Daily Mail reports.

After asking the staff in Spanish and English if the churros contained peanuts, they ordered the Argentine treat with a hot chocolate.

But soon after they had eaten, barber Harry started to feel unwell and feared he was having a reaction.



Naomi asked staff again if the churros contained peanuts and again received a “firm no” in response, an inquest in Truro heard.

After ordering and eating a second serving Harry began to feel seriously unwell again.

His girlfriend advised him to make himself throw up but he said he was feeling a little better, the court heard.

Naomi told the court how they took a tube back to their accommodation but his lips swelled and he began struggling to breathe.

She called emergency services and ran into the apartment to get an epi-pen (a medical device used to deliver a rapid dose of adrenaline) and injected him.



As Harry was rushed to hospital by an ambulance his heart stopped for about 11 minutes before it was restarted and he was taken into intensive care.

He died one-eek later from hypoxic brain injury and anaphylactic shock.

At the time of his death a representative of his family wrote on GoFundMe: “For over a week, he showed extraordinary strength and determination — the same strength that made everyone who knew him so proud.



“Despite the doctors’ tireless efforts and Harry’s incredible fight, the medical team confirmed that Harry was brain dead and there was nothing they could do.

“Harry passed quietly with his family around him. Our hearts are broken beyond words.”

The family managed to raise around £71,500 to help with the repatriation process from 2,000 donations.

“Harry fought so hard, and we have never been prouder of him. He was brave, strong, and full of love until the very end,” his loved ones said.

The inquest heard how Harry’s father and brother went to the same cafe a few days later and ordered the same dish.



They asked the staff if the churro and hot chocolate contained any peanuts and were told it did not.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But, when they took a sample to a lab to be tested, the churro was found to contain 20mg of peanut protein per kilo.

The inquest concluded Harry’s death was accidental.

News.title: UK’s national security adviser faces calls to be sacked after wife ‘posted antisemitic comments online’
News.content:
'INDEFENSIBLE' UK’s national security adviser faces calls to be sacked after wife ‘posted antisemitic comments online’







Next

THE UK’s National Security Adviser faced more calls to quit or be sacked after his wife allegedly made antisemitic comments online and publicly revealed his work.

Labour Against Antisemitism has written to PM Andy Burnham arguing that Jonathan Powell, pictured above, should get the boot.

Mr Powell’s wife Sarah Helm dismissed EU President Ursula von der Leyen’s support for Israel in the wake of the October 7 atrocity in 2023 as “empty dangerous glib tropes”, and later called it “puzzling” no rape victim had testified.

Ms Helm said last week: “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action. Sounds like Adam [Boulton] would have all our books swept off the shelves in a jiffy.”





She claims to have “spent a very long time in Gaza” and laments Hamas was “blackballed a terrorist entity”.

Labour Against Antisemitism’s Alex Hearn wrote to the PM and said: “Either Jonathan Powell lacks full clearance, vetting missed this, or saw it. Each is indefensible.

“You promised zero tolerance on antisemitism. Mr Powell’s position is untenable and his wife raises security concerns. He must resign or be sacked.”

The Campaign Against Antisemitism spokesperson said: “At a time of the worst antisemitism in living memory, how can British Jews be reassured when these sentiments are so close to the person charged with protecting us all?”

Shadow home affairs minister Alicia Kearns wrote to Mr Burnham asking if Mr Powell’s position is still tenable.

It is classed as a terror organisation but police say no action is needed over the post. No 10 said she “does not represent the Government in any capacity”.

It comes as a report has found three in five older Jewish pupils have seen or suffered antisemitic abuse.

News.title: Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences
News.content:
The UK government has approved production from the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.

Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.

But environmental campaigners said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the prime minister of "dithering" on Jackdaw and said a ban on new oil and gas licences should be repealed - but Andy Burnham said her party had "messed up" the original decision.

Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.

A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.

News.title: Websites taken down worldwide as critical cyber-security update issued
News.content:
International governments and agencies have urged websites to address two critical cyber-security flaws in a programming language which powers much of the internet.

The vulnerabilities were found within the PHP programming language, with a fix issued on Wednesday afternoon.

Multiple cyber-security agencies have urged organisations unable to apply fixes in time to consider taking their sites down, leaving bodies such as the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC to take pages offline.

The flaws were discovered by AI, with cyber-security firm Wiz saying they were the "most severe vulnerabilities ever discovered" by the tech, which is reshaping the cyber landscape.

Finland has temporarily shut down the government's public web services, while the Netherlands' cyber-security agency said it was taking its own website offline due to the vulnerabilities.

The US National Security Agency issued similar advice on X, external for organisations to take their systems offline if they were unable to update with the fix.

"These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database," it wrote.

Meanwhile, the White House said federal agencies were working with leading AI labs to speed up a fix to the issue.

And in a post on X, external, Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.

The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the online encyclopedia Wikipedia, said it was addressing the security vulnerabilities.

"We have taken down a number of other systems as a precautionary measure until they can be safely patched," it said.

That led some people to be unable to access parts of Wikipedia on Wednesday.

Edinburgh council's website has also become inaccessible, as well as the online homes for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors.

They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment.

News.title: Airbnb hosts can no longer make guests strip beds and wash dishes under new rules
News.content:
Airbnb has changed its rules to limit what property hosts may ask guests to do - including when it comes to cleaning.

The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and can also add other "reasonable" requests.

Airbnb states that guests - who are required to pay a cleaning fee - should not be asked to complete tasks normally done by a cleaner, including washing dishes and stripping beds.

The new rules will apply to all reservations booked on or after 20 November on the accommodation marketplace.

"House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb told the BBC.

"So, we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises."

According to the new requirements on the Airbnb website, hosts are generally not allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that "require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes".

The company said it may grant exceptions in some circumstances. For example, guests can be asked to limit shower time if there are local drought-related water restrictions.

A property's rules will be displayed to guests more prominently moving forward and will appear in the guests' reservation reminders.

Contracts will only be allowed in limited circumstances, including when required by law or homeowners association rules.

While a host will not be able to impose fines, they remain in control of their house rules and requests, the company said.

If a host's request does not follow Airbnb policies, the issue will be flagged and the owner can appeal if they disagree.

Guests have for years complained about unreasonable tasks they we required to complete before departure, especially as they are required to pay cleaning fees.

TikTok videos from Airbnb hosts Cassie and Jon that show them closely inspecting their rental property in the US state of Georgia after guests leave have gone viral recently for their attention to detail.

One video from the couple, for example, accuses guests of "disrespecting the house rules" for leaving a television remote out of place.

They have been criticised for their strict rules and high standards but said in response that their content had been misinterpreted

Their videos have inspired other content creators to parody stringent hosts.

News.title: Aberfan disaster 'most tragic of days imaginable' says King on 60th anniversary
News.content:
The King has described the Aberfan disaster which killed 116 children and 28 adults as the "most tragic of days imaginable" on its 60th anniversary.

Pantglas Junior School and a number of nearby houses in the village near Merthyr Tydfil, south Wales, were catastrophically engulfed in coal slurry after the colliery spoil tip collapsed on 21 October 1966.

King Charles III, Queen Camilla and the Prince of Wales joined survivors and bereaved families on Wednesday and laid wreaths and a posy with the last surviving teacher in the Aberfan Memorial Garden, located on the site of the school.

The King also paid tribute to the community's strength, resilience and "unconquerable spirit".

Warning: This story contains upsetting details that some may find distressing

About half the children from the school died when excavated mining debris from the Merthyr Vale Colliery was dislodged, and 150,000 tonnes of coal waste came thundering down the hillside.

Emergency services, miners and people who rushed to the village began an around-the-clock battle to dig out those trapped by the debris.

News.title: Don't Stop Believin'! - high school musical Glee set for reboot
News.content:
We never stopped believin'... now it's official: Glee, the Emmy-winning US high school musical comedy drama, is set to return.

Ryan Murphy's series, which chronicled the highs and lows of choir members from Ohio, premiered on Fox in 2009 and ran for six seasons until 2015.

The original cast included Lea Michele, Amber Riley, the late Cory Monteith, Jane Lynch and Matthew Morrison as Will Schuester, the optimistic teacher leading the fictional McKinley High's glee club.

The reboot was announced, external by Disney and Hulu via the show's social media team on Wednesday.

The show was a huge hit first time around, known for its big laughs and big heart, tackling topics such as sexuality, race, disability and mental health.

In the series, glee club New Directions helped misfit students find their voices through song and dance.

Lynch served as the club's main antagonist, the villainous cheerleading coach Sue Sylvester.

The choir's covers of Don't Stop Believin', River Deep, Mountain High and Smooth Criminal also brought older hit songs to the attention of younger audiences.

In 2010, the show was adapted for a concert tour in which was captured on film.

Around the same time, the cast overtook The Beatles as the non-solo act with the most Billboard Hot 100 appearances.

On Wednesday, the Wanted singer Max George told BBC Scotland that appearing in the show's sixth season was "an amazing experience", adding that he'd "love to do it again".

"I messaged the casting director from it, just with wide eyes from the announcement," he said.

Asked if it makes sense for the series to come back, he said: "I think soâ¦ It's been over 10 years, so I think that's a nice break.

"I think it was probably coming towards the end in terms of the storylines and everything, but 10 years has gone by, and Ryan Murphy will probably come up with something genius. So I'm expecting big things."

News.title: Google staff resign in backlash over its AI contracts with military
News.content:
Similar contracts were signed by OpenAI, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Oracle, Nvidia, and the start-up Reflection, to allow AI technology to be deployed across a range of military settings such as transport, planning and battlefield operations.

As the tech quickly evolves, concerns are growing about the use of AI in theatres of war.

"AI compresses the time an operator has to make a decision because it works much faster than a person, and that's especially risky in a high-stress environment," said Sarah Shoker, formerly head of OpenAI's Geopolitics team.

"When you have hundreds of targets that are selected by AI and a short amount of time, it is almost impossible for a human operator to meaningfully review the AI's outputs for errors."

Employees at Google have told the BBC that staff are scared to speak out about AI safety and its uses in warfare because their employment contracts prohibit them from publicly criticising the company.

"In principle I'm not allowed to criticise Google for the duration of my life," Sofia Liguori told the BBC. But she decided to do so "because I believe it's important for these things to be known and I also think that talking about facts is not criticising".

Liguori added that at Google "people are scared of retaliation and putting their career at risk. You feel you are being watched, you can't speak."

A current employee at Google DeepMind, who declined to be named for fear of retaliation, told the BBC that "a lot of motivated employees who signed up for [the company's] original mission could leave â but there's also a pipeline of people at the start of the careers who could fill those positions. It could be a changing of the guard."

Another Google DeepMind staff member, who also wished to remain anonymous, told the BBC: "A lot of people have left the company that feel strongly about this [how Google DeepMind has changed its ethics position]."

"Some people are putting up a fight, others are thinking: 'it's a big company. What do you expect to change?'", the employee said.

Google's agreements with Israel have also caused controversy. In 2024, the company was criticised by staff for a joint contract with Amazon worth $1.2bn (Â£960m) called Project Nimbus which provides Israel's government and military with AI technology and cloud computing infrastructure. At the time, Google said Project Nimbus "is not directed at highly sensitive, classified, or military workloads relevant to weapons or intelligence services".

Moreover, Israel's AI capabilities in warfare have been the focus of debate after they were featured in a recent documentary, Naza, which examines the role of AI-powered targeting systems to bombard the Gaza Strip, resulting in high civilian casualties. An Israeli government minister has said the claims presented in the film were false and distorted.

Former Google employee Andreas Kirsch believes AI technology in warfare is not ready for the battlefield. "Current AI models are not robust enough, and I don't think they have been trained for such tasks either," he said.

Additional reporting by Rosa Rahimi

News.title: Burnham proposes plan to cut standing charges from gas bills
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked ministers to develop a plan to remove standing charges from gas bills.

These are fixed daily fees that cover the costs of connecting to a supply. They vary by region and households must still pay them even when energy is not being used.

Industry body Energy UK said whether the proposed changes would make a difference to bills would depend on how or where the charges were reallocated on the bill.

But an influential research foundation argued it would be a progressive move that would help those on low-incomes and knock Â£27 off a typical annual bill.

During Prime Minister's Questions, Burnham said the "pragmatic decision" on giving the green light to the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea would allow the government to increase investment in renewables and "do more to help people with bills".

He said he had asked the Chancellor John Healey and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh "to look at whether we can remove standing charges from gas bills and to report back to this house at the earliest opportunity".

No details have been given on how removing standing charges would work in practice. But the suggestion has been made by research firm Nesta that they could be moved to the unit rate, external, so people pay for what they use.

This would probably benefit customers who don't use much gas, but heavy users could end up paying more.

For nearly two years, regulator Ofgem has run a series of consultations on standing charges, with a massive public response including vociferous opposition from low-energy users who can do nothing to cut standing charges.

Ofgem is running a pilot scheme on low standing charge tariffs, but is yet to draw any firm conclusions, suggesting there are no easy answers.

News.title: Will it bring down your energy bills?
News.content:
The UK government has approved production from the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.

Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.

BBC Verify correspondent Ben Chu looks at whether the approval of Jackdaw will mean lower bills for households and businesses.

News.title: Jailed former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson being investigated over alleged rape inside Parliament
News.content:
Jailed former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Jeffrey Donaldson is being investigated by London police about an alleged rape of a woman inside the Houses of Parliament, the BBC can reveal.

The disgraced former MP has been accused of raping the woman in Parliament in 2016, at the very heart of the political establishment.

Last week Donaldson was sentenced to 15 years in prison for a series of child sex offences against two victims, including one count of rape, which took place between 1985 and 2008. He is seeking to appeal against his convictions.

It is understood the woman has been interviewed by Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) officers.

The PSNI has now shared her claims with the Metropolitan Police, as the alleged incident happened in London.

While not naming the former DUP leader, the Met has issued a statement confirming a 63-year-old man is being investigated.

It said: "On Tuesday 13 October, the Met received a report referred to us by the Police Service of Northern Ireland relating to an allegation of rape in 2016, by a man now aged 63.

"The allegation relates to one victim who is being supported by specialist officers.

"The investigation is in its early stages. No arrests have been made and enquiries are ongoing."

In July, the Belfast Telegraph first reported that a woman from Northern Ireland alleged she had been sexually assaulted by Donaldson in the DUP offices at Parliament in 2016.

She claimed that he attempted to get her to drink vodka shots in his office, before trying to kiss her and put his hand up her skirt.

On Saturday, the newspaper further reported that the Met was set to investigate and interview Donaldson about these accusations.

But in response to BBC questions it has now emerged the same woman has also alleged Donaldson raped her.

Concerns about the ex-DUP MP's behaviour in London were raised in a BBC NI Spotlight film, earlier this year.

A former senior PSNI detective told the programme he had seen Donaldson drunk in the Houses of Parliament.

Two other former senior PSNI detectives also reported seeing him going into a gay sauna not far from Parliament in 2006, the same year in which Donaldson described homosexuality as "sinful".

News.title: Teenage boy guilty of trying to murder girl, 15, in school
News.content:
A teenage boy who had a hatred of women and an "obsessive interest" in killers has been found guilty of the attempted murder of a girl at his school.

The boy dressed in black and wore a face mask before stabbing the 15-year-old victim in the back at Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich, in March.

Armed police were called to the school, which went into lockdown, and the attack was caught on CCTV.

The boy, who is 16 and cannot be named for legal reasons, wrote notes about hating women and had an "obsessive and dangerous interest in killers and killing", jurors at King's Lynn Crown Court were told. He will be sentenced on 18 December.

Jurors deliberated for just under four hours before delivering a majority verdict at the end of a trial which began two weeks ago.

The teenager "went to school not to learn, but to kill" while armed with a kitchen knife, the prosecution said.

The school went into lockdown after the attack and there was an armed police response, while the girl was taken to hospital with a minor injury.

News.title: Tributes paid to 'bravest' woman who died of 'stab wounds' after crash
News.content:
Tributes have been paid to a woman who crashed a car into a wall after allegedly being stabbed.

Eleanor Barnfield, 47, died in hospital after police were called to the crash in Bridgend on Monday, where they found she had "puncture wounds unrelated to the collision", which the BBC understands were sustained in a stabbing.

A 61-year-old man from Bridgend has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a "significant" police operation at a retirement housing complex, and remains in custody.

Eleanor, who worked for housing association Valleys to Coast which runs the complex, has been described by her family as the "kindest, most loving, bravest person in the world".

South Wales Police said Eleanor was taken to hospital after officers were called to the crash on Coity Road at about 12:40 BST on Monday, but later died.

Police were also called to nearby sheltered housing retirement complex, Ger-y-Nant, where the man was arrested.

Describing Eleanor, from North Cornelly, Bridgend, her family said: "She meant everything to us and will be forever loved and missed deeply by her devoted family and friends. She was our rock."

Jo Oak, chief executive of Valleys to Coast, added the organisation was "devastated by the tragic death of our colleague".

"Eleanor was a much-valued member of the Valleys to Coast team, and her loss has been deeply felt by everyone who knew and worked alongside her," she said.

"She made an important contribution to our organisation and to the communities we serve, and she will be remembered with great warmth and affection by her colleagues.

"Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with Eleanor's family and friends at this unimaginably difficult time."

Oak said the organisation would "continue to cooperate fully with South Wales Police".

Ch Supt Jason Rees said: "Our thoughts remain firmly with Eleanor's family. I want to assure the community that teams of detectives and specialist staff are investigating.

"We appreciate the patience and support of residents, especially those displaced following the incident. Local communities may notice an increased police presence as our investigation continues."

News.title: Holocaust school lessons to be improved after 'shocking' antisemitism review
News.content:
The review into antisemitism in schools and colleges in England was led by former Ofsted chief inspector Sir David Bell and presented to Parliament on Wednesday.

Powell told the BBC it marked a "generational moment" to re-educate young people, among whom she said the issue of antisemitism was "particularly prevalent".

She said: "It's definitely a crisis and I think it's actually got worse since Sir David began this review. This has become a real challenge for Jewish people in our country, but also Jewish students and Jewish teachers working in our schools and colleges.

"I do really feel it is a generational moment to educate this generation and the next â that is the job of education â to understand what antisemitism is in the modern world."

Speaking on Holocaust education, the education secretary said new lessons will "challenge" some of the concepts that young people have.

The review also calls for stronger guidance on political impartiality for teachers.

Powell told the House of Commons "teachers should not bring their own political views into the classroom" but they should not avoid discussing important topics.

The review was launched following a series of high-profile incidents including the attack at Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester in October 2025, in which two men were killed.

Separate reviews were also commissioned into antisemitism in healthcare and into public order and hate crime laws.

The BBC revealed in August that the Bell review had found Jewish schoolchildren were experiencing regular harassment and abuse.

It also found that headteachers of some Jewish schools were spending more of their time dealing with security arrangements than educational matters.

The review also recommends that the government sets up a type of hotline where school leaders can access immediate advice on tackling antisemitism.

Bell, who is now vice-chancellor of the University of Sunderland, heard evidence from pupils, teachers, governors and parents across state and independent schools, as well as from community organisations.

He told the BBC: "This is not just a report for Jewish children in Jewish schools. This is for all children and young people in all schools and colleges. We know that antisemitism crosses all boundaries."

Earlier this month, the BBC was given rare access inside a Jewish school in Hertfordshire, where pupils and staff operate under tight security, amid heightened concerns about antisemitism.

Spencer Lewis, the executive headteacher of Yavneh College, said that security was an "innate part" of his role.

"When you come in in the morning, there are high gates, high fences, lots of security cameras. We have four full-time security staff. And it sort of just becomes part of what you do," he said.

"We think about it a lot."

In response to the recommendations, the government will also encourage schools to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA)'s working definition of antisemitism, although it cannot make it compulsory.

The definition is supported by mainstream Jewish organisations and has been adopted by 47 countries, including the UK, as well as most British universities.

However, some of the IHRA definition's examples of antisemitic behaviour have proven controversial.

The Board of Deputies of British Jews said that adopting the IHRA definition would provide schools with a tool "to deepen understanding of contemporary antisemitism".

In a statement, a spokesperson told the BBC: "Treating antisemitism in schools as a safeguarding issue will have the benefit of creating an explicit duty on all schools to address this as they would any other threat to children's safety, and will strengthen accountability."

Rabbi Charley Baginksy and Rabbi Josh Levy, co-leads of the Movement for Progressive Judaism, said that the report "exposes serious failures in how schools recognise and respond to antisemitism".

They said: "Alongside that urgent question of how schools deal with hatred and educate about Jewish persecution, we also need to ensure they teach about Jewish creativity, music, literature, humour and the extraordinary pleasure of belonging to this diverse tradition."

Dan Green, Chief Executive of the Anne Frank Trust UK, said the review "confirms what we see in classrooms every day".

"Antisemitism in our schools is real, it is widespread, and too often it goes unrecognised and unchallenged."

"One-off assemblies are not enough, and neither is sitting pupils in front of a video. Young people need the space to ask difficult questions, challenge their own assumptions and understand that antisemitism did not start or end with the Holocaust."

The National Education Union raised concerns about creating a "hierarchy of racism" and adopting the IHRA definition.

It said the latter risked "blurring the line between antisemitism and legitimate criticism of the Israeli government and the genocide in Gaza".

The union welcomed a "strengthened focus on antisemitism" while underlining that "no form of racism should be minimised".

Recent figures from the Community Security Trust, an organisation which provides security advice and support to the Jewish community, showed a spike in antisemitic incidents at schools.

It found in the first half of 2026 that antisemitism in schools had reached the highest level ever recorded for the first six months of any year.

News.title: Attempted murder arrests after boy, 16, attacked
News.content:
Two boys aged 15 and 16 have been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after a 16-year-old was seriously assaulted in Liverpool, police have said.

Officers were called to The Lutine Bell pub on Breck Road in Everton at about 14:15 BST following reports of a boy being assaulted nearby. He was taken to hospital with head and chest injuries where he remains in a serious condition.

A 37-year-old man and a 41-year-old woman have also been arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender. All four remain in custody, Merseyside Police said.

Det Ch Insp Paula Jones said: "We are continuing to appeal for anyone who was in the area of Breck Road shortly after 14:00 and saw, heard or captured anything to please get in touch."

Jones added: "You may also live or work nearby and witnessed people running off at the time. Pass on all information and we will make the assessment."

News.title: MP harassed for 'being English' by man who took axe to pub
News.content:
A man who harassed a Labour MP for being "English", and claimed he knew where he lived, has been given a suspended jail sentence.

Michael Glover, 59, left a note on Mid and South Pembrokeshire MP Henry Tufnell's office door in Haverfordwest, Pembrokeshire, on 10 March, and carried an axe to the pub the following day.

In the letter, which he signed, he also wrote that he had taken "a look around" Tufnell's family home and had "left some presents".

The MP said he felt "uneasy" that the defendant said he knew where he lived with his family, including his newborn baby.

Swansea Crown Court heard Glover, who is a wheelchair user and has "complex mental health difficulties", was "frustrated" because of a delay in his application for a blue badge.

The court heard that CCTV captured the defendant taping a bag, which contained the letter, to the front door of Tufnell's office. He then made "gestures" to the camera before driving away.

On 11 March, he carried an axe in a plastic bag to a local pub, and picked it up in front of a member of the public.

Glover was arrested that day, and later pleaded guilty to both charges at the magistrates' court.

Regan Walters, prosecuting, read a victim personal statement by Tufnell, who said the incident made him feel "uncomfortable".

"Knowing that Glover knows where I live with my wife and young child has made me rethink things, such as the security of my address," the politician said.

He said he had to be mindful that his "panic alarms and CCTV cameras are working" and that, when he worked away, he felt "on edge, wondering if [his family] are safe".

Joseph Hocquard, representing Glover, said his client had been in custody for the past four months for breaching a probation order, which he said had been "incredibly challenging" because of his mental health and disabilities.

Glover appeared via video link with his barrister in the cells at Swansea Crown Court because of a "technical issue" with the lift in the building.

Judge Mark Powell KC told him "members of parliament are there to advocate for their constituents".

He said: "They are entitled to go about their business, without being subject to the sort of threats and harassment that you carried outâ¦ regardless of if they are English or not English."

He also said that brandishing an axe in public would have been "extremely frightening for those around" but that he "didn't intend to harm anyone".

The judge told the court that it was "frustration" and a "deterioration in his mental state" that led to Glover committing the offence.

He said he was satisfied the defendant had shown remorse for both offences, and that he needed support and medication for his "complex mental health" needs.

Judge Powell gave him a six-month prison sentence, suspended for 12 months, as well as a five-year restraining order.

He was also ordered to pay a victim surcharge of Â£154.

News.title: Lawyer caught offering to make illegal-worker fine go away
News.content:
A solicitor has been secretly filmed by the BBC explaining how he could make a Â£45,000 illegal-working fine go away.

Mohammad Alias Yousaf - also known as Alias - made the claim to an undercover reporter, who was posing as a mini-mart owner facing a fine for employing an illegal worker.

The Bradford-based solicitor told his potential client he could avoid paying the fine, if he could find someone overseas prepared to declare themselves the owner of the mini-mart.

Alias has denied ever providing such advice to anyone, or giving false information to the Home Office.

At least Â£150m is currently owed to the government in uncollected illegal-working fines, according to Home Office figures obtained by the BBC.

In response to our investigation, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced a review of the way such fines are issued and collected.

In a statement, she said she wanted to thank the BBC "for exposing those who undermine our rules".

Many business owners do not take the fines seriously, a law enforcement official has told us anonymously.

She told us she had seen immigration fine notices, "some worth Â£40,000, stuffed in a box" on a mini-mart counter.

When she had asked a member of staff if the business owners intended to pay, she said she had been told: "'It's got nothing to do with me.'"

News.title: Woman told Russell Brand he 'treated her like an animal', court hears
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

One of the women who claims Russell Brand raped her later told him he had "treated her like an animal", a court has heard.

The comedian's trial at Southwark Crown Court in London has been hearing recorded police interviews with a female complainant, who claims she did not consent to anal sex with him at his house in 2009.

Brand, 51, denies three charges of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one charge of indecent assault. He has said he has never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity.

The allegations span a 10-year period from 1999 to 2009 and involve six female complainants.

On Wednesday, the jury heard an interview with a woman who says she first met Brand at one of his comedy shows at Hammersmith Apollo in 2009.

She said she had a boyfriend at the time but went to his dressing room, where she performed a sex act on him.

The woman said it was during their next meeting at his house when the sex was not consensual and she had only agreed to vaginal sex.

Asked by the detective in the interview whether there was ever a conversation about anal sex, she replied: "No."

She said she was surprised to receive a "random" text message from Brand six months later, saying he wanted to "push her further".

She said she replied asking: "Why are you even messaging me?"

"I remember his response, saying, 'Because you're dirty and I want to push you further'."

The jury heard that the woman did not respond straight away because she was upset, but then replied saying: "I think you've pushed me far enough, you treated me like an animal."

The woman added: "I do remember his response was immediate. He said, 'I'm sorry'."

News.title: easyJet offers to cover £66.50 passport fee for your next family holiday
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Parents booking an easyJet holiday can soon have the cost of their baby's passport covered, the operator has announced.

In a survey of 2,000 parents for easyJet, one in 10 admitted they did not know their baby needed their own passport until they started planning a holiday.

And one in four said when they did get around to applying for one, it took up to six attempts to get a passport photo approved.

Stuart Wright, customer director at easyJet Holidays, said: “Travel has a unique way of bringing families together, and a baby’s very first holiday is often one of those moments parents remember for years to come.

“By covering the cost of a baby’s first passport, we’re helping more families start making those memories that little bit sooner.”

open image in gallery Nine-month-old Emelia on board an easyJet aircraft ( PA )

During the promotional period, the £66.50 fee will be covered for a child up to the age of 18 months when parents book an easyJet holiday.

easyJet holidays reported a 10 per cent increase in infants travelling this year compared to 2025.

In the UK, a parent or guardian can apply for a first child passport for any child under the age of 16. It costs £66.50 to apply online and £80 to apply with a paper form from the Post Office, and is then valid for five years. Current processing times estimate a three-week wait.

Details on how to claim the offer will be available at easyJet.com/firstpassport.

The promotion ends 26 November at 11pm.

open image in gallery Access to e-gates at UK airports was expanded to include younger children ( PA )

Earlier this year, the Home Office announced that e-gates at UK airports would be made available to younger children.

Since 8 July, children aged eight and nine returning to the UK have been eligible to use the automated gates.

The gates use facial recognition technology for identity verification, which is generally quicker than manual inspections.

Children must be at least 120cm tall so they can be seen by biometric scanners and accompanied by an adult.

Previously, passengers under the age of 10 were prohibited from using the gates, often leading to longer queues for families at traditional passport booths.

News.title: MI5 monitored politician behind NHS for two decades, newly-released files show
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Aneurin "Nye" Bevan, the Labour icon who founded the NHS, was subjected to surveillance by MI5 for over two decades, newly released official records reveal.

Files made public at the National Archives indicate he initially drew the attention of security services during the 1930s as a prominent left-winger tied to key communists.

The monitoring continued throughout his time as a minister in the post-war Labour administration, during which he established the NHS despite fierce opposition from doctors.

At one point, the director general of MI5 was so alarmed by his contacts with a known Russia spy that he raised the matter directly with prime minister Clement Attlee at No 10.

However, members of the security service questioned the operation, highlighting that his activities were carried out entirely in the open on the floor of the House of Commons.

open image in gallery The documents reveal that MI5 first set up a personal file on Mr Bevan – then serving as backbench Labour MP for Ebbw Vale in South Wales – back in 1933 ( PA Media )

In a review conducted after his death in 1960, an MI5 officer observed: "Considering what a controversial character Nye Bevan was, the file is remarkably tame."

The documents reveal that MI5 first set up a personal file on Mr Bevan – then serving as backbench Labour MP for Ebbw Vale in South Wales – back in 1933.

Early entries include a report covering a Canadian anti-Nazi rally in Montreal, which Mr Bevan addressed in 1934.

“Bevan has inherited the evangelical fervour of his Welsh forebears and knows how to use it in the Communist cause,” it stated.

“He pictured the overthrow of the Nazi regime as meaning the commencement of a united Europe under Soviet rule.”

In 1943, Roger Hollis, a future director general, complied a summary of what they knew of Mr Bevan’s activities up to that point.

In 1933, he noted, the MP had been “in close touch” with Harry Pollitt, general secretary of the Communist Party of Great Britain, and others in the party who backed his plan to organise “workers’ freedom groups” to defend against the “capitalists”.

Against a background of mass unemployment and the Great Depression, he had been closely associated with the hunger marches of 1934, entertaining deputations of marchers in the House of Commons.

He soon fell out, however, with his communist allies, who complained he was not interested in workers’ unity and was intent on building “a movement of his own” – now named The Sons of Freedom – with “all the elements of a fascist organisation”.

open image in gallery There is nothing in the files to indicate that MI5 ever tapped Bevan’s phone ( PA )

By 1936 they had patched up their differences sufficiently for Mr Bevan to support an application by the Communist Party to affiliate to the Labour Party.

With the outbreak of the Second World War in 1939 he was said to have adopted a policy of “war on two fronts” – attacking the Germans abroad and Neville Chamberlain’s Conservative government at home.

That continued with formation of Winston Churchill’s coalition government – sharply criticising the prosecution of the war while accusing Labour ministers of “leaning too much to the right”.

Although there is nothing in the files to indicate that MI5 ever tapped his phone or intercepted his mail, some wondered why they were bothering with him at all.

“I do not think that Bevan’s activities are a matter in which we, the security service, should be involved,” one officer wrote in 1943.

“In fact he makes exactly the same remarks in the Houses of Parliament pretty frequently, as any copy of Hansard will show, and it would not therefore be possible to do anything positive.”

Nevertheless, the reporting continued after the war – albeit less frequently – when Mr Bevan was appointed minister of health in Mr Attlee’s new government.

In 1949, MI5 was becoming increasingly concerned about Mr Bevan’s friendship with Wilfred Macartney, “an unsavoury, unscrupulous character” who had been convicted of spying for Russia in 1928.

Recordings of his conversations suggested he was passing on information obtained by Mr Bevan to Mr Pollitt, the Communist Party leader.

In May of that year, the director general Sir Percy Sillitoe took the evidence to Mr Attlee – who dismissed Mr Macartney’s claims as a “tissue of lies” but agreed to “warn Bevan about Macartney in general terms without, of course, making any allusion to the conversation”.

One of the final reports dates from 1954 when Mr Bevan, by now back in opposition, was invited to meet the Soviet ambassador, Yakov Malik, over lunch at the Polish embassy in London.

The event “went off very badly” in part because the Russian had difficulty in understanding Mr Bevan’s Welsh accent leading to a bad-tempered misunderstanding.

“A great deal of drink was consumed, but the party broke up in a none too friendly atmosphere,” the report stated.

The file was not finally closed however until 1975 – 15 years after Mr Bevan had died.

News.title: ‘Glaring gaps’ in military capability leave UK exposed to Russian attacks in High North, MPs warn
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Critical flaws in Britain's High North military posture leave the public, subsea pipelines and the nuclear deterrent exposed to Russian aggression, MPs have warned, highlighting "glaring gaps" in defence capabilities.

The Commons Defence Committee stated that "dramatic progress" must be achieved to strengthen UK armed forces and naval vessels in the strategically vital region before 2030 – the year former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer suggested Moscow could launch an attack on Nato.

Security in the High North has become increasingly crucial for Britain, particularly as Vladimir Putin’s Russia dispatches regional spy vessels into UK waters while questions surround Washington’s commitment to European safety.

A failure to safeguard the area could leave critical underwater cables and pipelines carrying key data and energy exposed to deliberate peacetime sabotage, the committee noted.

It added that in the event of conflict, Russia would be positioned to target the British population, civilian and military infrastructure, and vital Atlantic supply corridors originating from the US.

Committee chairman Tan Dhesi said: “The High North poses a major strategic challenge for the UK’s security. This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage.

“The UK needs to be willing to address a hard truth: it does not currently have all the capabilities to operate successfully in the High North.

open image in gallery Lawmakers emphasised an acute deficit in anti-submarine warfare at a time when Moscow’s greatest threat stems from its submarine fleet and naval sabotage units ( Getty )

“Russian submarine and sabotage forces in the High North pose direct risks to the North Atlantic and the UK, including the nuclear deterrent.

“Despite this, the Ministry of Defence has accepted a serious anti-submarine warfare gap.

“Publicly available evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines calls into question whether the UK can meet its commitments in the High North.

“And if the UK Government means what it says – that Russia could attack Nato as soon as 2030 – then work to rectify these vulnerabilities cannot start soon enough.”

Lawmakers emphasised an acute deficit in anti-submarine warfare at a time when Moscow’s greatest threat stems from its submarine fleet and naval sabotage units.

While Royal Navy anti-submarine warships and nuclear-powered submarines remain the premier deterrent, these assets are increasingly old and frequently sidelined by ongoing maintenance work.

There are currently five Type 23 frigates, which track down hostile submarines and protect the UK’s nuclear weapons, and six Type 45 destroyers in service – just over half of the Royal Navy’s requirement for 19 vessels.

Eight new Type 26 frigates will eventually take over, but with construction slow, the Defence Committee urged ministers to ensure that none of the remaining ones leaves service in the meantime.

The committee’s inquiry also heard of “a shockingly low availability” of submarines, and that the UK appeared to have temporarily lost its ability to operate them beneath Arctic ice.

This would allow Russia in a conflict to conceal its nuclear submarines under the ice unchallenged while its attack submarines surge forward.

The committee also questioned whether the Joint Expeditionary Force (Jef), a UK-led military coalition of northern European nations, should focus more on threats in the High North rather than maintaining the same level of activity in the Baltic region.

open image in gallery Commons Defence Committee chairman Tan Dhesi ( House of Commons )

Mr Dhesi urged ministers to consider this “particularly if the UK has to plan for uncertainty over US support for Nato”.

And to offset the effects of any greater Jef focus on the High North, the UK may need to consider bolstering the current British Army force in the Baltics, notably in Estonia, he said.

The Kremlin is seeking to exploit the High North, loosely defined as the Arctic and parts of the North Atlantic, for minerals and for control over shipping routes as melting sea ice makes them more accessible.

It comes as Britain’s biggest warship, HMS Prince of Wales, departed Portsmouth Naval Base in Hampshire to lead the UK Carrier Strike Group on a deployment to the Arctic and North Atlantic.

The aircraft carrier left on Sunday, with dozens of people gathering to wave and take pictures as the warship made its way out of the harbour.

The deployment marks the second phase of Operation Firecrest, which will focus on operational readiness, training, and strengthening Nato interoperability.

The Royal Navy said stealth fighter jets would return to the skies in the High North.

It said deployment of the flagship aircraft carrier alongside Nato allies “is a powerful shield for the nation, ensuring that the critical energy, trade, and communication links we all rely on every day in the region remain secure”.

Conservative shadow minister for war readiness Stuart Anderson said: “This Defence Committee report exposes glaring capability gaps in the High North at a time when the threat of war with Russia is rising.

“If Nato could be at war with Russia as soon as 2030, as the former prime minister warned, that means time is just as important as money.

“To deter war we must be ready for it, that means spending money now, not kicking the can down the road until it’s too late.

“The Chancellor must come to the Budget with his plan for spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030 – anything less leaves Britain at risk in the High North.”

An MoD spokesperson said: “We are clear-eyed about the threat Russia poses. During his recent visit to Iceland, the Defence Secretary saw firsthand how HMS St Albans helps track and deter Russian submarine activity across the North Atlantic.

“Through the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force, we are leading allied activity across the High North, strengthening Nato’s northern flank and increasing our ability to respond rapidly to emerging threats.

“This government is also investing in the capabilities needed to meet those threats, with £1.5 billion backing Atlantic Bastion to deliver a next-generation Hybrid Navy and a further £330 million to strengthen the protection of critical undersea infrastructure.”

News.title: Prescription charges in England should be scrapped, experts say
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Prescription charges in England should be scrapped, pharmacy leaders have said.

A new survey indicates that 79% of the public consider it "unfair" that patients in England must pay for their medication, whereas those residing in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland do not.

The poll of 1,781 adults in England, carried out by Savanta for the National Pharmacy Association (NPA), also discovered that one in 10 people (10%) have gone without a prescribed medicine over the last year because of the cost involved.

Another 12% of respondents stated they had delayed collecting their prescriptions for the exact same financial reason.

Describing the policy as a "cruel tax on illness", the NPA urged the Chancellor to eliminate the charges in the upcoming Budget, stating that such a step would help relieve widespread cost of living pressures.

Phil Day, superintendent pharmacist at Pharmacy2U, said: “It’s concerning to hear that people are going without medication because of the cost of prescriptions, particularly those managing long-term conditions who depend on regular treatment.”

Prescription charges were abolished in Wales in 2007, in Northern Ireland in 2010 and in Scotland in 2011.

In England, the standard fee for an individual prescription item currently stands at £9.90.

open image in gallery Prescription charges were abolished in Wales in 2007, in Northern Ireland in 2010 and in Scotland in 2011 ( Getty/iStock )

Selected medications remain free, including contraception and hospital inpatient drugs, while exemptions apply to under 16s, those aged 16 to 18 in full-time education, individuals aged 60 and over, benefit claimants and patients who live with certain specific qualifying medical health conditions.

Mr Day added: “Prescription prepayment certificates can reduce costs for those paying for regular medication, but our research suggests only 8% currently hold one, and 30% of the population have never heard of one.”

NPA chairman Olivier Picard said: “No patient should ever see cost as being a barrier to accessing the medicines they need but this polling shows an alarming number do.

“It is a national scandal and deeply unfair that anyone could consider stopping vital medicines because of cost.

“This cruel tax on illness, where some patients are exempt but others are forced to pay simply because they have the wrong kind of illness, undermines the founding principles of the NHS.

“If the Chancellor wants to tackle the rising cost of living and health inequalities, he should bring England into line with the rest of the UK and scrap this unfair and complex prescription tax.”

The NPA, which has teamed up with a group of charities to call for the charge to be axed, has said it is a “national scandal” that people are deterred from buying medicines because of cost.

The Association, which represents around 6,000 community pharmacies, said pharmacists have reported that patients with multiple one-off medicines on a prescription have asked “which is the most important one to take?”

Sarah Sleet, chief executive of the charity Asthma and Lung UK, said: “For people with lung conditions like asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), being able to take medication shouldn’t come down to whether or not you can afford it.

“But because respiratory conditions aren’t included on the prescription charges exemptions list, people are left essentially paying for their right to breathe.”

open image in gallery John Healey has been urged to eliminate the charges in the upcoming Budget ( PA Wire )

The NPA said that an estimated 11.6 million patients paid prescription charges in 2025/26.

Some 3.3 million people paid for a prescription prepayment certificate which covers NHS prescriptions for a fixed fee and can reduce costs for people who need medicines regularly.

There is also a PPC for women taking hormone replacement therapy, with around 730,000 women using this in 2025/26.

Marianne Radcliffe, chief executive at Crohn’s and Colitis UK, added: “We support calls to scrap prescription charges in England.

“People with long-term conditions should not be forced to choose between their health and their finances simply because they need medication every day.”

Fiona Loud, from Kidney Care UK, said: “It’s simply not a fair system because it penalises ill health; everyone should be able to access the medication they need to stay well for free, without worrying about whether or not they can afford it.”

Laura Cockram, head of campaigns at Parkinson’s UK, added: “The upcoming Budget is an opportunity for the Government to take meaningful action. If they are serious about tackling the cost of living crisis and preventing avoidable ill health, the Government must scrap prescription charges in England, bringing us in line with the rest of the UK.”

The NPA has estimated that £732.8 million was raised by prescription costs in in 2025/26.

Dr James Davies, director of research and insights at Community Pharmacy England, said: “The Chancellor has an opportunity in this Budget to remove one of the most unfair costs facing patients.

“No-one should be forced to choose between paying for essential medicines and making ends meet, yet these figures show that too many people are doing exactly that.”

It comes as millions of NHS app users in England can now receive smartwatch and phone notifications when their prescriptions are ready for collection.

NHS England said the new service aims to prevent unnecessary calls and premature visits to the chemist to collect medication.

To receive these updates, individuals must turn on push alerts within the application settings.

The Department of Health and Social Care has been approached for comment.

News.title: Burnham backs pioneering clinical trial that could speed up Alzheimer’s treatments
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A pioneering clinical trial could dramatically accelerate the discovery of new therapies for Alzheimer’s disease.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, whose father Roy died with the condition in September, said he was proud to back the initiative in the hope it will deliver findings far quicker than conventional testing methods.

Roy Burnham, who previously worked as a telephone engineer, was living in a care home prior to his death. His illness meant he remained unaware that his son had become Prime Minister.

The new study, titled Ad-Smart (Alzheimer’s disease Systematic Multi-arm Adaptive Randomised Trial), is spearheaded by the UK Dementia Research Institute and Alzheimer’s Research UK, with financial backing from funders including the Government.

Experts state that the trial's innovative design has the potential to more than halve the time needed to evaluate Alzheimer’s drugs.

The project will assess multiple medications concurrently, starting with atomoxetine, an attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) drug, alongside metformin, which treats type 2 diabetes.

Scientists noted that existing evidence shows atomoxetine affects mechanisms linked to further degeneration in Alzheimer’s, while metformin also demonstrates potential across specific pathways.

Over time, additional therapies, comprising repurposed medicines for other conditions as well as novel Alzheimer’s treatments, will be introduced to the trial.

open image in gallery Burnham’s father Roy died in September ( Reuters )

Mr Burnham said: “I know how it feels to lose a loved one to dementia and have seen first-hand the devastating impact this illness has on families.

“That’s why I’m proud to see this trial being launched in the UK, so that cutting-edge treatments can reach patients here as soon as possible.

“I have made dementia research a national priority. I want Britain to be the leading nation, making the breakthroughs that change people’s lives.”

Alzheimer’s is the most common type of dementia, affecting around 600,000 people in the UK.

Experts in the new trial are looking to see whether treatments help with issues such as poor memory and thinking problems, and whether they can help people maintain a good quality of life.

The first people have been recruited at Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS Foundation Trust and Surrey and Borders Partnership NHS Foundation Trust.

Other sites include at Imperial in London, Edinburgh and Southampton, with up to 20 NHS sites expected to open over the next 18 months to include more than 1,000 people.

The first drugs should have conclusions by 2030, with people tested via scans and blood tests at regular intervals.

Chief investigator Professor Paresh Malhotra, from the UK Dementia Research Institute, said: “For too long, Alzheimer’s research has moved at the pace of one drug, one trial, one answer, sometimes taking a decade or more before we know if we’ve found something that works.

“We are applying advances from cancer and other conditions to accelerate testing of treatments for people with Alzheimer’s disease.

“The way Ad-Smart is set up means we’re testing several treatments at the same time, and those that don’t show promise can be quickly stopped.

“Then we can start testing something else. That’s the best way to get effective treatments to patients as quickly as we can.”

Prof Malhotra told a briefing that the team “want to look at the multiple mechanisms that are involved in Alzheimer’s disease”.

He said: “We know there are different processes that drive neurodegeneration, that drive deterioration, and so if we can compare and contrast different treatments that affect different processes, then we should find an effective treatment faster.”

While the treatments lecanemab and donanemab, which have been rejected for use on the NHS, have advanced the field of drug treatments, other medicines are far cheaper and experts know already about the risk of side-effects for some of them.

open image in gallery Alzheimer’s is the most common type of dementia, affecting around 600,000 people in the UK ( Getty/iStock )

Professor Siddharthan Chandran, director of the UK Dementia Research Institute, said it was a “very exciting time” in the field, with major advances in both diagnostics and treatments for Alzheimer’s, but more needs to be done.

For too long, treatments have been tested in a “grossly inefficient way” and it can take four or five years to find whether a drug works, he said.

He added: “Because of the way Smart trials are designed, biotech and pharmaceutical companies can also bring their drugs straight into the trial.

“That means more treatments tested more quickly, and for people living with Alzheimer’s, that could make all the difference.”

Dr Sheona Scales, director of research at Alzheimer’s Research UK, said: “For people living with Alzheimer’s disease, time is precious.

“We urgently need more treatment options that can help people live better for longer and stay connected to the people they love…

“We hope this new approach to clinical trials could help bring a future closer where people affected by Alzheimer’s have more treatment options — and ultimately, a cure.”

Profesor Tara Spires-Jones, professor of neurodegeneration at the University of Edinburgh and a fellow at the Academy of Medical Sciences, said: “There is extremely promising neuroscience coming through the pipeline that can be tested in this trial and beyond.

“Although only a limited number of people will be able to participate in this new trial, there are things we can all do to boost our own brain resilience and help scientists in the fight to defeat Alzheimer’s and other diseases that cause dementia.

“People can lead a brain healthy lifestyle, get involved in research studies, and support research through working with dementia charities and encouraging governments to fund research.”

Elsewhere, the Government said it had hit its target to speed up clinical trials, with delivery times cut by 35%.

The average set-up time for commercial trials in the UK dropped to 100 days in the three months to March this year, down from 153 in the same period last year.

All of the 24 commercial trials during those months were set up within 150 days.

News.title: UK City of Culture 2029: The four contenders in shortlist revealed
News.content:
