World.title: Jansen, Rabada put Proteas in sight of win over Australia
World.content:
GQEBERHA - Marco Jansen and Kagiso Rabada bowled South Africa to within sight of a series-levelling victory on the fourth day of the second Test at St George's Park on Wednesday.

Australia were 156 for four in their follow-on innings after being shot out for 99 earlier in the day. They were still 170 runs short of making South Africa bat again.

Travis Head survived an early chance and was unbeaten on 87. Steve Smith did not come out to bat in the second innings after appearing to be struggling with a neck injury while making top score of 28 in Australia's first innings.

Jansen took five for 33 as Australia crashed to their fourth-lowest total against South Africa and Rabada made two crucial breakthroughs in the second innings.

Rabada dismissed Australian opening batsman Nic Maddinson cheaply for the second time in the match and later bowled Matt Renshaw, who was man of the match in Australia's 214-run win in the first Test.

With a first innings lead of 326 runs, South Africa enforced the follow-on despite fast bowler Anrich Nortje being out of action with a groin injury. Nortje dismissed Marnus Labuschagne in the first innings but bowled only 3.3 overs before pulling up injured.

In Nortje's absence, South African captain Temba Bavuma used Rabada, Jansen and fellow seamer Wiaan Mulder in short spells and made extensive use of off-spinner Simon Harmer, who bowled 18 overs and took two wickets.

Harmer broke a 92-run second-wicket stand between Head and Labuschagne when the latter went for a big hit and was caught by Jansen running back from mid-on as the ball was held up in a stiff breeze.

Tall left-armer Jansen was superb in the first innings. He struck with his first ball of the match when he had nightwatchman Scott Boland caught behind in the second over of the day.

He followed up with the wickets of Head, Renshaw, Alex Carey and Beau Webster as Australia collapsed.

World.title: Gachagua, Sifuna eye joint presidential strategy against Ruto
World.content:
DCP leader Rigathi Gachagua hosts Edwin Sifuna and Linda Mwananchi leaders at his Wamunyoro residence on October 20, 2026. [Linda Mwananchi, X]

A powerful political wave is expected to sweep across the country from this weekend, when Rigathi Gachagua’s Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) and Edwin Sifuna’s Linda Mwananchi outfit hold their first joint rally in Nyahururu.

Fresh details emerging from a meeting held at Wamunyoro on Tuesday indicate that a series of joint meetings between the two camps will continue in the coming weeks.

World.title: Drama in church after Mudavadi, Wetang'ula walk out as Sifuna speaks
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna, Prime CS Musalia Mudavadi and National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang’ula join mourners at the late Burudi Nabwera's memorial in Nairobi. [Edwin Sifuna, X]

Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi and National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang’ula walked out of the requiem mass of former lawmaker Burudi Nabwera after Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna was invited to address mourners.

In a clip that has since gone viral, the two senior government officials are seen walking towards the entrance of Friends Church in Lang'ata on Wednesday, the venue for the memorial service, while Sifuna took the stage.

Sifuna appeared to acknowledge the departure with a "this is Nairobi" quip that drew laughter from mourners.

The incident appears to lay bare the deepening political divisions ahead of the 2027 General Election.

The two leaders’ departure came as Sifuna used the funeral gathering to condemn tribal politics, lament the breakdown of political friendships and pledge to restore the spirit of national unity that defined Kenya at independence.

“At the beginning of this country, when we got independence, we were all Kenyans; there was nothing like tribalism and everyone of us should be available to all of us to sell our policies,” he said.

The senator appeared to take a swipe at those seeking to restrict political associations along regional lines, saying leaders were being judged based on whom they were seen with.

“Some people saw me somewhere with someone and somehow they are telling us that there is a region in this country where none of us is supposed to associate with,” Sifuna said.

The sentiments appeared to castigate government leaders who he said "are not happy" with his association with former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua.

This happened just hours after he met the Democracy for the Citizens (DCP) party leader at his Wamunyoro home in Nyeri on Tuesday, in the company of other Linda Mwananchi movement leaders.

He pledged that, in honour of Nabwera, he would work towards reviving the spirit of unity that characterised the country at independence in 1963.

“I want to make assurance here, in honour of Burudi Nabwera, we will restore that feeling that was there at the beginning of our country in 1963, that all of us, irrespective of our tribe, are Kenyans and we all belong to this society,” he said.

Sifuna, also used the opportunity to woo the Nabwera's nephew, Nabii Nabwera, who is Lugari MP, with whom they have "shared a long political history."

Sifuna also expressed regret that political divisions had separated him from Nabii, whom he described as a friend with whom they journeyed together in ODM.

“Our politics is so petty that being seen with some of us, you are branded and told you are hanging out with Sifuna; you are now a bad person,” he said.

“I miss Nabii Nabwera. You know the things we have done together. You know the journey we have walked together in ODM. I want you by my side on this journey towards the presidency,” he said.

World.title: Judge certifies fresh bid to jail Sakaja, Charles Kerich over Sh76.7m debt as urgent
World.content:
Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja. [File, Standard]

The High Court has certified as urgent a fresh application seeking to have Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja, former Finance Executive Charles Kerich and two other county officials jailed over an alleged breach of a court-approved payment plan in a Sh106.7 million legal fees dispute.

Justice Francis Gikonyo certified the application by Kwengu & Company Advocates seeking to reinstate a three-month jail sentence previously imposed on Kerich and hold Sakaja, current Finance County Executive Committee Member Ibrahim Auma Nyangoya and Chief Officer for Finance Asha Abdi accountable for the alleged failure to pay Sh76.7 million.

World.title: Kenya confirms third Ebola case
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kenya has confirmed a third case of Ebola involving a 65-year-old woman who is a close relative of the first two patients.

The Ministry of Health, in a statement, said the woman developed a fever, sore throat and malaise while in quarantine, prompting her isolation and testing.

Her samples tested positive for Ebola at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI).

According to the Health Director-General Patrick Amoth, the patient has been transferred to an infectious disease unit, where she is receiving supportive care and being monitored.

“Having been in quarantine, she was diagnosed early and is currently receiving supportive care, improving her chances of recovery while limiting the risk of further spread of the disease,” the statement read.

The second patient, on the other hand, is in stable condition and responding well to supportive care.

The latest case brings the number of confirmed Ebola infections in Kenya to three.

According to the Ministry, of the 130 contacts identified so far, 127 had been traced and placed in quarantine, with efforts ongoing to trace the remaining three.

World.title: Motorists, households face fresh fuel price hikes
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

EPRA attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East. [FIle, Standard]

The Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) has increased fuel prices, raising the cost of super petrol by Sh12.93 per litre, diesel by Sh9.90, and kerosene by Sh28.49.

The new prices, effective from October 15 to November 14, 2026, will see motorists in Nairobi pay up to Sh226.96 per litre for super petrol, Sh227.76 for diesel, and Sh219.85 for kerosene.

EPRA Director-General Edward Mwirigi Kinyua attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East, which has disrupted petroleum supply chains and driven up the cost of importing fuel.

The rise in kerosene prices is likely to hit low-income households that rely on the fuel for cooking and lighting.

Meanwhile, higher diesel prices could raise the cost of transporting goods and operating public service vehicles, potentially driving up fares and commodity prices.

Diesel is a key fuel for the country's freight transport sector and a significant portion of public service vehicle operations, meaning the increase could have a ripple effect across the economy.

The latest review comes after EPRA maintained pump prices during the September 15 to October 14 pricing period, despite a decline in the cost of importing petrol.

World.title: Oburu Oginga to leave hospital soon - ODM
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

ODM SG Catherine Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician.

ODM Secretary General Catherine Omanyo has dismissed social media reports about the health of party leader Oburu Oginga, saying he is recovering well and is expected to be discharged from hospital either today or tomorrow.

Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician, accusing them of exploiting his health condition to attract online attention and increase engagement.

“It's unfortunate what I've been reading on social media. Those people who are seeking to have more likes or viewers, they will be disappointed because he's up, he's well, he's fine. In fact, he's headed home either today or tomorrow,” she said.

Omanyo insisted that the reports had exaggerated his situation, dismissing claims of his death and assuring the public that he was doing well.

She noted that health conditions could fluctuate, saying Oburu's position as ODM party leader had made his well-being a subject of heightened public interest.

“Everybody, everybody, including you and me, our health is not static. You can be under the weather any time. It's just that he's a party leader, and it makes breaking news,” Omanyo said.

She urged social media users to exercise restraint when discussing the health of public figures, warning against spreading unverified reports, particularly claims of death, before confirmation from credible sources.

Her remarks come amid growing speculation on social media about Oburu's health, with some users circulating unverified claims about his condition.

World.title: Kenya declares Ebola a formidable epidemic disease, sets new rules
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale, who declared Ebola caused by the Bundibugyo virus a formidable epidemic disease under the Public Health Act. [File,Standard]

Kenya has declared Ebola virus a formidable epidemic disease, introducing new rules governing screening, isolation, quarantine, contact tracing and the handling of bodies.

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale issued the declaration through a legal notice published in the Kenya Gazette on Monday, October 12, under Section 35 of the Public Health Act.

The declaration follows Kenya’s confirmation of its first imported case of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease on October 6, after a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo travelled through Uganda to Nairobi. The patient died despite receiving supportive treatment.

The case prompted health authorities to trace people who may have come into contact with the patient and strengthen screening at points of entry.

In an update on October 12, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Kenya had listed 127 contacts, with 94 in quarantine, and screened more than 665,000 travellers at points of entry.

WHO also supplied protective equipment and testing materials worth about US$70,000 to support the response.

The government published two legal notices on October 12. Legal Notice No. 203 declares the disease a formidable epidemic, while Legal Notice No. 204 establishes the Public Health (Ebola Disease) Rules, 2026.

The regulations provide for screening at points of entry, medical assessment, isolation, referral, quarantine and monitoring.

They also assign responsibilities to transport operators, health facilities, medical practitioners and laboratories.

Health authorities will conduct investigations and contact tracing, while designated health facilities will manage suspected and confirmed cases. The rules also provide for the inspection and decontamination of premises.

The regulations cover the safe and dignified disposal of bodies, burial procedures, record-keeping, transportation and repatriation. They also address public communication, media houses’ responsibilities in public sensitisation and assistance from enforcement agencies.

The rules provide for offences and penalties, although the Gazette extract does not specify the penalties for individual violations.

What the declaration means

Bundibugyo virus disease is a form of Ebola that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person or contaminated materials.

Contact with the body of someone who has died from the disease can also expose people to infection during unsafe burial practices.

Symptoms can include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache and sore throat, followed by vomiting and diarrhoea. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days.

WHO says no approved vaccine or specific treatment currently exists for the Bundibugyo strain, making early detection, isolation, supportive care and contact tracing central to controlling its spread.

The health agency has advised against travel or trade restrictions on Kenya, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo based on the information available.

The new rules establish a legal framework for managing the disease, from identifying suspected infections and monitoring contacts to caring for patients and preventing exposure during burials.

World.title: As midterms loom, Democrats learn to speak a new language: American
World.content:
“I’m a border security Democrat.”

With five words at a CNN and Jubilee Town Hall last week, Texas Senate candidate James Talarico sought to dodge the stigma of the Biden administration’s failure to secure the southern border.

Talarico is one of a crop of Democratic midterm election candidates choosing language that pivots away from past election failures. For future political viability, the Democratic Party must reclaim voters alienated by its perceived contempt for politically and culturally more conservative Americans — including those who were once the foundation of its blue-collar base but defected to President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement.

One way to do this is to craft messaging on issues like affordability that connect with working Americans and highlight the link between Trump’s decisions — like the Iran war — and the cost of groceries, gasoline and housing.

Democrats also face a linguistic minefield as they try to again talk like the voters they want to attract without angering the party’s new base of more liberal urban and highly educated voters.

In recent years, Democratic messaging has often seemed academic, esoteric, politically correct or choked with jargon. Terms like “unhoused people” and “birthing people” were adopted to include and respect people who are marginalized or vulnerable. Such language shows regard for the humanity and individual rights of others. But it has sometimes obscured meaning and baffled people who are not deeply political, or turned away voters with more conservative values.

In some cases, Republicans have used Democratic language to drive a wedge between the party and persuadable voters and to suggest it has tacked to the left. The most hard-hitting ad of the 2024 election season attacked Democratic nominee Kamala Harris over transgender issues, telling voters that “Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you.”

A demonstrator holds a sign reading “Defund the Police” during events to mark Juneteenth amid nationwide protests against racial inequality in New York City, in June 2020. Brendan McDermid/Reuters

The term “defund the police” became a national slogan after the murder of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer in 2020. Republicans soon co-opted it to argue that Democrats were weak on law and order — a narrative that circulated for several elections, even though senior party members like former President Joe Biden publicly repudiated it and its policy implications.

And in one of the most notorious examples of loose language haunting Democrats, 2016 nominee Hillary Clinton suggested some Trump fans belonged in a “basket of deplorables” — handing MAGA a rallying cry to underscore Trump’s claim that establishment elites viewed his voters with disgust.

‘I understand why you voted for Trump’

One reason — apart from Trump’s unpopularity — why Democrats are competitive in more states than expected during this year’s midterms is that they’ve selected candidates who sound like their states.

In North Carolina, Senate nominee Roy Cooper has developed a colloquial way to argue he’d “Make Stuff Cost Less.” He appears to be rebuilding the broadened coalition that made him governor twice in a reliably Republican state.

James Talarico during a CNN and Jubilee Town Hall in Fort Worth, Texas, on Wednesday, October 14. Tristen Rouse/CNN

Talarico speaks the language of faith in pious Texas to distinguish himself from progressive Democrats. His “border security Democrat” phrase balances his support for both a hard border and a softer immigration purge that would target only undocumented criminals rather than “small business owners, grandmothers and infants.”

In Iowa, which Trump won by double digits only two years ago, Democratic Senate nominee Josh Turek brands himself a “prairie populist” and tells voters, “I understand why you voted for Trump” before he lambasts the president for raising costs and starting the kind of war he vowed never to fight.

In Maine, Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson refused to apologize for telling Sen. Susan Collins to “shut up” during a debate. The incumbent Republican suggested he was guilty of sexism. But Jackson, a former logger, turned the conceit of supposed establishment contempt for working people against his opponent. He said on CNN’s “State of the Union” Sunday that, “What I’m not going to be is talked down to by Senator Collins.”

Collins and Jackson are seen during their debate at the Gracie Theatre in Bangor, Maine, on October 15. Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty Images

Jackson added: “I’m fighting for Mainers. And, I mean, I just think that was another situation where she was talking down to me.”

Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has meanwhile developed his own searing linguistic critique of Trump that links alleged White House corruption to the economic struggles of millions of Americans. “Under the failed president Donald J. Trump, it costs more than ever in American history to fill up your truck, stock your fridge, visit the doctor or power your home,” Ossoff said at a rally earlier this month. “They promised to drain the swamp. Instead, it’s the most corrupt administration of all time, and everybody knows it.”

Of course, Democrats have one big advantage that facilitates their linguistic balancing act: It’s far easier to find language to attack an incumbent Republican president over high prices and economic insecurity than it was for the party to defend the Biden administration for its struggles on the same issues in 2024.

And a party that failed to take advantage of a president who boasts about an economic “golden age” when Americans are paying $4.30 for gasoline and dread their grocery bills would be guilty of gross political incompetence.

‘Talk like a normal human’

In August 2025, the moderate think tank Third Way published a memo warning that the while Democrats spent “billions of dollars trying to find the perfect language to connect to voters” they used “an awful lot of words and phrases no ordinary person would ever dream of saying.” The memo concluded that “the effect of this language is to sound like the extreme, divisive, elitist, and obfuscatory, enforcers of wokeness. To please the few, we have alienated the many—especially on culture issues, where our language sounds superior, haughty and arrogant.”

In the wreckage of another defeat to Trump, some top Democrats agreed.

Former Obama administration White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel, a possible 2028 presidential candidate, told CNN’s Michael Smerconish a year ago that in 2024, the party allowed itself to be framed as “culturally, not only distant, but culturally isolated from where the general public is.”

Emanuel added: “You have to build a winning coalition, which means it has to be big. It has to be broad, and other voters have to be respected, something elements of our party don’t do. They like to lecture people to be exactly like them.”

Another possible Democratic presidential candidate, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, has been striking similar notes this year. He said at a dinner in Michigan that he was a “pro-diversity” governor but that to win, Democrats needed to “talk like a normal human.”

Governor Andy Beshear on the campaign trail at the University of Louisville on in 2023. Michael Clevenger/Courier Journal/USA Today Network/Imagn Images

He criticized terms like “food insecure” for hungry and “justice-involved population” instead of prison inmates. “Sometimes these terms make it feel like we’re talking down to people, like we’re talking at them, instead of to them,” Beshear said.

Matt Bennett, executive vice president of public affairs at Third Way, said Democrats this year were doing a better job of finding ways to connect with voters.

“For the most part, we’re delighted with the people that have won their primaries and the races that they’re running, and they seem very well suited,” he said, pointing especially to the example of Cooper, who has prospered in a state that last voted Democrat for president in 2008. “He has done what it takes to win the trust of these voters.”

The general election campaign has been kinder to Democrats so far than primary season, which threw up several viral moments quickly seized upon by Republicans to portray Democrats as extremists.

In an interview with Fox News, Democratic Socialists of America co-chair Megan Romer advocated abolishing the Senate, replacing the presidency and the Supreme Court, and defunding the Pentagon. She said prisons could be abolished under long-term plans, along with national borders. The encounter ran on a loop on conservative media for days as the GOP tried to define all Democrats by association.

But Republicans are now creating their own viral moments with language that seems deliberately aimed at excluding citizens and groups.

Trump has been inciting Islamophobia in the crudest and most inflammatory terms by mocking the name of Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayedand falsely calling him a jihadist. On Monday, Vice President JD Vance suggested that a protester — a person of color who shouted that he was an American citizen — must have crossed the border illegally.

Democrats may not be the only party with a language problem.

World.title: Drone strike on a market in disputed African region of Abyei kills at least 153
World.content:
Juba, South Sudan AP — A drone strike on a market in Abyei, a border region disputed by A drone strike on a market in Abyei, a border region disputed by Sudan and South Sudan, hit a nearby fuel depot, killing at least 153 people and igniting a fire that was still burning Tuesday, a local official said.

Yohanna Akol Ngor, the Abyei administration’s caretaker information minister, blamed Sudan’s military for Monday’s attack on Amiet Market, north of Abyei town.

“We have recorded 153 deaths,” Ngor told the Associated Press by phone Tuesday. He said the death toll continued to rise as the fire burned.

A senior Sudanese military officer said the army carried out a drone strike Monday targeting fuel tankers arriving from South Sudan that he said were bound for the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). He spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the press.

The officer said those killed were RSF members and people involved in fuel smuggling. “We do not target civilians,” he said. The AP could not independently verify his account of the targets or the identities of those killed.

The officer said the strike took place outside the demilitarized zone along the border with South Sudan.

Doctors Without Borders, known by its French abbreviation MSF, said more than 20 wounded people were brought to Ameth Bek Hospital, where MSF teams were working alongside staff from South Sudan’s Health Ministry.

“So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted,” said Dr. Christian Lindauer, MSF’s medical activities manager at the hospital.

South Sudan’s Foreign Ministry also blamed Sudan’s military, saying the attack hit multiple locations within the market, causing civilian casualties and extensive property damage.

The ministry said it summoned Sudan’s ambassador to protest and urged Sudan to “refrain from any actions that endanger civilian lives and property.” It called for issues concerning Abyei to be addressed through diplomatic channels.

Sudan’s military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have been fighting since April 2023, devastating large parts of the country and threatening stability along its borders.

Ngor said the strike hit around 11 a.m. Monday. He said the fuel depot supplied local businesses.

“It is a horrible and shocking situation,” he said.

MSF called on all parties to stop attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, expressing concern about people’s ability to safely reach healthcare and other essential services.

Amiet Market is a trading hub serving the Ngok Dinka and Misseriya communities.

The oil-rich Abyei region’s status was left unresolved by a 2005 peace agreement that ended decades of civil war, and it remained unsettled when South Sudan became independent in 2011. A proposed referendum stalled over disagreements about who could vote.

The region’s majority Ngok Dinka population favors joining South Sudan, while Misseriya nomads who use its pastures favor Sudan. Abyei has also experienced deadly communal violence, including fighting over land between Ngok Dinka and neighboring Twic Dinka communities.

World.title: As climate summit approaches, UN reports existing 1.5C warming limit is no longer achievable
World.content:
A UN climate report released Wednesday finds the globe will unavoidably slip past the Paris Climate Agreement’s 1.5-degree Celsius warming target in the next few years. The task now, the report states, is to make the period of warming “overshoot” as limited as possible, eventually bringing global average temperatures back down.

The annual UN Emissions Gap report is designed to inform decision makers headed into the next round of global climate talks in Turkey, known as COP31, next month. While past gap reports have expressed skepticism about meeting the 1.5-degree target, this one marks the first time that its authors have pronounced that missing the mark will be “imminent and unavoidable.”

“We are now saying this window has closed, but we can open it again by making the overshoot as brief as possible,” UN Environment Program Executive Director Inger Andersen said on a call with reporters. “This is about how to find a way back as shortly and as quickly as possible with as limited an overshoot as possible.”

Past reports have examined the distance between countries’ emissions reduction commitments and what it would take to limit global warming to 1.5 C above preindustrial levels.

However, this year’s report redefines the gap. Instead, it examines new emissions overshoot scenarios, and what it would take to limit peak warming to just 1.7 to 1.8 degrees C before bringing temperatures back down to 1.5 C through emissions cuts and the use of carbon removal technologies.

The report makes clear that every additional fraction of a degree of warming above 1.5 C “raises the risk of irreversible changes including in ice sheets, permafrost carbon, ocean circulation, and coral systems, along with devastating human impacts.”

Each added fraction of a degree of warming can have an “immense” impact “as measured in terms of damage, cost and loss of lives,” said climate scientist Michael Mann of the University of Pennsylvania. Mann was not involved in producing the UNEP report.

The LPG and chemical tanker Bertolle sails through the Bosporus in Istanbul, Turkey, on Wednesday, Oct. 7. Emrah Gurel/AP

No upbeat scenario for overshoot

According to the UNEP, which is based in Nairobi, the lowest overshoot scenario would keep peak warming to between 1.7 and 1.8 degrees C and return global average temperatures to at or below 1.5 C by 2100.

However, to follow such a pathway, global greenhouse gas emissions would need to be slashed by far more than anything currently on the table at the upcoming COP31 talks. This would require an 18% cut by 2030, 45% by 2035, and 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels.

Meeting this lowest-possible overshoot scenario would require a tripling of renewable electricity capacity by 2035, and dramatic cuts to fossil fuels, including the phaseout of coal by 2040, the report states.

In addition, there would need to be a major scaling up of carbon removal technologies, which so far have not been proven to work at such a large scale.

In stark contrast to these figures, the fulfillment of existing emissions reduction pledges would only yield a 5-to-8% emissions cut by 2030 and an 11-to-15% reduction by 2035, the report found. This would be associated with a peak warming of about 2.6 degrees C.

If countries simply follow their current policies, then warming could reach a peak of about 2.8 C. That estimate has increased since last year, in part because of the withdrawal of the United States from the Paris Agreement and retraction of its emissions reduction commitments, the report states.

Even the scenario that assumes countries meet their existing reduction commitments, and nations with net-zero pledges succeed in fulfilling them, still brings warming to a peak of 2.1 C.

Children look out of a window as a gas flare burns at the Cardon refinery in Punta Cardon, Venezuela, May 6. Gaby Oraa/Reuters/File

The bottom line

Clearly, overshooting 1.5 degrees C by the most limited amount possible and then coaxing temperatures back down over time is a tall order compared to what countries have pledged to do so far.

“Without urgent action, the lowest possible 1.5 C overshoot pathway will quickly fade,” the report warns. “Every five years of CO2 emissions at current levels pushes peak warming up by around 0.1 C.”

Mann said an additional 0.1 C of global warming “Permanently cuts global GDP by roughly 1.2% (over $1.2 trillion annually) and pushes approximately 140 million more people into life-threatening, dangerously hot climates.”

Overshooting the 1.5-degree target can be viewed as a milestone, but it doesn’t mean an absolute failure of climate science and policy, according to climate scientist Kate Marvel of Project Drawdown, a climate research and solutions nonprofit. Marvel was not involved in the UNEP report.

“There’s nothing special about any given temperature threshold,” she said. “The right unit isn’t degrees, it’s tons — of carbon dioxide, methane and other greenhouse gases. If we want to avoid the worst impacts, our task is and has always been to reduce these emissions as quickly as possible.”

“Passing 1.5 degrees is a sign that we’re not moving fast enough, but it doesn’t mean we’re doomed,” she said.

World.title: The anti-AI writing police are everywhere. What are they looking for?
World.content:
On October 6, the Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza won the Caine Prize for African Writing, for the short story “The Blue Fighter.” Less than a week later, The Atlantic published a piece declaring that the story’s narrator “has all the personality of a chatbot.”

“The AI detector Pangram flags almost the entire story as AI-generated,” the article reported.

Kundizeza denied that he had used any such technology. “For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote ‘The Blue Fighter.’ I did not use generative AI to write it. It is entirely my own work,” he wrote in a statement on X.

The Caine Prize, which comes with a £10,000 award, had become the newest front in a war engulfing the literary world, powered by AI writing tools and AI writing detectors.

Scandals about suspected AI use have spread up and down the writing industry this year. In March, the publisher Hachette canceled the US release of author Mia Ballard’s self-published 2025 novel “Shy Girl” after a New York Times report found that it may have been written using AI.

In May, a Trinidadian author named Jamir Nazir was accused of using AI to write “The Serpent in the Grove,” which won the Commonwealth Short Story Prize.

In July, researchers at Stony Brook University posited that H.M. Wolfe’s “Daggermouth,” a national bestseller, was 60% AI-written according to a data set shared with The Atlantic.

More accusations kept flying: debut author Jerry Falade lost a $2 million book deal in July after his agents pulled his debut novel over suspicions he had used AI writing tools. In September, a claim that a book by Haitian Canadian author Thélyson Orélien had failed an AI detection test led the jury for the prestigious Goncourt prize to remove him from its longlist.

Haitian Canadian novelist Thélyson Orélien was accused of using AI to help him write a story earlier this year. Joel Saget/AFP/Getty Images

As generative AI proliferates, it’s easier than ever for an author, or someone who wants to be seen as an author, to come up with a story- or book-shaped piece of text. It’s harder than ever for a reader or a prize judge or a publisher to be sure that the words on a page were produced by human thought and effort, rather than a machine prompt.

The result is a literary version of the ruined world in the movie “Blade Runner.” Anxiety and suspicion about robot infiltrators are everywhere — and so are people claiming to hunt the robots down.

Multiple companies now offer products that promise to spot the difference, with often contradictory, biased or erratic results. The makers of Pangram, an AI detection platform that has been cited as authoritative in many of the recent controversies, claim it can distinguish between human and synthetic writing with near-perfect accuracy.

“We’re trying to mitigate some of the harms that come from these powerful AI models,” said Max Spero, the CEO and founder of Pangram.

Spero is quick to admit that he doesn’t have a background in literature or creative writing. He is a machine learning engineer by trade, and worked as a software engineer at Google and an autonomous vehicle startup called Nuro before founding Pangram in 2023.

“I’m an avid reader. I’ve never been a writer. I haven’t lived in that world,” Spero said.

Nevertheless, Spero presents Pangram as a protector of the magazines and journals that make up the literary ecosystem.

“A lot of these outlets are getting flooded with submissions because they pay writers they publish and don’t charge anything to send in your work,” Spero said. “There are these perverse incentives that come from AI making it nearly free. Our goal is to help reduce the friction on the defensive side to help people understand what’s AI and what’s not.”

What does a robot sound like?

Pangram caught widespread public attention in May, after the Commonwealth Foundation announced that Nazir’s “The Serpent in the Grove” was among the winners of its competition.

The story was ornately written, with figurative language that struck some readers as extravagant or peculiar: “Hard living lays itself on a man like wet sacking; it never asks permission. His eyes narrowed against the glare outside and the darker glare inside him: old promises that never ripened, the ache where hope should live, a gnawing sense that land can own a man while making him swear the land belongs to him.”

But many people declared they saw telltale tics of chatbot writing. A folklore has quickly grown up around generative AI prose, describing various shibboleths that are supposed to betray the robot voice.

One early AI panic revolved around the alleged overuse of em-dashes — an especially funny notion to the many magazine journalists who’d been using them for in-sentence digressions for years — while other people swear the giveaways are “It’s not X, but Y,” grandiose descriptions like “load-bearing,” or lists of three things.

The reason such devices show up in AI writing, though, is that they were already in common usage among the legions of human writers whose work AI companies ingested to train their systems.

“AI slop is sort of indistinguishable from human-written slop because the AI is trained on bad writing,” said the author Patrick Nathan. “The reason AI writes badly is because the vast majority of writing is bad.”

To back up their confidence that something was wrong with the style of the story, then, the people accusing Nazir of using AI also appealed to Pangram numbers.

“Pangram flags at 100% but also, come on, if you know you know,” Ethan Mollick, a professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, wrote on Bluesky. Others posted screenshots of the story’s Pangram results like trophies.

It’s not lost on the writing community that some of the most gleeful AI hunters, like the tools they use, come from the tech sector, not from among their own ranks. Readers trying to understand what was going on with “The Serpent in the Grove” could encounter Nabeel S. Qureshi, a former engineer at Palantir, posting on X about “the ‘hums’ trope, and plenty of other obvious markers of AI writing.”

Suspicious patterns of suspicion

There’s also the glaring question of whose work gets fed into Pangram for investigation, and why. The originally anonymous accusation against Orélien was made by Samuel Fitoussi, a conservative French newspaper columnist at Le Figaro and the author of the book “Woke Fiction.” Many of the major scandals were also centered on nonwhite writers; Nazir is of South Asian descent, while Ballard, Wolfe, Falade, Kundizeza and Orélien are Black.

The conservative columnist Samuel Fitoussi revealed that he had accused Orélien of writing using AI tools on social media. Benjamin de Diesbach/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images

“Part of this has to do with a broader anti-woke and anti-Black tenor in a lot of conservative and right-leaning online discourse,” said Doyle D. Calhoun, a professor of postcolonial studies at the University of Cambridge.

Calhoun said that for decades the literary establishment was made up mostly of white men. Now that those demographics are changing and there are more non-white authors getting book deals and winning awards, there’s an emerging resentment, especially on social media.

“Once these accusations — many of them sort of unverified or unfounded — are out there, the internet media ecosystem just goes into sort of overdrive,” he said. Historically, these sorts of claims also tend not to “stick” to white writers in the same way they do with non-white writers, Calhoun said.

Spero said that Pangram is calibrated to call something AI-assisted only if the tool is extremely confident in its analysis.

The company’s own estimates claim that false positives — in which the tool wrongly reports that a piece of human writing was created — are 1 in 10,000 and shrinking. Peer-reviewed studies from the University of Chicago and the University of Brussels support that claim, though one 2025 study from the University of Maryland found that Pangram erroneously labeled 2% of documents as AI.

A widely referenced 2023 Stanford study that found AI writing detectors produced higher rates of false positives on writing from non-native English speakers was conducted before Pangram was created. Pangram ran an internal study using a database of non-native English texts and self-reported that false positive rate was around 8 in 10,000.

How do you prove you’re not a machine?

Prior to the emergence of AI writing tools, the cardinal sin of writing was plagiarism. But plagiarism requires two different parties and a measurable accusation. When one author steals another’s words, everyone can judge whether that’s actually the case or not. It’s not that simple with AI writing.

Publishing houses are twitchy about putting out potentially AI-written books and authors are tense about being accused of using AI to write lest they be asked to share their drafts and version history with the entire internet. Social networks are so inundated with AI writing —both real and imagined — that LinkedIn has installed a new post reaction option: “Looks like AI slop.”

Given the thousands upon thousands of pieces of writing published each day, a 1 in 10,000 chance of a false accusation — let alone an 8 in 10,000 chance — means that even the most trusted AI detector is going to be wrong, and wrong about a lot of people.

Pangram isn’t able to tell users the truth about someone’s writing, but it is able to introduce something much more complicated: doubt.

Unless an accused writer confesses to using an LLM, there is no bulletproof way to prove an accusation, short of being given full access to someone’s computer history and finding the chatbot prompts.

The Caine Prize judges said that they would using a “human centered approach” to determine the provenance of Kundieza’s story. Ellah Wakatama, chair of the Caine Prize’s board of trustees, told the BBC that the writer would send his draft history to the organization for review.

While draft version histories are not sacred texts, being asked to share them in exchange for exoneration does introduce some thorny social questions about how much writers need to show an audience — or accuser — in order to be trusted.

And once an accusation is made, there’s no consensus about what evidence would be sufficient to clear an author’s name. When Bryan Armen Graham, a sports editor at The Guardian, was accused of using AI to help him write articles, the publication called the allegations “preposterous.” That didn’t stop several others, including some journalists, from siding with the Pangram results over the word of a colleague.

Either way, a machine wins

To some people and institutions on the literary side, using automated AI writing detectors to fight the influx of AI writing is just trading one form of technological domination for another.

Pangram has entered the public consciousness at a time of distrust that goes beyond writing. “All of this is happening in a larger milieu of bullshit,” said John Warner, the author of “More Than Words: How to Think About Writing in the Age of AI.”

Readers, writers, and publishers are all anxious about AI writing and what AI detectors are doing to the industry. Aaron Ufumeli/AP

The ability to dam at least some of the daily overflow of misinformation and misrepresentation is one of the reasons for Pangram’s success and adoption, but Warner said that comes at a cost.

“Like all other technology of automation, that is going to de-skill people from discerning these things for themselves,” he said.

The Commonwealth Foundation conducted a review of the work of Nazir and the other nominees, but it chose not to use Pangram or other AI detection software in the process.

“Because the tools aren’t conclusive the jury is still out as to how much they can be relied upon,” Razmi Farook, director general of the Commonwealth Foundation, said. “For us, we didn’t want to rely on a singular indicator. We believe the fairest approach is to consider multiple sources of evidence.”

Those sources, Farook said, included the original reading and judging process, along with “supporting documentation” of the writers’ “creative processes, including working drafts, notes, and other relevant materials.” There were also lengthy discussions with each author about how their stories came together. Snippets of those conversations were included in a video promoting the award.

The foundation concluded that none of the writers, including Nazir, had used AI tools to write their stories. But the literary magazine Granta, which had published the story as part of an agreement with the Commonwealth Foundation, canceled its relationship for future competitions. Sigrid Rausing, Granta’s publisher, said in a statement that the magazine fed Nazir’s story into Claude as a way of gauging whether it was written with AI. “The response was long, concluding that it was ‘almost certainly not produced unaided by a human,’” wrote Rausing. (Claude is not designed to detect AI writing.)

The statement from Granta was far from conclusive, though, and it summed up the anxious ambivalence that many authors and readers are feeling in the AI age. “It may be that the judges have now awarded a prize to an instance of AI plagiarism — we don’t yet know, and perhaps we never will know,” Rausing wrote. “There is, however, a certain irony in the fact that beyond human hunches AI itself is the most efficient tool we have for revealing what is AI generated.”

Spero was unconvinced by the foundation’s investigation, but offered to take down a case study posted to the Pangram website if they shared the results and he was satisfied with the process. The foundation refused, citing legal and privacy issues. Farook said, however, that her team has asked Pangram for their input on how to secure the award process next year.

World.title: Who will be Egypt’s next president?
World.content:
No one can easily predict who will govern Egypt—no matter how clear the warning signs or preliminary conditions may seem.

Gamal Abdel Nasser emerged literally out of nowhere to dismantle the centuries-old monarchy of the Muhammad Ali dynasty.

Following Nasser, Anwar Sadat stepped out from the ranks of the Free Officers Movement to take the helm—a succession virtually no one had anticipated.

Sadat was the least flashy figure among his peers, a man hidden deep in the shadows who deliberately feigned passivity and deference until fate thrust him to the pinnacle of power.

Years later, from the commanders of the October 1973 War, Sadat selected Air Vice-Marshal Hosni Mubarak as his Vice President. Mubarak was neither the most prominent nor the highest-ranking officer in the military command chain, nor did he seek such a role; his highest personal ambition was to serve as ambassador to London or governor of Ismailia.

In a historical irony, Mohamed Morsi of the Muslim Brotherhood ascended to the presidency for a brief year, bypassing the group’s paramount figure, Khairat al-Shater, as well as its most prominent and influential leaders within the Guidance Bureau.

And most recently, General Abdel Fattah al-Sisi rose from the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces to the presidency, despite being neither the oldest nor the most visible member of the military leadership.

Each president came to power through a unique set of circumstances.

Viewed from within their own narrative and the sequence of events as they saw them, their rise might seem logical, structured, or even inevitable.

Yet, when observed from the outside, each of them arrived unexpectedly, one way or another.

History has documented the names of dozens of kings, presidents, caliphs, governors, and sultans who have ruled Egypt from Narmer (Mena) down to the present day. Some held power multiple times, such as Al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun; others inherited the throne as children, like Tutankhamun; and some were even crowned as mere infants, as occurred during the Mamluk era.

Throughout Egypt’s long history, the leader has almost always been a matter of preordained fate rather than popular choice—with only rare exceptions scattered across the historical record.

President Sisi’s insistence on stepping down at the end of his current term has opened the floodgates to speculation, questions, and expectations regarding potential succession scenarios.

Likewise, his reference to a carefully selected elite that will undergo specialized training programs has sparked even greater debate than his sincere and firm pledge to leave office at the conclusion of his term in 2030.

This raises a fundamental question: Should the next president be a public choice emerging from among several figures shaped by public life—individuals evaluated and scrutinized by the people through their long-standing positions, statements, and vision for national affairs over the years, or during pivotal defining moments?

Or should President Sisi engineer a selection mechanism that presents the public with a candidate possessing specific qualifications, drawn from a defined elite, and tailored to fit a precise mold?

Today, after all these years, President Sisi’s vision and underlying philosophy are clearly decipherable.

The President seeks to hand over power to a trusted successor—defined strictly by his own standards. Many believe he is prioritizing his personal definition of trust and stewardship over the public’s fundamental right to freely choose their leader and future path.

After all, history has shown that given the choice, the electorate once brought the Muslim Brotherhood to power; had Hazem Salah Abu Ismail not been disqualified, he might well have taken the helm of Egypt.

Despite lingering skepticism surrounding the mechanism for selecting the fifty candidates the President announced to prepare for the upcoming era, a swarm of critical questions remains.

These range from demographic balances—male to female, Muslim to Christian, military to civilian, technocrats to politicians—to the debate over drawing candidates with genuine public policy experience versus plucking individuals from complete obscurity simply because they hold a PhD, even if their dissertations were on pre-Islamic poetry or shade gardening – with all due respect to every academic discipline.

Furthermore, should the President appoint one or more vice presidents following the selection of the fifty candidates, what would their prospects be moving forward?

And what if unforeseen circumstances abruptly forge a leader from entirely outside those designated ranks?

Does such a committee possess constitutional grounding backed by logic, rigor, empirical precedent, and established political practice across different regimes?

Or will it remain a mere proposal, destined to erode with time and shifting realities?

Such advanced institutions may well serve to train capable cadres for ministerial duties and senior state roles.

Yet, can the presidency—with all its unique aura, strategic imperatives, and grave demands—be subjected to a pre-programmed filtering mechanism? One designed by current figures whose own convictions, views, and biases will inevitably dictate who is brought close and who is sidelined?

To be sure, several nations feature covert circles that shape leaders and presidents. Chief among them is the US, with its secretive and ideological networks that have successfully propelled their members to the presidency and beyond.

Other nations groom future leaders within political parties and public life; some refine them behind the scenes of military and security establishments, while others draw them from ruling dynasties, the educated elite, or affluent classes.

Amid all these critical questions, one must acknowledge and commend President Sisi’s decisive commitment to a peaceful transfer of power, as well as his genuine concern for the nation’s destiny and his resolve to ensure that the best possible successor assumes this duty.

So I return to where I began: throughout history, the one who comes to govern Egypt is, more often than not, someone who emerges entirely beyond expectations.

Author’s biography:

Ahmed al-Doreiny is a prominent Egyptian journalist, author, television presenter, and documentary filmmaker.

World.title: Agriculture Minister: “Egypt Forum” showcases state’s vision for next 3 years with participation of all segments of society
World.content:
Minister of Agriculture and Land Reclamation Alaa Farouk emphasized the importance of the “Egypt 2026 Forum” in showcasing the Egyptian state’s vision for the next three years, noting that the forum witnesses wide participation from various segments of society, political parties and decision-makers.

In a statement on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, Farouk stated that the forum reflects the Egyptian state’s keenness on societal participation and opening spaces between the government, the people, experts and specialists regarding public policies, national projects and development programs implemented over past years and their impact on improving citizens’ lives.

He added that the file of food security and rural development comes at the forefront of the Egyptian state’s priorities, contributing to turning challenges into promising opportunities.

He pointed out that the Egyptian state has adopted an integrated reform and executive path that balances giant horizontal expansion for land reclamation with vertical expansion based on scientific research and digital transformation, aiming to maximize added value, achieve self-sufficiency, narrow the import gap and provide safe food for citizens at affordable prices.

Farouk explained that the agricultural sector witnessed a radical transformation driven by the state’s vision towards horizontal land reclamation and the rational management of water resources.

The state implemented a package of the largest land reclamation projects in its history, which increased the agricultural area and doubled production. These include the New Delta project with an area of 2.2 million feddans, the Toshka project with an area of 1.1 million feddans, the North and Central Sinai Development project covering about 456,000 feddans, the New Egyptian Rural Development project spanning 1.5 million feddans, and projects in South Upper Egypt and the New Valley covering 650,000 feddans, he said.

Farouk noted that the state has taken numerous proactive measures to support urban development, particularly the agricultural sector, to secure the food and agricultural product needs of the great people of Egypt during periods when many countries—including developed ones—failed to achieve this goal and some even imposed restrictive policies on their agricultural exports.

He stressed that at a time when the world was losing millions of hectares annually due to desertification, soil degradation, drought and unfavorable climate change, the Egyptian state managed to add more agricultural land through reclaiming over 3.5 million feddans of desert.

World.title: Egypt seeks to accelerate oil, gas investments
World.content:
Minister of Petroleum and Mineral Resources Karim Badawi met with Cypriot Energy Minister Michael Damianos, East Mediterranean Gas Forum Secretary-General Osama Mobarez and executives of international oil and gas companies operating in Egypt to discuss ways to accelerate investment and increase production.

The meeting took place during a roundtable titled “The Future of Energy in Egypt,” held on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, as part of the Mediterranean Offshore Conference and Exhibition (MOC).

Discussions focused on accelerating the development of discoveries and connecting them to existing infrastructure, maximizing the economic returns from oil and gas resources, strengthening regional cooperation and consolidating Egypt’s position as a regional hub for energy trading and trade.

Badawi said partnerships with investors were based on mutual interests, stressing that the success of companies operating in Egypt translates into success for the country’s oil and gas sector and the Egyptian state.

He affirmed the ministry’s commitment to addressing challenges facing its partners and providing the necessary conditions for expanding investments to generate sustainable economic returns for all parties.

The minister said declining production had been one of the sector’s most significant challenges, requiring efforts to stimulate investment, accelerate exploration and development activities and improve operational efficiency. He stressed that the ministry was focused on strengthening cooperation with partners, addressing factors affecting production and establishing more sustainable foundations for growth in the coming years.

Badawi added that the current phase required more effective partnerships through direct dialogue with companies to identify their needs and proposals, determine measures to accelerate investment decisions and project implementation and enhance the competitiveness of investment in Egypt’s oil and gas sector.

He also highlighted the importance of regional cooperation among Eastern Mediterranean countries and leveraging available resources and existing infrastructure to generate greater economic value from discovered gas reserves and support the development of new resources.

Egypt has significant advantages that position it to play an increasingly central role in the regional energy system, Badawi said, citing its advanced natural gas infrastructure, transportation networks, gas reception and trading facilities and liquefaction capabilities, as well as its strategic location linking production areas with consumer markets.

The ministry is looking to work with its partners to maximize the economic benefits of these assets and facilities, reducing project costs, improving efficiency and enhancing investment viability, he added.

For his part, Mobarez said Egypt’s energy future was closely linked to the future of regional cooperation, given the Eastern Mediterranean’s discovered natural gas resources and promising potential, which require increased investment and the development of infrastructure to unlock their value.

The main challenge, he said, lies in accessing these resources and converting them into sustainable economic value by developing viable projects, accelerating the development of discoveries and connecting them to target markets.

Achieving this requires clear regulatory frameworks and investment-friendly policies that enable the private sector to play an effective role in financing and implementing projects, as well as developing the infrastructure needed to transport gas to markets, Mobarez said.

He added that the East Mediterranean Gas Forum works to strengthen cooperation among governments, oil and gas companies, technology and services providers, financial institutions and regulatory authorities. Its efforts aim to identify priority projects, attract further investment and accelerate the implementation of infrastructure needed to maximize the use of the region’s resources.

Company executives and international partners said Egypt had significant competitive advantages that strengthened its ability to attract investment and reinforced its role in the regional energy sector. These included advanced infrastructure, transportation networks and gas facilities, its strategic geographical location, accumulated technical and technological expertise and the availability of data to support exploration activities and investment decisions.

Participants said these advantages offered promising opportunities to accelerate project implementation and maximize the use of resources in Egypt and the Eastern Mediterranean. They emphasized the importance of continuing to develop government-investor partnerships based on transparency, mutual trust and shared interests.

They also said the settlement of outstanding dues owed to companies had helped strengthen confidence in Egypt’s oil and gas investment climate and encouraged new investments to accelerate the development of discoveries and connect them to the national grid as quickly as possible, boosting production and maximizing economic returns.

Sustaining investment flows, participants stressed, requires a stable and predictable investment environment, clear and flexible regulatory frameworks, and long-term partnerships between the government and private sector. Such conditions would help companies make investment decisions more quickly and ensure projects are implemented according to target schedules.

They further noted that the true value of resources lies not merely in discovering them, but in the sector’s ability to develop, produce and market them efficiently. This requires flexible and innovative business models and the adoption of advanced technologies and artificial intelligence tools to improve operational efficiency, reduce costs and accelerate exploration, development and production.

The discussions underscored the importance of greater integration and cooperation among Eastern Mediterranean countries and companies operating in the region, alongside the development of regulatory and commercial frameworks and coordinated efforts to develop resources, provide infrastructure, transport gas and connect supplies to markets. These measures would support energy security, optimize the economic use of resources and strengthen prospects for sustainable development across the region.

The Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources said the roundtable reflected its commitment to deepening direct dialogue with investment partners and identifying practical solutions to the challenges facing the sector. The efforts aim to increase investment, accelerate resource development, raise production levels, maximize the use of Egypt’s infrastructure and consolidate the country’s position as a regional hub for energy trading and trade.

World.title: Egyptian Navy celebrates 59th anniversary commemorating sinking “Eilat” destroyer
World.content:
The Egyptian Navy celebrated its 59th anniversary, commemorating October 21, 1967, the day Egyptian naval forces changed the concepts of naval warfare worldwide by successfully sinking the Israeli destroyer Eilat off the coast of the city of Port Said.

Speaking at a press conference on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, held to mark the occasion, Commander of the Egyptian Navy Lieutenant General Mahmoud Adel Fawzy affirmed that this historic anniversary serves as an inspiration and a driving force for building the future.

He noted that the Navy continues to implement its development and modernization plans in accordance with the strategic vision of the political leadership and the General Command of the Armed Forces. These efforts aim to strengthen combat capabilities, localize armament and naval shipbuilding and enhance the training and qualification of combat personnel, enabling the Navy to carry out all missions assigned to it across the country’s various strategic directions.

World.title: Liberia: Mo Ali Challenges Grand Gedeh University Graduates
World.content:
Mr. Mo Ali, Managing Director of the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation

Zwedru City, Grand Gedeh County — In a stirring commencement address during Grand Gedeh University’s historic convocation over the weekend, Mo Ali, Managing Director of the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation (LWSC), challenged both public officials and the graduates to measure leadership by outcomes rather than titles or ceremony.

By Franklin Doloquee From Zwedru City, Grand Gedeh

Speaking before a crowd of graduates, faculty, local officials, educators, government officials and community residents, Ali said appointments and honorifics are only the beginning.



He said real achievement is demonstrated by the tangible improvements leaders produce for ordinary citizens.

Colorful banners bearing the university seal fluttered in a warm breeze while applause rose and fell as his remarks underscored the convocation’s theme: “Accountability Is the Test of Leadership.”

‘Power must produce results’

Ali told the assembly, urging officials at every level to hold themselves to higher standards.

He described the too-common celebration of appointments — public congratulations, photographs and social media fanfare — as premature if they are not followed by measurable gains in service delivery.

“When someone is appointed to lead an institution, the appointment is not the achievement. The achievement is what that person accomplishes with the responsibility entrusted to them,” the LWSC boss stated.

He illustrated his point with concrete examples. For families who wait each day for clean water, an impressive title means little if taps remain dry.

For communities suffering from poor sanitation, a decorated office or an official vehicle offers no relief.

“A minister should be assessed not simply by meetings attended, but by policies implemented and improvements achieved,” he said, adding that legislators should be evaluated on the quality of representation, lawmaking and oversight, and public managers by how well their institutions perform.

He acknowledged that public institutions often operate under severe resource constraints, from tight budgets to aging infrastructure.

Yet he insisted those obstacles should spur creativity and discipline rather than provide perpetual excuses for inaction.

“Leadership is not the absence of difficulties. It is the responsibility to confront them and demonstrate progress,” Ali intimated, his voice steady as he paced a short stage set against the silhouette of the university’s main building.

Addressing the graduates directly, Ali urged them to be problem-solvers, innovators, entrepreneurs and professionals committed to serving their communities.

He reminded them that change does not require national fame. Small, local improvements a successful shop that provides jobs, a better-stocked clinic, a repaired school roof, or a community-led sanitation drive transform lives even if they do not make headlines.

“You do not have to wait until you become nationally prominent before contributing to Grand Gedeh,” he asserted.

Ali also counseled the new graduates on the nature of public life and the temporary privileges of office.

In a section he titled: “The Day Nobody Calls You ‘Honorable,’” he reminded them that official recognition and attention ebb over time.

“The official vehicle may be returned. The telephone may stop ringing.

The invitations may become fewer,” he said.

Rather than mourn this normal change, Ali suggested officials and citizens alike should focus on the substance of their work and the legacy of service they leave behind.

The convocation included several other speakers who echoed calls for accountability and community engagement, and the ceremony featured traditional music, student presentations, and the presentation of diplomas to hundreds of graduates who celebrated with relatives and friends.

In conversations after the ceremony, many attendees expressed optimism that the university’s new alumni, equipped with fresh skills and energy, will play active roles in improving local health care, education, water access, and small business growth across Grand Gedeh County.

Ali closed his remarks by challenging both officials and citizens to keep asking pragmatic questions about leadership: Will services become more reliable? Will public resources be managed responsibly? Will projects be completed on time and to standard? He said those questions should guide public assessment of leaders and serve as the yardstick for progress.

As graduates dispersed into the late afternoon heat, the convocation left a clear message: authority is not valuable for its own sake; it’s worth is proven by the concrete benefits it brings to people’s daily lives.

Thousands Turn Out to Celebrate Graduates at Historic Commencement Ceremony

Thousands of graduates, family members and well-wishers including many Liberians packed the grounds to celebrate the University of Grand Gedeh’s historic commencement ceremony.

The atmosphere was jubilant and colorful as crowds gathered to honor the students who received the university’s final batch of associate degrees before the institution transitions to full university status.

The eighth and final associate-degree commencement drew huge numbers from across the region.

Graduates marched in rows, their gowns and caps fluttering in the breeze, while proud parents, siblings and friends cheered from shaded stands and along the walkways.

Vendors moved through the crowds selling cold drinks, snacks and flowers and the air filled with congratulatory shouts, camera clicks and the low hum of excited conversation.

For many of the graduates, the ceremony was more than a formal rite of passage it represented hope and a tangible step toward improved opportunities.

Several graduates described the degree as a “big boost” for their futures, saying it will strengthen their chances for employment, further study, and community leadership.

One graduate embraced relatives and wiped away tears of joy, while others posed for photographs, their faces beaming with relief and pride.

Speakers at the event emphasized the milestone significance of this graduating class.

University officials lauded the students’ perseverance and dedication, noting the institution’s achievement in becoming a full degree-granting university. Government and community leaders who attended the program highlighted the positive impact the university’s upgrade will have on local education, job creation, and regional development.

The ceremony blended formal protocol with vibrant local culture. Traditional music and dances punctuated the program, and speakers often paused for rounds of applause and cheers. Guests waved national and university flags as the graduates processed; colorful fabrics and patterned attire added to the festive scene.

Organizers took care to ensure the event ran smoothly. Ushers guided guests, security personnel maintained order, and medical staff were on hand for any emergencies. Despite the large turnout, volunteers and staff coordinated seating, the diploma distribution, and the procession with practiced efficiency.

As the ceremony closed, many graduates lingered on the grounds, exchanging congratulations and making plans for the future. For the university and its community, the day marked both an ending and a beginning: a celebration of achievement and a hopeful look ahead now that the institution has attained full university status.

World.title: Liberian Senate’s Own Papers Bury Its Denial
World.content:
MONROVIA – On Monday, the Liberian Senate under the leadership of Pro Temp Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence, called FrontPageAfrica’s reporting on a staff salary plan “false,” “misleading” and “fabricated,” and demanded a retraction. What the Senate did not do is more telling. It did not dispute a single figure, did not challenge the authenticity of a single page, and did not say the plan does not exist.

By Rodney D. Sieh

It could not. The plan is on Senate letterhead.



What the documents say

On October 7, 2026, the Senate Committee on Rules, Order and Administration signed a “Proposal for the Standardization of Remuneration for Civil Servants and Personal Staffers of the Senate.” Six of the seven committee members signed it, including Chairman J. Gbleh-bo Brown of Maryland County and Vice-Chairman Johnathan B. Sogbe. On October 12, Senator Brown sent it to President Pro Tempore Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence. He asked for leadership’s endorsement and for the plan to be included in the Fiscal Year 2027 budget.

The numbers are the committee’s own:

* The Legal Counsel’s monthly pay rises from US$1,704 to US$2,920, an increase of US$1,216, or 71 percent.

* The HR Director rises from US$1,500 to US$2,000, and the Deputy Legal Counsel from US$1,500 to US$1,991.

* Senators’ chiefs of office staff rise from US$1,021 to US$1,500.

* The total annual cost is US$792,552. The covered payroll grows from US$1,830,648 to US$2,623,200, an increase of 43 percent.

The committee’s final recommendation asks the Senate leadership and plenary to approve US$792,552 for the 2027 budget. That is not a rumor. It is a funding request.

A denial that answers a different question

The Senate’s statement rests on one claim: the plenary never voted. That is true, and it is beside the point.

A proposal that six senators have signed, that the Pro Tempore commissioned, and that is formally headed for the national budget is news. Proposals are exactly when the public should hear about them, before the money is spent rather than after.

The statement also confirms the most important fact. It says the review was “mandated by the President Pro Tempore.” By the Senate’s own account, this plan began in the Pro Tempore’s office.

The fine print the statement leaves out

The statement describes the plan as a review “across the three branches of Government.” The documents cover only Senate staff. The other branches appear only as benchmarks for raising Senate pay.

The statement says the plan has not been “acted upon.” Yet section 2.0 of the committee’s report, titled “What Has Been Accomplished,” says the committee “has completed” standardizing fuel and gas benefits for directors, deputy directors, assistant directors, secretaries, drivers and other staff. The Senate should explain whether those benefits are already being paid.

The statement also accuses this newspaper of failing to verify the facts “through the Senate official spokesperson.” The verification is the documents themselves: the Senate’s letterhead, its committee’s signatures and its own arithmetic.

“Harmony” for whom?

The committee says the 2019 National Remuneration and Standardization Act requires the plan. It quotes the Act’s goal of narrowing “the inequality gap in government.” The tables point the other way.

The Legal Counsel’s raise alone, US$1,216 a month, is larger than the entire current salary of nine of the twelve central administration positions listed. At the bottom of the scale, the Executive Secretary gets US$96.

Today the Legal Counsel earns about three times as much as the Executive Secretary. Under the proposal, that would rise to about four and a half times. In dollar terms, the gap between them nearly doubles, from US$1,153 to US$2,273 a month.

A plan written to narrow inequality would widen it.

The comparison the Senate calls “emotional”

The Senate objects to comparisons with the national minimum wage and calls them “emotional.” They are arithmetic. Labour Minister Cooper W. Kruah has reminded employers that Liberia’s Decent Work Act sets a minimum monthly wage of US$143, and he has warned firms caught paying less.

The proposed raise for the Legal Counsel is roughly eight and a half times that minimum wage. The proposed salary is about twenty times it. That is not the language of emotion. It is the reality of a country where many families decide daily between food, school fees and medicine.

The staff have a case, and that is not the issue

Fairness requires saying this clearly: many Senate employees are underpaid, and their complaints are real. In December, staff spokesperson Roosevelt Tulay told reporters there had been no salary increment for Senate staff since 2015. He pointed out that the Senate’s own budget had grown from US$14.6 million to a proposed US$16.4 million for Fiscal Year 2026, while staff salaries stayed flat, and he warned of civil disobedience.

A serious reform would start at the bottom, with the clerks, secretaries and drivers. This plan gives its biggest dollars to the top. And the Senate’s answer to public scrutiny has been to call accurate reporting “fabricated.”

What the Senate should do

If the Senate believes the plan is sound, it should defend it in public. It should publish the full proposal and the attached spreadsheet, explain the 71 percent raise for its Legal Counsel, disclose whether the fuel benefits are already being paid, and commit to a recorded plenary vote.

What it should not do is demand that a newspaper retract a story built on the Senate’s own signed pages. FrontPageAfrica stands by its reporting.
