World.title: Africa: Africa Needs More Than Envoys to Secure the Red Sea
World.content:
analysis

The Horn's proliferating diplomatic appointments have done little to bolster African influence amid new Middle Eastern alliances.

In September, Ansarullah (the Houthis) took control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, shattering the assumption that the insurgency was confined to northern Yemen. The group is now at the epicentre of the Middle East conflict and is the channel through which crises flow between the Horn of Africa and the Middle East.

Countries on either side of the Red Sea have responded asymmetrically to this shared shock. The Horn has dispatched more envoys while Middle Eastern countries, led by Saudi Arabia, are strengthening political institutions and hardwiring them with military deals. These include the newly signed Mecca Joint Defence Agreement (MJDA) and the politically oriented 14-member Multinational Maritime Defense Coalition (MMDC).



Although the Red Sea has a history of instability, current upheavals are distinct. Ansarullah is not only at war with the Saudi Arabia-backed Yemeni government, but is linked to the Israel-Hamas conflict, the Israel-United States war with Iran, and escalating conflicts in the Horn. These interwoven crises require equally interlinked responses from both shores of the Red Sea.

Red Sea and bordering countries

The assertion by Iran, commentators and Ansarullah itself that its conflict is solely with Saudi Arabia is untenable. Iran's strategy of hedging its bets across the Middle East has enabled Ansarullah to evolve from an ally targeting Yemen's government into a self-tasking surrogate whose operations also serve Iran's interests. Having cultivated Ansarullah, Iran did not need to act on its earlier threat to close Bab al-Mandab.

Ansarullah's deepening ties with al-Shabaab have helped transform the Yemeni group from a transnational criminal actor involved in smuggling and illicit financial activity into a force choking a Red Sea gateway carrying nearly 15% of global trade. The two Islamist groups now run a corridor of instability, migration and economic disruption from Tehran to Nairobi and Kampala.

The Horn of Africa's four biggest conflict hotspots - Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia and Ethiopia - have become intertwined with Middle Eastern crises. Although conflicts on both sides of the Red Sea stem from local grievances, Middle Eastern actors are the main drivers of conflict in the Horn. The United Arab Emirates (UAE) alone is entangled with Ethiopia, Somalia, and Sudan and has multi-purpose investments in every country in the Horn.

In the past, the Horn's Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) and the League of Arab States coordinated over Somalia's crisis and conflict resolution in Sudan. But countries on either side of the Red Sea are now using markedly different tools to address their shared challenges.

In March, the AU designated former Tanzanian president Jakaya Kikwete as its High Representative for the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea. Kikwete, who opted to focus on South Sudan, joined a crowded field of IGAD envoys already deployed in the Horn - covering Somalia, Sudan and South Sudan. Others include the Special Envoy for the Red Sea and Maritime Affairs, and the AU High Representative for Sudan.

A corresponding bench of envoys from outside Africa also covers the Horn - from the UN, EU, China, Germany, Japan, France, Norway, United Kingdom, Netherlands and Switzerland. While each is responsible for a piece of the interconnected conflict resolution puzzle, this 'envoyflation' adds little leverage to individual portfolios or to the Horn's stability. Instead, Horn envoys and their external partners shuttle between capitals, with little progress to show.

Source: ISS based on open-source data

By contrast, Middle Eastern countries are moving away from institutions such as the Gulf Cooperation Council and Council of Arab and African Coastal States of the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, in favour of political-military frameworks. Although there are envoys in the region, they represent external powers, the United Nations (UN) and European Union (EU), not Middle Eastern countries.

The MMDC, established to safeguard freedom of navigation, was launched in Saudi Arabia on 30 July with members including Red Sea and non-Red Sea countries in Africa, the Arab world and Asia.

While it includes Djibouti, Somalia and Sudan, the exclusion of IGAD highlights the Horn's limited regional control over its coastline. This was already evident from Turkey's wardenship of Somalia's maritime defence, the UAE's port expansion in the region and numerous countries' military bases in Djibouti. Eritrea's absence from the MMDC reflects its rejection of military solutions to Yemen's conflict.

Days after launching the MMDC, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan unveiled the MJDA on 7 August. Conspicuously, it excludes Horn countries but includes non-Red Sea Pakistan and Turkey. On 5 October, Saudi Arabia conducted its first military operation against Ansarullah within the MJDA framework.

Both the MJDA and MMDC exclude landlocked Ethiopia and the UAE, which could weaken these frameworks. The exclusions reflect a political dispute over which countries qualify as Red Sea states - a debate that has undermined IGAD's Red Sea efforts. Eritrea's departure from IGAD in December 2025 further limits the organisation's diplomatic leverage over the coastline.

Ethiopia, meanwhile, wants access to the Red Sea but faces opposition from Eritrea and Egypt, a founding MMDC member. This conflates Nile water disputes with disputes over the definition of the Red Sea.

The Horn has military institutions that could help secure the Red Sea. The East Africa Standby Force and Eastern Africa Fusion and Liaison Unit could have complemented IGAD's efforts, but neither has a maritime focus. Consequently, African envoys are increasingly relegated to 'managing' inland conflicts, while their external counterparts are oriented towards the Red Sea.

Close 

Envoyflation reflects IGAD and the AU's political inertia and financial weakness. Envoys are appointed in temporary posts and rely on external donor funding. In the Horn, this has led to fragmented responses and the exclusion of African actors from conflict resolution efforts. Middle Eastern states, by comparison, largely fund their own interventions.

AU and IGAD efforts to institutionalise their position on the Red Sea and engage with the League of Arab States were appropriate steps. However, the league has also been weakened by the altered context.

Going forward, the AU and IGAD should be ready to capitalise on emerging opportunities, reconceptualise their maritime mechanisms, streamline existing diplomatic efforts and work closely with their Middle Eastern partners.

For permission to re-publish ISS Today articles, please email us. In South Africa, News24 has exclusive rights to republish ISS Today articles. In Nigeria, Premium Times has exclusive rights to republish ISS Today articles.

Moses Chrispus Okello, Senior Researcher, Horn of Africa Security Analysis, ISS Addis Ababa

World.title: Uganda: Uganda Has No Active Ebola Cases, Health Ministry Assures Public
World.content:
A tent used to isolate Ebola patients is disinfected in Bunia, DR Congo (file photo).

Uganda has reiterated there are no confirmed active Ebola cases, following reports of a confirmed infection in Nigeria involving a woman who travelled to the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) for business.

In a statement, the Director General of Health Services in the Ministry of Health, Prof. Charles Olaro

said preliminary information indicated that the woman transited through Uganda in early October without showing symptoms but developed them after arriving in Nigeria.

He cautioned against concluding that the infection originated in Uganda, noting that investigations were still underway to establish where the woman was exposed to the virus.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation," Prof Olaro said.

He added that Uganda had no confirmed active Ebola cases at the time of the statement and urged the public to remain calm as authorities continued to monitor the situation.

"We wish to clarify that, as at the time of this statement, Uganda has NO confirmed active Ebola cases," Prof. Olaro said.

The Ministry added that the government of Nigeria had not yet provided detailed information about the woman's travel itinerary and clinical history, which would help guide further investigations and determine whether contact tracing was necessary.

Meanwhile, the Ministry said it would work with relevant government agencies to strengthen screening and public health controls at Uganda's points of entry.

It noted that limited provisions had been maintained for humanitarian and diplomatic movement and that additional measures would be taken to reinforce public health safeguards.

The Ministry urged Ugandans to remain vigilant and observe preventive hygiene measures, including regular handwashing and the use of sanitiser.

"We urge the public to remain calm, vigilant and to practice regular handwashing and sanitising," the statement said.

The Ministry said it would continue to provide verified information through its official communication channels as investigations progressed.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 21, 2026
World.content:
Nigeria Confirms First Ebola Case as Outbreak Spreads

Nigeria has confirmed one case of Ebola in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) after a woman who recently travelled from Uganda tested positive. The patient is in isolation and receiving treatment at a private hospital. The authorities have begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. The government has called on health facilities to step up surveillance, isolate suspected cases and implement infection prevention measures. It also advised the public to maintain good hand hygiene and avoid contact with bodily fluids from suspected cases. Nigeria has become the latest country to report an Ebola case as the virus spreads across the region. Kenya has recorded nine infections. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases, but it later declared itself free of the virus.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

UN Warns Pulling Peacekeepers From CAR Will Fuel Regional Chaos

The United Nations has warned against a premature withdrawal of peacekeepers from the Central African Republic (CAR) as Sudan's war fuels instability along the country's eastern borders. UN Special Representative Valentine Rugwabiza told the Security Council that an attack on Am-Dafock on June 30 killed civilians and security personnel, displaced 17,000 people and injured six UN peacekeepers. She said the rapid response by the UN peacekeeping mission, MINUSCA, helped restore state authority and prevent further casualties. Between June and September, suspected Lord's Resistance Army fighters were linked to 26 serious incidents in the southeast, including sexual violence and the abduction of 68 civilians, about 40 of them children. Despite progress in disarming 1,907 fighters since July 2025 and establishing municipal councils in 127 of 177 municipalities, large areas remain unstable. Nearly two million people faced acute food insecurity between April and August, while the UN humanitarian plan was less than half funded. As the Security Council considers renewing MINUSCA's mandate, members remain divided over troop reductions, with the UN Secretary-General recommending a one-year extension that preserves the mission's capacity to respond rapidly to violence.

15 Years After Gaddafi's Fall, His Legacy Still Haunts Libya and the Sahel

Fifteen years after Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi was captured and killed in 2011, his political legacy continues to influence debates about Libya's instability and security across the Sahel. Libya specialist Virginie Collombier says Kadhafism combined the Green Book's proposed alternative to capitalism and communism with centralised rule, Arab and African nationalism, anti-imperialism and the redistribution of oil wealth. However, the regime was also marked by severe repression, restrictions on political opposition and policies that alienated sections of the population. Kadhafi's overthrow, following an uprising and Western-backed military intervention, left Libya divided between rival political and military factions, with insecurity spreading across the region. Some African leaders and political elites remain nostalgic for his investment and support for African development, while criticising foreign powers for removing him without a clear plan for the country's future. The assassination of his son Saif al-Islam in February 2026 has further weakened the movement, leaving supporters without a prominent leader or a clear political project. Collombier argues that Kadhafi's legacy reflects both his personalised rule and Libya's complex history.

South African Woman Dies in Shark Attack Off Eastern Cape Coast

A 65-year-old South African woman, Janine Lochrenberg, has died following a shark attack while swimming off Orient Beach in KuGompo City, formerly East London. Lochrenberg was swimming with her local open-water swimming club at about 08:00 when she was bitten on her thigh and upper arm. Fellow swimmers brought her towards shore, but she is believed to have died before reaching it. Her sister, Margot, said Lochrenberg had a deep love of the ocean despite being aware of the elevated shark presence in the area. Her partner, Barbara Briceland, described her as an experienced swimmer who regularly ventured into the breakers. The retired medical physicist was reportedly wearing a magnetic shark-repellent band when the attack occurred. Authorities have closed Orient Beach and another nearby beach following the incident. According to the Florida Museum's International Shark Attack File, fatal shark attacks in South Africa are rare, with about 10 recorded since 2012.

Morocco's First Female Prime Minister Faces Test on Women's Rights

Morocco's appointment of Fatima Zahra El Mansouri as its first female prime minister has been welcomed as a historic milestone but has also reignited debate over women's leadership and gender equality in the Muslim-majority country. Former justice minister Mustafa Ramid questioned whether a woman should lead the government, citing a religious saying that countries led by women will not succeed. Many younger Moroccans welcomed El Mansouri's appointment. However, conservative views remain influential, particularly on inheritance, polygamy, marriage and divorce. Women's rights advocates say reform of the country's family code, known as the Moudawana, will be a key test of whether the new government can deliver meaningful change. Education is another concern, with official figures showing that only 55% of girls aged 15 to 17 in rural areas attended school in 2025, compared with 100% in urban areas. However, analysts said that El Mansouri's ability to drive reform is constrained by the king's extensive powers and the influence of religious authorities. But critics also question whether her appointment is a true step forward, or simply an attempt to bolster the monarchy's image at a time of low voter turnout. Advocates argue that her record in office, rather than her gender alone, will determine whether the appointment translates into lasting improvements for Moroccan women.

World.title: Nigeria: Presidential Panel Submits Draft National Policing Bill to Justice Ministry for Review
World.content:
press release

The proposed National Policing Bill seeks to establish the constitutional and legislative framework for a dual policing structure, comprising a Federal Police Service and State Police Services.

The Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill has completed the drafting stage of its assignment. It has formally submitted the draft National Policing Bill (2026), along with 29 consequential amendment bills, to the Federal Ministry of Justice for legislative drafting, review, and validation.

The submission was made on 19 October to the Attorney General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, in line with the Working Group's work plan.

The ministry's review will ensure the bills conform to legislative drafting standards and conventions and do not conflict with existing laws.



The Ministry of Justice is expected to return the validated draft bills to the Working Group on or before Friday, 30 October. The Working Group will then give the validated bills final consideration before presenting them to President Bola Tinubu, thereby concluding its mandate.

The proposed National Policing Bill seeks to establish the constitutional and legislative framework for a dual policing structure, comprising a Federal Police Service and State Police Services.

The Working Group remains committed to a rigorous, transparent process that will deliver a comprehensive legislative proposal for the President's consideration and subsequent transmission to the National Assembly.

Work on preparing the National Policing Bill is proceeding alongside the States Houses of Assembly's ongoing consideration of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (Sixth Alteration) Bill, 2026, which must be completed before the Bill is transmitted to the National Assembly.

Femi Gbajabiamila, CFR

Chief of Staff to the President

Chairman, Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill

October 20, 2026

World.title: Kenya: Kenya Confirms Ninth Ebola Case, Says All Patients Improving
World.content:
Health workers in protective gear inside the Ebola treatment centre at Buniaâs referral hospital in Ituri province, eastern DRC, October 2026.

In a statement published on its X account on Tuesday and signed by Patrick Amoth, the Director-General for Health, the ministry said all nine cases belonged to one known cluster.

Kenya has confirmed a ninth case of Ebola, with health authorities saying all eight surviving patients are improving.

The latest Kenyan case involves a 24-year-old man who is a close relative of the first patient. He developed symptoms while in quarantine and tested positive on 19 October, according to the Kenyan Ministry of Health.

In a statement published on its X account on Tuesday and signed by Patrick Amoth, the Director-General for Health, the ministry said all nine cases belonged to one known cluster, with no evidence of transmission beyond the group.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Kenya's first patient was a 40-year-old man who travelled from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on 3 October. He died at a Nairobi hospital on 5 October.

Treatment and contact tracing

The ministry said the eight surviving patients were stable and responding well to supportive care. It added that it had received 500 doses of medicine to support treatment for confirmed patients.

Contact tracing has also progressed, with 134 of the 135 identified contacts (99.3 per cent) traced and placed in quarantine.

The ministry said contacts who entered quarantine on 6 October and remain symptom-free would complete their 21-day monitoring period and begin returning home from 25 October.

It added that authorities had distributed protective equipment, diagnostic kits, and sample-collection materials to high-risk counties, and established a dedicated laboratory at Kenyatta National Hospital to support testing and prevent disruption to other hospital laboratory services.

Kenya, it noted, has not imposed restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings. The cases in Kenya are linked to the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the DRC, where the Bundibugyo virus has caused thousands of infections and deaths.

WHO reported more than 8,700 confirmed cases and more than 4,200 deaths in the DRC as of 6 October, with transmission continuing across dozens of health zones.

Nigeria confirms first case

The Kenyan update comes as Nigeria confronts its own Ebola infection, with the federal government confirming the first case in Abuja on Tuesday.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that the patient was a woman who arrived in Nigeria on an international flight from Uganda. She is receiving treatment in isolation at a private hospital in the Federal Capital Territory.

Close 

In a statement signed by the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, the federal government said it had begun contact tracing and identified 44 close contacts, including healthcare workers, patients, caregivers, and travel contacts.

The government urged healthcare facilities nationwide to remain vigilant, promptly isolate suspected cases, maintain strict infection prevention measures and report suspected infections to public health authorities.

The development has heightened concerns about cross-border transmission, particularly as the outbreak in East and Central Africa coincides with frequent international travel and movement between countries.

Nigeria's response includes surveillance, laboratory testing, isolation and contact tracing to identify possible infections and limit further transmission.

World.title: Nigeria: 12 Years After First Outbreak, Nigeria Records Fresh Ebola Case
World.content:
A tent used to isolate Ebola patients is disinfected in Bunia, DR Congo (file photo).

Twelve years after Nigeria was declared free of Ebola following an outbreak that killed eight people, the country has confirmed a new case of the disease in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).

The federal government disclosed the case on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, following laboratory confirmation of the infection in a woman who recently arrived in Nigeria on an international flight from Uganda.

The patient had been admitted to a private hospital in Abuja, where she received treatment for several days before the diagnosis was confirmed.

The coordinating minister of health and social welfare, Prof. Muhammad Ali Pate, announced the development in a statement, adding that the woman was in isolation and receiving medical care.



He said 44 close contacts had been identified as authorities intensified efforts to contain the infection and prevent further transmission.

According to the minister, contact tracing had commenced, with public health teams working to identify and monitor people who might have been exposed to the virus, including healthcare workers, patients, caregivers and travel contacts.

He added that surveillance had been intensified and the hospital where the patient received treatment was receiving immediate support to strengthen infection prevention and control measures.

Pate directed public and private healthcare facilities nationwide to remain on high alert and maintain a high index of suspicion for possible Ebola cases.

He also urged healthcare workers to identify and isolate suspected cases promptly, observe strict infection prevention and control measures, and immediately report suspected infections to public health authorities.

The minister advised Nigerians to remain calm but vigilant, stressing that early detection and compliance with public health measures were critical to preventing further transmission.

He said containing the infection would require public cooperation and coordinated action by the federal government, FCT authorities and other partners.

Pate assured Nigerians that investigations were ongoing and pledged that the government would continue to provide accurate and timely updates.

Remembering Nigeria's 2014 Ebola Battle

Nigeria's first major encounter with Ebola occurred in July 2014, when an infected Liberian-American, Patrick Sawyer, arrived in Lagos by air.

Sawyer was admitted to a private hospital, where he died five days later. His arrival triggered an outbreak investigation in Lagos, a densely populated commercial city with extensive domestic and international travel connections.

The incident posed a significant risk of wider transmission because Sawyer had interacted with people at the airport and in healthcare facilities before his infection was confirmed.

However, Nigeria's response, including the sacrifice of the late Dr Ameyo Stella Adadevoh, demonstrated how rapid case identification, contact tracing, isolation, coordinated emergency management and public awareness could help contain a dangerous infectious disease.

According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), the outbreak resulted in 20 cases and eight deaths, including the index case. Nigeria was officially declared free of Ebola transmission on October 20, 2014, after completing the required 42-day period without a new case.

The response involved the Federal Ministry of Health, Lagos State authorities, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), international health partners and other stakeholders.

An emergency operations structure was established to coordinate the response, investigate suspected infections, identify contacts and monitor people who might have been exposed.

Public awareness campaigns and engagement with community, traditional and religious leaders also helped communicate the risks associated with the disease.

The successful containment of the 2014 outbreak established Nigeria as an example of how a country could interrupt transmission even when confronted with a potentially devastating epidemic.

However, the confirmation of another case 12 years later underscores the fact that previous success does not eliminate the risk of new infections entering the country.

Nigeria's Ebola Preparedness

Before the latest confirmation, Nigeria had intensified its preparedness following the spread of Ebola in parts of Central and East Africa.

On October 6, 2026, the NCDC announced heightened vigilance after Kenya confirmed an imported case linked to an outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

At the time, the agency said Nigeria had no confirmed Ebola case.

It also disclosed that preparedness activities were being strengthened in collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, Port Health Services, state governments and other partners.

The measures included surveillance, early detection, laboratory diagnosis, isolation and referral, contact tracing, infection prevention and control, risk communication, and the protection of healthcare workers.

The NCDC also reported that a national Ebola preparedness tabletop simulation exercise had been conducted to test response arrangements and identify gaps requiring attention.

LEADERSHIP reports that President Bola Tinubu established a Presidential Task Force on Ebola Virus Disease Preparedness and Emerging Public Health Threats in June 2026. The task force was created to strengthen national preparedness and prevent the importation and spread of the disease following outbreaks in the DRC and elsewhere in the region.

It is chaired by the Chief of Staff to the President, Femi Gbajabiamila, and comprises representatives of relevant ministries, departments and agencies, state governments and public health partners.

Its responsibilities include coordinating the national response, overseeing the implementation of Nigeria's Ebola preparedness plan, reviewing surveillance reports and coordinating decisions on emergency measures.

As part of the preparations, Tinubu approved the release of N10 billion in emergency intervention funding to strengthen the NCDC's operational capacity and support critical public health response activities.

The confirmation in Abuja now puts these preparedness arrangements to a practical test.

Expert Calls for Calm, Effective Risk Communication

Meanwhile, an infectious disease expert, Dr Oladipo Elijah Kolawole, has urged Nigerians to remain calm but vigilant following the federal government's confirmation of an Ebola case in the FCT.

Kolawole, an associate professor of infectious diseases, pathogen genomics and molecular epidemiology at Adeleke University and founder of Helix Biogen Institute, told LEADERSHIP that early detection and strict adherence to public health measures were critical to containing the disease and preventing wider transmission.

He advised Nigerians to practise regular hand hygiene, avoid direct contact with the bodily fluids of sick individuals and promptly report suspected cases to health authorities.

The expert stressed that public vigilance and evidence-based interventions, rather than panic, were essential to managing the situation.

He urged the government to prioritise rapid case investigation, contact tracing, laboratory confirmation and effective risk communication to contain the infection.

Kolawole also called for stronger infection prevention and control measures in healthcare facilities, noting that transparency, preparedness and a coordinated public health response would be crucial to preventing further transmission.

Close 

How Ebola Spreads and What Nigerians Should Know

Ebola is a severe viral disease that can cause serious illness and death.

The virus spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person who is sick or has died, or through contact with contaminated objects and materials.

It is not spread simply because an infected person is in the same room, nor through ordinary casual contact without the necessary exposure.

Symptoms

Symptoms can include fever, severe weakness, headache, muscle pain, vomiting and diarrhoea. Some patients may develop bleeding, although this does not occur in every case.

The incubation period generally ranges from two to 21 days.

Precautions

The federal government has advised Nigerians to practise regular hand hygiene, avoid contact with the bodily fluids of anyone suspected of having the disease and report possible exposure to public health authorities.

Anyone who develops compatible symptoms after possible exposure should contact public health authorities for guidance rather than visiting a healthcare facility without prior notification.

People identified by contact-tracing teams should cooperate with health officials and follow instructions on monitoring and other recommended public health measures.

Assurance to Nigerians

The Federal Ministry of Health has said Nigeria successfully contained Ebola in 2014 and has the experience and public health systems to respond to the current case.

However, the ministry stressed that containing the disease requires everyone to play their part.

World.title: Uganda: Prisons Say Lukwago, Besigye's Health Improving
World.content:
Dr Kizza Besigye in the dock at the military court in Makindye.

Uganda Prisons Service spokesperson Frank Baine says detained opposition figures Erias Lukwago and Dr Kizza Besigye are improving, as concerns persist over their health and access to specialised medical care.

Baine said Lukwago had been taken to Mulago National Referral Hospital for a medical check-up after his condition reportedly worsened, but maintained that there was nothing critical about his health.

Speaking on the sidelines of Victoria University's 10th graduation ceremony at Speke Resort Munyonyo, Baine said the prisons service was working with the detainees' personal doctors to ensure they received medical attention.

"Whether he is in the hospital or prison, he remains a prisoner," Baine said, adding that Besigye's condition was also improving by the day.



His remarks come amid concern from the families, lawyers and supporters of the two opposition figures over their wellbeing and access to specialised treatment.

On Monday, Medard Lubega Sseggona, one of Lukwago's lawyers, appealed to Ugandans to pray for his client, saying his health remained a major concern and that he needed specialised treatment in India.

Sseggona said Lukwago had been transferred to Mulago National Referral Hospital on Monday morning after his condition reportedly deteriorated while in detention. Lukwago had previously been receiving treatment at the Joint Clinical Research Centre (JCRC) in Lubowa.

Sseggona, who heads Lukwago's legal team, described the situation as worrying and called on Ugandans of all faiths to pray for the former Kampala Lord Mayor.

Lukwago, a lawyer and former Kampala Lord Mayor, has been in detention amid concerns about his health. His transfer to Mulago has renewed calls from his legal team for access to specialised medical care.

The People's Front for Freedom (PFF) also raised concerns about Besigye's health, saying he was undergoing speech therapy and learning to speak again, as well as working to regain his ability to walk.

The party's update on Tuesday, October 20, contrasts with Baine's assurance that the opposition figure's condition was improving, highlighting continuing concerns about his recovery while in custody.

Besigye, a four-time presidential candidate and long-time critic of President Museveni's government, has been in custody since November 2024 and faces treason-related charges alongside his co-accused.

Lukwago, who has also represented Besigye as a lawyer, was separately charged with misprision of treason in June 2026.

Washing and Hushing

Three weeks ago, this page demanded the public release of details of the much-publicised framework agreement on mining between Nigeria and the US. On Monday, ThisDay Newspaper published what appears to be the text of the agreement on pages 14 and 15. Although the publication was not attributed and the names and signatures of the officials were omitted, the fact that there is a movement in the transparency needle that should ordinarily thread such important bilateral cooperation between the two countries is worthy of mention.

However, the publication has raised cogent questions that deserve to be answered by the Ministry of Solid Minerals Development and the United States Government. In the spirit of dialogue and to encourage more transparency and mobilisation of public support for the just exploration, processing, and value-addition of Nigeria's rare earth and transition minerals, there needs to be more awareness of the community safeguards, beneficiation, and social licence to operate covered in this framework. There needs to be more information and engagement on how Nigerian entities, especially the private sector, can benefit, to create multiplier effects on the economy. There needs to be more assurance on how the Nigerian government intends to protect and promote national interest in the face of the fierce geopolitics over these transition minerals. There are many more questions, so let the engagement continue.

World.title: Making whiskey at home could land you in prison, but Supreme Court may change that
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Americans can legally brew beer and make wine at home, but producing even a small amount of whiskey could land them in federal prison.

Now, the U.S. Supreme Court is preparing to weigh in on a 150-year-old federal law prohibiting home distilling, a case that could have implications far beyond the liquor cabinet.

The justices agreed Monday to review the Reconstruction-era restriction, which dates to 1868 and was originally enacted to combat liquor tax evasion.

AMERICANS ONCE SURVIVED ON SQUIRREL PIE, WHISKEY AND HOMEMADE CHEESE AFTER BRITISH IMPORTS DRIED UP

Robert Alt, president and CEO of the Ohio-based Buckeye Institute, which represents challengers to the ban, told Fox News Digital the decision marks a significant development for home-distilling enthusiasts.

"This is a real opportunity for both whiskey and freedom," Alt said.

Among those challenging the prohibition is John Ream, an Ohio brewery owner and former aerospace engineer who wants to distill small quantities of spirits at home for personal consumption.

Ream's legal battle was previously highlighted by Fox News Digital as he awaited word on whether the nation's highest court would intervene.

MAN CHALLENGING 150-YEAR-OLD BAN ON MAKING LIQUOR AT HOME HOPES SUPREME COURT TAKES HIS CASE

Under federal law, producing distilled spirits at home can carry penalties of up to five years in prison, a $10,000 fine and possible property forfeiture.

The case centers on whether Congress' constitutional authority to collect taxes also allows it to prohibit an otherwise lawful activity inside a person's home.

"What this case boils down to is what is the scope of congressional power?" Alt said.

Two federal appeals courts reached conflicting conclusions earlier this year.

CLICK HERE TO 

The 5th Circuit struck down the restriction, finding that Congress' taxing authority did not justify the prohibition. The 6th Circuit upheld the law, concluding it was a permissible means of enforcing federal liquor taxes.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) maintains that the restriction is a legitimate tool for preventing tax evasion and protecting federal revenue. The DOJ declined to comment on the case to Fox News Digital.

"The founders would be rolling over in their graves at the suggestion that Congress had the authority to ban and make a felony out of this very American activity."

Alt, however, argues that allowing Congress to prohibit home distilling under its taxing authority could establish a troubling precedent for other private activities.

He pointed to hobbies such as gardening and working on cars as examples of activities that could theoretically face similar restrictions under the government's legal reasoning.

The attorney also noted that home distilling has deep American roots. President George Washington participated in home distilling, Alt said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"The founders would be rolling over in their graves at the suggestion that Congress had the authority to ban and make a felony out of this very American activity," Alt said.

A ruling favoring the federal government would leave the challenged restriction in place, although Congress could still amend the law, Alt said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Alt said his clients would be willing to pay applicable taxes on spirits produced at home, arguing that taxation should not require an outright prohibition.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Supreme Court has not yet scheduled oral arguments, but Alt said he anticipates arguments in late February or early March, with a decision potentially arriving by the end of June.

World.title: Former Chiefs, Falcons defensive end Allen Bailey dead at 37
World.content:
Former Kansas City Chiefs and Atlanta Falcons defensive end Allen Bailey died Tuesday at 37.

Bailey's brother, Alford Bailey Jr., told TMZ that Bailey's wife found him dead at their Florida home on Tuesday. Bailey's family believes he died of natural causes, according to TMZ. No official cause of death has been released.

"Allen Bailey was an excellent teammate, generous man, and kind soul. We're deeply saddened to hear of his passing, and our thoughts and prayers are with his family and friends," the Chiefs posted in a statement.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Bailey played in the NFL for 10 seasons. The Chiefs drafted him in the third round of the 2011 NFL Draft out of Miami.

Bailey spent the first eight seasons of his career with the Chiefs before signing a two-year, $10.5 million contract with the Falcons in 2019. In March 2020, the Falcons gave Bailey a one-year, $4.5 million contract extension, but released him in 2021 to save $4.5 million. He never played in the NFL again.

In 10 seasons, Bailey played in 133 games (including 70 starts), recording 248 tackles and 22 sacks. Chiefs coach Andy Reid called him one of his favorite players.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"Sad news, the passing of Allen Bailey. Our hearts go out to his family, prayers are with them. Way too young, obviously, one of my favorite players. Great kid, just sorry to see that happen to him," Reid told reporters on Wednesday.

Bailey stood 6 feet, 3 inches tall and weighed 288 pounds. Chiefs star quarterback Patrick Mahomes recalled a humorous story about Bailey while speaking to reporters on Wednesday.

"I tell this story kind of like every year, with [the quarterbacks], he was the first person I saw when I stepped into the locker room, I think it was after one of the drafts, they were in OTAs. I stepped in the locker room to see Allen Bailey and I’m like this isn’t the Big 12 anymore. It was surreal to see him. I tell that story every single year," Mahomes told reporters on Wednesday.



"Obviously, it’s terrible to hear the news that we heard. A great teammate, you see him, he’s one of the glue guys on the team. He makes plays, not necessarily the superstar but kind of the guy who makes everything go. It was terrible to hear that news later last night and we’re praying for his family, and know that as teammates we talked, and we’re going to do whatever we can to support those guys."

Tennessee Titans coach Robert Saleh defended Jordan Elliott after the team released the defensive lineman following a gun-related incident.

World.title: France in flames is preview of what 'DSA' Democrats want for US, senator warns

The chaos engulfing France is a preview of what Democrats want for America, Sen. Eric Schmitt warned, contrasting the unrest with new manufacturing jobs and a federal crime crackdown in Missouri that he credits to cooperation with the Trump administration.

"You see what’s happening in France. That’s exactly what they want here, the DSA Democrats," the Missouri Republican told Fox News Digital.

VIOLENT FAR-LEFT RIOTS IN FRANCE ARE 'CHILLING WARNING' FOR AMERICANS AT HOME, MIKE JOHNSON SAYS

With control of the House "up for grabs," Schmitt argued, Republicans need to make the stakes clear while showing voters what they have delivered.

INSIDE THE HOUSE GOP'S 4-WEEK BATTLE PLAN TO SAVE ITS MAJORITY

Asked what a Democratic House would mean for Trump’s agenda, Schmitt accused Democrats of obstructing Republican efforts on immigration, permitting reform and regulations.

'SQUAD' DEMOCRAT FORMALLY INTRODUCES BILL TO ABOLISH ICE, BORDER PATROL AND DISMANTLE DHS

He warned that Democratic control could jeopardize funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement and revive what he described as the political weaponization of government under former President Joe Biden.

KEY AMERICAN INDUSTRY SEEING BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM AS TRUMP'S RE-SHORING POLICIES PAY OFF

In Missouri, he highlighted Boeing’s selection to build the Air Force’s F-47 and the Navy’s next-generation F/A-XX fighter as a potentially transformative investment in American manufacturing.

Boeing secured the Navy contract in September after winning the Air Force program last year.

BERNIE SANDERS ADMITS DEMOCRATS FAILED WORKING-CLASS VOTERS ON ECONOMICS, DRIVING THEM TO DONALD TRUMP

Schmitt, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said the programs would mean 7,000 direct jobs, with additional opportunities for suppliers and surrounding businesses.

"It means that the goal we’ve been fighting for, which is that St. Louis is the defense tech capital of the United States of America, is coming true," he said.

TRUMP SAYS POLLS 'DON'T ACCOUNT FOR ONE THING,' AS HE PLEDGES TO DEFEAT COMMUNISTS 'ONCE AND FOR ALL'

Schmitt said he worked with Trump and administration officials to help land the programs, describing them as "generational opportunities" for Missouri workers.

"You think of the good-paying jobs that’s going to mean for generations to come, it’s just a game changer," he said.

He also tied the aircraft programs to the broader competition with China, saying the next generation of fighters would help meet military demands in the Pacific.

On public safety, Schmitt pointed to Operation Show Me Justice, an ATF-led enforcement surge that resulted in 435 arrests and the seizure of 166 firearms in St. Louis, according to the Justice Department.

Authorities also seized 81 kilograms of drugs and more than $1.25 million linked to suspected illegal gun and drug transactions during the operation, which officials announced had concluded Oct. 15.

Schmitt said his conversations with administration officials have carried a straightforward request for his hometown.

TRUMP’S LAW-AND-ORDER BLITZ MARKS ONE YEAR WITH EYE-POPPING HAUL OF SUSPECTS, GUNS IN BLUE CITY

"St. Louis, we need your help," he said.

The former Missouri attorney general described the toll of violence on families, including grandparents cleaning up broken glass and parents burying their children.

"We don’t need to accept this," he said. "We just don’t need to accept the idea that violent crime needs to be in the headlines every single day."

He pledged the effort would continue beyond the surge.

"This isn’t a one-and-done deal. There are more resources coming," Schmitt said.

OMAR'S NEW LEGISLATION TARGETING ICE SPARKS OUTRAGE WHEN THE INTERNET SEES WHAT'S IN IT: 'UN-AMERICAN'

For families wanting to send children safely to school, visit a park or attend a Cardinals game downtown, he said the goal is a better quality of life.

"I think the message is help is on the way, and there are real tangible results now, not just rhetoric, not just empty promises," Schmitt said.

"We’re not letting up."

Schmitt’s third major priority is modernizing St. Louis Lambert International Airport, an effort he linked to the region’s aerospace growth and aviation history.

His Modern Skies Act would fund improvements to air traffic control technology, towers and airport terminals. He said midsize airports need help securing investments that larger hubs can more readily finance.

"St. Louis is the gateway to the West," he said. "It deserves a world-class airport."

The proposal remains a legislative push rather than a guaranteed funding award for Lambert. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said during an October visit that airport funding would be competitive.

For Schmitt, those priorities form part of the argument Republicans need to make as voters weigh control of Congress.

He's very much in the owners' club, as proven by his attendance and participation in their meetings this week.

And so Tisch's contrite statement in which he regretted his Epstein association seems not quite so meaningful anymore.

"We had a brief association where we exchanged emails about adult women, and in addition, we discussed movies, philanthropy, and investments," Tisch said in that January statement.

"I did not take him up on any of his invitations and never went to his island. As we all know now, he was a terrible person and someone I deeply regret associating with."

All of this is, of course, a rough look for the NFL. It's bad optics.

World.title: Fox News Poll: Gender gap and pocketbook pain shape Ohio Senate race
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Powered by a clear favorability advantage, a large gender gap and voter discontent with both household finances and President Donald Trump, former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown has the edge over appointed Republican Sen. Jon Husted in the Ohio Senate race.

A Fox News survey of likely Ohio voters finds Brown leads Husted, 52% to 47%.

Brown’s advantage is anchored by his stronger personal standing, with his favorability rating 2 points above water (50% favorable, 48% unfavorable), while Husted’s rating sits 13 points underwater (42% favorable, 55% unfavorable).

FOX NEWS POLL: COST-OF-LIVING CONCERNS WEIGH ON GOP IN MIDTERMS

More Brown supporters (88%) than Husted backers (83%) say they’re certain of their vote.

FOX NEWS POLL: IT’S A LONE STAR SENATE SHOWDOWN BETWEEN TALARICO AND PAXTON

Economic unease creates another headwind for Husted because about 2½ times as many voters say their financial situation is worse than two years ago rather than better (46% vs. 19%). Those who say things are worse favor Brown by 49 points, while those who say their finances are better or the same favor Husted by 51 and 24 points, respectively.

The president’s standing in Ohio adds to Husted’s difficulties. Trump won the Buckeye State with 55% of the vote in 2024, but just 43% now approve of his job performance. A 57% majority disapproves, with 46% saying they "strongly" disapprove.

Meanwhile, 52% express concern that Husted is too close to Trump, including 38% who are extremely concerned. Brown faces similar concerns about being too liberal, as 50% are worried, though fewer, 30%, are extremely concerned.

In the matchup, women favor Brown by 14 points, while men support Husted by 4, an 18-point gender gap. Brown also has advantages among voters under 35, voters with a college degree, union voters and those living in urban and suburban areas. Husted relies on rural communities, non-college White men and married voters and has a narrow edge among those ages 65 and up.

Partisan crossovers further tilt the field toward the challenger. While Husted receives 90% of Republicans, 9% cross over to back Brown. Some 97% of Democrats support Brown, while just 2% choose Husted, and Brown carries independents by nearly two to one.

Voters who view both Senate candidates unfavorably prefer Husted by nearly 20 points.

Brown is up by 9 points among those who are extremely interested in the election and leads by 29 points among the 15% of Ohioans who say they have already voted.

Legislative preference tilts toward the Democrats, with Ohioans dividing 50% for Democratic control of the U.S. Senate and 48% for Republican control.

In the governor's contest, likely voters favor Democrat Amy Acton over Republican Vivek Ramaswamy by 50% to 48%. Women favor Acton by 10 points, while men back Ramaswamy by 7, a nearly identical gender gap to the Senate race.

CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE

Ticket splitting goes in both directions: 8% of Brown supporters cross over to Ramaswamy, while 6% of Husted supporters back Acton.

The survey was completed before a negative television ad from Ramaswamy’s campaign featuring Acton’s estranged mother became public.

Conducted October 15-19, 2026, under the joint direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News Poll includes interviews with a sample of 2,005 Ohio registered voters randomly selected from a statewide voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (219) and cellphones (1,306) or completed the survey online after receiving a text message (480). Results based on the registered voter sample have a margin of sampling error of ±2 percentage points, and, for the subsample of 1,592 likely voters, it is ±2 percentage points.

Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling error, question wording and order can influence results. Sources for developing weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis and voter file data. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education and area variables to ensure the demographics of respondents are representative of the registered voter population. Likely voters are based on a probabilistic statistical model that relies on past vote history, interest in the current election, intention to vote, age, education, race, ethnicity, and marital status. Results among subgroups are only shown when the sample size is at least N=100.

Fox News’ Victoria Balara contributed to this report.

World.title: Who is Stephen Hubbard, the retired American teacher freed by Russia?
World.content:
Stephen James Hubbard, a retired American teacher, was released by Russia on Wednesday after nearly five years in detention in the midst of an apparent warming of ties between Washington and Moscow.

The 74-year-old from Michigan had been living in eastern Ukraine for years when Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. He was detained two months into the war as Russia captured swaths of Ukrainian territory. Two years later, he was convicted by a Russian court of serving as a mercenary.

The news of his release came out of a meeting between President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday, where they were due to discuss an end to the Ukraine war.

Witkoff thanked Putin for freeing Hubbard during their on-camera talks. He later met Hubbard in person in St. Petersburg before boarding a flight back to the United States.

In a video from Russian state news agency Ria, Hubbard can be seen smiling as he met Witkoff. “Thank you very much for all your efforts,” he tells Witkoff as they shake hands. Putin sent Hubbard “blessings,” Witkoff tells him, adding “from today, it’s a new life.”

During the meeting, Witkoff said on X, Trump “called Stephen to check on him and reaffirm his unwavering commitment to bringing all Americans wrongfully detained home.”

Witkoff shared an image of Hubbard on a plane next to the American flag and several others, writing that he was “headed back home to his family.”

Martin De Luca, Hubbard’s lawyer, told NBC News in a phone interview Wednesday that he had spoken with Hubbard as he was “getting ready to take off” on a plane bound for the U.S. and that his client was overjoyed to be released.

“He was overwhelmed with joy,” De Luca said. “The No. 1 thing he was excited about was seeing his children and family, who will be waiting for him when he arrives in the U.S. tonight. He was in a fragile state, so it wasn’t a long conversation, but he’s OK, which is what’s important.”

Stephen Hubbard. Trisha Hubbard via Facebook

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin released Hubbard “on humanitarian grounds,” though Russia did not provide more details.

Hubbard’s family acknowledged both Trump’s and Putin’s roles in securing his release.

“We have been gravely concerned for his safety and health since his 2022 detention,” Hubbard’s son, Joseph Coleman, said in a statement on behalf of the family. “Never once did we waver as we prayed for success in these negotiations, and we must acknowledge that this humanitarian move by President Putin in this matter is deeply appreciated,” the statement said.

Coleman, a Greek Orthodox priest who lives in Cyprus, wrote Putin “a long and very emotional letter” last month, De Luca said.

In the letter, Coleman told the Russian leader that Hubbard’s family “feared he would die without ever seeing his kids or grandchildren,” De Luca said. Coleman had also outlined his father’s background and family history and emphasized his faith.

Trump cheered Hubbard’s return, framing it as a demonstration of the Kremlin’s “respect” for their American counterparts.

“Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Wednesday, shortly after Witkoff announced Hubbard’s release. “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return — an unprecedented situation for Russia.”

There was no “swap” necessary for this release, Trump added, though in a later post he said “those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt” had the U.S. gone ahead with sanctions that he waived last week.

Stephen Hubbard in Moscow City Court in 2024. Moscow City Court / via AP

Hubbard was sentenced in a closed-door trial in 2024, with very little information about his case reported by Russian state media.

At the time, Russian prosecutors alleged that as the Kremlin launched its “special military operation” in Ukraine in February 2022, Hubbard voluntarily joined a territorial defense battalion in the eastern city of Izyum, where he had been living since 2014. The prosecutors said Hubbard took part in the Ukraine war and regularly received financial compensation before his detention in April 2022 as advancing Russian forces captured the city.

“He was aware of the unlawful nature of his actions, yet — with the deliberate intent of personal enrichment — he carried out the orders of his superiors, which entailed direct participation in combat operations on the side of the Armed Forces of Ukraine against service members of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation,” according to Russia’s prosecutor general’s office.

Russian state media reported that he pleaded guilty to the charges. Following Hubbard’s release Wednesday, De Luca stood by his previous statements that Hubbard had told him the charges were false and that he was not part of any combat or military unit.

The New York Times reported last year that Patricia Hubbard Fox, Hubbard’s sister, disputes that he fought for Ukraine, as do three former Ukrainian prisoners of war held with Hubbard.

The paper also cited Fox as saying that her brother had a master’s degree in English, and had lived in Japan and Cyprus before moving to eastern Ukraine, where he had a Ukrainian partner. Fox also said that Hubbard taught English online when he needed money, and did not speak either Ukrainian or Russian.

Izyum, where Fox said her brother settled, was occupied by Russia for six months in 2022, but was later recaptured by Ukraine in a major counteroffensive. It is currently held by Ukraine and is not part of the four Ukrainian oblasts Russia has illegally annexed.

Hubbard’s release from Russian custody comes just months after former U.S. Marine Robert Gilman, who spent more than four years in a Russian prison, was set free in August.

Washington has accused Moscow of arbitrarily detaining American citizens in Russia for years, with their cases often used to negotiate prisoner swaps, including for state-backed intelligence operatives, detained around the world.

In some of the more high-profile cases, U.S. journalist Evan Gershkovich was released in a swap in 2024, alongside Marine veteran Paul Whelan — both had been jailed on espionage charges. WNBA star Brittney Griner, detained on drug charges in 2022, was freed after the Biden administration negotiated her release in exchange for a Russian arms dealer.

John Herbst, former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine and senior director of the Atlantic Council think tank’s Eurasia Center, said that despite the depiction of Hubbard’s release, “It was not a freebie. It was not a gift to the United States.”

He told the “Here’s the Scoop” podcast that it came after the release of a prominent Russian war blogger, Mikhail Zvinchuk, who was detained in Montenegro in October and freed after the U.S. opted not to extradite him.

“Russia’s got back a bad guy who we should have taken into custody, and we got back an American who was innocent. That’s the pattern,” he said.

Meanwhile, on the same day that Hubbard was released, Russia said it had detained a German national accused of serving in the Ukrainian army.

Russia’s Federal Security Service didn’t release the man’s name or any other identifying details, and did not say where or when the man was taken into custody.

World.title: Pope Leo will not require further treatment after lung surgery, doctors say
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV will not need further treatment following lung cancer surgery, his doctors said Wednesday.

The Vatican’s press office released an update from the pontiff’s doctors, saying final reports and analyses of tissue removed from his surgery were completed Wednesday.

00:41 Pope Leo rides popemobile for first time since surgery 00:00 00:00

“The results have confirmed that the condition was a pulmonary adenocarcinoma and that the disease was localized,” said his doctors, Dr. Luigi Carbone and Prof. Stefano Margaritora.

“A subsequent oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required,” the statement said.

The 71-year-old American had surgery earlier this month at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital to remove a lung nodule found during recent routine medical tests. Leo said the nodule was detected “at a very early stage.”

He was discharged on Saturday and returned to his public duties on Sunday with a prayer from the window of the papal apartment at St. Peter’s Basilica.

“This experience has made me feel particularly close to all those who are experiencing illness and a condition of frailty,” he said, thanking well-wishers.

Leo said that “having come through this delicate phase, as you know, I will now gradually resume my activities, always with God’s help and your prayers.”

The pope’s diagnosis and surgery left his upcoming trip to South America up in the air. He is still scheduled to depart on Nov. 6 for the 12-day journey to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

The trip will be a demanding one, covering 19,000 miles on multiple flights and two helicopter rides. His itinerary includes a stopover in Cuzco in the Peruvian Andes that sits at an elevation of 11,000 feet.

Pope Leo, 71, had received a surgery earlier this month at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital to remove a lung nodule found during recent routine medical tests. Massimo Valicchia / NurPhoto via Getty

Peru is a special place for Pope Leo, where he formerly served as bishop of Chiclayo and holds citizenship.

The pope’s surgeon, Margaritora, on Saturday told Vatican News that recovery from Leo’s type of surgery typically takes a couple of weeks.

“As for a long trip involving air travel in about three weeks, I would say there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place,” Margaritora said.

World.title: Woman sexually assaulted at fraternity near University of Chicago, lawsuit alleges
World.content:
A 19-year-old woman filed a lawsuit Monday alleging she was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house near the University of Chicago in February amid heightened scrutiny of sexual misconduct on college campuses.

The college student, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, sued in Cook County Circuit Court, alleging that the sexual assault took place during a party at the Alpha Delta Phi fraternity house on Feb. 7. It names Alpha Delta Phi Inc. and Chicago Society of Alpha Delta Phi as defendants.

“The grief that this has imposed upon me is indescribable,” Doe told NBC News in an interview. “It is the first thing I think about whenever I wake up every day and the last thing I think about whenever I fall asleep.”

Doe’s case comes weeks after a former Cornell University student claimed in a lawsuit that she was gang-raped at a fraternity party, causing national outrage, and just days after a woman reported that she was sexually assaulted at a party hosted by a different fraternity near the University of Chicago.

Monday's lawsuit filed by "Jane Doe" holds that a member of Alpha Delta Phi sexually assaulted the 19-year-old woman during a fraternity party on Feb. 7, 2026. E. Jason Wambsgans / Chicago Tribune via Getty

The University of Chicago, which does not recognize fraternities as official student organizations, said in a statement that it was “prepared to help the Chicago Police Department” in its investigation.

“These allegations are very disturbing to the University community,” said a university spokesperson, Gerald McSwiggan. “The University of Chicago is committed to addressing and preventing incidents of sexual assault.”

Alpha Delta Phi’s national team said in a statement that it is aware of the allegations and that it “suspended the member involved.”

“The conduct described is deeply troubling and inconsistent with our values,” it said. “We are committed to the safety and well-being of our members and communities and will cooperate with law enforcement as appropriate.”

Alpha Delta Phi’s Chicago chapter referred all requests to its national organization.

Doe — who is not a student at the University of Chicago — said she learned about the party on Instagram and had gone to parties at the fraternity house previously. That night, she said, she went to the party with several friends, none of whom are students at the university.

Doe said she was dancing with friends when a fraternity brother approached her. The fraternity brother offered her a shot, which she said immediately made her feel unsteady and lightheaded, according to the lawsuit.

She said she had had only two drinks before she took the shot, spaced out over roughly two hours. She described having the “spins” and feeling as though her “vision was underwater.”

“I know myself, and that was not the amount with how intoxicated I felt after the shot that I took with him,” she said. “I’ve never felt like that before.”

She added that she watched the fraternity brother pour the shot and did not notice anything “odd.”

The fraternity member then directed Doe to follow him to a secluded bedroom on a different floor of the fraternity house, according to the lawsuit. Doe expressed her unsteadiness and lightheadedness, which the fraternity member ignored, the lawsuit says.

The fraternity brother began to make “unwanted and nonconsensual sexual advances” on the woman, the lawsuit says. It says she “lost all physical and verbal ability to refuse” the fraternity member’s alleged sexual advances.

“I remember backing onto the bed because I knew what was about to happen, but I just — I didn’t feel like I was strong enough to get out,” she told NBC News.

The lawsuit says that although her verbal ability was limited, she managed to plead with the fraternity brother to wear a condom, which he refused to do. The fraternity brother then penetrated her “without her consent,” the lawsuit says.

After the alleged encounter, the man left Doe alone and unconscious, according to the suit. It alleges that other fraternity brothers initially blocked her friend from going upstairs to find her.

Her friend found her unconscious and helped her out of the house, according to the complaint. She said that she faintly remembers her shirt being on backward when she woke up but that she was not sure how she got her clothes on.

She struggled to speak and walk as they escorted her out of the home, according to the lawsuit. Doe said she slept over at her friend’s dorm room that night.

The next morning, Doe found bloodstains in her underwear and went to the hospital, where she reported the incident to the Chicago Police Department, according to a police report. Doe told police she believed the alcohol was laced with something, according to the report.

Police confirmed that a 19-year-old who reported a sexual assault at the fraternity house took herself to Illinois Masonic Hospital for treatment on Feb. 8. Doe received a sexual assault evidence collection kit at the hospital, according to the police report.

Days later, the woman was contacted by the University of Chicago Police Department, which she said was investigating her case. Doe said that university police spoke with her for roughly 30 minutes over the phone but that she has not heard from them since. The university police department declined to give Doe records related to her case without a subpoena, she alleges in her lawsuit.

A spokesperson for the city’s police department said it was investigating the incident; the spokesperson did not answer questions about the university police department’s involvement in the case.

Doe is seeking a trial by jury and an amount in excess of $200,000, plus costs.

Doe’s lawyer, Mike Grieco of Gould Grieco & Hensley, said the aim is to also “ensure that this doesn’t happen again, and to help reform” policies within the university.

The University of Chicago has been roiled in recent days by a separate allegation of a sexual assault at a fraternity party near campus. A 21-year-old woman told police she was sexually assaulted this month at a party held at the Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity house, just off campus. Chicago police said no arrests have been made in either case.

“At the end of the day, what happened to me is not unique, and it’s not rare. It happens way more than people realize,” Doe said. “There are so many other survivors out there who suffer in silence.”

World.title: Russians locked out of bank accounts and apartments as Ukraine hits data centers
World.content:
While most Yandex services have been coming back online, three people told NBC News they had been left locked out of their disposable cash and savings for days after disruptions to Yandex Pay, a digital payment service that many Russians use.

Irina, 21, said that in the future she will diversify her deposits across different banks and have a “substantial cash reserve” just in case.

Yandex said Oct. 9 that no employees were hurt and that it is working to restore service.

“Data centers are the iron heart of Yandex,” the statement said. “Their operation is critical for services that have become part of people’s everyday lives.”

Anastasiya Mityaeva, 25, who splits her time between Moscow and the southern city of Krasnodar, said she was “shocked” by the outages, which initially left her family worried about being able to pay down their mortgage after her account, her mother’s account and her grandmother’s account were all inaccessible.

“The uncertainty was scary,” said Mityaeva, who has 2 million followers on TikTok and is originally from Russian-annexed Crimea. “We realized just how much hangs on Yandex. We did not quite appreciate it before.”

Mityaeva, who regained access to her money after several days, also had issues calling a taxi on the first day of the outages and encountered problems with the system to enter her apartment building. Her Yandex home voice assistant, equivalent to an Amazon Echo, stopped responding to requests to play music and turn off the lights.

She did not blame the company, saying Yandex was a “hostage of the situation,” adding: “I understand that this was not up to them. This came from the outside.”

Others were more critical of the company. Viktoria, 30, a barista from Moscow, said she plans to stop using Yandex completely after she was unable to access her money during the outages, describing it as the last straw after other recent issues.

She said Saturday that she once again had access to her money through Yandex Pay but that the service was displaying the wrong balance on her account.

Three taxi drivers in Moscow, who use Yandex’s taxi application to take orders and get paid, all told NBC News they could not see how much money they were making and could not withdraw their earnings during the outage. One of the drivers said he has stopped working altogether until the problem gets fixed. He is originally from Kyrgyzstan and did not know why the outages were happening.

World.title: Arizona mom whose son was found alive in hospital morgue speaks out: ‘It’s an unexplainable feeling’
World.content:
The mother of a toddler found alive in an Arizona hospital morgue in February more than five hours after he was pronounced dead said Wednesday she thought she heard him breathing when she hugged him goodbye.

But instead of listening to her gut, Alexus Fiordilino said, she believed the doctor who told her those were 18-month-old Vincent’s last gasps and that any further attempts to save him would just prolong his agony.

“As a mom you don’t want to hear that,” Fiordilino, 30, said in an interview. “I didn’t want him to suffer. It seemed to be they’d done everything they could. And then he called it.”

Fiordilino was referring to Dr. Aryan Toosi, who pronounced Vincent dead at 6:20 p.m. on Super Bowl Sunday at Mercy Gilbert Medical Center in Gilbert, Arizona.

A little over five hours later, Fiordilino said, police were questioning her and her husband, Angelo, when a detective burst into the room and told them that a medical examiner’s employee who had come to collect Vincent’s body had discovered he was still alive.

“My husband and I just screamed in relief,” she said. “We were praising the Lord. We were crying. To go from hearing he was gone and then finding out he isn’t gone, it’s an unexplainable feeling.”

Fiordilino spoke out more than eight months after her son’s remarkable story of survival after he nearly drowned in the family swimming pool made national headlines and sparked multiple investigations into what happened on Feb. 8.

The Gilbert Police Department had recommended filing child abuse charges against both parents for losing track of Vincent while a Super Bowl party was going on at their residence.

“Both admitted to smoking marijuana the morning of the drowning,” the police report said.

But Maricopa County Attorney Rachel Mitchell announced in July that the Fiordilinos would not be charged.

Fiordilino’s lawyer, John Brewer, said he plans to file a formal complaint this week against Toosi and the hospital. He said a review of Vincent’s medical records shows that critical test results that Toosi cited to justify ending efforts to save the child were not completed until after the toddler was declared dead.

“The parents were faced with having to decide whether to keep trying to revive their son, and the doctor provided them with false information,” Brewer said. “That’s beyond a conscious disregard for human life.”

Brewer’s office turned its records over to the Gilbert Police Department, which said it forwarded everything to the state attorney general’s office for review. The AG’s office said Wednesday that it has not made a decision to review this case.

Toosi’s lawyer, Scott Holden, released a statement in response.

“Dr. Toosi’s thoughts are with the young patient and family, and he wishes the child continued healing and recovery,” it said. “His commitment to delivering high-quality care has always been rooted in a desire to provide healing, safety and comfort to his community.”

Meanwhile, the hospital called the situation “heartbreaking” in a statement.

“Out of respect for the patient’s privacy, we cannot share any information and we are unable to comment on those involved in patient care,” it said. “Patient safety and exceptional care are our highest priorities.”

Asked how Vincent is doing now, Fiordilino said, “He’s getting better.”

Brewer said that while the boy is home with his family, he has many health challenges.

“Vincent is severely brain-injured,” he said. “He can’t swallow. He seizes up. He can’t sit up on his own or crawl.”

The tragic turn of events began around 5:38 p.m. Feb. 8 with a 911 call for help after Vincent was found floating face down in the family pool and a relative tried to revive him by performing CPR, according to a police report obtained by NBC affiliate KPNX of Phoenix.

Vincent was rushed to the emergency room at Mercy Gilbert Medical Center, where an ER team that included Toosi took over the effort to save him.

At 6:13 p.m., according to the report, Toosi went out to deliver bad news to the boy’s parents.

Vincent Fiordilino. via GoFundMe

“As long as there are no objections, I’d like to call time of death,” Toosi said, according to the report.

Then, “at approximately 18:20 hours, Dr. Toosi called the time of death and requested a moment of silence.”

Just as Fiordilino told NBC News, police officers who had been in the ER said in the report that the child still appeared to be gasping for breath after he was declared dead.

A detective reported then hearing “another audible gasp” at around 7:18 p.m. as the ER workers were preparing to move Vincent from the trauma room to the “cold room” that serves as the hospital’s morgue and where the temperature is set at 36 to 39 degrees.

The same detective said that when he returned to photograph the body an hour later, he “again observed what appeared to be a gasp or air release.”

“The nurse again stated it was agonal breathing and explained it was due to compressions, oxygen, and possible pressure applied by family members while saying goodbye,” the report says.

And at 7:23 p.m., “the cold room door was closed,” the report says.

More than four hours later, when the medical examiner’s team arrived at 11:52 p.m. to retrieve the boy, “he was found breathing,” the report says.

“The family was notified immediately,” and the boy was airlifted to Phoenix Children’s Hospital.

Fiordilino said that when she saw her son again in the pediatric intensive care unit, “he was hooked up to all kinds of monitors and things.”

“He looked like a different baby,” she said. “It’s something I hope no other parent has to live through.”

World.title: Collins enlists Manchin to woo moderates as she distances herself from Trump
World.content:
Lewiston, Maine — Republican Sen. Susan Collins is campaigning on a simple idea: She can sit across the table from anyone. On Wednesday, she did it literally, sharing breakfast sandwiches with Democrat-turned-independent Joe Manchin and a roomful of Maine voters as she makes her case to people of every political stripe.

"She's not a Trump senator. She's not a Republican senator or a Democrat senator," Manchin told reporters after dining with Collins in the morning. "She's an American senator that represents her state of Maine."

Collins is the only Republican senator up for reelection in a state that President Trump lost. CBS News rates the race a toss-up. But Collins, who is running for a sixth term, has a history of surviving tough reelection battles and outrunning other Republicans. In 2020, she won by more than 8 points, even as Mr. Trump lost Maine by 9 points.

Both Collins and Manchin — who represented deep-red West Virginia in the Senate before leaving the Democratic Party and retiring in 2024 — have a history of clashing with their respective parties.

Collins worked to distance herself when pressed on Mr. Trump on Wednesday. While touring a local New Balance factory, she was asked about Trump envoy Steve Witkoff calling Russian President Vladimir Putin a "humanitarian" for releasing a jailed U.S. citizen. The question drew a visible reaction from Manchin, who shook his head. Collins responded with a flat "no."

"I would describe Putin as a warmonger, a thug. He's certainly not a humanitarian. He is the aggressor in the war against Ukraine," she said. She also said she does not support Mr. Trump's decision to waive new sanctions on Russia and strike a diesel deal with Moscow to import Russian diesel, arguing it will give Russia more funding to attack Ukraine.

Collins, who has long defected from parts of Mr. Trump's agenda, has also criticized the president's handling of the Iran war. In debates, she has said the president did not have a good plan and that the conflict should end. Her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, doesn't believe she's sincere in her rebukes.

"She's the chair of appropriations. If she wants to stop the war, she can cut the funding off for the war," Jackson said at a debate last week. "But she's not willing to do that because Donald Trump wants this and that's what is going to happen."

Similar skepticism popped up outside of Collins' breakfast stop. A group of protesters shouted for the incumbent to retire and held signs and cutouts of Brett Kavanaugh's face, a reference to her vote to confirm the Supreme Court justice. Collins' supporters, dressed in bright red, drowned them out with chants of "six more years," when she stepped outside to talk to the press and her tour bus blocked the demonstrators from view.

Elaine Makas, a Lewiston Democrat who served in the state legislature from 2002 to 2008, joined the protest. She said she's grateful for Collins' service and calls her "genuinely a nice person," but argued that is not enough.

"She's just voting wrong," Makas told CBS News. "She's fallen completely in line with the president."

Collins has argued that she frequently votes against Mr. Trump's wishes.

Makas echoed Jackson's line of attack. "She only disagrees with him when her vote doesn't matter," she said. She said she personally knows Jackson, a former state Senate president, from their time in the legislature and believes he'll "listen" to Mainers.
