World.title: Supreme Court upholds pause on Trump's anti-trans prison policy
World.content:
Supreme Court upholds pause on Trump's anti-trans prison policy

toggle caption i Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images

The Supreme Court ruled Wednesday that the Trump administration must continue providing gender-affirming care to transgender inmates in federal prisons.

The decision, in an emergency appeal, maintains a lower court's injunction on a federal Bureau of Prisons' policy that would terminate hormone therapy and other treatments for trans inmates.

The unsigned order offered no explanation behind the decision. It simply read, "The application for stay presented to The Chief Justice and by him referred to the Court is denied."

It also said Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito would side with the Trump administration and would grant the application for stay.

Sponsor Message

As the federal judge's injunction remains in place, the legal battle over the policy continues.

In January 2025, upon assuming office, Trump issued an executive order banning the use of federal funds that "promote" gender ideology. And prisoners brought a class action seeking reinstatement of the decades-long health policy. It contends that the Trump policy violates the Eighth Amendment's ban on cruel and unusual punishment.

A federal district judge barred the BOP from implementing its policy this summer.

A second court, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, also rejected the administration's request to pause U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth's order.

That's when U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the Supreme Court to intervene.

As the federal judge's injunction remains in place, the legal battle over the policy continues.

Li Nowlin-Sohl, senior staff attorney at the American Civil Liberties Union and a lawyer involved in this case, said the organization believes there are more than 2,000 people in BOP custody who identify as transgender. (The BOP stopped publishing data reflecting transgender inmates after Trump took office in 2025. It only records male or female individuals incarcerated in the federal system.)

Kingdom v. Trump represents 1,000 inmates who have a gender dysphoria diagnosis, Nowlin-Sohl explained. Of those, the ACLU believes there are about 800 who have been prescribed hormone therapy and many who are also receiving social transition accommodations, Nowlin-Sohl said.

Sponsor Message

In its request for an emergency stay on the earlier rulings, the Trump administration argued that providing this care poses several risks, including for recipients of this specialized care, who it argued would become "targets for attacks." They also said that it raises "fairness concerns" as it would "breed resentment" with other inmates.

Access to gender-affirming care is considered medically necessary to treat gender dysphoria, a medical term used to describe the deep discomfort caused by a mismatch between a person's assigned sex at birth and their gender identity. Without it, individuals can struggle severely with mental health issues such as heightened anxiety and depression, with some turning to self-harm and suicide.

Gender-affirming care can include "...hormone therapy, and gender-affirming surgeries among others," according to the World Professional Association for Transgender Health. (In its filings, the Trump administration questioned WPATH's standards of care, which were developed by experts in transgender health and used by organizations across the world.)

Some people who are transgender may require hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgeries; others may not require any of these interventions.

The BOP has treated people diagnosed with gender dysphoria since at least 1992, the ACLU said in response to the government's filings to the Supreme Court.

"Had BOP's doctors found this treatment unhelpful or harmful to patients or had the agency found that the treatment compromised security, surely BOP would have mentioned it in the administrative record," the ACLU wrote.

This is a "glaring omission" and appears to indicate that the government's arguments now are simply "contrived," the ACLU continued.

NPR previously covered the impact of the loss of hormone treatments on people who are incarcerated. One woman said she experienced severe physical and mental anguish when she lost access to hormone treatments.

The Supreme Court's decision is at odds with other rulings that support the Trump administration's anti-trans policy agenda.

Sponsor Message

Last June, the court ruled that states can ban transgender girls from participating in sports at publicly funded schools. And in 2025, the court upheld state laws that make it illegal for doctors and other health professionals to provide gender-affirming care for minors.

In one of his first executive orders of his second term, President Trump targeted the trans community with a declaration that his administration recognizes just two sexes, male and female. This order has been the basis for a host of anti-trans policies throughout the administration.

But at least for now, the emergency request on the prison policy was to no avail.

Waiting in the wings at the Supreme Court are other cases on transgender rights. Most prominently, the Alliance Defending Freedom, an anti-trans group, has filed an emergency petition at the court on behalf of a mother and her teenage daughter who contend that the daughter was "unknowingly" forced to face a transgender opponent in girl's high school wrestling. Later this year, the court will hear oral arguments in a case testing whether a religious preschool can receive state funding while excluding LGBTQ families. In a separate case, the justices will examine whether parents have the right to challenge a state law that allows runaway teens to receive gender-affirming care without parental consent.

NPR Legal Affairs Correspondent Nina Totenberg contributed reporting.

World.title: New human data hints at psychedelics' potential to combat inflammation
World.content:
New human data hints at psychedelics' potential to combat inflammation

toggle caption i Cannabis-Pic/Getty Images

Efforts to understand how classic psychedelics like psilocybin and LSD summon powerful changes in consciousness tend to focus on what's happening inside our head.

That's because these compounds bind tightly to serotonin receptors that densely populate certain structures of the brain, and a growing number of studies demonstrate they can exert long-lasting changes in mental health and well-being for people with a range of psychiatric conditions.

Increasingly researchers have started to probe how these drugs elicit other physiological changes, given that many cells and tissues beyond the brain possess those same receptors, known as 5-HT2A.

Sponsor Message

Now, new research offers some of the first evidence in humans that psychedelics may also hold potential for treating diseases characterized by inflammation and immune dysregulation throughout the body.

The data, published Wednesday in the medical journal JAMA Psychiatry, draws from a small pool of patients with Parkinson's disease, but it reflects what's been observed in lab studies with animal and cell models for years. For certain diseases, psychedelics appear to combat inflammation and even help restore stressed mitochondria, the energy-producing factories of the cells.

The team at the University of California, San Francisco, who conducted the study, used blood tests to measure five different signaling molecules involved in inflammation in participants, both before and after two sessions with psilocybin.

The participants had significantly lower levels of inflammation following the treatments, compared to baseline, and those changes persisted a month after their final dose of psilocybin. The researchers also tracked a blood marker of mitochondrial stress. Here, too, there were substantial improvements immediately after participants were given psilocybin, though not during the longer-term follow up.

"This gives us an initial biological signal to investigate," says Dr. Ellen Bradley, an associate professor of psychiatry at UCSF who helped lead the analysis.

Sponsor Message

The findings were based on 12 participants in a pilot study to evaluate the feasibility and safety of giving psilocybin to people with Parkinson's disease. Patients with neurodegenerative conditions are typically excluded from trials on psychedelics and mental health for safety concerns.

The original study, which was published last year, assuaged researchers' concerns about the risks. Bradley says they found a "really promising safety profile" and that "symptoms even seemed to get a bit better."

The researchers emphasize that the study has limitations: they did not have a control group, and the participants knew they were receiving the drug. So the data on what was happening in their blood needs to be confirmed in follow-up studies before making definitive claims, says Aoife O'Donovan, a professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at UCSF and co-author of the paper.

Still, O'Donovan says the findings reflect "objective markers" that changed over time and that gives them confidence to pursue this line of research.

Parkinson's disease is characterized by dysregulated inflammation and mitochondrial dysfunction. This data, Bradley notes, could help explain why the participants appeared to benefit from the drugs during the trial.

Beyond that, the results raise the proposition that psychedelics may help address others diseases that are characterized by troubles with inflammation, says D. Parker Kelley, a research scientist in the Mitochondrial PsychoBiology group at Columbia University who was a first author on the paper with Bradley.

"It's a potential jumping off point for a lot more research in this area," he says, "that may apply not only to Parkinson's, but also neuropsychiatric disorders like depression and anxiety, and even cardio-metabolic and inflammatory disorders."

While previous studies have looked at biomarkers of inflammation after psilocybin, those have generally included healthy volunteers – not people with real disease, says Charles Nichols, a professor of pharmacology, biochemistry and experimental therapeutics at LSU Health Sciences Center in New Orleans.

Sponsor Message

"I think it's really exciting," says Nichols, who didn't work on the study, but whose lab discovered that certain psychedelics could have powerful anti-inflammatory effects about fifteen years ago.

That insight came from studying lab-grown cell culture that simulated inflammation of blood vessels and hardening of arteries, also known as atherosclerosis.

In that experiment, they found a psychedelic acting on the 5-H2TA receptors functioned as a "potent anti-inflammatory," even at doses well below what would cause a psychoactive trip, he says.

Since then, Nichols' group has run numerous experiments in animal models of disease including asthma, arthritis, and cardiovascular disease, but the field has needed to test whether these protective effects hold up in humans.

He says this new study in Parkinson's patients is a proof of principle.

"We can only draw so much from those conclusions," he says. "But I do think it validates a lot of the pharmacology that we've been doing over the last 15 years on the anti-inflammatory, the mitochondrial protective effects."

World.title: Sentenced to death at 17, at 68, quilt artist receives solo museum exhibition
World.content:
Sentenced to death at 17, at 68, quilt artist receives solo museum exhibition

toggle caption i Sea Stachura for NPR

Imagine living all of your adult life behind bars for a murder you didn't commit and being released at 58. You're also a fabric artist, and the Smithsonian has acquired one of your quilts. That's the story of Gary Tyler, and now, the artist has his first solo exhibit.

At the Grand Rapids Art Museum in Michigan, Gary Tyler points to a black-and-white quilt that's based on a photo.

"That's a picture that was taken by my brother back in [19]74," he says.

He was a 16-year-old with a flair for fashion, living in Louisiana. One school morning, he dressed in a body shirt with a sweater overtop. Then he added fingerless gloves and a bandana.

Sponsor Message

"This body shirt was the shirt and bandana that I had the day of the incident," he said.

By dinnertime, Tyler was arrested. A white 13-year-old had been shot and killed during anti-school-integration violence. Tyler was put in a police car for "mouthing off." The next thing he knew, local police arrested and charged him with murder. He couldn't believe the charges would stick. He was still wearing the same clothes a month later, when his brother snapped the photo.

"You're looking at the innocence of a young, of a teenager, adolescent, you know, and who's who's at loss and and not knowing … what's definitely ahead of him," he says of the image.

toggle caption i Sea Stachura for NPR

A divorce lawyer incompetently represented him. Four friends testified against him, then recanted their testimony. The judge instructed an all-white jury to assume the 16-year-old meant to kill multiple people. It then convicted and sentenced him to death. Tyler maintained his innocence.

At the time, he was the youngest person on death row. He was sent to the Louisiana State Penitentiary, also known as Angola, and placed in a form of solitary confinement. His story isn't unique, says Wanda Bertram with the Prison Policy Initiative.

"There are a ton of people in prison who have shocking stories to tell about the defense they received, especially if they were indigent, the coercion they experienced from police and prosecutors," Bertram says.

Sponsor Message

Louisiana has the highest rate of incarceration in the U.S. Globally, it's second only to El Salvador. It also has one of the lowest parole rates.

The Louisiana Board of Pardons and Committee on Parole recommended Tyler be pardoned three times. Each time, the state's governor refused.

Eric Seiferth says sentences are often extremely long, especially at Angola. Seiferth is a senior curator at the Historic New Orleans Collection, in the French Quarter. He's also one of the authors of Captive State: Louisiana and the Making of Mass Incarceration.

"There are just more and more and more people than ever before in the history of the state who have received life sentences … that have no option to ever come home. They're convicted to die," he says.

Tyler was at Angola, watching other men die behind bars. In the late '80s, he and others created a hospice program.

"Men in prison, taking care [of] terminally ill men to, you know, end of life, it had the way of really transforming you, changing you," Tyler says.

The group raised money for coffins by making and selling quilts. That's how Tyler learned the craft. One of his quilts was raffled off at the Angola Prison Rodeo, a biannual public event, and raised $30,000 for the hospice program. Seiferth's museum has one of them, The Tree of Life.

"It has the names and people, you know, it's basically made of people. Essentially, of human forms," Seiferth says.

toggle caption i Sea Stachura for NPR

toggle caption i Sea Stachura for NPR

Tyler never received a pardon. A 2016 U.S. Supreme Court ruling required states to resentence all people who had been given life without parole as juveniles. As a result, the St. Charles Parish District Attorney proposed resentencing Tyler for manslaughter. Tyler was desperate to get out of Angola, so he agreed and was released soon after. The St. Charles Parish District Attorney declined to comment for this story.

Sponsor Message

For Tyler, the terms of his release were another injustice. "The [criminal justice] system is unfairly administered, especially to the people of color and poor people in the United States. There are better ways of being able to adjudicate, or punish a person in prison humanely," he says.

Now Tyler's art honors those still locked up. He points to portrait quilts featuring the incarcerated men and women he met behind bars.

"Because when you see Sandra Stall, Trinidad, Big Toe, Mary, and Bertha, that's my way of showing moral and spiritual support," Tyler says.

Only Mary and Bertha have been released.

At the opening reception of the exhibit, Caton Vance is admiring Tyler's work.

"I think it mostly has to do with dealing with consequences that are beyond imagining and somehow, despite the environment, finding hope," Vance says.

The exhibit, "Gary Tyler: Rebirth," runs through Jan. 3.

World.title: U.S. Embassy says Carney government brushing off 'potential interference' in midterms
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The U.S. Embassy in Ottawa says the federal government is brushing off concerns about "potential interference in U.S. elections" after Prime Minister Mark Carney insisted that Canada is not getting involved in the American midterms.

U.S. officials have in recent weeks warned against what they describe as potential Canadian interference ahead of their Nov. 3 midterm elections.

In a release on Wednesday, the embassy suggested that the "Canadian government brushes off" the Trump administration's concerns. The release lists a number of statements by Ontario Premier Doug Ford, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and other officials as examples of attempts to influence the midterms.

Both Carney and Ford were asked about the embassy's statement during a news conference on Wednesday. Both denied that they're trying to sway the vote south of the border.

"The United States initiated a series of trade actions. We've responded to those to protect Canadian jobs, to protect Canadian companies and develop our economy," Carney said.

"All of our actions are in the interest of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy."

WATCH | Carney, Ford respond to election interference claims: Carney, Ford respond to Trump administration's election interference claims | Duration closed caption 1:49 Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded to a fact sheet sent out by the U.S. Embassy on Wednesday claiming Canadian politicians have plans to influence American politics. 'All of our actions are in the interest of Canadian workers,' said Carney.

Ford followed up by saying he has "no interest at all interfering in American elections."

"We're going to focus on what we can do here in Ontario and in Canada to make sure we protect our economy, protect the people and protect communities," the premier said.

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said last week that American officials are "closely watching" Canadian politicians for signs of election interference ahead of the midterms.

Hoekstra pointed to Joly's comments about the strategy behind Canadian counter-tariffs and the Ontario government's now infamous Ronald Reagan ad that ran in the U.S. last year.

WATCH | Trade war a major issue in midterms: Canada-U.S. trade war emerges as key issue ahead of U.S. midterms | Duration closed caption 2:18 The Canada-U.S. trade war is solidifying itself as a major ballot-box issue in pivotal states ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

Wednesday's embassy release listed a number of grievances that Hoekstra raised last week but also added more, including Canada's consul general in Boston, Bernadette Jordan, appearing at a Canada-U.S. trade event with Democratic candidates — as well Liberal MP Anthony Housefather canvassing for a Florida Democrat during a primary vote earlier this year.

About half of the instances listed on the embassy's release occurred in 2026, and a handful point to events from last year, including a federal government billboard campaign from early 2025.

The release also alleges "Canada has the second-highest total of prosecutions for fraudulent or illegal voting of any country," while listing 11 Canadians who have been charged for illegally voting in past U.S. elections.

According to the release, while the alleged offences took place between 2012 and 2024 — the 11 Canadians were all charged or sentenced this year.

Joly pushed back against Hoekstra's previous comments, telling reporters last week that Canada would never engage in election interference and would "never accept that also being done to us in Canada."

WATCH | Canada 'absolutely not' interfering, Joly says: Canada 'absolutely not' interfering in U.S. midterms, Joly says | Duration closed caption 1:19 Asked about the United States Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra's comments about watching for Canadian interference in the U.S. midterm elections, Minister of Industry Mélanie Joly says 'we never do that and we never accept that also being done to us in Canada.' She says her recent visits to the U.S. were 'to attract investments' by American companies and she will continue to do so.

Joly said she has been to the U.S. in recent months and has met with Democrats and Republicans.

Carney also told Global News last week that Canada doesn't "get ourselves involved in [foreign] elections."

Peter Navarro, one of Trump's top trade advisers, also suggested Canada could interfere in the midterms during an economic conference in Washington last month.

"The problem you have is you lobby this country and you've been successful in the past and you think you can keep doing that," Navarro said of Canada's approach to trade talks.

"Memo to Canada: You cannot do that. That game is up and if you interfere in our elections in Maine or Michigan you will pay even more dearly."

WATCH | Trump adviser issues warning to Canada: 'You will pay': Trump adviser warns Canada not to 'interfere' with U.S. midterms | Duration closed caption 2:54 White House trade adviser Peter Navarro warned Canada not to 'interfere' with U.S. midterm elections in border states such as Maine and Michigan by lobbying against the Trump administration's tariffs. Navarro said Canada would 'pay even more dearly' for doing so.

The trade war has become a pressure point on Republican candidates running for the Senate in the two border states Navarro mentioned.

The Republican candidate for Michigan's open Senate seat released a new 30-second ad criticizing tariffs earlier this month.

"Here in Michigan we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now," Mike Rogers says in the ad.

Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who has represented Maine since 1997, has also tried to distance herself from Trump's tariffs.

The Globe and Mail reported recently that Republican political operatives were on the ground in Alberta earlier this year to help the separatist campaign. CBC News previously reported that Alberta separatists also attended meetings in U.S. State Department offices in Washington, D.C., last year.

Since returning to the White House, U.S. President Donald Trump has made a number of public statements backing candidates in various countries, including Argentina and Hungary.

World.title: Canada's Russian envoy returns with advice on how to hit back against Putin
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's outgoing ambassador to Russia has returned with advice for crafting a response to Moscow's "cognitive warfare" campaign against the NATO alliance and why keeping sanctions on oil and gas can frustrate Vladimir Putin's struggle to finance his war machine.

Sarah Taylor's three-year tour of duty in Moscow, which ended Oct. 8, was defined by the Russian president's invasion of Ukraine from her first day in the country to her last, and that conflict, she says in a rare interview with CBC News, has all but returned the country to a Cold War mentality.

Taylor says that while many in NATO, particularly in Europe, worry about a conventional invasion of their territory by Russia, she doesn't see that happening "at least in the short to medium term."

"But I do think already we are effectively under attack in a form of cognitive warfare and we maybe don't really realize just how bad that is," she told CBC Radio's The Current, in an interview that aired on Wednesday.

LISTEN | Outgoing ambassador to Russia on life in Moscow: The Current 19:08 Outgoing ambassador to Russia on life in Moscow Longtime diplomat Sarah Taylor has just wrapped up nearly three years on the ground in Moscow as Canada's ambassador to Russia, her final posting before retirement. She speaks with Matt Galloway about her conversations with Russian citizens and officials as the war in Ukraine continues, and the cognitive warfare she warns is already underway.

Taylor says Russia's use of propaganda is widespread and effective because it uses its knowledge of how the West works and key language skills to ensure its campaigns will have maximum impact.

She says the large Russian dissident community, including independent journalists, that are now outside Russia could be an effective counteroffensive on the cognitive battlefield.

"I think part of Putin's power lies in an ability to sort of project inevitability and to say, 'Well, you know, it'll always be Putin and only Putin. And this is just the way it is,'" she told host Matt Galloway.

"To have an active, open discussion that's going on, particularly if some of it is in Russian and can filter back into Russia to say, 'No, Russia doesn't have to be like this. There are alternative futures.' That's really important."

Another vulnerability Taylor sees is Putin's ongoing struggle to fund Russia's war machine.

"One of their weaknesses in this war is financing it," Taylor said. "It's become a hugely expensive undertaking for them, lasting much longer than the Russians expected … and part of the way they are funding this is through their sales of oil and gas."

Frustrating Putin's war machine

She says that while some sanctions on Russia are more symbolic in nature, such as the ones targeting people who "visibly support the war," others have a deeper strategic impact — like those on oil and gas, which U.S. President Donald Trump has moved to lift with his recent diesel deal with Putin.

"I do believe, personally, that it's very important to try and maintain those as much as possible because the more you do that, the more you increase the dilemma for the Russian government about how they are going to fund this war going forward," she said.

While the cost of invading Ukraine has been steep for the Russian government, Taylor says the state has "made a huge effort to make life feel as normal as possible" in cities like Moscow and St. Petersburg.

That reality held largely true, she says, until the last six months when Ukraine began targeting oil refineries, the warehouses of Russian e-commerce giants Wildberries and Ozon that some call the "Russian Amazon" and more recently, large data centres.

Smoke billows into the sky following Ukrainian drone strikes on warehouses of Russia's online retailer Wildberries, in St. Petersburg, Russia, in July. (The Associated Press)

"Those are starting to have an impact, a bit more impact on daily life," she said. "It's obviously nothing like what, say, our colleagues in Kyiv are living every day … but it does feel like you're in the middle of a Cold War."

While admitting she did not mix with a "completely representative sample of Russians" while serving in Moscow, she says support for the war is paper thin.

"I have yet to meet a single ordinary Russian who was enthusiastic about the war. And most of them just want it to end, really," she said.

But wanting, and having the capacity to do something to feed that want, are very different, she says.

"The vast majority of people who have in any way either demonstrated against the war, or even … supported Ukraine by making donations or anything of that sort are now almost all in jail," she said.

"It's very telling that there are now as many, if not more … political prisoners in Russian jails than there were in the Khrushchev era of the Soviet Union. So we're really back to a Soviet-like feeling of repression, of dissent."

World.title: El Niño breaks warming records in the Pacific Ocean, foreshadowing more extreme weather to come, UN says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The El Niño weather pattern could cause a record rise in ocean temperatures in the Pacific as it barrels ‌around the globe like a "wrecking ball" causing floods and droughts, UN officials said on Wednesday.

The new World Meteorological Organization (WMO) seasonal outlook predicted the El Niño event would become extremely strong, ​with temperatures in the central Pacific rising about ​3.8 C above normal between November and January, peaking around December.

"We have not seen in our records 3.8. We ​have seen around [3 C] in some record El Niños before, ⁠with very substantive ⁠impacts across the world. So we ‌are beyond that limit," WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said.

Celeste Saulo, World Meteorological Organization secretary-general, is warning of record temperatures during this El Niño. (Sergei Grits/The Associated Press)

El Niño is the warm phase of the naturally occurring El Niño-Southern Oscillation cycle — a climate pattern that influences weather around the world. It tends to ⁠cause higher global temperatures and disrupt rainfall patterns across large regions, meaning drought in some areas and heavy rains in others.

It is a natural climate ‌pattern and is not caused by climate change. However, global warming can make El Niños more intense because the baseline temperature is already higher.

El Niño-linked weather extremes could worsen pressure on housing, water, sanitation and health services, with flooding risks rising ​in southern Africa from November, the WMO said.

In Southeast Asia, warmer conditions and a ⁠lack of rainfall could impact agriculture and water supplies, while Latin America could ⁠see increased rainfall, according to the WMO.

The WMO and the UN ⁠under-secretary-general ⁠for humanitarian affairs and emergency ​relief coordinator, Tom Fletcher, called for urgent action to get ready.

"This El Niño ​is the behemoth, it ⁠is a wrecking ball. It will tear through Latin America, Eastern and Southern Africa, Asia and the Pacific with extreme heat, droughts and flood," Fletcher said, warning of massive humanitarian consequences.

Some 50 million people could face increased hunger, he ⁠said.

World.title: Alberta premier says UCP must be pro-Canada, separatists can 'join a different party'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Premier Danielle Smith says separatist UCP members should support the will of Albertans who voted to remain in Canada or leave the party.

That desire was clear in the results of Monday’s referendum, she told reporters at a news conference in Calgary Wednesday. She echoed the sentiment from her video message sent to UCP members earlier in the day.

“For those few who cannot reconcile this fact and remain intent on dividing and turning our party into a vehicle for the independence movement, I would respectfully invite them to join a different party,” Smith said in the video.

She said at Wednesday's news conference that she knows there are a lot of "hurt feelings," referencing those who voted to support the province holding a second, binding referendum on separation. But she said now is the time for them to recalibrate.

"You get to have your say, but you don’t always get to have your way.”

In the Wednesday video, Smith said she expects that, going forward, the UCP will be pro-Canada.

"The United Conservative Party is not an independence party," Smith said.

Smith said the party needs to be clear that "a strong Alberta within a united Canada is the position of our party and our government."

The premier said party members can hold whatever views they wish but candidates running under the UCP banner must be committed to the party's position.

Smith said the UCP also expects members of the provincial board and constituency boards to uphold the party's position on separatism. Smith said the party needs to focus its efforts on beating the NDP in the next election.

UCP legislature member Jason Stephan, who publicly said he was voting for a second binding referendum, announced Monday as referendum polls closed that he won't seek re-election.

Smith said Wednesday that Stephan decided to walk away on his own, and that she supported his decision.

University of Calgary political scientist Lisa Young said Smith drawing a line with party members could suggest the premier is concerned she can't win over Calgary or Edmonton voters unless the separation issue is stamped out.

"She clearly thinks that she's in trouble," Young said.

She said Smith has been successful as UCP leader because she is skilled at placating party members no matter their position.

"If you dance with the one that brung you, these are the ones that brung her," she said.

Referendum results

As of Wednesday morning, results are still trickling in on the 10-question referendum.

While CBC projected Monday night that Albertans strongly favour remaining in Canada, the results of other questions are too close to call.

Smith previously said that she would seek “majority rule,” meaning a 50 per cent-plus-one threshold, to act on the first nine questions, which deal with immigration and constitutional issues.

The five questions that focused on immigration seem to give the Alberta government a clear mandate to take greater control, she said, adding that other provinces share the sentiment and Prime Minister Mark Carney is “accepting the will of Albertans.”

"I think we're about to have a very honest discussion about returning to the kind of immigration system that worked and served us well for so many years, which is prioritizing economic migrants."

Cross Country Checkup is asking: A majority of Albertans voted in favour of non permanent Canadian residents paying an access fee for health care. What do you think? Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for this Sunday's show.

Smith said her government will look to Quebec’s 1991 accord for inspiration on how to share responsibility for decisions about who gets to move to Alberta and how many — "to make sure we're matching newcomers with the jobs that are here."

New legislation could be introduced in the spring, she said.

Smith said that the results show a divide between urban and rural voters, and that the constitutional questions are less of a priority overall.

"There's a reason to be skeptical that some constitutional amendments would be worth the effort," she said. "What I'm seeing is that Albertans would rather we spend our time focusing on things where we can make meaningful change."

Full referendum results are expected by Wednesday night.

World.title: Canadian government sites among those offline after flaw identified in widely used computer language
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Numerous websites, including Canadian government sites, went offline Wednesday in order to implement a fix after vulnerabilities were found in PHP, a widely used programming language.

PHP developers on Wednesday released urgent new fixes to vulnerabilities in their software, and encouraged website operators to implement the solution as soon as possible.

"If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now," the PHP Foundation said in a news release.

Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon said some federal government websites had been taken offline temporarily as a "precautionary measure," and urged organizations whose websites run on PHP to implement the security update.

"We are taking this situation extremely seriously," Solomon said in a post on social media. "The affected websites will be brought back online as soon as the fixes have been applied."

The websites for the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and Statistics Canada website appeared to be down for a period of time on Wednesday when CBC News attempted to access them.

The Newfoundland and Labrador government site was offline on Wednesday following a newly disclosed cybersecurity vulnerability. Multiple Canadian government sites were down on Wednesday because of the vulnerability. (CBC)

Provincial sites for Newfoundland and Labrador and Prince Edward Island were also offline, displaying messages saying the shutdown was due to a global security incident. The site for Elections B.C. was also down on Wednesday, the last day of advance voting before Saturday's provincial election.

Wikipedia, Cloudflare and Maple Health also addressed security vulnerabilities in PHP on Wednesday.

Vulnerability uncovered by AI

PHP is a language that dates back to the early 1990s and initially stood for "Personal Home Page." It underpins huge parts of the public-facing web and is baked into sites like WordPress, ​Drupal, Joomla and Magento.

When a visitor loads a page that uses PHP, a server running the language assembles the content and sends it to the browser. ⁠It is free, open source software, maintained by volunteers.

PHP is widely used across the internet — running roughly 75 per cent of websites whose programming language can be identified, according to web technology tracker W3Techs.

"When it comes to PHP in particular, that is foundational to the internet," said Ritesh Kotak, a Toronto-based cybersecurity and tech analyst.

Because of that, he says many websites are vulnerable to hacks until the fix is implemented, making the scale of the situation "absolutely scary."

Kotak said that bigger companies and organizations with large IT teams will be able to implement the fix more quickly, but says medium or small ones will be vulnerable for longer or may struggle to implement the fix because they don't have the same resources.

In a blog post, Alphabet-owned cybersecurity company Wiz also said it discovered the flaw in PHP using artificial intelligence.

WATCH | How AI hacked the Australian government and almost got away with it: How AI hacked the Australian government and almost got away with it | About That | Duration 2:58 OpenAI says one of its models, while in testing, went rogue and hacked an official Australian government website in a security breach that went undetected for months. Andrew Chang explains what we know about the hack and why Australian authorities say the manner in which they learned about the incident was 'entirely inadequate.' Images provided by The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images

The company said the vulnerable code had been present for more than a decade, and that they used multiple large language models to find the vulnerability and validate the patch for the problem while working with OpenAI on discovery and patching. They also co-ordinated with Automattic, AWS, Microsoft and others on the rollout of the patch, so they could give guidance to customers that cannot implement the fix immediately.

PHP Foundation said a possible exploit for one of the vulnerabilities was first "theorized" in 2024, but the foundation explained to CBC News in an email that each of the solutions it came up with caused new problems. A lack of resources and other issues taking precedence led to the delay in fixing the problem, according to PHP.

Kotak says while AI helped in this case to find the vulnerabilities and fix them, it can also be used by hackers to find those weak points and exploit them.

"With [AI], you could have thousands of hackers using the latest and greatest tools and knowledge that is out there going out and trying to get into systems and infiltrate databases," Kotak said.

For that reason, he expects to see more cybersecurity incidents in the future.

Elsewhere around the world, cybersecurity agencies in Europe, Australia, Japan and Britain also urged PHP users to make the fix, while governments in France, the Netherlands and other European countries proactively took their websites offline to make the fix.

World.title: Airbnb limiting the checkout chores hosts can ask guests to do
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As of late next month, guests staying in an Airbnb will have fewer chores to do before they check out after their stay.

The short-term rental company has updated its policies to restrict how much cleaning hosts can ask guests to undertake before they leave.

Here's what to know about the new rules, which apply to bookings made on or after Nov. 20.

What does the new policy say about cleaning?

The new guidelines, in short, asks hosts to "be reasonable" on a number of fronts.

When it comes to tidying up, hosts will no longer be allowed to ask guests to do any tasks that would take "significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner."

These jobs include stripping the bed, taking the garbage to an offsite location or washing and putting away used dishes.

With the change, Airbnb's cleaning fee should only cover a basic tidy-up between guests — and hosts are no longer allowed to charge guests if they don't finish a cleaning job on the checkout list.

Why now?

Airbnb cleaning duties have long been a topic of debate.

Hosts have shared stories about the messes guests left behind, while some post TikTok videos where they "reveal" the state of a property after checkout. On the other hand, guests have complained for years about paying a cleaning fee when they end up with a list of chores to do themselves .

"The biggest gripe that guests tend to have is around the cleaning aspects," said Makarand Mody, an associate professor who teaches at Boston University's School of Hospitality Administration.

"There was this discord between the fact that hosts were charging you cleaning fees and then you still have to follow house rules where you have to clean up, which is not how we as travellers experience the hotel."

CBC News has contacted Airbnb about the timing of its change.

WATCH | More travellers trading homes instead of paying for short-term rentals: Home swapping on the rise as Canadians try to cut travel costs | Duration closed caption 2:11

What else does the policy say?

On top of the information around cleaning, the guidelines says hosts will not be allowed to restrict use of amenities advertised in their listing. They won't be able to charge guests fines or penalties, either, because AirCover already protects hosts "in the rare event that their place or belongings are damaged by a guest."

House rules and requests will have to be visible on the listing for guests at the time of booking, and no new rules or requests can be added after the fact. These rules include information around check-in and check-out times, smoking, pets, quiet hours, the number of approved guests and commercial photography or video.

But hosts will be able to add "reasonable" requests, which can be updated at any time. The policy said Airbnb will assess whether a request fits within that definition based on a number of factors, like the type of listing and local context.

"We understand every home is unique," it reads. "For example, it may be reasonable to ask guests to limit shower time due to local drought-related water restrictions, or to dispose of trash in an animal-proof container in bear country."

Mody said he's interested to see how hosts respond to the change and how Airbnb enforces the new rules. He believes the company deliberately left the definition of "reasonable" open-ended to give hosts some wiggle room.

"Hosts are also their customers. They want hosts to have a good experience, to want to keep listing on Airbnb and to feel like they still have control over the property," the professor said. "And that Airbnb is not going completely, you know, guest-centric in that sense."

World.title: Carney, Ford announce $8.7B partnership to support steel, auto, critical mineral sectors
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Alongside Ontario Premier Doug Ford, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced an $8.7-billion support package for steel, critical mineral and auto sectors on Wednesday.

Ford said the federal-provincial agreement "will protect workers in key provincial industries from tariffs and will pave the way for new good-paying jobs" across Ontario.

The partnership with the Ontario government earmarks $2.5 billion over two years for the province's auto industry to build the "connected and electric vehicles of the future."

Ottawa is providing $1.5 billion of the auto funding, with Ontario providing the remaining $1 billion.

The support for auto companies comes at a time of uncertainty caused by the trade war with the United States.

"An integrated North American auto sector will be stronger, more competitive and provide better jobs for our workers," Carney said. "But we recognize these are not the objectives of the current U.S. administration. Their approach has changed, and so must ours."

WATCH | Carney announces plan with Ford: Carney and Ford announce $9B plan to 'protect' Ontario jobs | Duration closed caption 1:10 Standing with Ontario Premier Doug Ford, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Wednesday that new investments in Ontario's Ring of Fire critical minerals projects, the steel sector and the auto sector will protect up to 290,000 jobs across the province.

In August, U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to increase tariffs on all cars, trucks, auto parts and steel to 50 per cent on Jan. 1. That threat came after Carney announced he was retaliating with matching dollar-for-dollar tariffs on American goods.

The U.S. is already hitting finished vehicles and non-CUSMA-compliant auto parts imported to the U.S. with 25 per cent levies.

"Ontario and Canada are being challenged right now," Ford said. "We see it in every corner of our province where tariffs and trade uncertainty are leaving workers and their families worried."

Also in the joint package, Ottawa is easing greenhouse gas regulations as U.S. tariffs pressure Canada's automotive sector.

Canada's emissions standards are now set to flatline until 2030 — maintaining 2026 levels for new light-duty vehicles through the 2029 model year. Annual increases are set to resume in the 2030 model year.

Ottawa initially proposed increasing emissions standards from 2026 through 2035 to reach its goal of 75 per cent EV sales by 2035.

Brian Kingston, president of the Canadian Vehicle Manufacturers' Association, says the step will provide "some relief" to the auto industry.

"By pausing the regulation and flatlining to 2030, it gives companies some flexibility as they deal with a much more significant threat, which is of course U.S. tariffs," Kingston said.

At the same time, Evan Pivnick, associate director of public affairs at Clean Energy Canada, said the change is a setback for the government's EV sales targets.

Pivnick said that even though Carney acknowledges a global shift toward EV adoption, "the policies that are meant to help ensure Canadians are able to access a larger share are just delayed."

Ottawa's loosened emissions standards come after the Trump administration made similar changes on Monday.

The U.S. finalized rolling back fuel economy standards for new vehicles, reversing policies meant to boost fuel efficiency and promote using electric vehicles.

Because of the Canadian auto industry's close integration with the U.S., Kingston says Canada needs to remain "relatively closely aligned" with its southern neighbour on that front.

"We cannot diverge significantly from the United States if we intend to have an industry of the size and scale we have right now in Canada," Kingston said.

The Carney government is aiming to have three out of every four new vehicles sold in Canada to be electric by 2035. (Doug Ives/The Canadian Press)

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said on her way into a caucus meeting on Wednesday that the government wants to continue to provide support to auto companies impacted by the Trump administration's reversal in regulations.

"A lot of our auto producers have been deeply impacted, not only by the American tariffs but indeed by the fact that the American administration has decided to reduce massively its different protection regarding GHG emissions," Joly said.

Carney said Canada's imperative to invest in cleaner auto technologies is "reinforced by the radical transformation of the global auto sector" toward lower emissions, greater connectivity and more advanced manufacturing.

Carney said the investment is "the next major step forward" in positioning Canada as a global leader in EV production.

Measures for steel, critical minerals

The federal-provincial partnership also launches a $5-billion Joint Steel Action Fund — $3.55 billion from Ottawa and $1.67 billion from Ontario, both over five years.

Carney said the investment will allow steel mills to upgrade their machinery, manufacture more products that Canada needs and expand to meet demand from markets other than the U.S.

"When Canadian projects need specialized steel, they can increasingly count on Canadian mills, and Canadian steelworkers, to supply it," Carney said.

Ottawa is also setting out $1 billion over three years to match Ontario's investment toward building a road to reach the mineral-rich Ring of Fire region.

Ontario has been trying to get the federal government to help pay for and speed up development of the Ring of Fire.

Ford has called mining critical minerals in this area an "ace in the hole" that could help give Canada leverage against American tariffs.

Carney said Ottawa and Ontario are creating a co-ordinated process for federal and provincial permitting to open mines. Carney said the process for opening a mine in Ontario has historically taken over 15 years.

World.title: Ontario man convicted in U.S. terror probe gets additional 50-year prison sentence
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Mississauga man serving a 40-year sentence for terror-related charges in the U.S. was sentenced to an additional 50 years in federal prison for assaulting two corrections officers, the U.S. Attorney's Office announced Monday.

Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy, 28, pleaded guilty last November to multiple counts of assault, assault with intent to commit murder, possession of contraband inside a prison and providing material support to ISIS, according to a news release from the Middle District of Pennsylvania attorney's office.

The charges are related to a 2020 incident at a federal prison in Pennsylvania, where El Bahnasawy attacked two corrections officers using a weapon made from part of a steel desk in his cell, according to the news release. He stabbed one officer in the head and face and another officer in the hand when they intervened, it said.

The first officer lost his right eye as a result of the attack, the release said.

The release goes on to say that after El Bahnasawy was restrained, a note was "found in his sock" that read, "this is a terrorist attack for the Islamic State."

A pledge of allegiance to the Islamic State of Iraq and ISIS was also found in his prison cell, according to the release.

“Today’s sentence will further ensure that Bahnasawy remains in prison, where he can do much less harm, for a very long time,” John A. Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for national security, said in the release.

In his sentencing submission for the 2020 assaults, El Bahnasawy submitted a letter in which he said he was 'deeply sorry' for the incident. (bringabdulhome.ca)

El Bahnasawy expressed remorse after assault

In his sentencing submission for the 2020 assaults, El Bahnasawy submitted a letter, dated Oct. 15, in which he said he was "deeply sorry" for the incident.

"If I had been mentally well and able to think clearly, this would never have happened," he said. El Bahnasawy noted he's had mental health problems for years and struggled with being held in solitary confinement without "the right medication and care."

"All I can do now is stay committed to medication and treatment and prevent further harm. When I receive my medication, I am calmer and think clearly," his letter said.

In an interview with CBC News, El Bahnasawy's parents, Khdiga Metwally and Osama El Bahnasawy, said they couldn't sleep for "a week" after hearing about the incident.

"We don't support any type of violence," Osama said.

"I was crying for the guard, I was crying for my son," Metwally said.

History of mental health issues: court documents

In 2018, El Bahnasawy was sentenced to 40 years in U.S. federal prison after pleading guilty to terror charges.

His indictment detailed seven charges in relation to a 2016 plot to carry out "terrorist acts in and around New York City," which included plans to detonate bombs across the city's subway network and a car bomb in Times Square.

El Bahnasawy was 18 years old when he pleaded guilty. None of the attacks were carried out.

Sentencing memorandums filed by both the state and the defence acknowledge that he faced mental health and addiction issues. Both documents also state he was radicalized online.

Prior to El Bahnasawy's initial arrest, he was diagnosed with severe bipolar disorder and addiction problems and he had stopped taking his medication, his parents told CBC in 2021.

El Bahnasawy, right, with his father and mother. El Bahnasawy's family has been calling on his return to Canada to serve his prison sentence, citing a lack of mental health support and appropriate medication in U.S. prison. (bringabdulhome.ca)

In his 2018 judgment, New York District Judge Richard M. Berman recommended he be sent to a prison that has "greater proximity to mental health services" and is close to his family in Ontario.

That judgment also noted the court "does not oppose a treaty transfer to Canada."

Experts, family call for transfer to Canadian prison

El Bahnasawy's family, along with U.S. experts , have been calling for his transfer to a Canadian prison due to his mental health for the better part of a decade.

He is currently serving his sentence at The Administrative Maximum Facility (ADX) Florence , a supermaximum security prison designed to hold the United States' most dangerous prisoners and known for its solitary confinement conditions.

Metwally and her husband said they last saw their son in September, with Metwally saying it was "heartbreaking" to see him in an isolated environment where he can't get "full" mental health care.

The family is currently embroiled in a legal battle involving the RCMP and Canada's Director of Public Prosecutions to make the case for his transfer to Canada.

In an emailed statement Tuesday, Corrections Canada said it could not comment on specific cases but all applications "for an offender's international transfer are carefully considered."

Andrew Frisch, a New York attorney who's been representing El Bahnasawy in the U.S. since 2017, said he's "essentially" been prosecuted for his psychotic episodes by the U.S justice system.

"When you take a step back and look at the full context of the case and what's happened, it's just at odds with international consensus about mental illness and it's inhumane," he said.

CBC News has reached out to the U.S. Department of Justice for comment.
