World.title: Doha diary: A historian amid the Iran war
World.content:
(Renowned historian and author, Rila Mukherjee, was scheduled to fly from the USA to India by Qatar Airways [QA] on February 25, 2026. Her route—Shreveport–Dallas Fort Worth–Doha–Kolkata—was expected to bring her to Kolkata on the night of February 26 or in the early hours of February 27. However, as of March 8, she was still stranded in Doha. Qatar’s skies were closed due to the US-Israeli attack on Iran. QA’s commercial flights were suspended. At the time of writing, evacuation flights to India were scheduled to start soon. She reached home on 12 March.)

Today is 8 March. I am now camping out in Doha for the ninth day since 28 February. The Qatar airspace is shut and padlocked. The authorities have thrown away the key. Limited numbers of passengers are being flown to Europe and the Americas on evacuation flights (they are called ‘relief flights’) organised by QA, and relief flights to Africa and Asia will start from tomorrow. But for the time being, I am effectively marooned in Doha.

Doha is one of the largest airplane hubs in the world, and a cosmopolitan group of transit passengers has been put up by QA in the 4-star The Royal Riviera Hotel. The hotel is situated on Doha’s Corniche. It is an ageing hotel; not terribly posh, and the plumbing is a bit iffy. But it is well located, with comfortable rooms, and it is a clean and friendly hotel. I feel safe here. Its staff is composed of Asians (from Bangladesh, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, Nepal), North Africans (Algerians and Moroccans mostly) and some West Asians. All of them are helpful despite the pressures they are facing. They deal gracefully with the diverse demands and complaints of the passengers.

My room faces the Corniche and I can see the Persian Gulf from my window. As a maritime historian, this makes me very happy.

This country and its national airline are looking after us very well and, really, I have no complaints. QA’s representatives visit the hotel twice daily. There is no information forthcoming on my evacuation to Kolkata, and the greater part of passenger bags are still to arrive at the hotel. My South African neighbour says one of their bags has not been delivered; perhaps it is lost.

We are largely dependent on the clothes we have on our backs and those we had in our carry-on. Most of us are washing and drying them overnight. We have to use the hair dryer if they are still not dry.

My bags came in today, i.e., 8 March.

There are some elderly travellers. Many of them say that their medicines are running out. Mine will last another week.

Will I be able to get out by then?

We are told that a limited air corridor may open today; alternatively, we may be evacuated by the land route through Saudi Arabia to Riyadh (this would take around seven hours), where a leased QA aircraft may take us to India. But we have to make our own arrangements for the Saudi e-visa and overland travel. This seems a risky enterprise. And whether this potential leased aircraft would fly me direct to Kolkata is not known. There is no clarity to date.

***

But if I was scheduled to arrive in Kolkata on 27 February (and the war broke out a day later, on 28 February), how is it that I am still in Doha

Ah, thereby hangs a tale!

It is a cautionary tale on buying air tickets with multiple connections, and what ensues when the first connection does not take off as per schedule.

***

I had spent nine weeks in Shreveport with my son and daughter-in-law and was scheduled to leave on 25 February. Unfortunately, my flight from Shreveport to Dallas Fort Worth (DFW) by QA’s codeshare partner American Airlines (AA) did not take off. We were told that the incoming flight had nose gear problems and therefore could not land. Ultimately it made an emergency landing. Fire engines, firefighters, EMTs and ambulances were standing by. Luckily, there was no fireball and there were no casualties. The vice-chair of my daughter-in-law’s department was on that flight; I bumped into him in the terminal as he deplaned, and he said that the landing had been really scary.

There were no more AA flights to DFW that day. Roo and Stephanie came back to the airport and took me home. I spent a restless night. I hate flying at the best of times.

I was put on the same AA flight the next day, on 26 February, but when I reached DFW I was told that my connection flight to Doha was full. Apparently, the AA staff at Shreveport Regional Airport knew there were no seats on that flight; nevertheless they sent me on to DFW hoping I would ‘sort out’ the matter with AA’s customer care there. The only ‘sorting out’ that AA did at DFW was to put me on a later QA flight to Doha on the same day, that is, late evening on 26 February. It was a smaller aircraft (not the Airbus 350 on which I was ticketed), the flight was cramped and some of my co-passengers were not very well behaved. One lady kept on drinking; she skipped the meal service and was quite abusive. Another one, African American, told me that as an ‘American’ she was superior to Asians. Right, I thought, we all know how you as a Black person got there!!!

In all my years of travelling I have never encountered such blatant racism.

When we reached Doha very late on the night of 27 February (almost 24 hours later due to the time difference with DFW), I had missed that evening’s flight to Kolkata!

No problem, QA’s customer care said, we’ll talk with AA as it is their problem. This took a while, so I went off to buy myself a snack at Brioche Dorée in the airport’s food court.

By then it was early morning on 28 February.

Readers, note the date!

***

AA agreed to comp me a room for the remainder of the night at The Royal Riviera Hotel. I was granted a 48-hour emergency visa by Qatar Immigration and I was shifted to the hotel on 28 February at 2 AM. QA’s ground staff helped me throughout. The room was comfortable, the bed looked inviting, and I went to sleep, confident that my Kolkata flight would take off as scheduled at 18.45 hours on that day itself (that is, 28 February). At that point, I was going to reach only 24 hours behind my original schedule.

I informed Kolkata and asked my driver to collect me from the airport accordingly.

***

On 28 February, I was woken around 8 AM by a strange sound from my cell phone. It was a very loud, continuous screech. I don’t have international roaming and I wondered who was calling me and what was happening. I saw a ‘Security Alert’ on my screen but the text was in Arabic. I started hearing thuds and bangs. Another alert, still in Arabic, came in.

What was going on? I was mystified.

I was now getting alerts in English. It said the US and Israel had jointly attacked Iran. US bases and embassies and consulates across the Gulf were vulnerable. Qatar was in this critical area. Sirens were going off. I started watching Al Jazeera and Richard Engel on NBC.

This was Day 1.

Smoke rises following an explosion, after Israel and the US launched strikes on Iran, in Tehran, Iran, February 28, 2026. PHOTO: REUTERS

By Day 2, the Gulf was not just lying in a war zone; it had been converted into a theatre of war. Doha was undergoing regular drone strikes and missile attacks.

Day 3 was relatively quiet. Apparently, Qatar and Iran had a phone conversation, and Qatar urged Iran to stop the strikes. But our temporary visas were extended by Qatar. This was an indication that the phone call was not conclusive. This war was not going to end anytime soon.

The Qatar–Iran conversation does not seem to have yielded the desired result. There is no relief from Iranian attacks. These now form the backdrop to our daily life at The Royal Riviera. Drone attacks and missile strikes re-started from Day 4. None of them target the downtown area; they target only the US base and industrial areas in Qatar. Most of the drones and missiles are successfully intercepted; the few that are not cause localised fires. The attacks usually happen around breakfast and lunch, and sometimes they occur very late at night or in the early morning hours. This means we are always in a state of extreme alert. It is jarring on the nerves. We can neither eat properly nor rest. We are getting stressed out.

But I must also mention that the attacks and interceptions sound more like Diwali patakas than the very loud explosions that one expects.

*** Days 4 till 9 (that is, till date) have seen this regional war extending from land to sea: from the Hormuz Strait to the Indian Ocean. This is now becoming very serious. Critical choke points like this strait have become a curse. Ports across the Gulf are lying idle; almost no cargo is getting through. But we have had no alerts today. Does this mean that Iran will not strike Qatar for the time being? Is this a temporary reprieve? Will relief flights be able to take off? ***

Some bags arrived at the hotel on Day 5. Mine were not among them.

By Days 6 and 7 we have more or less settled into what is turning out to be our semi-permanent home. The hotel is no longer very ‘royal’; it has taken on the character of a London bedsit. Or a council housing estate in one of the UK’s inner cities! Children play noisy games in the corridors, an oddly comforting sound among the explosions, security alerts and sirens that go on regularly.

I see an enormous solidarity among the travellers, both on my floor and when we meet up at meal times. I have a very nice South African couple next door who check on me each morning, always asking how I am faring (‘please don’t hesitate to knock if you face any difficulties’). They have even offered to take me out to buy clothes (this was before my bags arrived). Elegant MENA (Middle East North Africa) people greet me each day at breakfast, a young Pakistani financial analyst from Toronto shares his insights with me at the breakfast table, and a British couple advise me to carry my passport with me at all times (especially when I leave my room in case of an attack and subsequent fire). They kindly offered to buy me my medicines, although they are at least a decade older than me. A young school teacher from Geneva shares my table at dinner. I have not seen her lately; perhaps she has already been repatriated on one of the relief flights to Europe which started operating from Day 7. The British couple and the South Africans are still here; the Pakistani man left for Toronto early this morning. He was given only two hours’ notice and he phoned my room to say goodbye at 1.15 AM this morning.

***

What does my daily schedule look like?

It is like what I imagine a day at boarding school would be. Because it is Ramadan, the hotel starts the breakfast buffet from 3 AM, lunch is from 12 noon, and dinner is over by 7.30. The food served (although mild in taste and quasi-institutional as regards the daily menu, which does not rotate much in terms of items), is nevertheless amazingly varied as regards the cuisine: Arabic, Turkish, Italian, Spanish and South Asian (the last is not good at all). A lot of lemon is used in the preparations, but practically no onions. This may be due to the fact that there was an onion shortage; onions came in from India only on Day 5. There are loads of different kinds of salads, some bland European cheeses and diverse types of hummus. In addition, there is feta cheese, stuffed vine leaves, green and black olives, veg and non-veg samosas and spring rolls, koftas, and baba ghanoush or baingan bharta. Good cappuccinos and lattes. Flaky croissants and brioches, pastries and amazing Arabian/Persian/Yemeni sweets. A decadent baked (and often caramelised) bread pudding called Umm Ali is served at dinner. Obviously, the Qatari supermarkets are still well-stocked with FMCG. The Indian-origin Lulu supermarket chain has flown in a whole lot of perishable and non-perishable food items.

Strangely, no fresh fruit!

***

Gas prices have shot up.

I have given up watching the death and destruction on TV, and watch Looney Tunes, Anthony Bourdain, Fawlty Towers and Mr Bean instead. Priyam Paul, my editor at The Daily Star, has sent me some e-books which help to pass the time.

When I am not reading, or watching sitcoms, cartoons and travel and food documentaries, I reflect on what brought us to this war. I see the Persian Gulf from my room; it is still a brilliant blue. But it is also desolate since the Hormuz Strait was closed off. I see no cargo ships or container vessels; there are no cruise ships or tankers. For a maritime historian like me, this is not the Persian Gulf I know. After all, it has been a crossroads since recorded history! My India in the Indian Ocean World (2022) documents this history of two thousand years at the very least. Now, mobility is severely constrained.

Persian Gulf. Photo: Collected

We are living now in a world of fragmented geopolitics, of accelerated climate degradation, and of critical demographic shifts. The world is undergoing these changes along with increasingly disaffected groups of peoples, perhaps terrorists, some of them. We are seeing the rise of AI which, to my mind, is linked, along with the toxicity of social media, with the increasing authoritarianism that we see worldwide. It horrifies me when I see a young nation declare it will bring ‘civilisation’ to Iran. It disregards the fact that Iran-as-Persia predates Arab culture and is one of the world’s oldest culture areas. Not just the glory of Shi’ite Safavid Persia (1501–1736), which political theorists and analysts invoke when describing this civilisational space and whose heritage modern Iran draws on: think of the period from c. 550 BCE to 651 CE (Muslim conquest and start of Islamisation by the Rashidun Caliphate), when four mighty Persian empires ruled a large portion of the then-known world: Achaemenid, Seleucid, Parthian and Sassanian. Persia challenged Egypt, Greece and Rome, and then it faced up to the Ottoman and Russian empires. This memory of resistance of 2500 years will not be easily erased.

However, the total disregard of international law and the collapse of the rules-based order will usher in a new regional order in West Asia. This will impact on the Gulf states. Once-biblical Lebanon is almost destroyed by a rampant Israel. Syria has closed its borders. As a rogue USA intimidates Persia and trains its eye on the Caucasus and Azerbaijan, it also destabilises Iraq. Iranian Kurds based in Iraq have been reactivated. How will this impact on the Turkish Kurds? Turkey, a NATO country, is already feeling threatened.

The relatively young post-WW1 statelets in the Gulf will lose out in the violent reshuffle in the greater region. The Dubai story was already over. And Oman had lost its sheen even earlier. Financial and service centres will shift eastward—to Singapore or perhaps to KL. As will global airline hubs. The Gulf states will see their importance in location, business and finance diminish. They will have to reconsider their dependence on the USA which has now become a double-edged sword. Iran will endure, but perhaps in a new form. But it will not be erased from the map of the world.

World.title: André Béteille: A sociologist Bangladesh should read
World.content:
My first encounter with the ideas of Professor André Béteille was in July 1966 in an introductory sociology course at the University of Dhaka (at that time in East Pakistan) through Professor Tom Bottomore’s book, Sociology: A Guide to Problems and Literature (1962). The emphasis on general theory of social stratification for an explanation of the Indian caste system found its empirical reflection, as Bottomore refers to, in the work of Béteille, especially in Caste, Class and Power: Changing Patterns of Stratification in a Tanjore Village (1965).

My second encounter with him was in the Fall of 1975 at Dalhousie University, Halifax where I was writing my Master’s thesis under Professor Bottomore, and he referred to read me Béteille’s “Closed and open social stratification” (1966). Reading Béteille after nine years under the Maple tree, I began to admire his empirical depth, comparative methodology, and theoretical clarity, which reshaped my understanding of social hierarchies in India.

In the Christmas of 1976, I had an occasion to share some of my understanding of Béteille’s work. At that time, I was at York University, Toronto where I was doing my PhD. Professor K. Ishwaran, one of our faculty members, who wrote Tradition and Economy in Village India (1966), invited me for Christmas dinner-- Turkey with cranberry sauce, cooked by his Dutch wife. There we talked about the contribution of both Béteille and his supervisor M. N. Srinivas towards understanding the impact of social change on Indian social stratification.

In order to realistically understand contemporary caste hierarchy, Béteille emphasised the “other factors such as class and power” that “have to be considered as independent variables” (1966). It appeared to me highly useful for comparative empirical research. It creates a distance from traditional essentialist and ideological perspective of inequality.

Borrowed from Max Weber, he focused on multidimensionality of stratification and examined how status, economic resources, and political control interact to shape multifarious social order. This was a tremendous contribution in the field of stratification studies. Though he focused on rural stratification, the model is also applicable to the study of urban social stratification.

It is puzzling that in Bangladesh universities, both sociology and anthropology disciplines overlooked and neglected the Weberian model of multidimensional stratification system: anthropology remained spell-bound under the dichotomous model of rural “ashraf-atraf”; and sociology was locked in the iron cage of simplistic Marxist model of “land ownership” under the name of peasant studies. In spite of teaching Weber’s “Class, Status, Party” (1922/1946) in the universities, there is a marked absence of the application of Weberian model in the study of rural and urban complex social hierarchy. Probably in Bangladesh, this shows the intellectual bankruptcy of these disciplines, which are suffering from morbidity.

In fact, in order to understand contemporary social change in Bangladesh, especially its regime of accumulation under crony capitalism, it is essential to understand the nexus between power and class. The determining power of traditional property ownership in the formation of classes and consequent class consciousness has diminished in Bangladesh.

The notion of political capitalism advanced by Max Weber is also useful in understanding Bangladesh social stratification, especially class formation. The party consciousness along with ruling party affiliation, may give legitimate or illegitimate access to economic resources, thereby determining class position in terms of life opportunities and life style. This in turn, heavily influence commodification of prestige and honour; and becomes marker of status.

André Beteille (1934 - 2026). Photo: Collected

The rural and urban dispossession, which is an integral part of neoliberal and crony capitalism’s regime of accumulation, is also the progenitor of emergent lumpen bourgeoisie, whose class position do not correspond with their demeaning status position. Again, the traditional status group in Bangladesh, as Béteille found in his Tanjore village study with respect to traditional caste, suffer from status dislocation, having less access to power and economic resources. The ontology of inequality and hierarchy can best be understood by the Weberian epistemology.

I think study of this process of social change, and its impact on inequality in Bangladesh, is vital towards understanding Bangladesh society. The internationally acclaimed Indian empirical model provided by Béteille can be one of the best guides to study the intersectionality of class, status and power in both urban and rural Bangladesh. It is unfortunate that social sciences in Bangladesh have neglected such a significant social dynamic that affects all our lives.

In March 1989, Professor Abhijit Dasgupta, a colleague of Professor Béteille, facilitated my direct meeting with him. Professor Dasgupta was kind enough to arrange a seminar talk by me in the sociology department of Delhi School of Economics. After the seminar, I paid a visit to Professor Béteille’s office room. He was very warm and hospitable to offer tea to me and my wife. He spoke in Bangla and affirmed his Bangali origin. I felt very comfortable to have a vibe of Bengal. I mentioned to him how I came to know of his work à la Bottomore and Ishwaran. I was so surprised to experience his stock of knowledge mediated by modesty and simplicity. The meeting with professor Béteille during the short-lived spring of Delhi was one of the most memorable events of my life. I wish his conceptual and methodological clarity inspire the young Bangladeshi sociologists to break the chain of ignorance, myopic framework, and the hegemony of intellectual infantilism.

A.I. Mahbub Uddin Ahmed is a professor in the Department of Sociology at the University of Dhaka.

World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

Shamsuddoza Sajen is a journalist and researcher. He can be contacted at [email protected].

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Tokyo and Osaka record latest-ever day above 30 Celsius
World.content:
Tokyo and Osaka topped 30 Celsius on Wednesday, the latest in the year both cities have ever recorded such temperatures, a Japan weather official said.

Warm, humid air from the south swept across Japan, particularly areas along the Pacific coast, sending temperatures unusually high for late October.

Tokyo climbed above 30 C by early afternoon, the threshold the Japan Meteorological Agency classifies as a “midsummer day,” JMA data science official Kazuhiro Shirono said.

It marked the latest 30 C-plus day recorded in the capital since observations began in 1875, he said.

Prior to this, the latest midsummer day record was Oct. 19, 2024, Shirono said.

Temperatures also rose above 30C in Osaka, breaking the city’s previous record for the latest midsummer day, set on Oct. 20, 1933.

Osaka began recording weather observations in 1883, according to the JMA.

Scientists say human-induced climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme heat events around the world.

Japan saw its hottest summer on record in 2025, with warmer days on the rise globally due to climate change.

This year, the weather office began using a new word — ”kokushobi” or “cruelly hot day” — when temperatures hit 40 C (104F), urging the public to treat extreme heat like a natural disaster.

World.title: ¥4 billion in lottery proceeds to go to quake-hit Kumamoto
World.content:
About ¥4 billion in proceeds from the Nenmatsu Jumbo series year-end public lotteries in Japan will be allocated to quake-hit Kumamoto Prefecture and its capital on a priority basis, it was learned Wednesday.

The policy was set by a public lottery association comprising relevant local governments, according to informed sources.

The money will be used for reconstruction projects in areas damaged by the powerful July 28 temblor, which measured up to shindo 7, the highest level on Japan’s seismic intensity scale.

Tickets for the year-end lotteries will be on sale between Nov. 24 and Dec. 25.

Of about ¥183 billion in estimated total sales of the Nenmatsu Jumbo and Nenmatsu Jumbo Mini lottery tickets, ¥10 billion will be set aside as resources for aid to disaster-hit areas. Proceeds after the deduction of winning amounts and other expenses are projected to total some ¥4 billion.

Takarakuji public lotteries in Japan, including the Nenmatsu Jumbo series, are sold by prefectural governments and major cities designated by a central government ordinance, with lottery proceeds shared among them.

Lottery proceeds are an independent revenue source for local governments and can be used for a variety of projects.

Following the massive earthquakes in Kumamoto Prefecture in April 2016, takarakuji proceeds were allocated preferentially to afflicted areas for the restoration of facilities, including roads as well as farmland.

World.title: Japan tourist spending rises despite drop in visitor arrivals
World.content:
Foreign visitor spending in Japan rose in the third quarter, according to data released Wednesday by the Japan Tourism Agency, despite a consistent decline in overseas arrivals.

Inbound visitors spent an estimated ¥2.21 trillion ($13.9 billion) between July and September, up 3.2% from the same period in the previous year. The increase came even as visitor arrivals fell 4.8% during the quarter.

In separate data from the Japan National Tourism Organization (JNTO), Japan had 3.10 million visitors arrive from abroad in September, down 5% from a year earlier. The decline followed a 9.6% drop in August, bringing the total for the first nine months of 2026 to 30.73 million, down 2.9% from the same period last year.

The figures come as Japan approaches the one-year mark since Chinese authorities began issuing advisories urging citizens to avoid travel to Japan in November last year. Beijing has issued multiple warnings along similar lines since then, according to JNTO, contributing to a sharp downturn in what had been one of the country’s largest sources of inbound tourism. JNTO also cited reductions in flight services to and from China as a factor behind the decline.

Arrivals from China fell 44.5% in September to 430,800, compared with 775,657 a year earlier. For the January-September period, Chinese arrivals plunged 55.5% to 3.34 million from 7.49 million a year earlier.

The downturn has extended to spending. Visitors from China spent ¥358.3 billion in the third quarter, down 39.8% from ¥595 billion a year earlier, although spending per person jumped 22.1%, to total ¥294,560. Their share of total inbound tourism expenditure fell to 16.2% from 27.8%.

Despite the overall decline in arrivals, visitors to Japan were spending more on average. Expenditure per visitor, excluding cruise ship passengers, climbed 6.1% to ¥233,677 in the third quarter. Accommodation accounted for the largest share of spending at 35.2%, followed by shopping at 27.7% and food and beverages at 22.9%.

Taiwan overtook China as the largest source of visitor spending, with expenditure rising 26.2% to ¥381.8 billion, accounting for 17.3% of the total.

South Korea recorded inbound figures to Japan jumping 25.6% to 842,300 in the month of September, supported by the Chuseok holiday period and increased airline capacity. Taiwanese arrivals to Japan rose 13% to 595,600. Seven markets, including South Korea, Mexico and the Middle East, recorded their highest September arrivals on record.

Meanwhile, the number of Japanese nationals traveling overseas rose 6.3% in September from a year earlier to 1.48 million. The increase brought the total for the first nine months of 2026 to 11.21 million, up 3.2% from the same period last year.

World.title: Newly appointed farm minister apologizes over donation scandal
World.content:
New farm minister Arata Takebe on Wednesday apologized over a weekly magazine report stating he allegedly received a political donation from a public works contractor.

“I instructed relevant officials to promptly investigate the facts and take action to return the money or correct the political funds disclosure report accordingly,” Takebe told reporters at parliament.

News website Bunshun Online reported Tuesday that a district branch of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party in Hokkaido that is headed by Takebe received a political donation from a local contractor engaged in national public works.

The donation was made on the first day of official campaigning for the 2014 election of the House of Representatives, potentially violating the public offices election law.

“I didn’t know the company had won a national public works project at the time the donation was received,” Takebe said.

Takebe took office only last week, succeeding Kazuo Yana, who resigned on Oct. 14 over his remarks on cutting the budgets of municipalities whose mayors did not support him in a general election, as well as his provision of free shuttle bus transportation for supporters in an election campaign, possibly in violation of the public offices election law.

After the Bunshun Online report, Takebe said that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has instructed him to confirm the facts and provide a proper report.

World.title: Japan braces for 30th named storm this year as Typhoon Champi heads for Okinawa
World.content:
Typhoon Champi is moving in from the Pacific Ocean toward the south of the country, including Okinawa Prefecture, in the coming days, prompting authorities to urge people to be on alert.

The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) forecast on Wednesday that the typhoon, the country’s 30th named storm of the year — which is known in Japan as taifū No. 30 — will reach the Sakishima Islands of Okinawa Prefecture between Friday and Saturday.

The JMA predicted that Typhoon Champi will then make its way toward western Japan and is due to affect parts of Kyushu from the weekend onward.

As of Wednesday, the JMA said Typhoon Champi was tracking northwest toward Japan at a speed of 25 kph from a position east of the Philippines.

The typhoon could bring extreme weather conditions, with maximum wind speeds of up to 216 kph. It has been categorized as a super typhoon — the strongest of the agency’s five-level system.

Compared to a tropical storm, a typhoon is a more intense weather event and brings wind speeds of 119 kph or higher, according to the JMA. Typhoon Champi is predicted to be particularly severe since it is at the upper end of the scale.

Okinawa Prefecture is expected to experience the brunt of Typhoon Champi on Friday, with the JMA forecast showing that the center of the typhoon could reach approximately 160 kilometers from the coast.

Forecasters are also cautioning people to be wary of heavy rain and rough sea conditions, including high tides, particularly around Okinawa Prefecture.

Reaching as many as 30 named storms in one year is rare for Japan. There are an average of 25 in the country each year — meaning 2026 will have already seen 20% more than the average.

There have already been flight cancellations because of Typhoon Champi. Japan Airlines and All Nippon Airways announced Wednesday that a number of flights scheduled to and from airports in southern Japan would not be running over the next few days.

Events in Okinawa Prefecture have also been canceled as the typhoon approaches. The 50th Okinawa Industrial Festival, which was to take place from Friday to Sunday and was expecting hundreds of thousands of visitors, has been called off.

World.title: Education ministry calls for University of Tokyo to review president selection
World.content:
The education ministry has requested that the University of Tokyo review how it selected its new president after the institution chose a woman for the role for the first time despite her finishing second in a faculty vote. The selection raised questions over how the screening body came to its decision.

It was the first time for the government to make such a request regarding how a university selected its president.

“A self-directed review of the process behind the presidential selection to ensure the University of Tokyo’s governance is fulfilling its accountability obligations is the first step toward reform,” education minister Yoshihiro Seki said on Tuesday, adding that the request called for an inspection by the university’s management policy council.

World.title: One year on, LDP-JIP partnership still has some holes to fill
World.content:
A year after Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi forged a hasty coalition government with the Japan Innovation Party (JIP), what began as a political marriage of convenience is evolving into a deeper relationship after some parliamentary successes.

But with controversial legislation still to be enacted and not everyone in Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic Party enthusiastic about a long-term relationship with the JIP — also known as Nippon Ishin no Kai — the coalition’s future remains uncertain, even though a divorce anytime soon appears unlikely.

After being elected LDP president last October, Takaichi faced her first crisis when Komeito, the LDP’s coalition partner since 1999, announced it was departing because it could not support her conservative, hawkish policy approach.

World.title: As residents of flood-hit Chiba Prefecture rebuild, concerns about the future linger
World.content:
While residential areas in Chiba Prefecture are finally clear of floodwaters one month after heavy rain from Typhoon Dujuan doused the region, many people are concerned about the future.

In the Mabashi district in the town of Shisui, where 15 houses were flooded after a collapsed embankment blocked a river, floodwaters receded on Oct. 13.

“I’m hesitant to repair my home until I get assurance that I’ll be safe in the future,” said Sanae Suzuki, 56, who was clad in protective clothing while cleaning the mess left behind. Floodwaters had reached about 55 centimeters above floor level in her home.

“I can’t decide whether to continue living here or relocate elsewhere,” she said.

“We’re finally at the starting line,” said Yuta Hoshina, 44, whose home needs new tatami due to the flooding.

Levees were breached in four locations at Inbanuma, a major lake in northern Chiba Prefecture. Emergency restoration work has since been completed, however, the surrounding farmland remains covered in mud.

Akihisa Suzuki, a 76-year-old resident of the city of Narita who mainly grows radishes, eggplants and asparagus, saw his farmland of about 5,000 square meters, including four greenhouses, flooded for 10 days, destroying all of his crops.

His greenhouses are still caked with dried mud and all of his heating appliances and tillers are broken. “I won’t be able to grow vegetables again until around next spring,” Suzuki said.

Restoration work on the Anegasaki-Nagaura section on the Uchibo Line of East Japan Railway, which was hit by landslides, is expected to take another two months to be completed.

As a measure to remedy the situation, the Chiba Prefectural Government and JR East have started lending power-assisted bicycles free of charge.

Noting that it takes about 25 minutes by bicycle, much shorter than around 40 minutes on a replacement bus, Ayumi Hirano from the city of Kisarazu said, “I plan on using the bicycle when it’s nice outside, and the bus when the weather is bad.”

“I just want it to be restored as soon as possible,” 31-year-old Hirano said of the train section.

According to Chiba Prefecture’s disaster response headquarters, 10 people were killed and 37 injured in the prefecture by the typhoon as of Tuesday. A total of 795 houses were either destroyed or severely damaged and 1,534 houses were flooded. Damage related to the agriculture, forestry and fisheries sector exceeded ¥25 billion ($158 million).

World.title: Could Hong Kong’s student housing boom lure property giants off the sidelines?
World.content:
Hong Kong’s largest landlords and developers could get their first formal route into the rising student accommodation market after the government announced plans to tender land for a purpose-built student hostel this quarter, according to analysts.

Development Secretary Bernadette Linn Hon-ho announced on Thursday the inclusion of a 1,100 square metre (11,840 square foot) site for student accommodation as one of two land tenders in the October to December quarter.

The plot – at the junction of Yuen Shun Circuit and Yuen Hong Street in Siu Lek Yuen, Sha Tin – is expected to provide 600 hostel places.

“The tender of a dedicated PBSA [purpose-built student accommodation] site could be an important catalyst for Hong Kong’s major developers to take a closer look at the sector,” said Kathy Lee, head of research and retail consultancy at property consultancy Colliers in Hong Kong.

World.title: “Talent in, Impact Out”: Inside The Education University of Hong Kong's vision for an interconnected world of talent and expertise
World.content:
“Partnerships are not one-off events but sustained, ever-growing relationships,” he adds. “As we mark the 10th anniversary of the University’s retitling, our next decade is about education with impact: attracting and nurturing talents who contribute to social good in Hong Kong SAR, China, and the world.”

“We live in an interconnected world that goes beyond the West, and it should be viewed as a highly connected whole,” says EdUHK President Professor John Lee Chi-Kin. “When we welcome students and scholars from diverse backgrounds, they bring different approaches to learning, teaching and research, and help cultivate global citizens who respect every culture.”

The Education University of Hong Kong (EdUHK) pursues a dual internationalisation strategy: attracting talented students, scholars and researchers from around the world while exporting educational and research expertise to communities beyond Hong Kong.

[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]

The journeys of three faculty members bring this vision to life.

Bringing international expertise to Hong Kong

Professor Andrew Mark Edwards joined EdUHK in 2025, among a growing number of international scholars drawn to the University. He now serves as Associate Dean (International Engagement) of the Faculty of Liberal Arts and Social Sciences (FLASS). He previously held senior academic positions in the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand, and is internationally recognised for his research in exercise physiology and psychophysiology.

“I was drawn to Hong Kong by its ambitious and highly supportive higher education environment. Higher education is deeply valued here, and the opportunities to make an impact through research and teaching are strong,” he says.

“EdUHK offers a distinctive focus on education while embracing interdisciplinary research and innovation. Within my first year at EdUHK, I secured a competitive General Research Fund grant. The University has been highly supportive in helping me establish my research programme, including supporting an international PhD student from the Netherlands to join my research group.”

The University's commitment to building international networks and fostering global collaboration left a strong impression on Edwards. Shortly after joining EdUHK, he was invited by the President to help the Head of Department organise a major international conference. "Shaping the Future: Sport, Health and Education 2026", which will be held in November.

As Associate Dean (International Engagement), Edwards is also helping to advance a wider programme of international engagement across FLASS, covering staff mobility, international partnership development and global impact initiatives.

“What impressed me most was its openness to new ideas and international collaboration. The University provides a supportive environment where academics can exchange ideas, expand global networks and create research with real-world impact,” he notes.

A strategic focus on Belt and Road countries

EdUHK actively promotes international educational collaboration, with a particular focus on Belt and Road countries. One notable example is its longstanding partnership with Kazakhstan, which includes the establishment of the EdUHK-Kazakh Academy of Education in Almaty, and a major student recruitment initiative.

Dr Artem Zadorozhnyy, now an Assistant Professor in the Department of English Language Education at EdUHK, first encountered the University at a recruitment talk promoting its PhD programmes at Nazarbayev University in Astana, Kazakhstan, while he was pursuing a master's degree in multilingual education.

Inspired by the opportunities available, he chose to undertake his doctoral studies at EdUHK under the highly competitive Hong Kong PhD Fellowship Scheme. After completing his PhD, he secured a grant under the RGC Postdoctoral Fellowship Scheme, placing him firmly on the path towards becoming a promising early-career researcher.

The appeal of EdUHK lies in its generous support, world-class research environment and strong reputation in technology-enhanced language education, Zadorozhnyy explains.

“I found an inspiring academic community at EdUHK, where scholars are engaged in rigorous, collaborative, and socially meaningful research. What particularly appealed to me was EdUHK’s emphasis on interdisciplinary collaboration, where fields such as language education, digital learning and computer science intersect to generate innovative research,” he says.

Exporting research expertise and creating global impact

Integral to EdUHK’s internationalisation strategy is the export of expertise through international research partnerships and capacity-building projects that create tangible benefits for communities worldwide.

One example is the work of Dr Deng Wenjing, Acting Head of the Department of Science and Environmental Studies and Associate Professor at FLASS, who has built an international research collaboration from a project examining environmental risks in schools. Aligned with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, the initiative demonstrates how EdUHK translates research excellence into practical solutions while informing policymaking in several Belt and Road countries.

“Our team was the first in Hong Kong to identify endocrine-disrupting chemicals in indoor school environments,” Deng says. “By working closely with international partners, we have transformed research findings into practical tools, STEM learning programmes and school-based interventions that help create healthier learning environments across Belt and Road countries.”

Deng’s team has developed monitoring technologies, educational resources and policy-support tools that help schools better understand environmental health risks and respond effectively.

“Because environmental challenges vary across regions, we work with local universities, schools and education authorities to co-create solutions tailored to each community’s needs,” she explains.

Through portable air-quality sensors, hands-on monitoring activities and STEM learning resources, the team empowers local educators and students to improve their own environments.

“Through initiatives in Sri Lanka, Nepal, Malaysia, Indonesia and Guangxi, Chinese Mainland, we have reached more than 3,000 students and educators.”

“The success of this work demonstrates how international collaboration, built on local ownership and co-creation, can generate lasting impact,” Deng adds.

Deng’s achievements also reflect EdUHK’s commitment to fostering an inclusive academic ecosystem that provides opportunities for talented and dedicated scholars regardless of gender or background.

“I am grateful for the many opportunities at the University. I think I have made a mark as a woman in science,” she says.

EdUHK’s internationalisation strategy demonstrates how Hong Kong serves as a welcoming, dynamic and globally connected education hub, where scholars from diverse backgrounds and at different stages of their careers can thrive, contribute and create meaningful global impact.

World.title: A Tale of Two Cities, retold in style
World.content:
The opening also comes as the role of the brick-and-mortar bank branch is now very different from what it was even less than a decade ago. As everyday transactions can now be handled easily and securely through digital channels, the value of physical branches increasingly lies in conversations that benefit from professional advice, privacy and trust.

That proximity is part of the reason why OCBC has chosen the prime location of 35 Queen’s Road Central for its Central Branch. Here, clients can access wealth management services close to where they work or spend their time, in a cosy, private setting, while eligible Premier Private Clients can also access health and wellness support available in the same building. Fewer separate journeys can leave more time for work, family and life outside both.

For many of Hong Kong’s high-flying executives and entrepreneurs alike, Central is already part of their working day.

[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]

For affluent clients, that can mean discussing investments, succession or other important financial needs face to face. OCBC’s Central Branch is taking an early lead in this direction, combining private advisory and meeting spaces with hospitality, lifestyle offerings, while selected wellness services are available to eligible Premier Private Clients.

Reimagining the branch experience

Held on September 29, the grand opening was attended by senior management, government and business leaders, partners and singer-songwriter Hanjin Tan. The occasion also marked the introduce of its new Premier Private Client Centre and the unveiling of a 3D LED display wall on the building façade.

With the addition of its newly opened second and third floors, the expanded premises give OCBC considerably more room to rethink what eligible Premier Private clients can do during a branch visit.

The approach also draws on OCBC’s Singapore origins and long presence in Hong Kong. That relationship is expressed in its latest campaign, “A Tale of Two Cities, For Your Wealth and Beyond”, which presents the two financial centres as complementary bases for serving clients whose business, wealth and families may increasingly cross borders.

A façade inspired by the Hong Kong spirit

OCBC’s 3D LED display brings a cast of animated characters inspired by Hong Kong’s entrepreneurial spirit to Queen’s Road Central. A 3D LED display wall on the branch façade introduces an original cast of animated characters inspired by qualities associated with Hong Kong people. “Manager Cat” represents innovation and entrepreneurial spirit, while the “Prosperity Dog “ embodies trust and reliability, and the “Agile Monkey” represents adaptability and an ability to recognise opportunities.Reflecting the spirit of the Twin Hubs, the characters give wealth planning ideas a more playful expression. Seeking opportunities, protecting accumulated wealth and preparing for the future are represented by personalities encountered on Queen’s Road Central instead of being confined to a banking brochure.

There is an Instagrammable side to the campaign, too. Until October 31, visitors can photograph the display from a designated location outside Loke Yew Building at 50–52 Queen’s Road Central, with at least one of the cat, dog or monkey characters visible. After posting the photos on Facebook, Instagram, WeChat or Xiaohongshu with the specified campaign hashtags, visitors can redeem a limited-edition OCBC character blind box at the Central Branch, subject to terms and conditions.

The installation gives passers-by a reason to interact with the branch even without a banking appointment, while the blind box turns the digital characters into something tangible.

A Hong Kong story with Singapore roots

Singapore-born singer-songwriter Hanjin Tan brings his own tale of two cities to OCBC’s new campaign, having established his career in Hong Kong and written and composed its theme song. The same two-city idea is explored through music in OCBC’s new advertising campaign. Hanjin Tan has a tale of two cities of his own. Born in Singapore before establishing his career in Hong Kong, the singer-songwriter and Hong Kong Film Award winner embodies the connection at the centre of the campaign. He appears in the TVC and also composed and wrote its theme song.Inspired by the spirit of Hong Kong, the campaign follows aspirations at different stages of life. Creating wealth may dominate earlier years; preserving it can become increasingly important as responsibilities grow; later, succession and preparing for the next generation can become a priority.

Tan’s career has crossed the same two cities that OCBC uses for its regional proposition, allowing the campaign to talk about wealth through personal ambition, family and long-term planning instead of financial products alone. “The sense of being at home, the trust, and the peace of mind are what OCBC Premier Private Client offers,” said Tan, who is also an OCBC Premier Private Client, at the Central Branch grand opening.

Embedding wellness into the wealth journey

The new Premier Private Client Centre occupies the second and third floors of the Central Branch, with Singapore-inspired interiors, private meeting areas and a garden terrace. Through its “Navigating Your Wealth & Wellness Together” proposition, OCBC offers eligible Premier Private Clients access to personalised wealth management, wellness privileges, regional banking, lifestyle experiences and legacy planning services.

Through a partnership with Fullerton Health, eligible Premier Private Clients can access personalised one-to-one nutritionist consultations at a dedicated consultation room conveniently located within the same building, as well as cross-border medical referral services and regional healthcare support, subject to applicable terms and conditions.

[Premier Private Client Centre]

Commenting on the grand opening of OCBC’s Central Branch and the soft launch of its new Premier Private Client service in Hong Kong, Mr. Wang Ke, Head of Greater China of OCBC and Chief Executive Officer of OCBC Hong Kong, said, “Hong Kong remains a key wealth management hub in Asia and an important market for OCBC. The opening of our Central Branch and the soft launch of Premier Private Client mark an important milestone in our growth journey in Hong Kong.

Mr. Sunny Quek, Head of Group Consumer Financial Services, OCBC, added, “OCBC Premier Private Client is a key offering of our wealth franchise, supporting our customers’ increasingly sophisticated wealth needs. We are now extending the experience to Hong Kong as we strengthen our Singapore-Hong Kong twin wealth hubs to capture rising Asian wealth flows.

Ms. Josephine Lee, Head of Consumer Financial Services, OCBC Hong Kong, said, “Hong Kong’s affluent customers are increasingly seeking trusted advice that extends beyond investment returns to address wealth preservation, liquidity management, retirement planning, healthcare needs and legacy planning for the next generation. By bringing together personalised wealth management, wellness support and regional connectivity, OCBC Premier Private Client aims to support customers’ financial, family, lifestyle and wellness aspirations through different stages of their wealth and life journeys. This reflects our purpose to enable people and communities to realise their aspirations.”
