Do you think the military is afraid of Aung San Suu Kyi herself or of what she continues to represent?

They’re definitely afraid of her. Why else would they keep her locked up?

And she really is a symbol for the people. People in Burma recognise how much she has sacrificed for them over the past 30 or 40 years. They know that she has been willing to stay in Burma, to remain with them and go through the same hardships they’ve had to endure.

Your mother remains a symbol of democracy for many people. But is there anything from her time in government that you personally disagree with? I’m thinking, for example, of the Rohingya crisis.

No, I’ve never had a problem with any of her decisions. She was in an extremely difficult position, and the international community failed to understand just how delicate that situation was.

I think it’s much clearer now that she simply wasn’t able to do everything she might have wanted to do. But I believe she did more for the Rohingya than anyone else, and people don’t realise that.

They say she remained silent on the issue, even though what she actually said about it would fill entire volumes. They say she went to The Hague to defend the military. But they say that without ever having properly listened to what she actually said there. So my advice to people is this: go and listen to what she said. Find out exactly what she did to help the Rohingya.

She initiated the establishment of the Kofi Annan Commission the day after she came to power. That was before the issue had even become a major concern for the international community. She was taking steps to help the Rohingya, and representatives of the Rohingya community I’ve spoken to have told me that she did everything she could for them.

Most people associate Aung San Suu Kyi with politics or the Nobel Peace Prize. Was it difficult growing up with someone who was both a parent and such a prominent public figure?

I grew up with it, and I think that, when you’re a child, everything just seems normal. You don’t know any other way of life, so you don’t really know what’s normal and what isn’t. From a very early age, I was aware of what she represented, but I don’t think those two things are mutually exclusive. She can be my mother and, at the same time, a very prominent political figure.

You’ve said before that you never wanted to become involved in politics, and that your mother didn’t want that for you either. Yet here you are, travelling, campaigning and speaking publicly about Myanmar. When did you realise that staying out of the spotlight was no longer an option?

When they put her in prison five years ago, I realised I had to speak out. After all, I’m her son. And if I don’t do anything, how can I expect anyone else to stand up for her?

How much of what you’re doing today is about your mother personally, and how much is about Myanmar itself? If your mother were released tomorrow, would you continue campaigning for democracy in Myanmar?

I think my mother would do a pretty good job of that herself. If I manage to secure her release, then I can feel that I’ve done my job well too.

For much of her life, Aung San Suu Kyi was seen as the daughter of Aung San, the general who played a key role in Burma’s struggle for independence from British colonial rule. Do you sometimes feel that you, too, are defined by your mother’s name?

I suppose I do, to some extent. After all, it’s very difficult not to have that image hanging over you. But at the same time, I’m doing this because I want to. I think it’s important that we all try to do whatever we can. People often don’t realise that they’re capable of doing much more than they think.

As a child, did you understand why your mother chose to stay in Myanmar rather than live a safe life with her family in Britain?

Yes, I did. I was actually with her when she was first placed under house arrest, so I saw what was happening with my own eyes. In some ways, it felt like a natural continuation of what had been happening before, because we’d been watching the situation in Burma gradually deteriorate.

I can’t say it was easy, but I think that, because I was a child at the time, I was somehow able to accept it. It’s difficult to explain. I think adults often find it harder to deal with change. And if she’d been imprisoned five years ago without my having already spent decades living with our separation, I think it would have been much harder.

What was it actually like when your mother was first placed under house arrest? Can you describe what happened?

When they first came to arrest her, they arrived with several trucks to take away the student revolutionaries who were staying in the house as well. I remember watching them being taken away. Then they put barbed wire around the entire compound, set up guard posts, cut the telephone lines and stopped us from leaving the house.

But at least we were still in her own home, and her own doctor was allowed to visit her. Even after I returned to England, I could send her parcels, and sometimes we were able to communicate. The past five years have been completely different.

You mentioned the student movement earlier. Is the revolution still visible on the streets of Myanmar today?

Yes, it is. It may not be as visible as it once was, but there is still an enormous amount of resistance across the country. In some places, like Yangon, things might appear quite normal. Other journalists I’ve spoken to who have been there have told me that everything looks remarkably normal. But it certainly isn’t. There are still huge numbers of people doing everything they can to change the situation. They’ve simply gone underground, so they’re not as visible as they used to be.

Do you ever feel that the junta has forced you into a role you would never have chosen for yourself?

Yes. I wouldn’t be doing this otherwise.

And what would you be doing?

Spending time with my children and working. I’m a trained carpenter.

How do you explain to your children what’s happening to their grandmother, and what’s happening in Myanmar more generally?

We’ve been talking about it for years, and they’ve had to come to terms with it too. They understand what’s happening in Burma. I still try to protect them as much as I can. Being in the public eye isn’t easy, and I want to keep them as far away from all that as possible.

Do you believe you’ll ever see your mother again?

Yes, I do. She’s been released before, and the situation in Burma could change at any moment. Even if the resistance doesn’t achieve victory in the near future, I think there’s still a chance that she could be released.

The interview first appeared in Czech at Seznam Zpravy. Daniela Kucerova is the new outlet’s foreign news department editor. Her main area of focus is Asia, particularly China and neighboring regions.

World.title: China Moves to Cement Myanmar Influence After U.S. Talks With Regime
World.content:
As Washington resumes direct engagement with Myanmar’s military regime, Beijing moved to cement its overarching influence last week by meeting with nine political parties in Yangon to gauge public sentiment.

The Chinese delegation was led by Peng Xiubin, director‑general of the Chinese Communist Party’s International Liaison Department. Present at the meeting were representatives of the military’s proxy Union Solidarity and Development Party, the National Unity Party, People’s Party, People’s Pioneer Party, Shan and Nationalities Democratic Party, Arakan Front Party, Kayin People’s Party, Unity and Development Party, and New Chinland Congress Party.

Participants said the Chinese side raised five key points, including Myanmar public attitudes toward China and challenges in bilateral relations.

“The Chinese side asked how the Myanmar people view them,” one participant told The Irrawaddy. “Some parties noted that sections of the public hold negative or skeptical views. They urged China to do more to show how it is helping Myanmar so that people understand.”

Anti-China sentiment in Myanmar has surged since the 2021 coup, triggered by Beijing’s support for successive military regimes, supplying them with battlefield hardware, technology and diplomatic cover. China is a key arms supplier and the biggest investor in post-coup Myanmar, propping up an embattled regime shunned by much of the international community and sanctioned by the West.

Most of the parties present at the meeting took part in Jan.-Feb. regime elections that were widely dismissed as a fraud to cement military rule.

However, leaders of the National Democratic Force (NDF) and the Shan Nationalities League for Democracy (SNLD)—Htet Aung Kyaw and Sai Kyaw Nyunt—joined the talks despite their parties being dissolved for defying the regime’s electoral roadmap. One party leader said the duo attended in a personal capacity after being invited individually, rather than as representatives of their banned organizations.

The CCP delegation also asked about priority areas for cooperation, and parties’ views on peace, the economy, and domestic issues.

The meeting came as coup leader Min Aung Hlaing made progress in securing formal engagement with Washington. U.S. officials held their second round of talks with regime representatives in Tokyo earlier this month after Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance flew to Naypyitaw for talks with coup leader Min Aung Hlaing in September.

“The Chinese side made no mention of the recent U.S.-Myanmar talks, focusing instead on gauging our views,” said one participant. “Some parties stressed that they prefer engagement with China, a neighbor.”

Party leaders said they also discussed trade policy and technical support for agriculture while urging China to help reopen the Muse–Mandalay highway, a vital trade corridor. After losing control of major trade routes with China in northern Shan, the regime has imposed a near total blockade on Chinese imports to starve ethnic armed organizations of tax revenue.

Saw Han Aye, chair of the People’s Pioneer Party, said: “We asked the Chinese to increase investment and reopen trade routes as soon as possible, and Beijing affirmed it wants more frequent exchanges.”

While Beijing rejects accusations of interfering in Myanmar’s internal affairs, the belief that its investments prop up a military regime waging war on its own people is widespread within the country. Anti-China sentiment soared to new levels in 2024, when Beijing pressured ethnic armies to halt northern Shan offensives that were threatening the regime’s grip on power.

When China’s Asia envoy Deng Xijun called for ethnic autonomy during a Naypyitaw ceremony marking the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement’s anniversary last week, critics pointed out that northern Shan State is already controlled by ethnic armies under Beijing’s thumb.

World.title: Migrants Urge Thai Gov’t to Let Them Work Free of Myanmar Regime Extortion
World.content:
Myanmar migrants are urging the Thai government to let them work legally without so-called Certificates of Identity (CI), which they say the military regime back home is weaponizing to extort money from them.

CI, issued by the regime under a quota system for overseas laborers hired in Myanmar, allow workers to register for work permits and renew their visas in Thailand.

Starved of hard currency, the regime has recently moved to harness CI issuance to grab the hard-earned money of migrant workers, saying it will not renew the papers unless workers remit a portion of their earnings back home through official channels and pay two percent income tax.

Under remittance rule introduced in late 2023, workers must send at least 25 percent of their monthly salaries home through regime-controlled banks, which means a fixed, artificially inflated exchange rate. Traditionally workers rely on the informal “hundi” system, which offers better exchange rates.

In response, the Myanmar Migrant Workers’ Representative Coordinating Committee in Thailand (MMWRCCT) has launched a campaign calling on Thai authorities to abolish the CI requirement for visas and work permits and instead allow employment solely based on the Pink Cards issued by the Thai government to regularize the status of migrants and refugees

Since Oct. 18, workers have staged an online photo campaign to press their demands.

Myanmar’s shadow National Unity Government (NUG) has expressed support for the campaign.

Workers say they are not willing to pay any form of tax to the regime which does little to protect and promote their rights.

“The regime does not even provide proper passport services, so why should we pay them any money?” said a Myanmar worker in Chonburi.

The campaign began after the regime opened new CI issuing centers on Oct. 14 in Samut Sakhon, Samut Prakan, Surat Thani, Chiang Mai and Chonburi in order to prey on migrant workers whose permit cycle expires in December. There they must show evidence that they have remitted their due share of their earnings through the regime’s banking channels.

Pouring oil on the flames, Labor Minister Maung Myint earlier this month told migrant workers in Thailand to “think of the money as a donation.”

“We are campaigning to live and work with Pink Cards only,” said Khaing Gyi of the Aid Alliance Committee. “The regime’s demand for 25 percent remittance and tax payments can only be stopped by the workers themselves.”

He insisted this is not a protest against Thailand, but “simply a request to be allowed to work legally with Pink Cards.”

Workers complain that the CI centers are expensive, Byzantine and riddled with corruption in the form of demands for unofficial fees. Many laborers, who may be barely literate and speak little official Burmese, have to reply on brokers, which makes them prone to overcharging and fraud.

Campaigners have petitioned both houses of the Thai Parliament to abolish the CI requirement and crack down on brokers profiting from migrants.

MP Sia Jampatong of the House of Representatives committee said the government “must seriously review the CI center system, because the labor registration process must exist to certify status and protect rights, not be left to become a channel for officials to make a living, or provide an opportunity for the military government to exercise power over the lives of working people,” according to news outlet The Reporters.

And Senator Thewarit Maneechai pledged to bring the demand to the consideration of the Senate Labor Committee “to consider further relevant actions,” it added.

Thai activists also expressed solidarity. The Thailand Migration Reform group warned that allowing Myanmar’s regime to control migrant registration “undermines Thai sovereignty and fuels corruption.” It urged Thai authorities to review the CI system and revert to the Pink Card framework used before 2009.

Until then, migrants lived and worked legally in Thailand with Pink Cards alone. “If workers could survive with Pink Cards before, why not improve that system and use it again?” said one migrant who has lived in the country for over 30 years.

According to Thailand’s Labor Ministry, there were nearly 3.5 million registered Myanmar workers with work permits in the country as of August this year, of whom only about 430,000 hold CI cards. The regime recently admitted that remittance has become a major source of foreign currency income for Myanmar.

World.title: Thousands Flee as Regime Troops Push Into Myanmar’s Oil Hub
World.content:
Regime troops backed by airstrikes are pouring into Magwe Region’s Myaing Township as the battle for Myanmar’s oilfields escalates, forcing thousands of residents to flee.

Reinforcements from the Light Infantry Division in Pakokku, an hour to the south, are bolstering the offensive to seize territory — nicknamed “Anyar Dubai” for its oil wealth — from resistance groups.

Resistance forces have controlled the area since 2022, repelling repeated efforts to choke off their crucial revenue stream. However, a regime offensive backed by 1,000 troops gained a foothold on May 24, seizing the Well-2 oil field in Tae Gyi village.

The latest push began on October 18, when regime reinforcements arrived in Kamma town, Pakokku Township while gyrocopters bombed the nearby village of Ohntaw, killing five people, including children, and injuring four others.

On Monday, the troops arrived in Myaing’s Twinma village, controlled by regime-aligned militia, and set up camp there. According to Sayar Htwe from the Anyar Myay Civil Society Organization, up to 5,000 residents fled neighboring villages as airstrikes and troops advanced.

“We have no information on where the troops are heading, but we can assume they are reinforcements for Tae Gyi village,” Sayar Htwe told The Irrawaddy.

Regime troops suffered heavy losses in the three-month battle for Tae Gyi, where they are now encircled and entirely reliant on airdrops for ammunition and supplies.

On September 28, the regime reported that troops had seized 131 small-scale oil rigs in the area, torching some to prevent them from falling back into resistance hands.

On Monday, the Magwe resistance’s Anyar Myay Coalition urged the public to remain on high alert for airstrikes and attacks, as regime troops were mobilizing in Pakokku, Myaing and Pauk townships. It warned that regime troops camped in Tae Gyi had killed around 50 civilians and torched 600 houses since May.

World.title: Regional Body Expels Myanmar Regime’s Human Rights Fig Leaf
World.content:
The South East Asia National Human Rights Institutions Forum (SEANF), a regional umbrella group, has expelled a fig-leaf human rights body controlled by Myanmar’s military regime after it refused to cooperate with a compliance review.

SEANF on Monday said it has terminated the membership of the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission (MNHRC) because it is not an independent institution promoting and protecting human rights.

Established in 2007, SEANF now consist of just five national human rights commissions aiming to strengthen regional cooperation, from Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, the Philippines and Timor-Leste.

The decision, made on Oct. 1 and put into effect immediately, came at the 11th hour before Myanmar was to assume the umbrella group’s rotating chairmanship in 2027.

It follows a review of whether the MNHRC still met the Paris Principles standards for independence, effectiveness, and integrity, which SEANF uses to define a national human rights institution.

SEANF told the MNHRC in early September to respond, but the MNHRC refused, saying the review “did not comply with” the network’s procedural rules—a frequent fallback by the putschist regime in dealing with regional organizations of which it has fallen foul.

SEANF then decided unilaterally that the MNHRC “no longer satisfies the definition of a national human rights institution under amended Article 1 of the SEANF Rules of Procedure,” namely being independent to promote and protect human rights, it said in Monday’s statement. The decision was made in “a fair, transparent and evidence-based manner,” it added.”

The MNHRC was also kicked out of the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI) and the Asia-Pacific Forum (AFP) in 2025.

SEANF added the MNHRC can reapply for membership if it can demonstrate efforts to comply with the Paris Principles.

Established under the quasi-civilian Thein Sein administration in 2011 and once recognized as a “partially independent” body, the MNHRC went rapidly downhill when its leadership was replaced with regime loyalists after the 2021 coup.

It has since remained conspicuously silent about the regime’s glaring human rights violations while offering it a veneer of respectability and protection from scrutiny. Anecdotal evidence suggests that anyone coming to the MNHRC with a complaint could expect a knock on the door from the regime’s enforcers soon after.

Rights groups in Myanmar and beyond have long called its removal from global networks.

Prominent activist Khin Ohmar of Progressive Voice told the Irrawaddy that SEANF’s decision was “a long-awaited principled action” and “strips the criminal military junta-controlled MNHRC of regional legitimacy.”

“This decision sends a clear message that this body can no longer hide behind a SEANF membership card,” she added.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Bombs Civilians While Claiming Military Operations Serve Peace
World.content:
Framing its aerial bombardment of civilians as a peace initiative, the Myanmar regime continued aerial attacks across five regions and states over the weekend, killing over two dozen civilians.

Addressing humanitarian concerns raised in the media over the targeting of civilians, newly appointed Defense Minister Lieutenant General Yar Pyae, who is also chair of the National Solidarity and Peacemaking Negotiation Committee (NSPNC), claimed that the current military operations—a reference to the bombing of civilians in resistance-held territories—were conducted in the pursuit of peace.

He made the remark at the closing ceremony of an event marking the 11th anniversary of the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement (NCA) in Naypyitaw on October 16.

At the event, the regime again called on ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) to join its purported peace talks while encouraging the People’s Defense Force (PDF), the armed wing of the civilian National Unity Government (NUG), to surrender.

Meanwhile, from October 16-18, the regime bombed civilian targets in Magwe, Sagaing and Mandalay regions and Rakhine and Chin states, killing at least 27 people and injuring 11, according to media reports.

On Friday evening, regime aircraft bombed a Starlink-based WiFi shop in Thitgyitaw Village in Yesagyo, Magwe Region. The attack on the shop, which locals rely on to bypass the regime’s restrictions and access the internet, killed at least 12, including two children aged 1 and 10, and injured two, the NUG said on Sunday.

The number of casualties was likely to increase as bomb damage was making it difficult to determine the number and identities of the dead, the NUG’s Human Rights Department said.

“This is a blatant violation of international humanitarian law and a war crime,” it said.

The operation was carried out by two Russian-made Mi-35 attack helicopters, two fighter jets from Magwe and Nyaung Oo, and two drones from the Pakokku-based No. 101 Light Infantry Division, the NUG said.

However, local media reported that at least 15 civilians were killed in the incident.

On the same day, the regime bombed Magyikan Village in Sagaing’s Myaung, injuring one.

The regime’s airstrikes continued on Sunday, as Y-12 utility aircraft bombed Arakan Army (AA)-controlled ethnic Rakhine villages in Rathedaung. Wai Hun Aung, a prominent ethnic Rakhine writer and aid worker, said five people were killed.

The regime also bombed a jetty in AA-controlled Paletwa, Chin State, on the same day, resulting in 20 casualties according to media reports, though there has been no official statement yet.

A regime drone attacked Shwebayet Village in Mandalay’s Singu Township on October 18, killing three people and injuring four women and girls, including a 5-year-old, the Singu People’s Defense Force reported on Monday.

Three regime gyrocopters bombed Ohntaw Village in Magwe’s Pakokku Township on Sunday, killing five including children and senior citizens. Local media reported that four were injured, including a 2-year-old.

At the NCA anniversary event, regime leader Min Aung Hlaing invited 2015 signatories that have been fighting the Myanmar military since the 2021 coup—the Karen National Union, Chin National Front and All Burma Students’ Democratic Front—to join his peace process. The regime demands that the PDFs surrender.

Lt-Gen Yar Pyae insisted the aerial bombing was conducted for peaceful purposes. “Some parts are military actions, while others are steps to achieve peace,” Yar Pyae said.

World.title: Detained Aung San Suu Kyi Receives UK Royal Package: Regime
World.content:
YANGON—Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi received a package from Britain’s King Charles III on Monday, authorities said, releasing the first pictures of the detained Nobel laureate in two months and describing her as a “special female prisoner.”

It is the first time Myanmar authorities have used the term to describe Aung San Suu Kyi, who was deposed in a military coup in 2021, triggering an ongoing civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to monitor ACLED.

The coup leader and former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president in April following elections that did not include Aung San Suu Kyi’s party, and she was moved to house arrest soon afterwards.

Home Ministry officials met her on Monday to deliver a package of two books about soil, “one sealed envelope, and a sealed diplomatic communication sent by King Charles III of the United Kingdom to the special female detainee,” Myanmar’s presidential spokeswoman said on her Facebook page.

Britain is Myanmar’s former colonial power and the monarch is known to have a keen interest in gardening and the environment.

Accompanying the statement were two images of Aung San Suu Kyi meeting two men with their backs to the camera.

The pictures appeared to be in a similar room to the last released images of her, when she met a Red Cross representative in August, her first publicized meeting with a foreign official since her ouster.

Fact-checkers from AFP examined the latest photos and found no evidence of manipulation using Meta Generative AI or OpenAI tools.

Aung San Suu Kyi remains detained on charges rights groups say were concocted to return power to the military, which has historically ruled Myanmar since independence.

“I have been extremely lenient toward her,” Min Aung Hlaing said in an interview with Time magazine published last month.

In response to questions from AFP, the Foreign Office in London did not say whether British diplomats had sought to deliver the package in person, or been refused permission to do so.

Britain condemns what it describes as Aung San Suu Kyi’s “arbitrary detention” and calls for her immediate and unconditional release.

World.title: Kazakhstan Seeks to Deepen Spiritual and Diplomatic Ties With Egypt and Arab League
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is seeking to expand cooperation with Egypt and the League of Arab States in diplomacy, religious education and interfaith dialogue, as Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi held separate meetings with the region’s senior religious and diplomatic leaders during his official visit to Cairo on Oct. 21.

Tileuberdi met with Grand Imam of Al-Azhar Sheikh Ahmed Al-Tayeb to discuss preserving traditional spiritual values, promoting interfaith dialogue and advancing religious education, the ministry’s press service reported.

Tileuberdi also held talks with Nabil Fahmy, the newly appointed secretary-general of the League of Arab States (LAS), on strengthening ties between the Arab world and Central Asia and addressing regional and international challenges.

Kazakhstan and Egypt expand religious and educational cooperation

During the meeting with Al-Tayeb, the officials highlighted the longstanding historical, cultural and spiritual ties between Kazakhstan and Egypt, describing cooperation in religious and educational fields as an important dimension of their partnership.

They pointed to the ceremonial reopening of Cairo’s historic Sultan Baybars Mosque following extensive restoration and the activities of the Egyptian University of Islamic Culture Nur-Mubarak in Kazakhstan as examples of bilateral cooperation.

Tileuberdi thanked Al-Tayeb for his continued support for the Congress of Leaders of World and Traditional Religions, held in Astana, and invited the Grand Imam to pay a working visit to the Kazakh capital.

They agreed to strengthen cooperation in spiritual and educational affairs for the benefit of the peoples of both countries.

Kazakhstan and Arab League seek closer regional dialogue

In his meeting with Fahmy on Oct. 21, Tileuberdi congratulated the new LAS secretary-general on assuming office and underscored the organization’s role in upholding international law and maintaining regional stability.

The talks focused on opportunities to strengthen the partnership between the Arab world and Central Asia. The officials also discussed the potential signing of a new memorandum of understanding to formalize joint efforts to promote peace and security in the Middle East.

They exchanged views on pressing regional and international topics, reaffirming their interest in expanding dialogue and cooperation.

The two meetings reflect Kazakhstan’s efforts to deepen its engagement with Egypt and the wider Arab world through diplomatic dialogue, religious cooperation and educational exchanges.

World.title: Stories We Inherit: Almaty Exhibition Explores Women’s Memory and Ancestral Knowledge
World.content:
ALMATY – An international exhibition exploring women’s heritage, ancestral knowledge and cultural memory through contemporary art opened at the Tselinny Center of Contemporary Culture in Almaty on Oct. 15, bringing together 21 artists and thinkers from Central Asia and other parts of the world.

Titled “Himoya: Matrilineal Energies, Oracular Kin,” the exhibition is curated by Natasha Ginwala and will run until April 4, 2027. It features newly commissioned works, existing projects and site-specific installations, alongside a research program, workshops and educational events.

The exhibition takes its name from the word “himoya,” which conveys ideas of protection, care and safeguarding vulnerability across several linguistic traditions, including Uzbek, Arabic, Azerbaijani and Sanskrit. Through sculpture, sound, installation and performance, participating artists explore how knowledge and traditions pass between generations, particularly through women and family relationships.

The project also examines how colonial histories, social repression and the loss of languages, rituals and ways of life have shaped cultural memory across Central Asia and beyond.

“For Tselinny, Himoya is the culmination of conversations that began back in 2021,” said Alima Kairat, the center’s artistic director. “Conversations about matrilineal memory, rituals, protection, inherited languages of shame and care that continue to live within us, even when we stop being aware of them.”

Kairat said these topics are deeply rooted in the experiences of Kazakhstan and Central Asia, where memory is transmitted not only through archives but also through the body, gestures, everyday practices and intergenerational relationships.

“Turning to ancestral knowledge, the exhibition invites us to see it not as evidence of the past, but as a living force capable of reinterpreting the present and opening up new horizons for the future,” she said.

Women’s stories and overlooked histories

Among the exhibition’s works is “Iron Mother” by Uzbek artist Aziza Kadyri, an interactive installation based on the story of her grandmother, Umida, one of the few women to oversee the construction of the Tashkent TV Tower. Umida later became its first director.

Despite her professional achievements, Umida’s personal recollections of the male-dominated power structures of Soviet Uzbekistan remained unpublished. Kadyri transforms this family history into an installation resembling a dismantled television studio and control room. Visitors take the position of a person operating a broadcast, gaining the ability to determine how Umida’s voice is heard. The work explores how women’s stories, long confined to family circles or excluded from official historical narratives, can gain a public platform.

Another featured project comes from Colombian artist Ana María Millán, who visited Almaty in March and conducted a role-play laboratory with local participants at Tselinny. The workshop used collaborative storytelling to develop characters, their abilities and scenarios that could be explored through choreography and motion capture.

The process is informing a new animated work in the format of a video game, connecting Kazakhstan and Colombia through protection, women’s autonomy, care and the reimagining of the monster. Rather than arriving with a completed project, Millán developed the work through collaboration with participants in Almaty, making the creative process itself part of the exhibition’s exploration of shared experience.

Sound, mythology and cultural connections

South Korean artist Haegue Yang presents “The Bear-Woman’s Story in the Sand Cave,” an audio installation originally created in 2009 and adapted for its presentation in Almaty.

With support from the Korean Cultural Center at the Embassy of South Korea in Kazakhstan, the work has been recorded in four languages: Kazakh, Russian, English and Koryo-mar, the language of ethnic Koreans in Kazakhstan. Local participants’ voices feature in the different versions.

The installation combines the Korean myth of Dangun with Japanese writer Kobo Abe’s 1962 novel “The Woman in the Dunes.” In Yang’s interpretation, a bear-woman lives in a dark cave with a tiger and must continuously remove sand to prevent the cave from being buried. Her endless labor, largely unnoticed by others, becomes a way to explore solitude, endurance, survival and invisible work.

Research conducted by Yang in Almaty and its surroundings, including visits to archaeological sites and ancient petroglyphs, informed the visual development of her new sculptures. The traditional Kazakh percussion instrument asatayak also served as a source of inspiration, with its form, symbolism and sound reflected in the works.

During her visit, Yang also went to the State National Academic Korean Theater of Musical Comedy, where she explored the history and culture of ethnic Koreans in Kazakhstan. This encounter contributed to the decision to incorporate local voices, including Koryo-mar speakers, into the audio installation.

An international dialogue on ancestral knowledge

The exhibition brings together artists including Ahmed Umar, Almagul Menlibayeva, Ariz Katki, Chitra Sasmita, Güzel Zakir, Jazgul Madazimova, Nara Beibit, Rajni Perera, Ritika Pandey, Umida Akhmedova, Yelaman Mukhtarhan, Zarina Mukanova and Zilola Saidova, among others. Drawing on Tengrian traditions, ancient Turkic mythology, spiritual cosmologies and forms of kinship, the exhibition considers artistic practice as a means of preserving memory and rethinking inherited narratives.

Its architectural and exhibition design, developed by Diogo Passarinho Studio, responds to the history of Tselinny’s building as a former Soviet cinema. The design reimagines the space as a setting for shared experience, collective imagination and non-imperial forms of cultural expression.

The exhibition is supported by the SÄR Foundation. Other partners include the Korean Cultural Center in Kazakhstan, the Office for Contemporary Art Norway, Geneva-based gallery FORA and the AMA Foundation.

Through its combination of contemporary artworks, research and community participation, the exhibition explores how women’s experiences, ancestral knowledge and cultural traditions continue to shape identities and creative practices across generations.

World.title: Kazakhstan Proposes AI Network, Transport Integration at SCO Meeting in Dushanbe
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has proposed establishing a network of artificial intelligence centers under the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) and integrating regional transport corridors under a unified strategy through 2035, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov said at an Oct. 20 meeting of SCO heads of government in Dushanbe.

Bektenov attended a collective meeting hosted by Tajik President Emomali Rahmon and SCO Council of Heads of Government sessions in narrow and expanded formats, bringing together representatives of member states and partner countries, the Prime Minister’s press service reported.

Welcoming the participants, Rahmon highlighted the SCO’s role as a platform for constructive dialogue, peace and stability amid changing global conditions. He called for expanding trade and investment, strengthening transport links, deepening industrial and agricultural cooperation, advancing digitalization and green technologies, and reinforcing energy and food security.

Rahmon also emphasized joint efforts to combat terrorism, extremism, cyber threats, drug trafficking and transnational organized crime. He highlighted the importance of establishing an SCO Anti-Drug Center in Dushanbe and called for greater cooperation in artificial intelligence, innovation and workforce development, reported Kazinform.

He also noted Tajikistan’s initiative, supported by the UN General Assembly, to declare 2027-2036 the International Decade for Strengthening Peace for Future Generations. Other priorities included climate change adaptation, environmental protection, glacier preservation and the sustainable use of water resources.

Addressing the expanded session, Bektenov outlined Kazakhstan’s priorities for strengthening trade, transport connectivity, digital cooperation and regional energy and water security.

Trade and transport connectivity

Kazakhstan called for removing trade barriers, simplifying customs procedures and expanding the use of national currencies in cross-border settlements. National currencies already account for nearly 70% of Kazakhstan’s cross-border payments with SCO member states, according to Bektenov.

To improve regional connectivity, Kazakhstan proposed integrating China’s Belt and Road Initiative with existing and planned transport corridors and incorporating common priorities into an SCO Transport Connectivity Strategy through 2035.

Bektenov also called for accelerating the modernization of maritime and dry ports under the SCO Action Plan for the Development of Ports and Logistics Centers through 2030.

The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route was identified as a platform for practical cooperation, with annual freight volumes targeted at 10 million tons.

AI and digital cooperation

Kazakhstan proposed establishing an SCO network of artificial intelligence centers to pool technological expertise and support member states in exchanging and scaling AI solutions.

Bektenov also highlighted the potential of the UN Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific’s Asia-Pacific Center for Digital Solutions in Almaty to facilitate technology transfer and cooperation.

“Only over the past five years, our IT services exports have grown 34-fold, reaching $1.1 billion,” Bektenov said, adding that Kazakhstan aims to strengthen its position as a regional digital hub under its Digital Qazaqstan strategy.

Energy and water security

Kazakhstan raised energy and water security as priorities for regional cooperation, including implementing the SCO Strategy for Energy Cooperation through 2030 and establishing an SCO Center for Water Issues Analysis.

Bektenov said the economic scale, geographic proximity and complementary production capacities of SCO member states created opportunities for more ambitious joint initiatives, including stronger production chains and industrial projects.

The meeting also reviewed reports on the activities of the SCO Business Council and Interbank Consortium for 2025-2026.

Following the sessions, participants signed documents covering multilateral trade and economic cooperation, transport connectivity and investment projects in industrial cooperation. Among them was a decision to establish an SCO digital platform to facilitate international multimodal freight transportation.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Ice Cream Exports Surge Nearly 50-Fold in Nine Years
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s ice cream exports reached $59.5 million in January-August, up from $1.2 million in the same period of 2017, marking an almost 50-fold increase over nine years.

Kazakhstan exported 15,300 tons of ice cream in the first eight months this year. Compared with the same period last year, export volumes rose 28.9%, while export value increased 50.3%, reported QazTrade, Kazakhstan’s trade policy development center, on Oct. 20.

Russia remained the largest market for Kazakh ice cream, importing 10,700 tons worth $41.6 million. The country accounted for nearly 70% of Kazakhstan’s total ice cream exports.

The Kyrgyz Republic ranked second, importing 3,400 tons worth $11.6 million, followed by Uzbekistan, which purchased 965 tons valued at $5.1 million.

Kazakhstan is also expanding its export geography. Shipments to Tajikistan increased 3.2-fold in volume, while exports to Azerbaijan rose 2.1-fold. Kazakh ice cream also entered the Georgian market this year.

Meanwhile, Kazakhstan strengthened its trade surplus in the ice cream category. Imports totaled $39.1 million in January-August, while the trade surplus widened from $3.6 million to $20.4 million year on year, an almost 5.7-fold increase.

Total foreign trade in ice cream reached $98.7 million during the reporting period, up 30.5% compared with the same period in 2025.

World.title: US and Central Asian Countries Outline Shared Vision in Joint Statement at C5+1 Meeting
World.content:
ASTANA – The United States and five Central Asian countries reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening economic, energy, security, and cultural cooperation at the C5+1 Ministerial meeting in Samarkand on Oct. 19.

In a joint statement, the foreign ministers of Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan, and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio shared a vision for an enduring U.S.-Central Asian partnership, grounded in respect for sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity, reported the U.S. Department of State on Oct. 19.

As the Central Asian countries celebrate 35 years of independence and the United States marks 250 years of independence, the governments expressed their commitment to a more peaceful, prosperous future.

“We envision the United States and Central Asia as enduring partners of choice,” the statement said.

The countries pledged to strengthen transportation links, invest in infrastructure along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, and forge digital connections, including through English-language training and education.

They also committed to developing regional economic integration through expanded intraregional trade, improved transport connectivity, harmonized customs procedures, and stronger industrial cooperation.

The statement highlighted opportunities to increase two-way trade and investment, expand e-commerce, and create commercial opportunities for American companies in Central Asia and Central Asian enterprises in the U.S. market.

The countries identified energy cooperation and critical minerals as key priorities, aiming to develop integrated, high-value supply chains, expand mineral extraction and processing, and increase production of value-added goods for international markets.

The governments also pledged to strengthen security cooperation, notably in countering terrorism and transnational organized crime, enhancing border security, and addressing human trafficking, illicit drug trafficking, arms trafficking, and cybercrime.

They reaffirmed their commitment to nuclear security, safeguards, the physical protection of nuclear material, and the peaceful use of nuclear energy.

The statement also emphasized preserving cultural heritage and expanding professional, cultural, and educational exchanges.

Speaking at the meeting, Rubio described Central Asia as a historic crossroads for East-West trade and an increasingly important destination for investment and exports.

“The C5+1 represents not only America’s interest in – but America’s commitment to – fostering closer, peaceful relations with Central Asian countries,” Rubio said.

He noted that the previous C5+1 meeting in Washington had yielded $25 billion in new deals across transportation, energy, finance, and other sectors.

“This group has an opportunity to partner and radically grow our countries in ways unseen in recent history,” he said.

Uzbekistan Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov said the partnership’s next stage should focus on strengthening economic connectivity, attracting advanced technologies and investment, and expanding access to global markets.

He also proposed advancing a strategic partnership in critical minerals, from geological exploration and mineral processing to the establishment of local industrial clusters.

Saidov said Uzbekistan, assuming the C5+1 Secretariat’s co-chairmanship, intends to build on previous achievements and focus on turning agreements into practical results.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan’s Tourism Sector Grows 45% as Industry Revenue Rises
World.content:
ASTANA — The number of people using tourism services in the Kyrgyz Republic reached 5.3 million in 2025, a 45.2% increase from the previous year, as the sector recorded growth in revenue, business activity and investment, according to an analysis by Finprom published Oct. 19.

The figure includes visitors who used organized tourism services, such as hotels, travel agencies and health resorts, as well as an estimate of visitors to private guesthouses and households. The latter accounted for 32.1% of the total, according to data from the National Statistical Committee of the Kyrgyz Republic cited by Finprom.

The organized tourism sector recorded approximately 3.7 million visitors in 2025. Of these, 2.9 million were Kyrgyz citizens and 770,000 were foreign visitors. The number of foreign visitors using organized tourism services increased by 30.5%, or approximately 180,000, compared with 2024.

These figures cover users of organized tourism services and should not be confused with the total number of foreign nationals entering Kyrgyzstan, which also includes people traveling for purposes other than tourism.

Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Russia were the leading source markets for inbound tourism, according to the report.

Tourism’s economic contribution increases

Tourism’s contribution to the country’s gross domestic product rose from 3.2% in 2021 to 3.8% in 2025. The government aims to increase the sector’s share of GDP to 7% by 2030.

Gross output in the tourism sector reached 136.8 billion Kyrgyz soms (US$1.56 billion) in 2025, up 26.8% from the previous year. The figure was 52.8 billion soms (US$603.8 million) in 2021.

Exports of tourism services approached $1.1 billion in 2025, an 8.1% annual increase. Retail trade turnover associated with tourism rose 41.6% to 74.6 billion soms (US$853.1 million). The total value of tourism services reached approximately 21 billion soms (US$240.1 million), around a quarter more than in 2024.

Accommodation providers, including hotels, hostels and other lodging facilities, accounted for 11.1 billion soms (US$127 million) of tourism services. Travel agencies generated 7.6 billion soms (US$86.9 million), while sanatoriums and other health resort organizations accounted for 2.4 billion soms (US$27.4 million).

Tourism service prices increased by 7.6% in 2025. The rise in the sector’s financial indicators therefore coincided with both expanding activity and higher prices.

Investment and tourism businesses expand

Foreign investment in the construction of tourism facilities in the Kyrgyz Republic reached $87.8 million in 2025, the highest level in recent years, according to Finprom. Investors from the Netherlands accounted for $63.9 million of the total.

The report identifies several major tourism development projects, including the Ramada by Wyndham Issyk-Kul sports and hotel complex, the Ala-Too Resort ski resort in the Ak-Suu district of the Issyk-Kul Region, the Mövenpick Ak Keme Issyk-Kul Resort and the Azimut park hotel in the Issyk-Kul Region.

The number of business entities operating in the tourism sector increased from 14,600 in 2021 to 20,700 in 2025.

The Issyk-Kul Region remains a key area for tourism development, including beach and winter sports tourism. The Osh and Chuy regions also contribute to the country’s tourism offering.

Regional air connectivity provides additional travel options. In summer 2025, Asman Airlines and FlyArystan introduced direct flights between Issyk-Kul and Almaty, with four weekly flights planned between the destinations during the summer season.

As the sector expands, its contribution to the economy will depend not only on visitor numbers but also on the development of tourism infrastructure and the quality of services available across the country.

World.title: Tokayev to Deliver Annual State-of-the-Nation Address on Oct. 28
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev plans to deliver his annual state-of-the-nation address on Oct. 28 in the first half of the day.

Tokayev announced the plans in a post on his X account on Oct. 20, saying he was working on the text of the address.

“I plan to deliver my annual state-of-the-nation address on Oct. 28 in the first half of the day. I am working on the text of this important document,” Tokayev wrote.

World.title: Central Asia is Shaping Terms of Cooperation With China, Experts Say
World.content:
ALMATY – Central Asian countries are increasingly shaping how China invests, builds infrastructure and develops technological partnerships in the region, challenging the perception that Beijing follows a single model of global engagement, experts said at an Oct. 20 discussion in Almaty.

Organized by the Almaty-based CAPS Unlock think tank and the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, the discussion examined how local governments, institutions and businesses influence China’s activities across different regions. Experts stressed that Central Asian states are not merely responding to China’s growing presence but are using their own development priorities and bargaining power to influence the terms of cooperation.

At the same time, intensifying competition between the United States and China could make it more difficult for countries in the region to maintain diversified international partnerships, even as global uncertainty creates new opportunities for them to advance their interests.

From a single China model to local adaptation

Carnegie launched the China Local/Global initiative nearly six years ago to study Chinese engagement across seven regions: Central Asia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, Latin America, Africa, the Middle East and North Africa, and the Pacific.

Evan A. Feigenbaum, vice president for studies at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said the initiative was designed to examine how Chinese engagement differs according to local political, economic and institutional conditions.

“While that may be part of the story, it is very clearly not the whole story,” Feigenbaum said of the assumption that China imposes a uniform model on countries around the world. In many cases, he noted, Chinese actors adapt to local practices and partner with domestic stakeholders.

For Central Asian countries, the question is not only how to attract Chinese investment, but also how to ensure that cooperation supports domestic priorities, including economic growth, employment, technological development and the creation of higher-value industries.

CAPS Unlock Executive Director Aida Aidarkulova said the partnership was intended to bring regional expertise into international debates rather than simply introduce foreign perspectives to Central Asia.

“We believe such exchanges enrich everyone involved,” she said, describing the think tank’s broader goal as generating knowledge about Central Asia from within the region and contributing to a regional research agenda.

Investment is shifting beyond raw materials

Djoomart Otorbaev, former prime minister of the Kyrgyz Republic, emphasized that China’s economic engagement in Central Asia has evolved over the past three decades, with a growing emphasis on foreign direct investment, industrial localization and more structured approaches to borrowing.

“Engagement between China and Central Asia is not merely borrowing now, but a structural shift towards FDI, foreign direct investment, industrial localization, and far more disciplined sovereign borrowing,” Otorbaev said.

According to the figures cited by Otorbaev, accumulated Chinese foreign direct investment in Central Asia reached $56 billion by mid-2025, nearly doubling over the previous decade.

While raw materials accounted for approximately 68% of Chinese investment in the region a decade ago, that share has since declined to 54%. Manufacturing now represents 22%, while energy, including renewables, accounts for 12%.

“Today manufacturing accounts for 22% of Chinese FDIs in Central Asia. In energy, including renewables, 12%. This is industrial embedding to my classification,” he said.

Kazakhstan remains the largest single recipient of Chinese investment. Uzbekistan has emerged as an increasingly significant competitor for capital, Otorbaev said. He pointed to the expansion of Chinese investment in Uzbekistan as a reason for Kazakhstan to strengthen its own investment environment.

“Yes, we are competing very, very hard with each other to be better,” he said. “So now I think, with all my excuses, it is a wake-up call for Kazakhstan.”

“What we want from China is cooperation in new 21st century economies. China’s most disciplined expansion is happening in Central Asia,” he added.

U.S.-China rivalry puts pressure on regional choices

Feigenbaum cautioned, however, that the growing role of local governments could be challenged by intensifying strategic competition between Washington and Beijing.

“The way I would describe the change is the securitization of everything, by which I mean that every issue, including economic flows, goods, capital, people, technology, data, are being refracted by both Washington and Beijing through the prism of national security in their own competition,” he said.

“If you’re sitting in this region, as in most regions of the world, I often use a mathematical metaphor. The mathematical operations that matter are addition and multiplication, not subtraction and division,” he added.

He warned that the growing rivalry could make it harder for regional governments to maintain that flexibility.

Temur Umarov of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center similarly urged analysts to pay closer attention to political and economic changes originating within Central Asia.

“I do believe that we pay too much attention to what is happening outside of Central Asia, not so much to what is actually happening here,” Umarov said. “And I think that this is one of the biggest problems that we have as people who write, observe, and analyze events in Central Asia, because it is not just unfair, it is wrong.”

He said international developments, including the geopolitical shocks and U.S.-China tensions, influence the region, but should not overshadow the agency of Central Asian governments themselves.

“The initiative in that activity is not coming from Washington,” Umarov said, stressing that regional political leaders have used international uncertainty to attract attention and expand their diplomatic and economic options.

He added that a new generation of actors is emerging across Central Asia’s political institutions, businesses and civil society.

“It is actually happening on all of the layers of government or any other institution, body, company, business, NGOs. Everywhere you see the new generation appearing,” Umarov said, highlighting that the current international environment, despite its instability, creates opportunities for countries located between major powers to strengthen their own positions.

The discussion also featured how regional experience can inform policymakers beyond Central Asia, reinforcing the organizers’ argument that understanding China’s global role requires attention to local conditions rather than assumptions about a single, universal model.

World.title: Russian-led EAEU bloc warns Armenia of possible ‘serious blows’ to its economy
World.content:
Report on suspension of Armenia’s membership of EAEU

Four countries in the Russia-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) may discuss suspending Armenia’s membership of the bloc. A report prepared by experts from the intergovernmental council of Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan says so.

The report’s main argument is that Armenia would face serious economic difficulties if it left the Eurasian Economic Union. These would include a 15.6% contraction in GDP.

“All the figures in this report are exaggerated by around 50%,” Armenian Economy Minister Gevorg Papoyan said in response.

He assured journalists that the impact on the country’s economy would be negligible, at around -0.61%. Papoyan cited figures from a study conducted in Armenia. The country set up a working group to assess the potential consequences of leaving the EAEU. It included representatives of the Central Bank and two ministries: the economy and finance ministries.

Unlike members of the ruling party, the parliamentary opposition considers the figures in the report alarming. Arthur Khachatryan, an MP from the Armenia bloc, said that even if the forecast proved only half accurate, the consequences would be “apocalyptic”.

Moscow has yet to comment on the document. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the presidential administration had not yet reviewed the report.

Context

At a meeting of the Supreme Eurasian Economic Council in Astana on 29 May 2026, the presidents of Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan issued a joint statement. They expressed concern about Armenia’s moves to strengthen ties with the European Union. In their view, European integration by an EAEU member could pose risks to the economic security of the bloc’s other countries.

They urged the Armenian authorities to hold a nationwide referendum as soon as possible on whether to choose the EAEU or the EU.

“We are working within the Eurasian Economic Union and will continue to do so until a choice between the European Union and the EAEU becomes unavoidable,” Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan replied at the time. He stressed that the people would make the decision in a referendum. However, he said he currently saw no grounds for a nationwide vote on the issue. He explained that Armenia’s European integration process had not yet reached the stage at which citizens could make such a choice: “Until Armenia officially applies for EU membership or comes close to obtaining candidate status, holding any referendum would make no sense.”

The heads of state also instructed their representatives to prepare a report by December 2026 on “the possible consequences of suspending the Treaty on the Eurasian Economic Union in respect of the Republic of Armenia”.

A closer look at the report

According to the report, Armenia’s actions contradict an obligation set out in Article 3 of the EAEU Treaty. The article requires member states to help create favourable conditions for the union to fulfil its functions and to refrain from actions that threaten its objectives.

The authors apparently mean a law adopted by Armenia’s parliament to launch the process of joining the EU. The EAEU may also have taken note of Armenia’s more active political dialogue and growing economic ties with the European Union.

The report again calls for a referendum in Armenia on “the EAEU or the EU”. The authors note that if the decision to suspend Armenia’s EAEU membership goes ahead, the suspension could remain in force until the referendum takes place.

However, the authors themselves acknowledge that the EAEU Treaty contains no explicit mechanism allowing member states to unilaterally suspend another country’s membership.

Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan nevertheless invoke the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties. The report says the four countries could consider adopting a joint decision to suspend Armenia’s membership under the convention’s provisions.

The document specifically warns that suspending Armenia’s membership would reduce the total volume of trade with other EAEU member states by 55.6%. The EAEU report also warns of the following consequences:

the reintroduction of customs controls and duties, comprehensive sanitary inspections and taxation of goods;

a 30–50% decline in exports of Armenian-made goods and a reduction of more than 90% in the re-export of goods;

a 15.6% contraction in the country’s GDP, a 14.9 percentage-point rise in inflation and a 14.6% fall in consumption;

an increase in the price of gas for Armenia from $177.50 to $300 per 1,000 cubic metres, a rise of 69%;

tighter restrictions on labour migration for Armenian citizens.

How Yerevan has responded to the report

“Armenia has always honoured its obligations to the EAEU in good faith”

Economy Minister Gevorg Papoyan said Armenia had always honoured its obligations to the EAEU in good faith.

“There are no obligations that we have failed to fulfil. We see this as an economic dispute, one that also concerns economic restrictions.”

Papoyan said Yerevan had lodged a complaint with the Eurasian Economic Commission and was awaiting a meeting on the issue, scheduled for 3 November.

“What do the EAEU rules say? They say that if you believe you have been treated unfairly — for example, if someone has imposed unjustified restrictions on you — you have the right to file a complaint.”

The dispute concerns economic restrictions that Russia imposed on imports of Armenian products. They have been in force since May and remain in place. Other EAEU member states have also backed them.

Although Armenia has already filed a complaint, the minister doubts it will secure a favourable ruling. He noted that the commission requires consensus, meaning all member states — including Russia — must agree.

As for the threat of higher gas prices, Papoyan expects a negative impact.

“A change in gas prices can have varying effects: one scenario could see a 5% impact, another 7% or more. Even a 1% increase in the price would be highly undesirable.”

However, the minister said that even a rise in gas prices would not have consequences so severe that Armenia’s economy could not cope with them.

“In principle, I find this acceptable, even normal. Everything should be paid for at market prices. If we do not pay the market price for something, we ultimately pay for it in some other way.”

Amid debate over a possible increase in the price of Russian gas, some Armenian experts and residents say that “Armenia has spent decades paying for cheap gas with its sovereignty”.

“They cannot expel Armenia from the EAEU”

Hasmik Hakobyan, an MP from the ruling Civil Contract faction, is not worried about Armenia being expelled from the EAEU because no such procedure exists.

“They cannot expel Armenia from the EAEU, even if every other member state wants to.”

She stressed that Armenia is not leaving the union and has expressed no intention of doing so. Under EAEU rules, the only way to end membership is for the country itself to decide to withdraw.

“We want to continue cooperating in the same spirit and, where possible, discuss all issues and challenges at the negotiating table,” she said.

Commentary

According to analyst Vahe Davtyan, the most interesting part of the document concerns the potential losses for other EAEU member states. It says that suspending Armenia’s membership would not cause them serious economic problems. In Russia’s case, for example, the projected decline in the total volume of imports and exports of goods and services would not exceed 1%.

“The report’s political message is crystal clear. Economic pressure on Armenia could prove virtually painless for the other EAEU countries, while dealing a heavy blow to Armenia itself,” he argues.

He warns that if Armenia leaves the EAEU, the sectors hardest hit would include agriculture, food processing, alcoholic beverage production and light industry.

“These are industries for which the Russian market has been one of the main destinations for sales for many years.”

On the possibility of higher prices for Russian gas, the analyst notes:

“Suspending membership of the EAEU does not automatically mean that gas prices will be revised. The inclusion of this scenario in the document can therefore be seen as a political signal.”

In Davtyan’s view, the report’s authors have overlooked an important detail: bilateral agreements between Armenia and Russia also govern gas supplies. Nevertheless, he stresses that any change in gas prices would inevitably affect electricity generation costs and the competitiveness of Armenian industry.

Report on suspension of Armenia’s membership of EAEU

World.title: German foundations leave Georgia: what the crisis in Berlin-Tbilisi relations means
World.content:
Two German foundations, the Konrad Adenauer Foundation and the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, have ceased operations in Georgia, where they had worked for more than two decades.

The move follows the adoption of a law on grants that requires foreign foundations to obtain government permission to operate in Georgia. The two foundations failed to secure approval and announced their withdrawal from the country.

Two other German foundations, the Heinrich Böll Foundation and the Friedrich Ebert Foundation, have resumed operations after a pause — at least for now.

The problems facing German foundations in Georgia are not viewed in isolation. Instead, they are seen as another consequence of repressive legislation and a clear sign that relations between Tbilisi and Berlin have reached an impasse.

Germany was among the first countries to support Georgia and express solidarity with it in the early years after independence. However, relations between Georgia and Germany have deteriorated over the past several years.

The crisis deepened in 2024, when the Georgian government’s decision to suspend European integration, its adoption of repressive laws and its crackdown on protests drew sharp criticism from the German government.

The Georgian authorities responded by launching a campaign to discredit Germany’s ambassador and the country as a whole. Germany, in turn, imposed visa restrictions on some members of the ruling Georgian Dream party. It also suspended planned development projects worth €237 million with the Georgian government.

Germany is more than just a partner country for Georgia. It is one of the European Union’s most influential political players, while Georgia remains a candidate for EU membership. The deterioration in Georgian-German relations therefore goes beyond diplomatic disagreements.

What German foundations did in Georgia

All four German foundations had operated in Georgia since the early 2000s. Their aim was to support the country’s democratic development and strengthen civil society. They worked with government agencies, civil society organisations, young people, researchers, women and minority groups. Their activities covered a wide range of areas, and they implemented dozens of projects across the country that benefited hundreds of people.

Dea Metreveli, who holds a doctorate in philology, headed the state-run Book Centre for many years. She says it would have been very difficult for the centre to attend prestigious events such as the Frankfurt Book Fair without support from the German foundations. Georgia’s participation, which also brought Georgian authors to the fair, had been a major achievement.

“When we prepared for the fair in 2018, the foundations had already laid the groundwork for our participation. They helped us organise various events. Much of this tremendous success came from our cooperation with them,” Metreveli recalls.

Giorgi Butikashvili, a lecturer at Ilia State University, worked for 12 years as a programme manager at the South Caucasus office of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation.

He recalls, among other things, joint Georgian-Abkhaz projects and dialogue between religious communities. The foundation’s support made these initiatives possible. He says Georgian government agencies took part in all these projects.

“When projects involving Abkhaz participants began, for example, everything was coordinated with the Ministry of Reconciliation. We planned everything in line with the government’s strategy. Germany was not pursuing its own interests; it was helping Georgia pursue its national interests. The German government provided resources that the Georgian state itself lacked.”

Metreveli also remembers a specific project involving Abkhaz participants: a joint collection of works by contemporary Georgian and Abkhaz women writers, published in Georgian and Abkhaz. It was one of the last projects the Konrad Adenauer Foundation helped implement.

“Imagine a single book featuring four contemporary Georgian women writers alongside four Abkhaz women writers living in Sukhumi. They worked together for a year, discussed the concept of the publication together and became friends.”

The Soviet Past Research Laboratory (SOVLAB) also worked with all four German foundations at various times over many years. Irakli Khvadagiani, a historian and researcher at the organisation, says their support enabled SOVLAB to publish a range of works on the Soviet and Russian occupation, state terror and the stories of countless individuals.

“From 2012 onwards, the state effectively pursued a passive-aggressive approach. It had no agenda for memory politics. On the contrary, it left the door wide open to Russian disinformation. Then, from the late 2010s, the authorities moved into a more aggressive phase: attacks on us and civil society, and the closure of archives. Under these conditions, we were able to keep working largely thanks to these foundations.”

Khvadagiani says the foundations helped fill the vacuum that the Russian regime was creating in the fields of historical memory, research and the teaching of contemporary history. None of this work would have been possible without the support of Germany’s partners.

Beyond the foundations’ work in Georgia itself, the German government also supported hundreds of young Georgians in pursuing higher education in Germany. One of them is Mamuka Andguladze, chair of the Media Advocacy Coalition. Funding from Germany’s DAAD programme enabled him to earn a doctorate in media law in Germany.

“It was very important to me to have the opportunity to study in Germany. Hundreds of young people had the same opportunity. And what happened to the knowledge they gained? They brought it back to our country. You get an education and return home to help build better institutions, a better court system and better elections.”

Why the problem facing the foundations is about more than the foundations themselves

Tina Khidasheli, Georgia’s former defence minister and now head of the organisation Civic IDEA, believes the problems facing German foundations should not be viewed solely as a consequence of repressive legislation.

In her view, this is the first clear sign of deteriorating relations between Georgia and Germany. She says Germany has historically played a key role in the development of the Georgian state, dating back to the early 20th century. Georgia’s state institutions are rooted in German legislation, law and institutional structures. Politicians from successive generations have attached particular importance to relations with Germany, making the current situation unprecedented.

For Giorgi Butikashvili, the situation clearly confirms an attempt to consolidate autocratic rule in Georgia.

“The closure of foreign foundations was the final stage in Russia, Belarus and Azerbaijan, when the authorities decided to consolidate autocracy once and for all. This is a symptom of autocratic regimes,” Butikashvili stresses.

What does the tension with Berlin mean for Tbilisi?

According to Irakli Khvadagiani, the crisis in relations with Germany means that Georgia remains behind an Iron Curtain.

“This is a continuation of the imperialist and aggressive policy Russia pursued, including during the Soviet era. Its sphere of influence — the territory it claims, which it sees as encompassing much of Eurasia — must remain behind an Iron Curtain. No outside influence, no ties, no cooperation.”

Tina Khidasheli, meanwhile, does not believe the Georgian Dream government singled out Germany in particular. She points out that its representatives have used similar rhetoric against other European countries. Nevertheless, she sees this as a dangerous sign.

“We are talking about a country that belongs to the G7. A country that is the strongest economically, or by any other measure. Moreover, since Brexit, Germany has become the most important player in the European Union. It carries the greatest weight internationally when it comes to European policy,” Khidasheli says.

She recalls that Germany blocked Georgia’s path towards NATO membership in 2008. It is therefore logical and natural that Georgia’s state policy has always aimed to establish and maintain good relations with Berlin.

“Germany’s veto, Germany’s opposition, mean that we have no chance not only of joining any future round of enlargement, but even of establishing serious relations with either the European Union or NATO.”

Meanwhile, relations between Georgia and Germany have reached an impasse despite the fact that several senior Georgian officials built their professional careers in Germany.

From 2003 to 2020, Georgian Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili worked for the German Agency for Technical Cooperation (GTZ) and the German Agency for International Cooperation (GIZ), including as head of the Georgian team.

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze earned a doctorate in law at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf.

Another Georgian Dream member, Nikoloz Samkharadze, who chairs parliament’s Foreign Relations Committee, also studied in Germany on a Konrad Adenauer Foundation scholarship. In 2003, the foundation funded his master’s degree in European studies at the University of Hanover.

For Tina Khidasheli, the Georgian government members’ ties to Germany are the main reason for the current problems.

“[Georgian Dream founder] Bidzina Ivanishvili demanded that they ‘sort things out’ with Germany, but they failed to do so. This subsequently gave way to aggressive rhetoric,” Khidasheli believes.

She adds that if Georgia wants to make progress towards joining the European Union or NATO, it is crucial for Berlin to support Tbilisi. Otherwise, such progress is impossible. In her view, however, this is precisely what Georgian Dream wants to prevent.

“That is their goal: to squander the opportunity for European integration and then make it look as though they are not to blame.”

World.title: Old enemies in same cell: crime boss beaten, codes and politics. What is happening in Georgia’s prisons?
World.content:
The beating of crime boss Peikrishvili in Georgia

A scandal has erupted at Gldani Prison No. 8 in Tbilisi. Davit Peikrishvili, a well-known crime boss, was taken to hospital twice in two days with multiple injuries.

According to his lawyer, on 16 October, prison authorities placed five inmates whom Peikrishvili considers his “underworld enemies” in his cell. They included Vato Kipiani and Avtandil Bilanishvili, known as Katsro. Authorities had arrested them the previous day over a fight at a restaurant.

The lawyer says the men beat Peikrishvili for several days and demanded the codes to his phone.

Background: Crime bosses Davit and Giorgi Peikrishvili were arrested on 22 September 2026 on charges of violence and extortion. Authorities arrested Kipiani and Bilanishvili on 15 October on charges of group violence. Georgian media often describe Bilanishvili as a friend of Bera Ivanishvili, the son of billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili, who is widely regarded as the country’s power behind the scenes. The alleged links between those involved and Georgia’s elite have long attracted intense discussion in the media and on social networks. Their arrests have caused a major public stir.

In January 2020, law enforcement agencies in Georgia and Ukraine announced that they had foiled a plot to kill brothers Davit and Giorgi Peikrishvili. According to investigators, the perpetrators planned to use a remotely detonated explosive device. Vato Kipiani was charged in connection with the case.

Now, six years later, Peikrishvili’s lawyer says Kipiani and Davit Peikrishvili ended up in the same prison cell.

The Special Penitentiary Service, however, insists that nobody mistreated Peikrishvili. Kipiani’s lawyer says the two men were never held in the same cell.

The Ministry of Justice has launched an investigation into the case.

Davit Peikrishvili (left), Vato Kipiani (right)

This is not the first such incident at Gldani Prison No. 8

Financier Giorgi Bachiashvili was beaten there in suspicious circumstances in 2025. Bachiashvili formerly served as executive director of an investment fund belonging to billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder and honorary chairman of the ruling Georgian Dream party, whom many regard as the country’s “power behind the scenes”.

Bachiashvili said at the time that, before the beating, the prison governor had advised him to hand over his financial data to Bidzina Ivanishvili as quickly as possible. The State Security Service later claimed that Bachiashvili had staged the beating.

Opposition politicians are now linking the Peikrishvili case to cryptocurrency wallets, fraudulent call centres and the Ivanishvili family. Peikrishvili’s lawyer rules out a political motive.

A cell without cameras

The Peikrishvili brothers’ lawyer, Paata Gogiashvili, described the incident in an interview with Formula TV.

He said that after their arrest, both brothers had stayed in cells equipped with CCTV. Prison staff then moved them to different cells and placed Davit Peikrishvili alone in a cell that, according to the lawyer, had no camera.

At 20:00 on 16 October, five more inmates joined him in the cell: Vato Kipiani, Shota Kipiani, Avtandil Bilanishvili, Kacharava and Gotsiridze. Earlier that day, on Friday, Gogiashvili had visited his clients, the Peikrishvili brothers. The lawyer…

On 17 October, journalist Keta Tsitskishvili wrote on Facebook, citing a source, that someone had beaten Peikrishvili in prison. The Penitentiary Service press office denied the report in an interview with Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.

On 19 October, Davit Peikrishvili called his mother and told her he was fine. However, she continued to insist that someone had beaten her son, although she admitted that she had not witnessed the incident herself and that his lawyer had not confirmed it to her.

That same day, lawyer Gogiashvili went to the prison.

He said he found Peikrishvili badly beaten. The prisoner had four broken ribs, fractures to his skull and facial bones, and bruises.

His mother says he had five broken ribs and a double jaw fracture. Based on Peikrishvili’s account, the lawyer alleges that all five cellmates took part in the beating.

According to the lawyer, the cellmates told Peikrishvili that he and his brother had landed them in prison. They demanded access to the brothers’ phones. The lawyer does not know what information the phones contained. He says investigators seized the brothers’ phones and laptops during a search.

The lawyer alleges that prison officials knew about the conflict between the inmates.
