World.title: Families of missing Azerbaijanis hold rally in Brussels (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 21. On October 21, 2026, families of missing Azerbaijanis held a rally organized by the public association "Karabakh Families of Missing Persons" Public Unionin Brussels’ central Schuman Square—home to the main institutions of the European Union. This event followed a demonstration held the previous day in the square in front of the European Parliament in Brussels.

This was reported by the Agency for State Support to Non-Governmental Organizations of Azerbaijan.

During the event, it was emphasized that Armenia has still not provided information regarding the fate of 4,010 missing Azerbaijanis and continues to withhold information about them. Particular attention was paid to the importance of providing information about missing persons as part of advancing the peace agenda.

Families of missing Azerbaijanis have stated that the European Parliament—which consistently advocates for Armenia and is viewed in international relations as an example of anachronism and atavism—has never once raised the issue of the missing Azerbaijanis.

Konul Behbudova, chair of the "Karabakh Families of Missing Persons" Public Union, stated that actions dedicated to the missing persons will continue.

As part of the event, a special installation was presented, featuring photographs of missing Azerbaijani citizens, along with their clothing and envelopes containing letters. The poignant messages, written on behalf of those who have gone missing, left a deep impression on visitors. Attendees expressed their solidarity with the families of the missing by leaving words of support, tying commemorative ribbons, and laying flowers.

The "Families of the Missing in Karabakh" Public Union has emerged as a winner in the 2026 grant competition held by the Agency for State Support to Non-Governmental Organizations of Azerbaijan, with its project titled "Echo of Absence."

World.title: Families of missing Azerbaijanis meet with EU representatives in Brussels (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 21. A meeting with members of the “Karabakh Families of Missing Persons” public association was held on October 21 at the European External Action Service (EEAS) of the European Union in Brussels.

The families of missing Azerbaijanis met with Okke Bouwman, Political Adviser to the EU Special Representative for the South Caucasus and the crisis in Georgia, and Marco Cardinali, Coordinator for Relations with Azerbaijan.

During the meeting, which lasted about an hour, the families of missing Azerbaijanis stated that Armenia had provided no information about their loved ones, even after the end of the conflict.

Konul Behbudova, chairperson of the public association, noted that on October 20, the previous day, families of missing Azerbaijanis had held a protest at Place du Luxembourg in front of the European Parliament in Brussels and adopted a statement.

She stressed that Armenia bears direct responsibility for the fate of missing Azerbaijanis and is obliged to share information with Azerbaijan about the locations of mass graves. Behbudova noted that 32 mass graves have been discovered to date in Azerbaijan’s territories liberated from occupation.

The meeting also addressed another protest held by families of missing Azerbaijanis in Brussels that day, at the central Schuman Square. It was emphasized that the families would not remain silent until they received information about their loved ones and would continue to hold regular protests.

World.title: Lamarre-Condon double murder trial shown five hours of CCTV
World.content:
A NSW court has released nearly five hours of CCTV footage showing what prosecutors say are the movements and alleged attempts to cover up a double murder by Beau Lamarre-Condon after he is accused of shooting a young Sydney couple.

Surrounded by shoppers at multiple Bunnings stores in the days following the deaths of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies on February 19, 2024, the footage shows the then-police officer picking out supplies and making cash purchases.

Emergency services on Triple Zero (000) if you need immediate care

It shows various changes of vehicle from Mr Lamarre-Condon's Tesla, to a hired Mazda, and a hired white van which he allegedly used to transport the men's bodies.

He made various returns to Mr Baird's street in Paddington, where it is alleged Mr Baird and Mr Davies were shot with the defendant's police pistol before their bodies were stored in surfboard bags.

The 31-year-old has pleaded not guilty in the NSW Supreme Court and is arguing self-defence, with his lawyers indicating it is his case the two men died during separate struggles involving the gun in the share house.

Mr Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty and is claiming self defence over the deaths of Jesse Baird (left) and Luke Davies. (Instagram)

Bunnings, surgery and sushi with a friend

The Crown alleged Mr Baird and Mr Davies were murdered on a Monday morning.

On the Tuesday, Mr Lamarre-Condon visited Bunnings in Alexandria for items including gumboots, a drill, hi-vis clothing and dust masks.

He made stops at ATMs and had sushi with a male friend in Cronulla.

On the Wednesday, he was dropped by an Uber at St Vincent's Private Hospital early in the morning for what the jury heard was a minor procedure.

The CCTV compilation shows more stops at ATMs before a trip to Bunnings in Rockdale for a tarpaulin, two sets of white overalls in different sizes, gloves, bin bags, a shovel, a wheelbarrow, and six bags of quick-set concrete.

The court heard that in the afternoon, he picked up a friend known during the trial by the pseudonym Elizabeth Kennedy in a white van.

Ms Kennedy testified they booked accommodation for an upcoming trip before he asked if she wanted to go for a drive.

Beau Lamarre-Condon's messages about Jesse Baird Texts between double-murder accused Beau Lamarre-Condon and a colleague show how he perceived his on-again-off-again relationship with alleged victim Jesse Baird.

She recalled the vehicle smelled "lemony" and saw a blue tarp in the back.

Ms Kennedy, who at times communicated with the accused in messages or calls on encrypted app Signal, gave evidence she was told to turn off her phone, and during the two-hour drive to Goulburn, the windows were kept down and the air conditioning was on.

The CCTV shows the pair stopping at Bunnings in Goulburn, where she says Mr Lamarre-Condon asked her to pay for an angle grinder.

According to Ms Kennedy's evidence, they then arrived at a farm which had dams.

She claimed Mr Lamarre-Condon said he knew the owners and had to "break in and save the cattle" which were going to get out.

She said she refused his request to help put garbage bags over the van's number plates.

"I just thought he was up to something," Ms Kennedy told the court.

The witness recalled being left at the gate for 30-to-40 minutes while Mr Lamarre-Condon drove towards a dam on the property, during which time it started getting dark and she had a panic attack.

"I was hyperventilating and crying," she said, recalling how Mr Lamarre-Condon was in gumboots when he returned.

Witness recalls 'freezing' car trip

She described the return to Sydney as "an awful drive" because "it was freezing".

Ms Kennedy said Mr Lamarre-Condon made "cryptic" comments, including about her medication, having nightmares, and whether she had thought about suicide.

She testified he told her he would need to return to Goulburn and would be "up all night", requesting she buy him a peach iced tea for the caffeine.

The blue tarp she previously noticed was gone from the rear of the vehicle, Ms Kennedy said.

The prosecution alleged Mr Lamarre-Condon unsuccessfully attempted to sink the men's bodies in the dam using cement and weights.

Police at the property in Bungonia, south-west of Sydney. (ABC News: Isobel Roe)

They were ultimately found near a monastery in the Bungonia area.

When Ms Kennedy was cross-examined, defence counsel John Stratton SC asked her about her mental health diagnoses, including borderline personality disorder and bipolar disorder.

He suggested, through his questions, an alternative version of the trip, putting to the witness Mr Lamarre-Condon had called her on Signal, told her about the deaths and asked if he should go to police.

But Ms Kennedy denied she replied with: "I watch a lot of crime documentaries — we have to hide the bodies, they won't believe you."

She also rejected suggestions she had made a reference to Taylor Swift by saying it was like the song No Body, No Crime.

Mr Lamarre-Condon is on trial over the alleged murders of Mr Baird and Mr Davies. (Instagram)

"He was the one who put that song on in the car," Ms Kennedy said.

Mr Stratton suggested his client told the witness, before the trip, that "if you don't want to help me, I understand", and lifted the tarpaulin to show her the head of Mr Baird in the van.

"He never mentioned anything about helping him with anything … he definitely didn't want me to know there was anything in the back," she said.

The jury heard Ms Kennedy gave an induced statement to police; representing a promise what she told them could not be used to prosecute her.

She was granted a certificate which had the same effect in relation to her evidence in court.

Jurors heard the arrangement did not extend to protection against potential falsity of evidence or perjury.

During cross-examination, she rejected suggestions Mr Lamarre-Condon had warned her if she helped him she could be charged with being an accessory, saying she did not know anything about the alleged murders.

She denied she had worn one of the pairs of white overalls and a mask, and had used a knife to put holes in a surfboard bag containing Mr Davies's body when it would not sink.

Asked during her evidence-in-chief about repeated attempts to call Mr Lamarre-Condon the following day, Ms Kennedy said she "wanted answers about his behaviour" having seen news about Mr Baird's disappearance.

She claimed a panicked Mr Lamarre-Condon, who was by that point planning to meet with police on the Friday, told her on a call: "If I can't go to Europe with you I'm so sorry, I love you."

"It sounded like a final phone call," she told the jury.

The trial, now in its fifth week, continues on Friday.

World.title: Melbourne man arrested by passers-by after attempted carjacking with axe
World.content:
A man has been arrested for allegedly trying to steal a car while armed with an axe during a multi-vehicle collision in Melbourne's north.

Police say they were called to reports of an eight-vehicle collision at the intersection of Sydney Road and Bolinda Road about 7am this morning.

Officers were told one of the drivers involved in the collision, a 29-year-old man from Altona North, was armed with an axe and attempted a carjacking.

Police say a vehicle struck him and then passers-by detained him in a nearby side street, until police arrived and took him into custody.

He was taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries under police guard.

No-one else was injured, police said.

Officers want any witnesses with footage or information of the incident to contact Crime Stoppers, to assist with their investigation.

World.title: Eastern Sydney beaches close after whale carcass washes up
World.content:
Coogee and Maroubra beaches in Sydney's east have been closed after a whale carcass, suspected of being a young humpback, was spotted floating against the coastline.

The dead whale was spotted at Lurline Bay this morning.

Randwick Council announced the beaches would be closed to swimmers pending the carcass's removal.

"Maroubra and Coogee Beaches will remain closed until further notice while lifeguards monitor the situation and work with local stakeholders and authorities to arrange the whale's removal," the council published in a social media post.

Whale scientist Vanessa Pirotta said sharks would likely be drawn to the area.

Loading Instagram content

"We do expect to see whales pass during this time," she said.

"The population is large and more individuals mean we are likely to see this."

"I would strongly advise not swimming in the area."

While the council identified the whale as a baby, Dr Pirotta said it was likely a young adult or teenaged humpback whale.

The whale is not the first to wash up on Sydney's coast this year.

A juvenile humpback whale calf washed up on Greenhills Beach in Sydney's Sutherland Shire in July and was tested for H5N1 bird flu, coming back with a negative result.

In April several beaches in the Royal National Park were closed for days after a carcass that attracted sharks washed up on the rocks at Era Beach.

Drone footage from a local operator appeared to show material wrapped around one of the whale's fins.

World.title: Victorian public schools to be fully funded — but only by 2034
World.content:
The basketball court at Pembroke Primary School has not seen a game in two years.

The court is full of potholes, and parent James Dunn said the school in Melbourne's outer east cannot afford to fix them.

"When you've got 90 kids running around and you've got half your playground fenced off, it's pretty frustrating," said Mr Dunn, who has been treasurer on the school council for three years.

A large section of Pembroke Primary School's basketball court has been fenced off due to potholes. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Pembroke students were missing out altogether on school camps and extracurricular activities because the school was "running on a shoestring", Mr Dunn said.

Yesterday Victorian Premier Ben Carroll announced his government had finally signed off on a promised deal with the federal government on school funding.

Victoria currently only pays 70 per cent of the agreed School Resource Standard, recommended by the Gonski review in 2012, while the federal government contributes 20 per cent.

Mr Carroll confirmed Victoria will lift its contribution to 75 per cent after a move signed off by state cabinet this week, calling it the "biggest investment in schools ever" by the Victorian government.

However, state schools will not receive 100 per cent of the school resourcing standard until 2034.

Mr Dunn said that the deal had only been made a month out from the state election, after Labor had run Victoria for 12 years, was disappointing.

"It feels like the kids are now a political football," he said, expressing frustration over the prolonged timeline for full funding.

" Things have got to be done now. "

Principals, union cautiously welcome deal

The Australian Principals Federation welcomed the deal but said the proposed timeline meant full funding remained years away.

"The challenges facing our schools are immediate," said Victorian branch president Andrew Cock.

"It is essential that meaningful funding increases are delivered progressively, rather than schools having to wait until the end of this period to see the benefits," he said.

" Our message continues to be simple — if we expect Victorian government schools to deliver a world-class education, we must fund them to do so. "

Australian Education Union Victorian Branch president Justin Mullaly said while the announcement was welcome and provided greater certainty, there was devil in the detail.

"Victorian public schools will not receive some of the additional funding as soon as other states and territories," he said.

Justin Mullaly says funding delays have consequences for schools. (ABC News)

"The delay in signing and the decision to back-end the deal, will short change Victorian public schools by hundreds of millions of dollars over the next few years.

" Funding delays have real consequences, and this needs to be addressed. "

Mr Carroll said: "If we can bring forward the timeline and meet the 75 per cent earlier, we will."

Voluntary contributions policy remains a sore point

Prior to yesterday's announcement, tensions had already been growing over parent contributions to keep state schools functioning adequately.

Last month, Victoria's Department of Education instructed schools to tell parents that all curriculum-based instruction and resources, including textbooks, are free and that there was no obligation to pay for school contributions.

Schools can ask for contributions for extra-curricular activities like camps and excursions or learning materials to keep.

Deputy Premier Gabrielle Williams also serves as education minister. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Education Minister Gabrielle Williams defended the guidance, telling the ABC it was "updated to make it absolutely clear that school contributions are voluntary".

Kim, a librarian at a Melbourne public high school not given permission to speak publicly, said her school would cover items for lower income students, but could not afford "extras" like school camps.

"Our school is 'free' but it's falling apart, any couches are from hard rubbish and the roof is leaking," she said.

James Dunn says parents are fed up with state funding not covering basic repairs on government school infrastructure. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

"School is free, but with 12-year-old science textbooks … free with old humanities textbooks with no covers.

"It's not a recipe for a winning education offering."

Australian Catholic University researcher Sarah Langman has analysed how voluntary parent payments were characterised in annual reports from 1500 Victorian public schools in 2024.

She said parent contributions were important for "a wide range of things, everything from school libraries to first aid offices to general programs, excursions and camps".

" The concern is then: what are schools going to be left with if they aren't able to provide these opportunities to their students? "

Ms Langman predicted the new Education Department advice would make budgets tighter.

"We would expect that this problem is probably going to become a lot more widespread as these policy restrictions come into place," she said.

"The real question we want people to consider is whether access to educational opportunities should depend on schools' ability to attract voluntary contributions."

Weeds have grown through the cracks in the bitumen of Pembroke Primary School's basketball court. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Parents Victoria chief executive Gail McHardy said payments should not feel like a "moral obligation or source of pressure" for families struggling with the cost of living.

"School leaders and school councils should not be made to feel responsible for passing government funding shortfalls on to parents," Ms McHardy said.

Back at Pembroke primary, Mr Dunn was lukewarm on the Gonski funding announcement and whether it would be enough to repair his school's aging facilities.

"We'll see. Politicians aren't at the top of my trust list," he said.

World.title: Mine on tropical island plans to pump pit water into ocean
World.content:
South32 plans to spend $100 million to pump water from its Northern Territory manganese mine into the ocean as it battles to keep the site open.

The Groote Eylandt Mining Company (GEMCO) has faced huge financial challenges due to ongoing flooding in its pits on the remote island, and the company is planning redundancies.

GEMCO, majority owned by South32, plans to construct about 12 kilometres of pipelines to take up to 80 gigalitres per year from the mine and discharge it into the island's Milner Bay.

The plan has the support of traditional owners via the Anindilyakwa Land Council (ALC), and it has environmental approvals from the NT government.

Traditional owners expect the mine to close in the early part of the next decade.

The new water infrastructure would be in place for the rest of the mine's life.

Mining operations on Groote Eylandt filled with water from Cyclone Megan in 2024. (Supplied)

It is understood South32's production costs have nearly doubled due to excess water management, and it needs to cut about $129 million out of the business.

In its quarterly report, released this week, the company said all production forecasts for next financial year were dependent on the infrastructure being built.

Production for 2025/26 was also below initial forecasts.

In a statement, an ALC spokesperson said it had been discussing the plan with GEMCO and the NT Environment Protection Authority (NT EPA) for more than three years and had confidence in the environmental plans in place.

Further consultation is required because the infrastructure extends beyond GEMCO's mining leases and into Aboriginal-owned land. Work cannot begin without traditional owner consent.

"The ALC is satisfied with the NT EPA's response, and this coupled with the other environmental practices are designed to meet the traditional owner expectations that risk for environmental harm is minimised," the ALC spokesperson said.

An NT government spokesperson said it wanted the mine to continue operating and that the plan had been approved with strict environmental conditions.

"GEMCO is one of the Territory’s most significant mining operations and a major employer and contributor to the Groote Eylandt economy," the spokesperson said.

"The ALC acts for the traditional owners, and on Aboriginal land its consent is a legal requirement. Those discussions are continuing.

"The NT government has supported these discussions where appropriate, while respecting that the agreement is required between independent parties."

The MV Anikitos crashed into a loading wharf on Groote Eylandt due to Tropical Cyclone Megan. (Supplied)

A South32 spokesperson said the water would be clean and it would work to "safely and effectively manage elevated water volumes".

"GEMCO currently manages excess water through a range of pathways, including bush discharge and riverine discharge … water is also used at processing facilities and for dust suppression," the spokesperson said.

"The excess water disposal project is intended to become GEMCO’s primary pathway for managing excess water."

The island and mine site were hit hard by Tropical Cyclone Megan in 2024, but it is understood heavy rain in multiple wet seasons was also a factor.

South32's website says it is the world's largest producer of manganese, a key alloy in the production of steel and aluminium.

World.title: Man United captain branded 'disgrace' for comments following latest loss
World.content:
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes has been labelled a "disgrace" after questioning manager Michael Carrick's tactics following a Champions League defeat to Como.

Fernandes said his side failed to apply enough pressure and adopted a "mood of defeat" after conceding early in Thursday morning's 4-1 loss, a result that increased scrutiny on Carrick.

Como opened the scoring in the second minute and United collapsed, with only a stoppage‑time consolation goal from Joshua Zirkzee making the scoreline slightly less severe.

"We started on the wrong foot and they scored very early," Fernandes told TNT Sports. "There was not enough pressure on the ball and not many good movements off the ball. There were many things not going our way.

"It's a decision from the [coaching] staff not to press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence.

Asked if his comments amounted to criticism of Carrick's tactics, Fernandes said: "That's on the manager and staff to see, not me.

"Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable."

The Manchester United captain was heavily criticised by former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher for his comments.

Carrick raised his arms up in an apology as he approached Manchester United's travelling supporters after the full-time whistle. (Getty Images: Marco Luzzani)

"For Bruno Fernandes to do that, it's a disgrace really," he said on CBS Sports Golazo.

"Last season he got Player of the Year, that was on the back of Michael Carrick becoming the manager, he wouldn't have got that award without Michael Carrick.

"When you think of him as a footballer, he's a talent, but in terms of attitude and the way he goes about things, it's not right at all.

"He's reacted like that because he's been brought off and he's embarrassed tonight by the manager.

"When he talks about pressing … for years, Bruno Fernandes has meant Manchester United can't press because he does things for the crowd.

"I commentate on games watching Man United, and he runs all over the place like a kid in the schoolyard, for the supporters.

"They all think he's working hard, he's not, he's killing the rest of the team.

"Watching him play every week, throwing his arms up at the other players constantly in the game is an absolute disgrace what he's done there, considering how he's performed this season.

"Awful attitude and not what a Manchester United captain should be."

Carrick's position has come under increasing pressure with United now winless in seven matches, and he responded by questioning the players' lack of willingness to run.

"There's a little bit on whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run and you don't run forward and you don't run back, you ain't gonna win," he said in his press conference when notified of Fernandes's criticism.

"It was more than disappointing," the 45-year-old manager said in a separate interview for TNT Sports. "I think everybody's got to take responsibility for that. I'll take responsibility for the overall team and performance, it stops with me and I'm fine with that.

"But as a supporter of this football club, to see a performance like that is unacceptable, I have to say."

Carrick said his side had failed to show the required intensity.

"It's the motivation and the purpose and the intensity of a game of football that you have to bring. We didn't bring that today," he said. "I've got to apologise for the performance."

Fernandes also questioned United's mentality after the early setback.

"Conceding early makes us go into the game with a mood of defeat," he said.

United have three points from their opening three Champions League matches and host AS Roma in their next fixture in the competition.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Breaking: Man charged after allegedly taking nunchucks to WA MP's office
World.content:
A man has been charged after he allegedly wielded a pair of nunchucks and made threats at the electoral office of WA Local Government Minister Hannah Beazley.

Police said they responded to reports of a man causing a disturbance at Ms Beazley's office in Victoria Park, 4 kilometres south-east of the Perth CBD, around 1.15pm yesterday.

The 56-year-old man allegedly threatened staff at the office while in possession of an "improvised martial arts weapon".

Nobody was injured in the incident and the man, from the nearby suburb of Bentley, was arrested at the scene.

Ms Beazley was not in the office at the time.

The man has been charged with making unlawful threats, being armed in a way that may cause fear and possessing cannabis.

His bail was refused and he is expected to face Perth Magistrates Court later today.

World.title: Diamonds looking lost and panicked as Constellation Cup woes continue
World.content:
We are halfway through the Constellation Cup and it is hard to know whether to panic about the state of the Diamonds.

Australia finds itself in a 0-2 hole after losing in Auckland 56-50 and in Christchurch 62-50, with two Tests still left to come in Sydney and Melbourne.

This is the last opportunity the Diamonds have to prepare against international opposition without another series scheduled between now and the 2027 home Netball World Cup.

The Diamonds are hoping to defend their Netball World Cup title in Sydney next year. (Getty: Steve Christo)

The Diamonds have looked uncharacteristically lost and panicked, while the coaches have struggled tactically. Some of Australia's greatest ever players are out of form but still getting a starting position, and fans are questioning why more hasn't been done to develop the next generation of talent.

The recent events at the Commonwealth Games probably feed into the worry, seeing the side fall short of the gold medal match for the first time in August.

If the Diamonds concede all four Tests to New Zealand, they are also expected to be knocked off their number one world ranking, a status they've held since 2013.

So, is the series a lost cause? Are injuries to blame? Or should we hold our breath and hope home-crowd advantage swings momentum? Here are the main talking points at the midway point of the Constellation Cup.

Missing key players

Jo Weston's (right) work out front makes it easier for the goal keeper to win ball. (AAP: James Ross)

Australia is dearly missing defenders Sunday Aryang and Jo Weston.

25-year-old Aryang has been out of action since rupturing her ACL in the last Constellation Cup series. Veteran Weston made herself unavailable for selection to give her body a much-needed break and focus on her Masters studies.

Their work rate at goal defence and wing defence make a huge difference. Weston is a relentless tagger, wearing down the opposition and slowing play outside the circle.

Could she be coaxed into changing her mind? After all, a similar situation happened in 2022, when Weston was originally rested from the series but received an SOS call to cover injury with Australia trailing 2-0. Her team went on to win the final two games at home.

Kate Moloney was ruled out of game one due to a nasty finger injury. (Getty: Ross MacDonald)

The team has also had to rejig its midcourt following injuries to Kate Moloney and Jamie-Lee Price. Moloney was ruled out of the game on Sunday after suffering a finger laceration while trying to catch a ball at training. She returned to play on Wednesday with stitches.

Price appeared in the first match but sustained a calf injury that prevented her from playing in the second. In both instances, head coach Stacey Marinkovich decided to play Liz Watson out of position at centre before subbing her off in the third quarter. It hasn't been the captain's best performance.

Jamie-Lee Price may not be able to return for the rest of the series. (Getty Images: Graham Denholm)

Whether Price will be able to make it back is unclear, but the Diamonds desperately need to do something different defensively. They've been unable to consistently hold up New Zealand's ball speed and the feed into target Grace Nweke.

In Auckland, they were behind on the gain stat 13-6 and in Christchurch it was just as bad, 9-2.

Home-crowd advantage

Silver Ferns smash the Diamonds 3-0 to clinch Constellation Cup The Diamonds were swept aside in Perth by 18 goals, as New Zealand clinch the 2024 Constellation Cup with one game to go.

Since 2014, the Constellation Cup has been played as a four-Test series, granting each country equal hosting rights, and that home-crowd advantage is no joke.

Over the past five series, the team hosting has emerged victorious in 18 of the 20 Tests played.

Because of this, we're unlikely to see either national body agree to hold an uneven number of Tests in the future. Even if it'd be more exciting for fans to see a team win outright than by goal aggregate.

It's certainly been tough going in New Zealand again this year. The Silver Ferns have been the better side in six of the eight quarters and have forced the opposition to make 29 changes, scrambling to find answers.

It's been five years since the Diamonds last won a Test across the ditch. That outing was Marinkovich's second in charge and Watson's first as captain.

In fact, Marinkovich's winning record in New Zealand only sits at 7 per cent since taking on the top job in August 2020. But does that really matter if the team wins the overall series, you may ask? Well, in the 10 series preceding her appointment, Australia only lost it once.

Australian coaches Stacey Marinkovich and Nicole Richardson were left scratching their heads after the loss. (Getty: Fiona Goodall)

In the five completed since, Australia has conceded it twice. A loss in 2026 would give Marinkovich a 50 per cent Constellation Cup success rate. Although she is contracted through to the end of 2027, there is a lot hinging on these results.

New Zealand last beat Australia two years ago in Perth to claim the 2024 trophy. It was the first time in history they'd won three consecutive games within the series.

Now there's a real chance it could happen again.

However, if we're to borrow a cricket analogy, it's important to wait till both teams bat before we place our final judgement. Home-crowd advantage tells us there's a possibility that we could be sitting here in a week's time in a very different state of mind, with two wins on the board.

High penalties

Umpire Gary Burgess officiates a match at the Netball World Cup. (Twitter: Gary Burgess)

A key area holding the Diamonds back has been the lopsided penalty count.

New Zealand has conceded 100 penalties so far, while Australia has conceded 145. That's a lot of time standing beside your player, unable to contribute to play.

What didn't help in the second game was the repeated offensive contacts called against the shooters, as they pushed off the body of Kiwi defender Kelly Jackson, trying to get free.

Donnell Wallam was called four times in 11 minutes of play. Sophie Garbin was called three times across 50 minutes. Kiera Austin tallied up to 12 penalties to finish as the third-most penalised Diamonds player on the night.

As per the typical etiquette in international netball, two neutral umpires have been appointed to officiate the series: Welsh umpire Alison Harrison and English umpire Gary Burgess.

"We had some offensive contacts, so we've just got to seek some clarification from the umpires as to what it is they're seeing so we can adjust for that in the future," Marinkovich said post-play.

"The fact that we also rotated our whole defence line from wing defence to the keeper, I don't think that we're that ill-disciplined throughout the entire unit and we've got to understand what it is that we're doing so we can adjust.

"In history, for the last four years, we've been penalised in New Zealand and it kind of shifts when we're in Australia … But I don't think our game plan changes too differently."

Silver Ferns captain Karin Burger and Diamonds captain Liz Watson. (AAP: James Ross)

That's an interesting observation as the umpires' calls should be consistent no matter where a game is played. But Silver Ferns captain Karin Burger had a similar thought.

"Obviously, knowing that Australia has the home crowd next and 50/50 calls always tend to go in the home side's way, it means the scrap is going to be even harder," Burger said.

"Later in the series there's going to be more tired bodies and defenders are going to need to be really smart about their line to the ball … so that we're contesting clean ball."

How much it means

The scary part is how much New Zealand is gunning for the trophy.

The Silver Ferns have already been brimming with confidence and head coach Noeline Taurua said they believed the Constellation Cup was just as big a pinnacle as the Commonwealth Games gold they won in August.

"You always have that trans-Tasman rivalry, and you've got to back up four straight outings against the one team," Taurua said.

"It is definitely the battle of the minds and the hearts and the bodies."

ABC Sport will live blog game three of the Constellation Cup in Sydney, starting at 4pm AEDT.

You can find this casual-chic diner smack bang in the middle of crowded Darling Square, serving tart cocktails and big plates of generosity. Cuong Nguyen’s dishes beckon diners to dig in, starting with rich chicken-liver mousse on mung- bean bread with soft herbs and pickles.

Follow up with a refreshing charcoal grilled octopus papaya salad (goi bach tuoc) that doesn’t hold back on the zing. Desserts are fine (Vietnamese ice-coffee trifle, say), but we reckon it’s more fun to fill up with a crunchy coconut- and turmeric-laden banh xeo, the crepe cradling meaty prawns, or the DIY rice paper rolls with crushed peanuts and barbecued pork jowl.

The food arrives quickly, as do the good times, although grilled wagyu with a pho demi-glace can be a half-hour wait. Is the $80 steak worth it? You bet.

World.title: Hanasuki
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

When Hansuki opened it felt like exactly what Sydney was missing: an upscale shabu shabu restaurant, where diners could sate their appetite for platters of premium produce to swish through simmering broth. Who knew?

If it’s your first visit, staff make things easy: choose one of four broths from a handy printout – mushroom, say, or the delicate kombu-based signature – add a cartoonishly bountiful platter of vegetables, then add your “delicious plates”: a selection of wagyu, perhaps, featuring marbled chuck roll, sirloin and knuckle, or a mini seafood platter, with oyster, scallops and prawn paste, which cooks into dumplings in the simmering broth.

Ponzu and sesame sauces are on hand for dipping, and mochi kinchaku are an essential, bursting add-on. The space, dressed in wood and beaten copper, may be minimalist, but this is maximal enjoyment, made for sharing with sake and umeshu on hand, right through to the last swish.

Good to know: Still hungry? Ask a waiter to turn the last of your broth into zousui by adding rice and an egg to the cauldron.

World.title: ‘I would strongly advise against swimming’: Sydney beaches closed by decomposing whale carcass
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWWhales ‘I would strongly advise against swimming’: Sydney beaches closed by decomposing whale carcass Angus Dalton Updated October 22, 2026 — 10:02am ,first published 9:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Authorities have closed two Sydney beaches and warned residents of increased shark activity after a whale carcass was discovered floating close to shore in the eastern suburbs. Lifeguards reported the dead whale floating in Lurline Bay, a rocky enclave between Coogee and Maroubra, just before 8am on Thursday. A whale carcass washed up in Lurline Bay in South Coogee. Audrey Richardson “As a precaution, Maroubra and Coogee Beach will remain closed until further notice while lifeguards monitor the situation and work with local stakeholders and authorities to arrange the whale’s removal,” Randwick Council said in a statement. Whale carcasses can attract sharks, which can detect decomposing flesh and blood from kilometres away and come in close to shore to feed.



The carcass appears to be an adult or subadult humpback and is fairly decomposed. “It looks like it could have been dead for a while and washed in,” whale scientist Dr Vanessa Pirotta said. “I would strongly advise against swimming.” The washed-up carcass coincides with the likely return of bull sharks to Sydney’s waters. The species migrate north to Queensland during the cooler months and swim back towards Sydney when coastal temperatures reach 19 or 20 degrees.



While the sharks’ prefer temperatures of 22 degrees, and peak in activity during January and February, research has shown the first sharks are arriving earlier in October each year – and staying around Sydney about a fortnight longer than they used to – as water temperatures climb under climate change. Crowds gather as a whale carcass washed up in Lurline Bay in South Coogee. Audrey Richardson The humpback is believed to have died some time ago. Audrey Richardson In April, a 25-tonne sperm whale washed up near Era Beach and forced the closure of all beaches in the Royal National Park due to the risk posed by scavenging sharks. An estimated 50,000 humpbacks are migrating south to the Antarctic after travelling to warm tropical waters near the Great Barrier Reef to breed and give birth.

There’s no question. The soup here is #thicc and like nothing else around. That’s why you’ll find a queue of devout loyalists every night, keen for its souped-up collagenic intensity achieved by boiling fresh pork bones for 14 hours.

The standard tonkotsu is already enough for most diners to handle, but you can request extra back fat to take it to the next level. Or try the fish tonkotsu boosted with katsuobushi flakes for an extra layer of umami. (Mercifully, a new oat-noodle ramen is a lighter option with lean pork if the original broths prove too much.)

Add-ons including a Flintstones-sized spare rib increase the protein, and we also rate the sweet glaze of the barbecued pork skewers. At least one jammy boiled egg is a must, not to mention pickled cabbage and scallops with garlic sprouts for a palate-cleansing boost.

Good to know: You can pick up a frozen tonkotsu ramen kit to cook at home.

Tucked inside a 160-year-old building, Gundaroo’s offering of “local heart and country soul”, as described by owners Kurt and Tanya Neumann, is all about seasonality.

Rye bread is courtesy of Three Mills in Canberra; entrees begin with house-smoked pork jowl brined for two days and teamed with the acid and crunch of pear, witlof and dates. A portobello tart with manchego and porcini is a flaky pastry affair that carries citrus notes and a nutty cream to highlight the mushrooms’ umami.

Lamb rump from Gundagai is blushing and tender, accompanied by celeriac, braised cavolo nero and a punchy anchovy butter. Sweets might be something rustic such as baked quince clafoutis topped with an earthy chestnut ice-cream.

Service is jolly and jovial, but also backs it up with quickfire answers and recommendations (plus wit) for a wine list that celebrates the region.

Must order: House-smoked Berkshire pork jowl, pear, witlof, walnut, date.

World.title: Frankly Nick’s
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

There’s a lot to be said for a restaurant with a landline as its only means of contact. As customers bite into lush cheese garlic rolls or the supple Cossaca Marinara pizza, they hear the voice of Georgio Panousos, who opened Frankly Nick’s with his childhood friend William Kay in late July.

This is old-fashioned restaurant noise, and diners stream in from all angles, grabbing seats at the tomato-red tables indoors and on the footpath to eat in a spot that feels like an old-school pizzeria mixed with a traditional ristorante.

Kay and Panousos grew up in restaurants, and it shows in the service and on a one-page menu ranging from charred, stretchy cheese and garlic rolls, to puffy edged pies that range from classic to “Sacrilege”, a twist on ham and pineapple that sees the fruit infused with whisky liqueur. Conchiglie alla vodka is oven-baked, tomato salad is impressively simple and gelato-affogato is a cute finish. Frankly, how good.

Good to know: A phone-only ordering system for pick-up has been expanded to include online ordering, with cute merch also available.

World.title: Flyover Fritterie
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

There are no chaiwalas calling you to this skinny, split-level restaurant and chai bar, but its sweet scent of cardamom, clove and ginger works much the same way. At first glance, Flyover Fritterie may not look like the bustling street food stalls huddled beneath the overpasses (flyovers) of Delhi or Mumbai, but inside it feels just as lively, with communal counter seating and an open kitchen and bar, where slow-simmering chai kettles infuse the room with spice.

Then there’s the pleasure of picking up a hot pakora with your fingertips and dredging it through cooling beetroot yoghurt or a sweet-sour tamarind chutney. Purple cabbage fritters can – and should – be used as a spoon to scoop up coconut lime khichri, a soothing daal-like stew of lentils, chickpeas and rice. The chai, like everything else here, is steeped in tradition with a dash of modern flair.

Good to know: Like the chai? You can also get a one-litre bottle to takeaway.

World.title: Brisbane parkland on site of former sewage plant and abattoir wins national award
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPlanning Brisbane parkland on site of former sewage plant and abattoir wins national award Nick Dent October 22, 2026 — 10:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Leaky pipes are not normally a cause for celebration, but on an unseasonably hot Sunday in October the water spilling from the joins of three bright-yellow drainpipes provides cool relief for children playing at the Archerfield Wetlands District Parkland playground. The leakage looks like a plumber’s nightmare, but it’s deliberate. Like the industrial-looking tube slide and the metallic catwalks, it’s part of the playground’s design that pays homage to the site’s former purpose as a wastewater treatment plant. Archerfield Wetlands District Park has won the inaugural Landscape Australia – Public Design award. Christopher Frederick Jones Opened in 2024, the Durack playground is at the centre of the council’s $22 million Archerfield Wetlands Parkland project, itself part of a broader $100 million commitment to transform Oxley Creek.



Now the project has taken out a Landscape Australia Public Design award, beating 26 shortlisted projects from around the country. Brisbane Sustainability Agency turned the 150-hectare site back into a wetland, with a network of walking and cycle trails, play areas, picnic sites, event spaces and a community centre. More than 150,000 native plants were planted to rebuild habitat, and more than 170 bird species, gliders and possums have returned to the formerly heavily polluted wetland. The playground, designed by Urbis in collaboration with Playscape Creations and Epoca Constructions, pays homage to the former water treatment plant. Christopher Frederick Jones “It’s about transforming a site that was really underused and degraded into a site that’s a public asset,” awards jury chair Emily Wong said.



“I think it’s part of a bigger trend of bringing nature into the cities and seeing them as part of the one broader ecology.” Brisbane city councillor Tracy Davis said the project turned a former industrial site into something Brisbane families could enjoy for generations. “Archerfield Wetlands Parkland shows we don’t have to choose between protecting nature and creating more to see and do. We can do both,” Davis said. More than 150,000 native plants were planted in the wetlands. Cathy Finch A major feature of the development is the adaptive reuse of concrete tanks, channels and piping from the former sewage plant into landscaping attributes.



“These remnants have been transformed into seating, feature gardens, informal gathering spaces and stormwater management features, giving the parkland a unique character that connects visitors with its past,” Brisbane Sustainability Agency chief executive Tracy Melenewycz said. The former Inala Wastewater Treatment Plant was commissioned in 1958 to service the growing residential population of the area, originally known as Servicetown. Related Article Architecture Annie and Jim wanted an undercover pool. They ended up with the Australian House of the Year The plant operated for almost four decades before being decommissioned in 1997. The area was also used for cattle grazing, the former Oxley Bacon Factory, and landfill. Wong said the project’s approach to flood management was another reason it won the award.



“Rather than trying to keep the water out, it absorbs the water and slows it down, and also cleans it. That means that the spaces can be open to the public relatively quickly after that happens.” Other projects nominated for the inaugural award included the Barangaroo Station Park in Sydney, the new Sydney Fish Markets, Duncraig Adventure Hub in Perth and the Girraween Visitor Precinct in Girraween National Park. Brisbane’s Green Grid, a proposal for the city’s urban landscape for the Olympics, was named co-winner of the Landscape Australia Award for Analysis and Planning. World.title: Ho Jiak Haymarket
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

It’s hard not to have fun at Ho Jiak (once you’re done queuing and land a table). Owner Junda Khoo says he wants it to remind him of his amah in Penang, and the village atmosphere is casual and warm.

The menu is huge, with all your favourites from char kwai teow to Hainanese chicken rice, and soon-to-be favourites like the char koay kak of wok-fried rice cakes in soy caramel. The kitchen works hard to deliver the true flavours of Malaysia, then takes it further, making them jump with chilli, garlic, belacan, and fermented duck eggs.

Playful dishes – har gau with chilli crab, and roti stuffed with chicken curry – are just as successful as the tried-and-true. Jumbo prawn laksa is generous, rich and creamy, with two different noodles for those paying attention. Bowlfuls of flavour, fun and family.

Must order: Slow-cooked bone-in chicken curry and rice. Classic.

The bar at The Herring Room.

There’s a cosiness about The Herring Room, a vibe that’s somewhere between a stylish grandparent’s dining room and a superior local bistro. But there’s also adventure to the menu, which approaches seafood from all types of different cuisines and angles.

A whole deep-fried baby snapper makes for a grand centrepiece, and has plenty of flaky, slightly sweet flesh to daub in a slick of ginger-laden soy glaze. Dishes like a scallop sashimi artistically drizzled with avruga caviar and a green apple and sudachi dressing show a flair for intricate plating, while slow-cooked octopus with a punchy gochujang and ’nduja vinaigrette demonstrates how to elevate seafood cooking with bold flavours.

Dessert, like a decadent, buttery banana rum baba, can dazzle too. The service is warm and attentive, rightly proud of a restaurant too good to stay a Northern Beaches secret.

Good to know: You can BYO wine for $10 a head.

You can find this casual-chic diner smack bang in the middle of crowded Darling Square, serving tart cocktails and big plates of generosity. Cuong Nguyen’s dishes beckon diners to dig in, starting with rich chicken-liver mousse on mung- bean bread with soft herbs and pickles.

Follow up with a refreshing charcoal grilled octopus papaya salad (goi bach tuoc) that doesn’t hold back on the zing. Desserts are fine (Vietnamese ice-coffee trifle, say), but we reckon it’s more fun to fill up with a crunchy coconut- and turmeric-laden banh xeo, the crepe cradling meaty prawns, or the DIY rice paper rolls with crushed peanuts and barbecued pork jowl.

The food arrives quickly, as do the good times, although grilled wagyu with a pho demi-glace can be a half-hour wait. Is the $80 steak worth it? You bet.

World.title: Hanasuki
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

When Hansuki opened it felt like exactly what Sydney was missing: an upscale shabu shabu restaurant, where diners could sate their appetite for platters of premium produce to swish through simmering broth. Who knew?

If it’s your first visit, staff make things easy: choose one of four broths from a handy printout – mushroom, say, or the delicate kombu-based signature – add a cartoonishly bountiful platter of vegetables, then add your “delicious plates”: a selection of wagyu, perhaps, featuring marbled chuck roll, sirloin and knuckle, or a mini seafood platter, with oyster, scallops and prawn paste, which cooks into dumplings in the simmering broth.

Ponzu and sesame sauces are on hand for dipping, and mochi kinchaku are an essential, bursting add-on. The space, dressed in wood and beaten copper, may be minimalist, but this is maximal enjoyment, made for sharing with sake and umeshu on hand, right through to the last swish.

Good to know: Still hungry? Ask a waiter to turn the last of your broth into zousui by adding rice and an egg to the cauldron.

World.title: ‘I would strongly advise against swimming’: Sydney beaches closed by decomposing whale carcass
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWWhales ‘I would strongly advise against swimming’: Sydney beaches closed by decomposing whale carcass Angus Dalton Updated October 22, 2026 — 10:02am ,first published 9:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Authorities have closed two Sydney beaches and warned residents of increased shark activity after a whale carcass was discovered floating close to shore in the eastern suburbs. Lifeguards reported the dead whale floating in Lurline Bay, a rocky enclave between Coogee and Maroubra, just before 8am on Thursday. A whale carcass washed up in Lurline Bay in South Coogee. Audrey Richardson “As a precaution, Maroubra and Coogee Beach will remain closed until further notice while lifeguards monitor the situation and work with local stakeholders and authorities to arrange the whale’s removal,” Randwick Council said in a statement. Whale carcasses can attract sharks, which can detect decomposing flesh and blood from kilometres away and come in close to shore to feed.



The carcass appears to be an adult or subadult humpback and is fairly decomposed. “It looks like it could have been dead for a while and washed in,” whale scientist Dr Vanessa Pirotta said. “I would strongly advise against swimming.” The washed-up carcass coincides with the likely return of bull sharks to Sydney’s waters. The species migrate north to Queensland during the cooler months and swim back towards Sydney when coastal temperatures reach 19 or 20 degrees.



While the sharks’ prefer temperatures of 22 degrees, and peak in activity during January and February, research has shown the first sharks are arriving earlier in October each year – and staying around Sydney about a fortnight longer than they used to – as water temperatures climb under climate change. Crowds gather as a whale carcass washed up in Lurline Bay in South Coogee. Audrey Richardson The humpback is believed to have died some time ago. Audrey Richardson In April, a 25-tonne sperm whale washed up near Era Beach and forced the closure of all beaches in the Royal National Park due to the risk posed by scavenging sharks. An estimated 50,000 humpbacks are migrating south to the Antarctic after travelling to warm tropical waters near the Great Barrier Reef to breed and give birth.

World.content:

There’s no question. The soup here is #thicc and like nothing else around. That’s why you’ll find a queue of devout loyalists every night, keen for its souped-up collagenic intensity achieved by boiling fresh pork bones for 14 hours.

The standard tonkotsu is already enough for most diners to handle, but you can request extra back fat to take it to the next level. Or try the fish tonkotsu boosted with katsuobushi flakes for an extra layer of umami. (Mercifully, a new oat-noodle ramen is a lighter option with lean pork if the original broths prove too much.)

Add-ons including a Flintstones-sized spare rib increase the protein, and we also rate the sweet glaze of the barbecued pork skewers. At least one jammy boiled egg is a must, not to mention pickled cabbage and scallops with garlic sprouts for a palate-cleansing boost.

Good to know: You can pick up a frozen tonkotsu ramen kit to cook at home.
