Tucked inside a 160-year-old building, Gundaroo’s offering of “local heart and country soul”, as described by owners Kurt and Tanya Neumann, is all about seasonality.

Rye bread is courtesy of Three Mills in Canberra; entrees begin with house-smoked pork jowl brined for two days and teamed with the acid and crunch of pear, witlof and dates. A portobello tart with manchego and porcini is a flaky pastry affair that carries citrus notes and a nutty cream to highlight the mushrooms’ umami.

Lamb rump from Gundagai is blushing and tender, accompanied by celeriac, braised cavolo nero and a punchy anchovy butter. Sweets might be something rustic such as baked quince clafoutis topped with an earthy chestnut ice-cream.

Service is jolly and jovial, but also backs it up with quickfire answers and recommendations (plus wit) for a wine list that celebrates the region.

Must order: House-smoked Berkshire pork jowl, pear, witlof, walnut, date.

World.title: Frankly Nick’s
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

There’s a lot to be said for a restaurant with a landline as its only means of contact. As customers bite into lush cheese garlic rolls or the supple Cossaca Marinara pizza, they hear the voice of Georgio Panousos, who opened Frankly Nick’s with his childhood friend William Kay in late July.

This is old-fashioned restaurant noise, and diners stream in from all angles, grabbing seats at the tomato-red tables indoors and on the footpath to eat in a spot that feels like an old-school pizzeria mixed with a traditional ristorante.

Kay and Panousos grew up in restaurants, and it shows in the service and on a one-page menu ranging from charred, stretchy cheese and garlic rolls, to puffy edged pies that range from classic to “Sacrilege”, a twist on ham and pineapple that sees the fruit infused with whisky liqueur. Conchiglie alla vodka is oven-baked, tomato salad is impressively simple and gelato-affogato is a cute finish. Frankly, how good.

Good to know: A phone-only ordering system for pick-up has been expanded to include online ordering, with cute merch also available.

World.title: West Papuan civil society calls for UN and Pacific access to region
World.content:
Audio player for " West Papuan groups push for UN action " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/pacific/2070620%2Fwest-papuan-civil-society-calls-for-un-and-pacific-access-to-region

West Papuan groups push for UN action Pacific Waves Download MP3 6m

West Papuan civil society organisations have called on Indonesia to allow access to their region for the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, and to open up genuine, inclusive dialogue.

Claims of persistent human rights abuses continue as violent conflict has deepened in the rugged interior of the Indonesian-controlled Papua region in recent months, causing an increasing number of Internally Displaced People (IDPs).

In recent weeks, numerous Pacific countries have echoed the 2019 call by the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) for Indonesia to allow the UN rights office to visit Papua to assess claims of widespread rights abuses.

Seven years on and the visit is yet to occur, although Indonesia's government told RNZ Pacific last month the visit remains "on track".

However, the patience of Pacific island countries has been tested - the call was again made at last month's PIF summit by the countries in the Melanesian Spearhead Group (MSG) bloc.

Human rights advocacy group Elsham Papua's director Paul Mambrasar said that the request is one of a series of calls to action and demands the civil society groups have made.

"The first one is unconditional international access by the UN body, and also from representatives from MSG and PIF, which is the result of the recent communiqué to visit West Papua," Mambrasar said.

"It is an invitation which needs to be made by Indonesia."

Nona Gae Luna, a Minister Counsellor at Indonesia's Permanent Mission to the United Nations in New York. UN TV

Speaking at this month's UN General Assembly in response to recent calls by Pacific governments, including Solomon Islands and Vanuatu, Indonesian diplomat Nona Gae Luna said the government "takes all credible claims of human rights violations seriously".

"Our national institutions and legal mechanisms, including the Independent National Human Rights Commission, is working continuously to address such allegations," she said.

West Papuan human rights defender Rosa Moiwend said Jakarta has long dismissed concerns about rights issues in Papua.

"The Indonesian government is always promoting the positive image of the human rights situation in West Papua, while the real situation on the ground is still getting worse, especially around the military operations and the impact to the people," Moiwend said.

"We now have like 127,000 IDPs waiting for the right time to go back home, and this is something that happened for a long time."

This photo was shared by ULMWP on 10 February 2026, claiming a makeshift refugee camp in Puncak Regency of was bombed, and that many villagers have been displaced. RNZ Pacific has not independently verified the image. ulmwp.org

Access to Papua is also restricted for international humanitarian organisations who could help the IDPs.

Jakarta's sensitivity over any attempts to internationalise the Papua issue was evident at the UN.

"Arrangements for any visit by the High Commissioner should be agreed between the host state and the office of the High Commissioner - they are not set by a third (party) or any regional body," Gae Luna said.

Nonetheless, Moiwend said the renewed Pacific Islands push for access to West Papua was welcome and timely.

"This is very consistent because the leaders already made a communiqué before, and the West Papuans, especially the CSOs, was really happy with that because the consistency is still there," she said.

"However, they need a clear action, and they also urged the Indonesian government to respond constructively with the statement made by the leaders."

Military forces

Mambrasar said the renewed call by Pacific countries is also timely because Papua is now more militarised than ever as Indonesian troops deploy in greater numbers to fight the disparate guerrilla forces of the West Papua Liberation Army.

"They use more advanced military equipment to fight insurgencies. They now have drone unit, and then, for example, they now use aeroplane to bomb the insurgent fighters," he said of the evolving tech used by Indonesia's military (TNI).

"They use the Brazilian-made Super (Tucano) Toucan aeroplane to bomb. It's not only a law and order issue, which in the past has been the main domain of the police, but now the military is also engaged."

The Indonesian government considers the Liberation Army to be an armed criminal group, and rarely refers to the Papuan struggle for independence.

Gae Luna underlined that Indonesia makes no apologies for the presence of security forces in Papua

"Any serious discussion of Papua must reflect the full picture. Innocent civilians, teachers, health workers, and many others have fallen victim to violence by armed criminal groups.

"Indonesia has a responsibility to protect all of its citizens. Law enforcement must and will remain subject to Indonesia's laws and our international human rights obligations."

Paul Mambrasar, the director of human rights advocacy group Elsham Papua. Supplied

Dialogue

One of the other calls by the civil society groups is for a credible, inclusive, and meaningful political dialogue to resolve the root causes of the Papuan conflict permanently,

Mambrasar said that Jakarta may ignore the troubled history of Papua's incorporation into Indonesia, but each new generation of Papuans comes back to the problem, and that needs to be acknowledged.

"When you engage with issues otherwise, you'll go nowhere," he told RNZ Pacific.

"Because it's been going for decades, and young generations of Papua keep on coming, emitting the same issue, so we're going in same thing over and over again.

"So, what Indonesia must do now is to sit and invite all the genuine representatives of West Papuans to sit and talk, and you know to discuss the best ways to go forward.

"Once you sit together and you know equally, and you see West Papuans as human beings, then you know we can find something.

"I believe things have happened in East Timor in South Africa and in some parts of Africa and South America, why don't we just look at those experience and maybe pick up one or two, and we can use it here."

World.title: Inflation tumbles to 3.7%, but expected to rise again soon
World.content:
Consumer prices rose 0.7% in September quarter, but the annual rate eased from a two-year high to 3.7%

A temporary dip in fuel prices eased CPI pressures from higher food, energy, building costs, airfares, and rates

Higher fuel, electricity, housing, electricity drove an annual increase

Underlying inflation pressures are touching the top of the RBNZ target band

The latest surge in fuel costs sent local prices to record levels; inflation is expected above 4% by year end

There are strong odds of Reserve Bank rate hike next week

Inflation retreated from a two year high as a temporary fall in fuel prices eased some of the pressures on household and business budgets.

Stats NZ data showed the consumer price index rose 0.7 percent in the three months ended September, with the annual inflation rate easing to 3.7 percent from 4.1 percent in June.

Petrol prices eased 6.5 percent during the quarter, and other vehicle oils fell 4 percent, during a lull in Middle East hostilities and improved global supplies.

Watch Finance Minister Nicola Willis react to the result below:

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407202628112

"Lower petrol prices were the largest downward contribution to the quarterly inflation rate," prices spokesperson Nicola Growden said.

For the year petrol prices rose 19 percent accounted for just under a fifth of the about 17 percent of the annual inflation rate.

Excluding food, fuel and household energy the quarterly inflation rate would have been 1.1 percent and the annual rate 2.9 percent.

International airfares were the strongest driver of the quarterly CPI increase, rising 14.3 percent.

"This was the largest quarterly increase in international airfares since the December 2022 quarter. The increase was mainly driven by higher fares to Europe and Asia," Growden said.

Domestic inflation raises its head again

Domestic prices - non-tradables - such as power, and rates were among the bigger items to rise, up 3.3 percent for the year, and by 1.0 percent for the quarter.

Construction of a new house rose 0.5 percent for the quarter, and by 3.2 percent for the year.

"Respondents reported that the higher costs for materials, subcontractors, labour and fuel contributed to rising prices for new housing," Growden said.

Rents, which had been a big driver of previous years' inflation measures, continued to be flat with no increase in the quarter and rising 0.2 percent annually.

Electricity prices were 9.3 percent higher than a year ago, reflecting higher lines charges.

The latest update of local body rates was incorporated in the data, and were 6.2 percent higher.

These offset falls in audio visual equipment, and some food items such as butter, and olive oil.

Finance Minister responds

National's Finance spokesperson Nicola Willis - the finance minister - says Thursday's inflation figures were encouraging but pressures remain "because of events overseas and the international oil shock".

Willis said that supports the government's approach of "choosing not to spend up large", saying if she had the inflation figure would be higher and New Zealanders would be paying higher prices.

"There are people who have faced a range of different circumstances. There are also always people who've had a promotion, people who've fixed on a lower mortgage rate, people whose circumstances have changed for the better.

"We can never generalise all New Zealanders because people have such different circumstances. What we know is that we are focused on the underlying drivers of your household budget, and that is keeping inflation under control."

She points to Australia's inflation rate at 4 percent as "significantly higher than New Zealand's".

Asked about energy costs, Willis blames Labour's 2018 "oil and gas ban" which prevented new exploratory drilling for oil and gas fields in New Zealand's offshore waters which was overturned last July.

Those who support the ban point to the last viable oil field having been discovered in 2003. The government this year granted the first new exploration licence for an area in the Taranaki Basin.

"Like many things, we've been doing the clean up. We have been fixing the underlying foundations, and New Zealand will be seeing the rewards if we stick to the plan," Willis says.

Inflation dip to be short lived, more RBNZ rate rises to come

The September quarter inflation rate was at the low end of economists' expectations.

Various measures of underlying inflation pointed to an annual rate in a range between 2.6 and 3.2 percent.

The September quarter's inflation relief has already evaporated amid the resurgence in global fuel costs, which have sent local pump prices to record highs.

Inflation is now expected to rise to as high as 4.5 percent in the December quarter, raising the prospect it will spill over into the price of other goods and services, and prompt stronger wage demands.

The RBNZ signalled in September that a pause in rate rises was likely this month, but forecasters and financial markets are now betting on a 25 basis point rate rise on October 28 and a 50 percent chance of a similar sized rise in December.

World.title: Warning for NZ as websites go dark around world in security scare
World.content:
New Zealand's National Cybersecurity Centre says it's aware of a website security scare that has led to the shutdown of government websites around the world.

The websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline on Thursday (NZT) after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language sent operators around the world scrambling to protect their language systems, Reuters reported.

Developers of the PHP programming language on Thursday (NZT) released urgent new fixes to vulnerabilities that had quietly been lurking in their software for years until they were uncovered using AI, saying that all users were "encouraged to update immediately."

With tech firms warning some hackers were already exploiting the flaws, government agencies across Europe were among those that took sites offline as a precaution.

Because a fix is now public and artificial intelligence tools are able to reverse engineer the bug with little effort, experts said they were bracing for a wave of intrusions as hackers jumped to get ahead of the updates.

Tech firms are warning that some hackers were already exploiting the flaws 123RF

AI was powering a "race to exploit," said Costin Raiu, co-founder of cybersecurity research and incident response firm TLP:Black. He said the next step was the "mass compromise of every vulnerable web server on the internet."

The National Cyber Security centre was encouraging New Zealand organisations to apply the recommended fix as soon as possible after the flaws in websites using the PHP programming language were exposed on Thursday (NZT).

The centre was also urging organisations to investigate unauthorised access, or compromise, of the kind of commonly used website or web application affected by the threat.

PHP - a language that dates back to the early 1990s and initially stood for "Personal Home Page" - underpins huge parts of the public-facing web and is baked into WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento sites, meaning that any critical vulnerability potentially has enormous knock-on consequences.

"All servers using any version of PHP released in the last 20 years will be vulnerable," said Tiffany Farriss, the interim chief executive of the Drupal Association. "This issue impacts the majority of the Internet."

Cybersecurity agencies around the world have urged PHP users to update immediately or take websites offline until patches can be applied.

According to data from Censys, the internet intelligence firm, about 1.5 million out of 2.6 million hosts report running a version of PHP for which there is no fix.

The Dutch cybersecurity agency itself went offline, saying it had done so as a precaution because of the vulnerabilities. The operator of the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia also said it had taken down an unspecified number of systems until they could be safely patched, while the Internet Archive, the sprawling online library, said it also briefly went offline to deal with the issue.

Even some world leaders, who don't typically get involved with software updates, weighed in. The Dutch prime minister said he was closely monitoring the situation. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in a post on X said website owners should "check whether your live site uses PHP and prepare to apply the new fix."

World.title: Tauranga residents to vote on future of its Te Awanui Māori ward
World.content:
Tauranga residents will vote on the future of its Te Awanui Māori ward next year.

A binding poll will be held on 23 March 2027, the city council decided this week.

Most councils held polls on Māori wards at last year's local elections, but Tauranga was exempt because it had already held an election the year before.

Those polls came after a 2024 amendment which required any councils that had previously introduced Māori wards without polling residents to do so retroactively.

Tauranga councillors voted in June to retain Te Awanui, and it was given until the end of March 2027 to hold a poll.

Voters have until 11 January 2027 to enrol before voting on 23 March 2027.

World.title: Rabuka defends Fiji election timeline as opposition claims he plans to 'abort' polls
World.content:
Fijians are being reassured by the country's prime minister and his senior government ministers that they will head to the polls before the 6 February 2027 deadline.

Sitiveni Rabuka, who is currently on a nationwide public consultation tour leading a special parliamentary committee on a constitutional reform process, is repeatedly assuring voters that the general election will proceed as planned.

In interviews with local media, the prime minister confirmed that the next election will be held under the existing electoral laws by the deadline.

Rabuka has not announced an election date yet, but previously told RNZ Pacific that he would do so after the constitutional reform process is complete, including a potential national referendum in December 2026.

Fijian PM Sitiveni Rabuka RNZ Pacific / Fiji Parliament

The Fijian Elections Office (FEO) has told RNZ Pacific that election campaigning is still ongoing, after the prime minister announced earlier this month that he had written to the Electoral Commission to suspend campaigning.

According to the FEO, more than 723,000 eligible voters have registered to cast their ballots as of 30 June.

Rabuka's coalition government came into power in December 2022. Under Fiji's 2013 Constitution, his administration's term ends on 24 December 2026.

One of the minor partners in Rabuka's coalition, the Social Democratic Liberal Party (Sodelpa), warned that the ongoing constitutional amendment process "must not create unnecessary uncertainty about the electoral timetable or distract from the preparations required for the next general election".

"The people of Fiji deserve timely, accurate information and confidence that the democratic process will proceed lawfully," Sodelpa leader and Rabuka's Education Minister Aseri Radrodro said in a statement.

More than 723,000 eligible voters have registered to cast their ballots as of 30 June, according to the Fijian Elections Office. RNZ / Philippa Tolley

Meanwhile, the Labour Party, which holds no seats in parliament, has accused the government of planning to "abort" the polls.

The party said that Rabuka's government is "so unpopular" and "is likely to" be voted out.

Labour leader and former Prime Minister Mahendra Chaudhry has called on the government to explain certain clauses in the Constitution (Amendment) Bill 2026 which concern the government's term in office without holding a general election.

However, Manoa Kamikamica - one of the two deputy prime ministers - told parliament two weeks ago that elections will be held before February 2027.

"Some naysayers would say that [the government] would try to delay the elections," Kamikamica said.

World.title: National promises more affordable homes for older people
World.content:
National is making a pitch to older voters, promising to reserve them at least one of every five homes supported by a government's affordable housing fund.

Leader Christopher Luxon made the announcement at Pacific Lakes Retirement Village in Tauranga on Thursday, noting that people aged 65 or older made up 15 percent of those waiting for social housing.

"Not every senior can - or wants to - move to a retirement village," he said.

Watch the announcement below:

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407200396112

"New Zealand needs many more low cost, affordable pensioner housing units."

Under its plan, National would earmark at least 20 percent of Housing Flexible Fund places for seniors, including social housing and affordable rentals such as those provided by Abbeyfield.

The fund allows housing organisations to build and provide homes with discounted rents. It was set up in 2025 with about $40m in operational funding and $60m in capital funding to stretch over four years. Another $70m was allocated in this year's Budget for a second tranche of homes, beginning in 2028/29.

National's election pledge does not include any additional funding, but guarantees seniors a minimum share of future places

National would also let more small homes be built without the usual council approvals, extending its granny flat rules to tiny homes on wheels.

Granny flats could also be built on empty sections, without needing an existing house alongside them.

Luxon said the changes would help families who wanted older relatives living nearby.

"We know many families want to embrace inter-generational living, but councils make it too difficult," Luxon said.

Labour has separately promised to help charities and other housing groups borrow more cheaply so they can build more homes.

The Greens want to build tens of thousands of homes for people who cannot afford market rents and limit rent increases to 2 percent.

World.title: Labour promises to hire 1000 more teacher aides
World.content:
Labour is promising to fund an extra 1000 teacher aides.

Education spokesperson Ginny Andersen said it would mean more individual support for students who need it, more help in busy classrooms, and greater confidence for parents that their children aren't being left behind.

Watch the announcement below:

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407201376112

"Too many teachers are stretched trying to meet the needs of every child, while schools are dipping into their budgets or fundraising to pay for learning support," Andersen said.

The policy costs $80 million over four years, with the party also promising to build on a 2022 review to find and close gaps in learning support.

Meanwhile, National's Education spokesperson Erica Stanford said the government's $750m investment into learning support last year was having an effect, with thousands more children receiving early intervention.

She said 896,210 additional teacher aide hours were delivered in 2025/26; over 1000 more children were receiving high-needs support from the Ongoing Resourcing Scheme; more than 6100 Year 1 children were benefiting from Early Intervention Services; early intervention wait times were 16 days shorter compared to December 2025 after contracting an extra 1000 private sector specialist places; 474 more schools had learning support coordinators; and 190 more learning support specialist roles had been filled.

Stanford said Labour never delivered on its Learning Support Action Plan while in government, promised learning support coordinators were stopped after the first tranche, a High Needs Review went nowhere and the party failed to uncap ORS funding as promised.

World.title: Search efforts continue for missing PhD student Sam Newton-Jones
World.content:
Police say they are using a range of resources in the hope of finding missing man Sam Newton-Jones.

Search efforts are focusing on the area around Piha beach in West Auckland after the PhD student's car was found at a nearby walking track.

The 33-year-old was last seen at his workplace in the suburb of Henderson on Tuesday.

Police say his car was later found at the Mercer Bay Loop car park near Piha but there was no sign of Newton-Jones.

In a statement, Newton-Jones' family said he was a much-loved son, husband and father-of-two, and his disappearance was "deeply concerning".

It said he was "warm, empathetic and incredibly generous".

"He plays a significant role in the lives of his family and friends. They are deeply concerned that he is missing."

Newton-Jones had been an engineer, but decided in his mid-20s to re-train as a psychologist.

"He is currently in the final stages of completing his PhD. He has a passion for working with children and young adults and helping them to navigate adversity.

"Like many New Zealanders, Sam has experienced his own mental health challenges. However, he recently described himself as feeling optimistic about the year ahead."

The family said his disappearance is highly out of character.

"Sam's family urge members of the public to contact police with any sightings, observations or information that may help to locate him. Sam's car was last seen at Mercer Bay, so Piha locals in particular are asked to stay aware of Sam. The family appreciate prayers and support at this difficult time."

World.title: Scatterbrained Australian approach opens door to South African victory
World.content:
Among those who fret over the ongoing primacy of Test cricket in the face of the T20 onslaught, Australia's tour of South Africa had long shaped as an enticing proposition: the two best sides in the world squaring off, a clutch of veteran tourists confronting ghosts of controversies past, and Australia commencing a year-long run of battles its aging superstars see as legacy-shaping.

Some of that probably distracted us from what a bittersweet prospect it was, too. For how, as anyone glued to this contest in the past two weeks will have asked themselves at some point or other, can a game so awash with money have conspired to deny us regular helpings of this fun and fascinating South African outfit? Of real cricket that matters?

Twenty-four hours ago, it was centurion Temba Bavuma reminding the world not only of his life-affirming resurgence as a batsman, but of the great shame that in the last two years, he's only had eight other opportunities to strut his stuff at Test level.

Quick hits: Sore Smith doesn't return as Marnus throws it away on horror day Steve Smith reaches a major milestone but doesn't return and Marnus Labuschagne makes a mockery of an enormous reprieve on a disastrous fourth day for the Aussies in Gqeberha. Here are the quick hits from South Africa.

Early on day four at Gqeberha, the focus shifted to beanpole all-rounder Marco Jansen, fresh from his swashbuckling 85 with the bat, now tearing through the Australian batting order like the Grim Reaper. Lurking not so much in the shadows as slightly off to the side of the stage, stirring up drama and intrigue, there was also the imposing figure of Proteas attack leader Kagiso Rabada.

That and a few subtler problems added up to an unmitigated disaster for Australia. Replying to South Africa's declared total of 425, the scatterbrained and frankly embarrassing tourists were skittled for 99 in their first innings and asked to follow on.

By default, Australia fared a little better in the afternoon, finishing the day at 4-156 with Travis Head undefeated on 87. But with its deficit of 170, and a neck injury to Steve Smith — who hasn't appeared to bat yet in the second innings — it will take something truly remarkable for Australia to pull this game out of the fire on the fifth and final day.

The main impression Australia's performance left was of the sheer needlessness of the entire debacle. What was the first innings batting plan, if any? Why were so many batsmen in such a hurry in a scenario from which Australia was never going to win?

Travis Head was the only Australian batter to show a bit of fight in the face of South Africa's onslaught on day four. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Richard Huggard)

Which is not to take the focus of South Africa's unstinting excellence. Another emblematic figure in that sense was off-spinner Simon Harmer, who many thought should have been dropped for this game.

Instead, he's made big runs, caught everything that has come his way, and chipped in with two key wickets. Australia has had no such unassuming star.

Jansen, with 5-33 from 11 overs in the first innings chaos, was the chief destroyer, but there were wheels within wheels. The mere presence of Rabada, who was missing from the first Test, seems to have transformed South Africa's collective energy from a little too amiable in Durban to ruthless and faintly menacing here.

Jansen was the most visible example of this phenomenon. In Durban, he'd bowled with pace and incision to spark Australia's initial collapse. But as his influence waned and Matt Renshaw got going, he silently brooded away in his own world, looking a little like Alain Delon's expressionless assassin in Le Samourai.

Today he was an entirely different man — gregarious, energetic, fired up. To his usual bouncers he added fist-pumps and fiery send-offs. Like Rabada in the memorably testy corresponding game eight years ago, he got up in Australia's grill and wouldn't go away.

Marco Jansen was back to his menacing best as Australia crumbled under his pressure on day four. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

A brief catalogue of Australia's worst misdemeanours in the first innings bears mentioning. Marnus Labuschagne again drove with hard hands, slightly off balance, with his bat plane all wrong, therefore couldn't complain about the bad luck of departing to a one-handed screamer by Harmer in the cordon. Alex Carey, Beau Webster, Mitchell Starc and Pat Cummins each either walloped or wafted at deliveries they should have respected, especially given the dire state their team was in at the time.

In the second innings, Nic Maddinson again nudged lamely at Rabada to be caught behind the wicket. As in Durban, Labuschagne again squandered a promising start when a break in sight, heedlessly thrashing Harmer into the deep to hole out for 39 when drinks were about to be brought on. And Webster, again neither looking comfortable nor batting with due caution, was dismissed cheaply at the worst possible time. Renshaw, who had looked relatively comfortable, shouldered arms to be bowled by Rabada.

And for all that, and Australia's loss of 13 wickets for the day, South Africa's attack was a man down for most of the day after lionhearted quick Anrich Nortje suffered a groin injury in his fourth over. Things could actually have been worse.

Only a day ago, one felt the confluence of luck, momentum and a single special innings had changed the game's course without any great culpability on Australia's behalf. The feeling is very different now. South Africa will arrive for the final day with victory in its mind — in this game, foremost, but also perhaps in a series that is now thrillingly alive.

World.title: Quick hits: Sore Smith doesn't return as Marnus throws it away on horror day
World.content:
Steve Smith doesn't return after reaching a major milestone and Marnus Labuschagne makes a mockery of an enormous reprieve as Australia is sent barrelling towards a chastening defeat in Gqeberha.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Fiery Marco tears through the Aussies

Fresh from his swashbuckling 85 on day three, the towering Marco Jansen continued to terrorise the Australians on day four.

The left-arm seamer was at his fiery, probing best, with his aggression and accuracy proving all too much for the tourists in their first innings.

Jansen dismissed both Scott Boland and Travis Head early in the day, before a few tense exchanges with Marnus Labuschagne appeared to light a fuse somewhere deep in the big man.

Labuschagne and Jansen had a few tense exchanges on day four. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

He proceeded to treat Matt Renshaw to a send-off — seemingly in Afrikaans — upon having the Yorkshire-born Queenslander caught at short leg, before sending Alex Carey packing in a double breakthrough in the shadows of lunch.

Unfortunately for the Aussies, Jansen wasn't done there, with the South African having Beau Webster caught in the cordon to claim his fifth wicket and continue Australia's horror day.

2. Sore Smith reaches 11,000 and doesn't return

Amid the carnage up the other end, Steve Smith was just about hanging in there.

Struggling with a neck issue, the Australian received running repairs at multiple points during his innings and never quite looked his usual self.

Smith received multiple rounds of treatment for a stiff neck. (AP Photos)

Even so, Smith was at the crease long enough to become just the 12th batter to score 11,000 Test match runs, joining Ricky Ponting and Allan Border as the only Australians in that rare air.

But the Australia vice-captain was in serious discomfort throughout his innings, and departed promptly after joining that exclusive club.

The stiff-necked Smith was bowled through the gate by Wiaan Mulder for 28 as Australia was asked to follow on after being skittled for just 99, their fourth-lowest Test total against the Proteas.

And in a massive blow for his team, the Australia vice-captain did not recover in time to return to the crease as wickets started falling in the tourists' second dig, remaining in training gear in the dugout as Australia limped towards stumps.

3. Two remarkable grabs, two very different reactions

We have been treated to some seriously sensational slip catching in Gqeberha.

Following in the footsteps of Renshaw — who made a stunning low catch late on day two — Simon Harmer produced his own moment of magic early on day four.

With Australia 3-45 in its first innings and already beginning to teeter, the desperately out-of-touch Labuschagne drove unconvincingly, sending his thick edge flying low and hard towards the cordon.

Harmer dived dramatically to his left, using his sizeable left hand to pluck the quickly dropping ball from the air in front of second slip.

It was a stunning reflex grab from Harmer. (Fox Cricket)

And the off-spinner was absolutely pumped with his effort, throwing his head back and roaring as he got to his feet.

It provided quite some contrast to Renshaw's bewilderment after pouching his similarly excellent catch earlier in the Test.

Harmer and Renshaw had very different reactions to their similarly excellent catches. (Fox Cricket)

4. Marnus throws it away after enormous reprieve

With Australia beginning its second innings needing 326 runs to just make South Africa bat again, Labuschagne had a golden opportunity to revive his sputtering Test career and make up for his rash dismissal earlier in the day.

Coming in after the early departure of Nic Maddinson, the signs were good for the Queenslander, who knuckled down with Head to push Australia towards 100.

And it was beginning to feel like Labuschagne might have finally been on for a score when he was the beneficiary of a huge reprieve in the 28th over.

Given out LBW to a Harmer off break, Labuschagne reviewed the decision in a blink and it was high drama as both camps waited for ball tracking to take an unusually long time to build.

Eventually, the technology projected the ball to be missing leg stump by what surely wasn't much more than a coat of paint.

Labuschagne survived by the skin of his teeth. (Fox Cricket)

Helmet off and head back, Labuschagne was making no secret of his relief.

But only moments later, he threw it all away, mistiming his slog and holing out to long-on for 39.

Labuschagne's relief was short-lived. (Fox Cricket)

It was an ugly, ugly dismissal and one that left Australia once again on the rack with shadows lengthening in St George's.

5. Consecutive night shifts for Boland

With Australia proceeding to lose both Renshaw and Webster late on, Boland once again found himself batting in the dying embers of a day.

It was the second consecutive evening the Victorian had been called on as nightwatchman, and for the second consecutive evening, he made his way through to stumps.

Again, he betrayed no hint of annoyance with his sacrificial role, instead digging in and bravely finding his way through a couple of overs of twilight finger spin.

It was another committed shift from Boland — but boy, it's some reward for taking a five-wicket haul on his return to the team.

He'll begin day five alongside Head (87*) with Australia 4-156 and still 170 runs away from making South Africa bat again.

World.title: Smith to return despite injury as Australia looks to save second Test
World.content:
Steve Smith is expected to bat on day five despite dealing with a sore neck as Australia stares down the barrel of a huge defeat in the second Test against South Africa in Gqeberha.

Being made to follow on for just the third time this century, Australia's collapse came in stark contrast to the recovery of South Africa when faced with a similar situation on day three.

The Proteas were reduced to 6-110 before battling to 9-425.

The tourists, though, were skittled for just 99 runs in their first innings, a whopping 326 runs behind South Africa's score, the largest first innings deficit Australia has faced since 1984.

Marnus Labuschagne was dismissed twice on a day to forget, leaving his Test career firmly in the balance. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Richard Huggard)

They were then reduced to 4-156 at the close of play, still 170 runs short of making South Africa batting again, with Smith yet to bat as a sore neck forced him to sit out of the start of Australia's second innings.

Despite Smith being in visible discomfort for much of his knock in the first innings, Australian coach Andrew McDonald said he would be able to take to the crease on day five.

"We felt it was best to hopefully get the batting unit through to tomorrow and then hopefully he's better placed," he said.

"We've seen the physio working on him, so he'll bat tomorrow.

Marco Jansen (left) was devastating with the ball on day four, ripping through Australia's batting line-up. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

"It's not something that will rule him out of the innings, but it was just a little bit more time than we expected on the back of the first innings.

"Sometimes he changes his technique when he's fully fit too, but he was limited in what he could do."

A chastening morning saw a steady procession of Australian batters traipse back to the dressing room after making starts.

Night watchman Scott Boland did not last a single ball in the morning session, edging Marco Jansen (5-33) behind to Ryan Rickelton and setting the tone for a disastrous day.

Travis Head fell soon after, LBW to Jansen for 14, a decision overturned on review by the Proteas.

Australia's most profitable partnership was worth just 23 runs between Smith and Marnus Labuschagne, before the latter was spectacularly caught by Simon Harmer off the bowling of Anrich Nortje (1-5).

That was to be Nortje's only wicket of the day after he aggravated a groin injury and played no further part.

Tellingly for Australia, the Proteas didn't miss him, smashing through the batting line up despite being a bowler down as Kagiso Rabada (2-33) and Wiaan Mulder (2-14) stepped up.

Matt Renshaw (12) fended a rising Jansen ball to Harmer at third slip, with Alex Carey (0) following him just two balls later after feathering behind to Rickelton, leaving Australia 6-65.

Beau Webster (13) became Jansen's fifth victim after fending a rising ball to second slip, with a clearly uncomfortable Smith (28) bowled soon after by Mulder, precipitating a rapid collapse.

Having enforced the follow on, Australia got off to the worst possible start with Nic Maddinson (8) edging Rabada behind with a shot that made him look hopelessly out of his depth.

With Smith indisposed, the partnership between Head and Labuschagne took on extra importance and, for a while at least, the two obliged.

Travis Head scored 50 in response. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Richard Huggard)

However, their 176-ball, 92-run partnership came to a juddering halt when Labuschagne (39) attempted to loft Harmer over the long on boundary, where he was well caught by Jansen.

As ever, the Queenslander showed several bright moments in his 98-ball stay at the crease, but ultimately his 39 runs and calamitous ending further highlighted his lingering issues in the line up.

Renshaw (11) was bowled by Rabada, and Webster (8) was trapped LBW by Harmer before Boland came out as night watchman for the second time in as many nights.

He remains unbeaten on 2, with Head on 87 and within touching distance of a first century away from home, facing a tremendous task to save the game on the final day.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Diamonds go down again as Ferns take control of Constellation Cup
World.content:
The Diamonds trail the four-game Constellation Cup series 2-0 after a 62-50 loss to New Zealand in Christchurch, continuing a five-year losing run across the ditch.

The series moves back to Australia for the final two matches — in Sydney on Sunday and Melbourne next Wednesday — as the Diamonds try to hang on to the trophy they reclaimed last year.

If the Silver Ferns win all four matches of the series they are expected to dethrone Australia from its number one world ranking for the first time since 2013.

After the six-goal loss in the opening match in Auckland, the Diamonds made a better start in game two but once again let the lead blow out to double digits by the third quarter.

The Diamonds regained the momentum and cut it to a two-goal difference just before three-quarter-time, but again the Silver Ferns responded and started the final term with a 10-3 run.

New Zealand captain Karin Burger praised her team for maintaining their focus even as the Aussies closed in.

The Silver Ferns were up and about as they took a 2-0 lead. (Getty Images: Joe Allison)

"Our training has been focused on staying really composed," she told Sky.

"In the past we've been guilty of letting that lead slip and then not being able to fight back."

The Diamonds shot just 82 per cent compared to New Zealand's 93, did not nab any intercepts, committed 18 turnovers to the Ferns' 11, lost the rebound battle 6-4 and, crucially, were penalised 31 more times in the game.

Captain Liz Watson credited the World Cup and Commonwealth Games champions, but suggested the Diamonds shot themselves in the foot more than a few times.

"Critical moments, turnovers, basic errors, those sort of things. Disappointing, really disappointing," she said.

"Sometimes it is perceived pressure rather than actual pressure. It could be the crowd, it could be [umpires'] calls, it could be what the Ferns are doing as well.

"They're a great team and when go hard they go really hard, so that can force errors, but we've got to be able to stay calm in those moments and read the game for what it is and not get caught up in what's happening around us."

Look back at how game two in Christchurch unfolded in our live blog below.

World.title: How Antonelli can become F1's youngest world champion this weekend
World.content:
Italian F1 driver Kimi Antonelli has his first chance to win the world championship this weekend, as the 20-year-old closes in on a maiden title in just his second season.

The Mercedes driver has been a class above the rest in 2026, with eight grand prix wins and a further six podium places across 17 rounds.

This Monday's (AEDT) United States Grand Prix will be Antonelli's first match point where he can officially seal a championship that has felt like his for many months.

The equation for Kimi Antonelli is very simple: win and hope for other results.

Antonelli enters this weekend's grand prix on 340 points, 102 more than teammate George Russell and 111 ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton.

The Italian needs to have a lead of 125 points or more to seal the drivers' championship at the United States Grand Prix.

That will happen if Antonelli wins the race, Russell finishes ninth or worse, and Hamilton finishes fifth or worse.

Antonelli Russell Hamilton Championship result Win 9th or lower 5th or lower Antonelli becomes champion Win 8th or better 5th or lower Hamilton eliminated Win 9th or lower 4th or better Russell eliminated Win 8th or better 5th or lower Championship remains alive 2nd or lower Any Any Championship remains alive

After this weekend, there will be five grands prix left in the season — Mexico, Brazil, Las Vegas, Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

There will be a maximum of 125 points left to win.

If Antonelli finishes exactly 125 points ahead of either Russell or Hamilton in Texas, mathematically either of those drivers could end the season level on points — if they won every race and Antonelli failed to score another point.

Even in that unlikely scenario, Antonelli would still become champion through a tie-break, having won more grands prix than the others.

When is the United States Grand Prix?

Here is when the F1 United States Grand Prix begins in your state or territory.

Monday, October 26

7am AEDT: NSW, Victoria, ACT, Tasmania

6:30am: ACDT: South Australia

6am AEST: Queensland

5:30am ACST: Northern Territory

4am AWST: Western Australia

World.title: Australians run 80 hours or more in 'crazy' race with no finish line
World.content:
It sounds like a metaphor for torture: a running race with no finish line.

About 900 runners from 67 nations, including 15 Australians, crossed the start line of the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship at 11pm on Saturday AEDT at Kembla Grange in the New South Wales Illawarra.

In a deceptively simple test of physical and mental grit, each athlete completes a 6.7-kilometre course loop on the hour, every hour, until one runner remains.

They squeeze food and minutes of sleep into the remaining time, in an event that can stretch beyond four days.

Jonathan Ash was the first Australian to pull out, succumbing to injury on Monday afternoon after he exceeded the hour limit on his 41st lap.

He told the event's live stream that knee bursitis and muscle tightness from the 16th lap slowed him down.

"Basically every muscle in my body started to get knotted at some point," Ash said.

"We had to get a physio in to push that out.

"[It was] probably one of the most painful experiences of my life."

Jonathan Ash, 43, took up running in his 30s and is now one of Australia's top endurance athletes. (Supplied: Snapped Sport Pics)

The Shellharbour engineer is the second-ever Australian to complete 100 laps, equal to 670 kilometres, over four days in 2024, behind Phil Gore, who sits injured on the sidelines this year, tending to fellow athletes.

Gore broke the world record last year after running 119 laps, or 797.3km, after five days on a southern Queensland farm.

Each Australian runner has a team of supporters stationed in tents ready to provide first aid, food and water between loops. (Supplied: Snapped Sport Pics)

Melbourne's Brandon Lee Gretch tapped out after lap 73 about midnight on Wednesday and said he was proud of his effort, having achieved a personal best.

"I came in with 20 seconds to spare and had a shooting pain down my back. That was just killing me from about yard 67 onwards," he said.

"It was hell."

Brandon Lee Gretch, 32, described the world championship event as "running with 14 of my best friends". (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

The 32-year-old was cheerful as he snacked on chicken nuggets this morning with heavily bandaged feet.

"Myself as an eight-year-old would be so proud to know I got to put on the green and gold," Gretch said.

"It's weird because I am so sleep-deprived, I feel like my body automatically goes into recovery mode.

Dozens of local volunteers have helped coordinate the Backyard Ultra World Championship at the grassy Kembla Grange course. (Supplied: Snapped Sport Pics)

"The only bad thing is I always wake up [with] stiff legs, so I'll have to get moving again soon."

Backyard ultras were invented 15 years ago by Gary "Lazarus Lake" Cantrell and hosted at his Bell Buckle property in Tennessee.

"He wanted to challenge people to complete 100 miles in 24 hours," Australian race director Red Barnett said.

"It just grew in popularity as people pushed beyond the 24-hour mark.

"It is a bit of a crazy event."

Ash described the event as "the lesson that every person is incredibly capable of much more than they think they are".

"You don't know until you give it a shot," he said.

Dan Camac crossed the finishing line of lap 81 with about 10 minutes to spare on Wednesday morning, shortly after teammate Ben Nicholls. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

All but one Australian runner ran more than 60km, but only two passed the 80km mark.

"There's a mixture of fatigue, not getting their nutrition right, body ailments that are going on," Ms Barnett said.

"So unfortunately, we just had one after the other [drop out] and are left with two [Australian competitors].

" If all goes well, these guys [Dan Camac and Ben Nicholls] are hoping to get to 100 hours, which is Thursday morning. "

Red Barnett started hosting Backyard Ultras in Wollongong's south in 2020 and is now managing the Australian course of the World Championship. (ABC Illawarra: Brooke Chandler)

Ms Barnett said things would become "drastically harder" for the remaining Australians.

"When there is only two left, they really need to work together," she said.

"Having a lot of people around to support and cheer them on, even through the nights, all that really helps, but it's going to be a huge mental test."

Dan Camac was the last Australian left standing, completing the 87th lap, with the Australian team finishing the event with a combined 1,069 laps.

World.title: PNG Chiefs unveil new logo ahead of 2028 NRL entry
World.content:
The PNG Chiefs have unveiled the club's inaugural logo and jersey ahead of its debut NRL season in 2028.

Revealed at a breakfast rich with singing, dancing and performance, the designs reflect Papua New Guinea's diverse cultures, according to the franchise.

Fashion designer Tabu Pelei, the artist behind the jersey, said finding a motif that could unite a country with over 800 different tribes was a challenge.

"I thought what better way than a kundu [drum], which is a cultural item that is found in every part of Papua New Guinea," she told the ABC.

A kundu drum is a musical instrument made from wood and animal skin that is often used in traditional performances.

Pelei said she also drew inspiration from the country's natural landscape and a tattoo from her own tribe, which represents sweat and tears.

Tabu Pelei designed the PNG Chiefs jersey. (ABC News: Marian Faa)

"I needed to include that in the design because of the process that it took to get the country through to the NRL," she said.

It is also a theme that will resonate with foundation Chiefs like Jerome Luai, Alex Johnston and Brian To'o.

"These are sporting icons for … not PNG alone but all over the Pacific and Australia. They'll be wearing one of my designs, [I'm] so extremely proud and excited," Pelei said.

With several marquee signings already announced, PNG Chiefs CEO Lorna McPherson hinted at more to come.

"November 1 is looming so you will see lots of things happen in the next couple of weeks but I can't reveal any of those secrets at this point," she told the ABC.

There has been speculation the Chiefs are looking to recruit star half back and Penrith Panthers player Nathan Cleary, who is free to begin contract negotiations next month.

But for now, McPherson is focused on the branding reveal, which she described as a defining moment for the new club in a nation obsessed with rugby league.

She said the unveiling of the logo marked "one of the most significant milestones in the journey of the PNG Chiefs".

"This is the first time that our club has its true, complete identity — a logo and jersey that our players, partners and fans can hold to as their own," McPherson said.

"The logo of the PNG Chiefs tells a story about Papua New Guinea — our people, what makes us strong and what makes us unique.

"The jersey of the PNG Chiefs is more than what players wear when they take to the field; it is a symbol of belonging, unity and the opportunity to represent millions of Papua New Guineans on the national stage.

"We know the responsibility that comes with establishing this club and we are incredibly proud to show our club to the world today.

"We strive for the PNG Chiefs to be something our country is proud of in every way — not because of the success that we will achieve on the field, but for the opportunities and legacy we will create for our country."

Elements of the PNG Chiefs logo

As per the PNG Chiefs media release

The feather headpiece: Inspired by Papua New Guinea's ceremonial plumes, the five feathers represent strength, beauty, chiefly status and national pride, with the Southern Cross connecting the club to the nation's flag.

The cassowary bone: Inspired by warrior traditions, the cassowary bone symbolises chiefly status, courage, power and the fighting spirit of the team.

The face: The chief's face represents the shape of Papua New Guinea, with ceremonial red paint showing a nation united through one warrior, one team and one purpose.

The kina shells: Representing traditional wealth, trade and prestige across Papua New Guinea's coastal, island and highland communities, the kina symbolises the value, legacy and future the club is building for the nation.

World.title: Snooker player in tears, hugged by presenter, after emotional and raw interview
World.content:
Former world number one snooker player Mark Allen has given an emotional and tearful interview, which involved a hug from the presenter and the admission that he may give up the game.

Allen, 40, took a break from playing after losing a dramatic semifinal in April's World Snooker Championship in April.

The Northern Irishman is understood to have taken time away from the game to deal with private matters, and it has cast doubt over the 40-year-old's future in the sport.

Loading Instagram content

Allen returned to the table for the first time since the world championship semi, where he missed a match-ball black that would have sent him to the decider, with a 4-2 defeat in the first round of the Northern Ireland Open to good friend Jordan Brown.

After the defeat, Allen did an interview with TNT Sports presenter Rachel Casey, where he admitted he was strongly considering throwing away the game he loved.

"I'm in a bad place at the minute, so even just to go out there and try was tough," Allen said.

"I think if I weren't playing Jordan, I wouldn't have come back.

"I felt like if I was going to play one last time, playing here at the Waterfront, where it all started in 2005, against one of my best mates — I thought that was a better way to sign out."

Asked if he was genuinely considering retirement, the winner of 12 ranking tournaments said it was a real possibility.

"I've been flooded with support but the problems are within. I just don't see a future with snooker in it, if I'm honest," he said.

"It's sad to say, because it's all I've loved to do since I was 12, but the last few months has been really difficult, and it's put snooker into perspective for me. At the minute, I'm just trying to survive."

In a touching moment, the interview was paused as Casey gave a clearly distraught Allen a comforting hug.

Allen also gave an interview with BBC Sport NI, where he said he was not prepared to retire now, but he had contemplated it "for a while".

Allen is a former world number one with 12 ranking titles in his career since turning professional in 2005.

He has won his home Northern Ireland Open twice, as well as two of the three Triple Crown events — Masters (2018) and the UK Championship (2022).

Loading Instagram content

Brown, who advances to the final 32 in Belfast with his win, described the match against his friend Allen as " the hardest match I've ever had to deal with".

"I don't even know what to say, I'm lost for words," he told Casey on TNT Sports.

"I've missed him, I love him. Just a great guy, through and through."

Tech.title: Data centers could erase decades of air quality gains
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A rush of new data centers could bring air pollution roaring back to levels not seen since the 2000s in Texas, which has become ground zero for the physical infrastructure behind generative AI.

New and proposed data centers are demanding a tremendous amount of electricity. How developers and utilities meet that demand — with gas turbines or renewable energy — will determine just how dirty things will get. So far, though, things are looking grim.

Tech companies and data center developers are devising new ways to get enough electricity, including building out their own power sources. But if all planned data center projects were to plug into the electricity grid in Texas and be powered by the anticipated grid mix, soot and smog-forming pollutants would skyrocket, according to a new report from the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC). In just five years, it would be enough pollution to wipe out decades of gains in air quality.

“There is a good chance that our children and grandchildren will breathe dirtier air than we did.”

In that scenario, fine particle pollution or soot from the power sector would more than triple, reaching its highest level since 2006. Smog-forming NOx emissions would increase 136 percent, approaching pollution levels from 2004. Planet-heating carbon dioxide pollution would climb 90 percent above what they were in 2025.

That’s not set in stone, of course. HARC modeled different outcomes based on three different projections for data center energy demand. Many proposed data center projects are speculative and could fall by the wayside. And developers can limit the environmental impact of a data center by building solar and wind farms onsite.

NOx emissions could be up to 10 times lower if data centers pair grid power with renewable electricity generated onsite. But if developers decide to build gas engines on site to power their data centers as a way to avoid long wait times to connect to the grid, the opposite could also play out, resulting in the highest pollution levels possible.

Data center capacity is typically measured by how much power they draw, and Texas has become the leading data center market in this measure with 26 gigawatts of existing and under-construction capacity. Texas is also bracing for four times more proposed data center capacity running on power generated onsite than any other state, according to a separate Wood Mackenzie report published in March. And in many cases, developers are turning to less efficient gas turbine technology in order to speed construction — another trend that’s making the data center boom more polluting than it needs to be.

“There is a good chance that our children and grandchildren will breathe dirtier air than we did,” John Hall, HARC CEO, said in a press release. “The transportation sector, the state, and other stakeholders have been working for decades to successfully bring these [emissions] numbers down, and that progress is now at risk.”

Tech.title: Meta to create a new class of shares to fund AI push
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta says it’s issuing a new class of shares to fund its AI initiatives. As part of its third-quarter earnings report released on Wednesday, the company says the non-voting stock will also go toward potential acquisitions and employee compensation, with trading beginning in 2027.

“The scale of investment required to compete, sustain growth, expand infrastructure, and pursue new strategic initiatives amidst the AI transformation taking place in the industry is significant,” Meta says in the press release. Susan Li, Meta’s chief financial officer, added during an earnings call that the new class of shares will “expand our funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business driven by AI.”

Meta has poured billions of dollars into the AI race as it builds (and promotes) sprawling data centers, poaches top talent from other companies like OpenAI, and builds AI models capable of rivaling those from other tech giants. The company expects capital expenditures between $135 billion and $145 billion this year, up from the previous $130 billion and $145 billion estimate.

It’s been a busy past few weeks for Meta, which launched its AI agent, Muse, in September. Like other AI agents, Muse can do things like clean out your email inbox, book restaurant reservations, and plan trips. The Muse app shot to the top of app stores shortly after its rollout, and hit 10 million downloads in the US this week. Meta also rolled out its Muse Wonder model this week.

Muse’s launch hasn’t come without some snags. Amid concerns about user privacy, a tech YouTuber reported that the agent gave out his address to a stranger on Facebook Marketplace. The company has also had to pause Muse’s conversation-sharing feature after researchers discovered chats publicly available on the web.

Tech.title: New York’s first microdrama film festival searches for its audience
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

It remains to be seen if people really want to watch vertical content on horizontal TV screens, but many filmmakers and creators were confident that their latest projects would play well at Alza — New York City’s first microdrama film festival. Founded by former Tribeca Festival chief operating officer Pete Torres, Alza, which took place October 16th through 18th, was billed as a showcase for the “the creativity, innovation, and growing cultural impact of stories made for the vertical screen.” The festival featured a selection of microdrama and film premieres as well as industry-focused panels with executives who all seemed to genuinely believe that vertical entertainment is going to be an integral part of the future.

Most fans of vertical videos and microdramas consume them through their mobile devices, but platforms like Instagram and Vurt have been rolling out dedicated smart TV apps that are designed to keep vertical video viewers glued to their couches. The popularity of YouTube — which you can access in so many different ways — has spooked major streaming services like Disney Plus, Netflix, and HBO Max into experimenting with feeds of vertical clips. Alza was filled with people who were confident that they were leading the charge to legitimize vertical content as an art form that’s going to revolutionize the entertainment industry. There’s no denying that some microdramas have been wildly successful, but Alza’s programming left me doubtful that the future is vertical.

The Alza red carpet. Image: The Verge / Alex Parkin

As odd as I personally found much of what was playing at Alza, it did seem to entertain some of the festival’s other attendees, many of whom were middle-aged women. None of the screenings were packed, but while watching a few steamy, romance-forward dramas, I was surprised to hear peals of laughter and gasps coming from the front of the theater, where festival staffers encouraged people to sit in order to have the best viewing experience.

“We’re making content that speaks to mainstream women who are part of this mobile-first movement.”

Appealing to female viewers has been one of the primary goals of GammaTime, the microdrama platform founded by former Miramax CEO Bill Block. When I spoke with Block and GammaTime’s head of development, Amy Sullivan, they told me the platform’s library of content has been designed to appeal to viewers and their general moods at different points throughout the entire day.

“We’re making content that speaks to mainstream women who are part of this mobile-first movement, who are on their phones in the mornings, the afternoons, at night,” Sullivan explained. “We have easy watches, we have rom-coms, and we have stuff that’s a little spicier — but not too salacious — for perhaps later at night. We’re trying to meet everyone where they are at every time of day.”

Block pointed to daytime TV watchers as one demographic that GammaTime has been especially interested in bringing into the fold. Though soap operas are still very popular in the US, their overall ratings have been declining in recent years as people’s attention has been pulled elsewhere. Block insisted that rather than disappearing, traditional daytime TV viewers have been migrating to other sources of entertainment, like on-demand streaming services and social media platforms.

“They’re still here, but they’re watching this while they’re pretending to work a little bit at the office,” Block said, referring to people who fire up microdrama apps for a quick hit of fun. “They’re at home, too, but this is the new daytime, the new 5–6PM, and the new 10PM plus.”

Block and Sullivan noted how, even when overall production costs are kept low, operating as a successful studio is still very expensive. It takes a lot of money to reach different demographics of potential viewers while maintaining various ad partnerships, which is why GammaTime has outsourced much of its marketing efforts overseas.

“We’ve got an edge in Tel Aviv, and I would honestly say the brains of the operation is our partner Slava Mudrykh and his customer acquisition, AI, and marketing teams,” Block said. “Because this is all Instagram and TikTok — that’s where you’re acquiring [new users.]”

“There’s so much nebulosity in this space, and it just seems like a lot of times, nobody actually watches the stuff they’re making.”

“Companies like ReelShort and DramaBox were kind of the first wave of these newer verticals, but because they’ve gone so crazy with AI, I think of them like cruise ships that have run themselves aground,” Paskowitz told me. “Now there are a lot of American companies that smell an opportunity, but there’s so much nebulosity in this space, and it just seems like a lot of times, nobody actually watches the stuff they’re making.”

Paskowitz believes that filmmakers owe it to their audiences and the brands that they work with to put out projects that actually look good. He also thinks that because studios that want to become the “HBO of verticals” now have an “AI slop button to press,” they’re losing sight of what people really want to watch. Paskowitz was adamant that using gen AI in any capacity for film production is a slippery slope that can quickly lead to the erasure of the human element. That, he said, is why Layover was produced traditionally.

Image: Andru Marino

“I’m even against doing hybrid productions because it’s easy to start cutting corners, and the public is going to see,” Paskowitz explained. “That idea sends chills through my body because it starts with ‘Let’s replace that tree, let’s replace all these buildings, let’s replace all the background work.’ And then at some point, it’s ‘Look, we’ve come so far. Let’s just replace all the actors.”

Something that struck me as the festival continued was how — while some projects featured AI elements — the vast majority of them starred human actors who all seemed very proud of their work and excited to share it with the public. These microdramas might not win any awards outside of Alza, but there are real people making them. That might also be why I was so surprised to hear Block jokingly say that the rise of vertical content “is all part of the decline of the West.”

After our interview, Block and Sullivan repeatedly stressed that he wasn’t being serious, which may be true given the line of work they’re in. But even if Block was just kidding, his words stuck with me because it feels like there may be some truth to the idea of decline. Verticals / microdrama production has become a multibillion-dollar industry because we live in a society that encourages us to engage with almost every aspect of our lives through the tiny screens that stay in our pockets. It’s no surprise that Hollywood sees vertical microdramas as the next big thing. But their cheesiness, lackluster production values, and formulaic stories don’t exactly make them feel ready for the red carpet treatment.

Additional reporting by Andru Marino.

Tech.title: Meta says it would’ve made over $22 billion if it didn’t have to pay a child safety settlement
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta had to shell out $9.89 billion to pay for a chunk of the child safety settlement it reached with US attorneys general. That’s according to the company’s third-quarter earnings report released on Wednesday, which says Meta’s income from operations would have been $22.89 billion without the settlement.

In August, Meta agreed to pay $17.1 billion to settle a massive nationwide lawsuit that claimed the company harmed children by making its social media platforms “addictive” by design. It will also only pay $5.3 billion of this amount if YouTube and TikTok implement stricter settings and safeguards for kids, which Meta also agreed to as part of the settlement.

Meta’s total costs and expenses amounted to $51.61 billion, including the amount it agreed to pay as part of the settlement. The company may have even bigger litigation costs in its future, as a New Mexico court ordered Meta to pay $25 billion over the Cambridge Analytica scandal on Wednesday.

Even with the fees associated with its legal battles, Meta reported earning $64.60 billion in revenue, marking a 26 percent increase from the same time last year. “We hit major milestones this quarter toward delivering personal superintelligence for everyone,” Meta CEO Zuckerberg says in the press release. “Our investments are paying off, the core business is strong, and we’re seeing velocity across the board.”
